Indian Civilisations [FC-0201] [FC-0201-1]

Faculty
Amar Farooqui [amar.farooqui@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The study of India’s past in the modern period has produced diverse understandings of Indian civilizations. This course looks at some of the ways in which these understandings have evolved, by discussing the writing of history, notions of heritage, anti-colonial resistance, nationalist thought and memories of exile. We shall explore how histories of representative monuments, rulers, cities or commodities allow us to comprehend the historical processes that have shaped Indian civilizations.

Learning Outcomes

To acquaint students with some of the methods historians have found useful for understanding India’s past; to introduce them to aspects of Indian civilizations; and provide some context to reflect on the meanings of civilization.

Indian Civilisations [FC-0201] [FC-0201-2]

Faculty
Gaurav Churiwala Garg [gaurav.garg@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course takes an intellectual history approach to the study of Indian civilizations. It considers civilization as an actor category. It explores how different conceptualizations of civilization have shaped India, and how India has shaped the concept of civilization. We will focus mainly but not exclusively on British/Western colonialists and thinkers on one hand and South Asian intellectuals on the other to embark on a journey that will begin from the middle of the eighteenth century and go right up to the present.

Learning Outcomes

The course will give students a fresh perspective on and a critical re-introduction to Indian history, how historical knowledge (including the kind of history that is taught in schools) is produced, and the many consequences of such knowledge in the making of our past, present, and future.

Indian Civilisations [FC-0201] [FC-0201-3]

Faculty
Nayanjot Kaur Lahiri [nayanjot.lahiri@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This is a small course about a large and fascinating subject, that of Indian Civilizations. It has been structured in a way that it can be immersed in, one hopes, with enjoyment. The course will draw out civilizational elements from prehistory till the present – through accounts of travels and lives, through ideas and  through art – in which small phenomena are linked to the larger frame of the Indian subcontinent and beyond. The course will explore a varied and rich tapestry that includes rock art, the Harappan Civilization, iconic emperors like Ashoka and Akbar, the words of the Buddha and the Bhakti saints, modern statesmen like B.R. Ambedkar and Jawaharlal Nehru. How social and gender inequalities cut across Indian history will also  be explored.  Indian civilizations, as the course will emphasize, are not   part of the 'old' and  ‘dead’ past but  are made up of elements that continue to be present in contemporary India. Readings will be electronically shared with students.

Learning Outcomes

A nuanced understanding of India's past and present through the civilizational lens

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Readings will be electronically circulated.

Week One: Civilization

Indian Civilisations [FC-0201] [FC-0201-4]

Faculty
Indivar Kamtekar [indivar.kamtekar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What is the ‘Indian civilisation’ which we inhabit, and when was it formed? Was it created in antiquity? Or was it a product of the colonial encounter? Discussions about Indian civilisation are usually attentive to ancient times, or to what has been labelled as a ‘composite culture’ fostered by the advent of Islam in medieval times. This course will suggest that the term ‘composite culture’ is perhaps more appropriate to describe the modern Indian living conditions, habits and identities which burgeoned during British rule, and have flourished thereafter. It addresses the making of modern Indian civilisation, not so much by looking at a distant past, but by examining developments in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. We shall discuss politics and economics, but also – among other topics – food and dress, technology and health, the adoption of new technologies, and new items of mass consumption. To a greater extent than many people wish to admit, we are constituted by colonialism. Even the drinking of tea and coffee, so much a part of our culture now, dates to our relatively recent past, and provides a fascinating history to explore.

Learning Outcomes

Appreciation of the diversity of narratives; location of ourselves in various narratives; awareness of historians’ sources and their varying credibility; learning how to use a newspaper’s online archive; insight into how histories are constructed from selected facts; historicization of everyday life; historical thinking more generally. In general, the aim is to increase our thinking capacity about the world around us.

Mind and Behaviour [FC-0503] [FC-0503-1]

Faculty
Aarthy Vaidyanathan [aarthy.vaidyanathan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Emotions, Responsibility, and Morality
Anger can sometimes be counterproductive. Can such anger be morally valuable nonetheless? Blaming seems detrimental in some clinical contexts. How can clinical service providers hold users morally responsible for wrongdoing without blaming them? We sometimes judge actions as morally right or wrong. But what makes an action morally right or wrong?  This course will introduce you to such questions about emotions, responsibility, and morality from a philosophical perspective. 

Sample readings:
Rachels, ‘The Challenge of Cultural Relativism.’
Selections from Mill, Utilitarianism
Singer, ‘Famine, Affluence, and Morality’
Pickard, ‘Responsibility without Blame’
Srinivasan, ‘The Aptness of Anger’

Learning Outcomes

Students of this course will learn to explain the core ideas we engage with clearly and succinctly. They will also learn to critically engage with philosophical arguments and to articulate and support their views.

The purchase of this course pack is required for participation in the course. Students will not be permitted to use laptops and other electronic devices (including phones) in class. Mind and Behaviour [FC-0503] [FC-0503-2]

Faculty
Bittu R [bittu@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course will introduce you to questions of mind and behaviour and their relationship to the brain and body, and will encourage you to think critically and scientifically through your own ideas around these relationships. In this course we will try to understand ourselves, the people and animals around us, and all the ways in which our interactions produce learning. Every conversation, every memory, even your reading of this course outline, structurally and functionally changes your brain, but not everything that the brain processes seems to make it to the realm of conscious perception. We will think about various seemingly intangible aspects of the mind and try to imagine how to make sense of them.

We will take a look at complex and interesting phenomena such as motivation, emotion, language, consciousness and attention. We will explore the specific question of how we learn, how we absorb and retain new material, the ways in which our brains tend to conflate correlation and causation, how we make decisions, and what critical thinking means. We will think through inter individual behavioural differences and what kinds of evidence we require to draw conclusions about group behaviour. We will focus on the limitations of what we collectively understand and the ways in which we might imagine advancing our collective knowledge about the mind and behaviour.

Learning Outcomes

The goal of the course is to provide you with the tools with which to ask these questions and begin answering them. The specific learning outcomes we hope for are:

1. That you develop an understanding of critical scientific thinking as a method for thinking through major life decisions.

2.  That you lose your fear of primary scientific research and become comfortable going to the source of evidence - a necessary life skill

3. That you develop specific tools of critical scientific thinking: critiquing the scientist as observer, distinguishing pseudoscience from science, distinguishing correlation from causation, controlled experimental methods, distinguishing absolute versus relative changes in data, sampling, etc.

4. That you specifically learn about cautionary checks necessary to understanding behaviour: placebos, categorical validity, objectivity vs subjectivity, etc.

5. That you apply these methods to think through interesting questiong about mind and behaviour: pseudoscience in psychology, personality and IQ assessments, conformity bias, criminal and forensic psychology, neurodiversity, emotion, rationality, decision making, consiousness, AI and the self.

Faculty
Kranti Saran [saran@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What kind of creature are you? A human being, no doubt. But what kind of creature is that? How should such a creature live? We will critically explore influential models of human nature in the Indic and Western philosophical traditions and their profound implications both for how we ought to live and our place in the social world. Readings include selections from the Upanishads, Vasistha's Yoga, Plato, Aristotle, Hume, Freud, Mill, Railton, Santideva, Korsgaard, Foot, O'Neill, Frye, Haidt, Milgram, Hobbes, Rawls, Bilgrami and others.   

Note well: this is a fast-paced and demanding course for students who take pride in producing their own work rather than relying on AI. If you haven't read a single novel or a book over the summer, this course probably isn't for you.

Mind and Behaviour [FC-0503] [FC-0503-4]

Faculty
Rachel Kathleen Harbin [kathleen.harbin@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Is the essential nature of the human mind its capacity to reason, to feel, to grasp certain aspects of the world? Are our minds and ways of thinking fundamentally different from those of animals or various forms of artificial intelligence? By exploring a range of answers to these and other challenging questions, this course examines the nature of the human mind and what it can tell us about ourselves and our place in the world. We will consider whether the mind is identical with physical or brain processes or instead is something else over and above the physical world. We will explore the question of whether our minds enable us to make truly free choices or rather only to channel the influential forces in our environment. Finally, we will seek to understand some distinctive modes of thinking, such as the experience of awe.  

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students should gain core reading, writing, and critical thinking skills. These skills are foundational for further study at Ashoka and for lifelong thoughtful intellectual engagement. Students should also understand course content at a level that prepares them for further study in philosophy and related disciplines.

Reading: the capacity to analyse challenging texts; this includes the ability to locate, understand and evaluate arguments in texts across multiple disciplines and time periods.

Writing: the capacity to persuasively articulate well-reasoned arguments in support of a thoughtfully considered point of view, both orally and in writing.

Critical thinking: the capacity to identify strengths and weaknesses in arguments, the understanding of common argument patterns and logical fallacies.

Content: an understanding of important perspectives on the nature of the mind and key arguments attempting to support or refute them, of how perspectives about the mind and the human capacity for action relate to questions about choice and freedom, and of whether the human mind is fundamentally different from other kinds of minds.

Mind and Behaviour [FC-0503] [FC-0503-5]

Faculty
Nandini Chatterjee Singh . [nandini.singh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Vision/Philosophy/Purpose

This foundation course seeks to address overarching questions about the human brain, mind, and behavior which form the core of human experience. The brain is the biological foundation for mental processes, the mind creates the internal experience of these processes, and together they are manifested in behaviour in the form observable actions and responses. Using theoretical frameworks, cool psychological experiments, and state of the art brain imaging methods, this course will unravel how human beings acquire language, learn to read, develop number sense, experience emotion, feel music, pay attention and exhibit kindness, from a psychological and neurobiological perspective. The course will raise significant questions about cognitive processes, brain organisation and processing, psychological constructs and human diversity. Students will be encouraged to find answers using approaches that blend both the sciences and the arts.  

 

The course will be structured into three parts as described below

In the first part students will be introduced to terminology and vocabulary in psychology and neuroscience. They will also be introduced to the organisation of the brain and different cognitive processes.

The second part of the course will discuss different cognitive abilities like reading, number processing, emotion processing, attention etc.. from a psychological and neurobiological perspective.

The third part of the course will discuss neurodiversity - how some of these cognitive processes vary across the human condition and thus render each human unique.

Learning Outcomes

To introduce the broad areas and varied approaches that comprise the field of psychology and neuroscience.

Learn about different cognitive processes.

Develop an understanding of how different cognitive processes work in concert to develop skills/abilities.

Identify the value brought in by the sciences and the arts in understanding human behaviour. Understand the design and contributions of experiments in neuroscience and psychology in our understanding of the brain.

Use knowledge of neuroscience and psychology to understand nature and nurture.

Name and identify regions of the brain and their role in processing information and skills like memory, motor skills, etc.

 

By the end of this course, students will learn to: 

To recognise and identify diversity of human thought and perspective.

To develop flexibility in ideas, approaches and response.

To appreciate the power of empirical and replicable research

Mind and Behaviour [FC-0503] [FC-0503-6]

Faculty
Rachel Kathleen Harbin [kathleen.harbin@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Is the essential nature of the human mind its capacity to reason, to feel, to grasp certain aspects of the world? Are our minds and ways of thinking fundamentally different from those of animals or various forms of artificial intelligence? By exploring a range of answers to these and other challenging questions, this course examines the nature of the human mind and what it can tell us about ourselves and our place in the world. We will consider whether the mind is identical with physical or brain processes or instead is something else over and above the physical world. We will explore the question of whether our minds enable us to make truly free choices or rather only to channel the influential forces in our environment. Finally, we will seek to understand some distinctive modes of thinking, such as the experience of awe.  

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students should gain core reading, writing, and critical thinking skills. These skills are foundational for further study at Ashoka and for lifelong thoughtful intellectual engagement. Students should also understand course content at a level that prepares them for further study in philosophy and related disciplines.

Reading: the capacity to analyse challenging texts; this includes the ability to locate, understand and evaluate arguments in texts across multiple disciplines and time periods.

Writing: the capacity to persuasively articulate well-reasoned arguments in support of a thoughtfully considered point of view, both orally and in writing.

Critical thinking: the capacity to identify strengths and weaknesses in arguments, the understanding of common argument patterns and logical fallacies.

Content: an understanding of important perspectives on the nature of the mind and key arguments attempting to support or refute them, of how perspectives about the mind and the human capacity for action relate to questions about choice and freedom, and of whether the human mind is fundamentally different from other kinds of minds.

Introduction to Literary Theory [ENG-1002] [ENG-1002-1]

Faculty
Mandakini Dubey [mandakini.dubey@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The field of English is shaped by literary theory, with its profound engagements with big questions of language, reality, identity, power, desire, history – most broadly, the self and the world. When studying literature, we often seek out ways of uncovering the workings  of these engagements in the texts we read. This course turns to the questions and answers posed by theory itself, rather than applications through the reading of literary texts. 

Theory can seem complex and intimidating, but its questions are fundamental: how do we make meaning? How do we constitute texts, and how do texts constitute us? How are we to know those parts of ourselves that refuse knowledge? How do our bodies, our given identities, and the material conditions of our lives shape who we are and how we feel, think, act, desire, and read? Keeping these and other basic questions in mind, this course will survey the key approaches and texts of contemporary literary theory.

Introduction to Literary Theory [ENG-1002] [ENG-1002-2]

Faculty
Huzaifa Omair Siddiqi [huzaifa.siddiqi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Introduction to Literary Theory

Literary theory encompasses texts by phenomenologists, existentialists, linguists, psychoanalysts, Marxists, structuralists, deconstructionists, feminists, queer theorists, Critical Race and anti-caste theorists. What this course seeks to explore is why the study of literature needs ‘theory’ in all its various guises. What kind of relation does literature have with theory that is manifestly different, and indeed incompatible with, the traditional understanding of object and knowledge in philosophy and the sciences? The advent of ‘theory’ (as contrasted with ‘philosophy’ and ‘science’) has to be seen, not just as the beginning of a radical critique of the purportedly self-evident notions of subject, class, caste, race, gender and identity but also as a revolution in the very concepts of knowledge, truth and reality themselves. What happens to these concepts when literature (which has for so long been the catch-all term for illusion, falsity, imitation and error) becomes the site of truth; when theory replaces philosophy?

This course seeks to enter into these questions raised by literary theory. We will read texts by major theorists to see how theory displaces traditional philosophy and necessitates a practice that may be artistic, political, ethical or a combination of all three.

Overview

Addressing the self-reflexive imperative that lies at the root of “theory,” this class will step back from individual texts of fiction to think through bigger questions about literature. What counts as literature? What is the role of history in the production of literature? Does literature reflect reality or create it? Does gender play a role in the kind of literature we read and write? Why do we desire to read? What do we read when we read? Theory not only reads the whats and whys and hows of texts, but it also asks to be read itself as a text. In this class, therefore, we will undertake that double session of reading and writing about texts that think about reading and writing.

Introduction to Literary Theory [ENG-1002] [ENG-1002-4]

Faculty
Eesha Kumar [eesha.kumar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The emergence in the 19th and 20th centuries of interpretative frameworks such as Marxism, feminism, postcolonial theory, psychoanalysis — and, significantly, semiotics — had a transformative and lasting impact on the institutional study of literature. This introductory course posits that these frameworks can be understood as modes of investigative reading. With the conceptual anchor of “suspicion”— and the associated figures of depth, doubt, unveiling, exposure — this course occasions an immersion in literary theory, and the ruptures and developments of intellectual history that it names. 

We will learn the stakes of interrogation with the “masters of suspicion” Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, and encounter the “usual suspects” of literary theory, including Gramsci, Althusser, Saussure, Barthes, Derrida, Lacan, Foucault, Deleuze, Said, Fanon, Butler, Jameson and Sedgwick. Thinking across the creative and the critical, we will deepen our discussions of theory by reading together Laurent Binet’s 2015 novel The Seventh Function of Language, a fictional investigation of (the death of the author of) “The Death of the Author.”

We will conclude the course by bringing this investigative spirit closer home, reading modern and contemporary theorists of caste (such as Aniket Jaaware and Gopal Guru), and by making connections with contemporary debates in criticism about surface, depth, paranoia, and forms of textual intimacy and distance. 

Learning Outcomes

This course is designed to introduce students to the best known texts and figures of literary theory. Students will receive a supportive framework for the study of challenging texts, and, being immersed in traditions of critical thinking, they will practice close-reading, annotating, and writing in accordance with academic conventions. Students will gain an understanding of the historical and material conditions that produced literary theory as we know it, and they will enter ongoing scholarly conversations about “post-theory” and the futures of literary criticism.

The main objects of study in this course are groups and rings. (These words have a precise mathematical meaning.) 

 

Groups are an abstract way of modelling the symmetries of an object, and rings are an abstract way of modelling ordinary number systems.

 

Abstraction leads to sharper intuition and wider applicability. As a result, Algebra is used not only throughout mathematics but also in many other sciences such as physics, chemistry and informatics.

 

The emphasis in this course will be on precise definitions, rigourous proofs, and clear understanding.

Statistics and Research Methods I [PSY-2001] [PSY-2001-1]

Faculty
Supriya Ray [supriya.ray@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

"The business of the statistician is to catalyze the scientific learning process." ― George E. P. Box

"Without data, you’re just another person with an opinion" ― W. Edwards Deming

“I couldn't claim that I was smarter than sixty-five other guys--but the average of sixty-five other guys, certainly!”― Richard P. Feynman [In 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman: Adventures of a Curious Character']

 

In this course, you will learn how to use statistical tools (central tendency, variability, probability, hypothesis testing (e.g., t-tests, ANOVAs), regression, etc.) to answer questions of psychological interest. The emphasis will be given on understanding statistical concepts and performing basic statistical analyses, not on mathematical formulas and derivations. Many students, for whom the world of numerals and symbols has been a ‘no-go’ area, begin their statistics course with a fear of doing mathematics. However, statistics is not about (re-)learning summation; instead, statistics summarizes the data in a comprehensive manner.

Learning Outcomes

This course is primarily designed for undergraduate students. By the end of this course you will be able to

  • Understand basic theoretical and applied principles of statistics.
  • Gain proficiency in using statistical software for data analysis.
  • Appreciate why data triumphs anecdotes.
  • Understand basic theoretical and applied principles of statistics.
  • Interpret complex statistical findings.
  • Communicate quantitative data in statistics, graphs, and tables
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Text Books:

"Explaining Psychological Statistics" by Barry H. Cohen (Wiley)

"Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology" by Hugh Coolican  (Hodder Education, Taylor & Francis)

Overview

Faculty
Sneha Shashidhara [sneha.shashidhara@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course is currently undergoing design and modification. Please check this location frequently for updates and changes.

Cognitive psychology is the study of how we think, and how we make sense of the external (and internal) environment using our prior experiences, and determine how to respond to an ever changing environment. While the main purpose of this course is to introduce you to the scientific study of the mind, you will also begin to understand the central role cognition plays in our everyday lives. 

In developing this course, we have remained attentive to the realities of a rapidly evolving era of artificial intelligence. Our curriculum is crafted to harness the possibilities offered by AI, while foregrounding those uniquely human capacities that remain irreplaceable. We place special emphasis on original thinking, ethical reasoning, and imaginative synthesis—abilities that continue to define human intellect.
 

Learning Outcomes

Upon completing this course, students should be able to:

  •  Understand major cognitive theories and models.
  • Critically evaluate experimental results.
  • Analyze the neural bases of cognitive processes where applicable.
  • Apply cognitive principles to real-world issues.
  • Develop foundational skills for cognitive research.

We will explore how the presence of others shapes and influences our motivations, cognition, attitudes, emotions and behavior, by looking at group processes involved in cooperation, conflict and competition.

Poonam Yadav [poonam.yadav@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Social psychology is a major branch of psychology that explores how individuals’ thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are influenced by the social world. It examines the ways people perceive, interact with, and are affected by others, as well as how social norms, culture, and group membership shape human behavior. The field bridges the gap between individual psychology and broader social processes, helping explain how personal actions are connected to social environments. We will explore how the presence of others shapes and influences our motivations, cognition, attitudes, emotions and behavior, by looking at group processes involved in cooperation, conflict and competition.

 

Learning Outcomes

● To introduce major theories, concepts, empirical findings and debates in social psychology

● To familiarize students with methods within social psychological research

● To critically engage with social psychological findings and explore how they apply to our

cultural contexts

● To understand the intersections between ‘social’ and ‘individual’ and multi-layered

problems that social psychologists examine

● To facilitate the development of interest in exploring social psychological questions of

enquiry among students

Develop a working knowledge of psychology’s content domains

Algebra II [MAT-2002] [MAT-2002-1]

Overview

Field theory/Galois theory can be considered as one of the fundamental courses considered as 

learning outcomes in undergraduate mathematics (Others being Complex Analysis, Fourier theory with applications

to basic PDE, some bit of number theory).  

 

The classical problems which the Greeks raised but

could not solve are the following: using ruler and compass constructions,

can one trisect any angle? can the cube of unit length be doubled and finally

can the circle be squared. To this, we can add the problems of explicitly solving higher

degree polynomial equations in one variable, just as it can be done for the quadratic

equation; or which regular n-gons can be constructed?

 

The solutions to this questions come from a study of

polynomial equations, what is known as field theory.

The answer given by Galois (Gauss, Abel and others) is to consider

the symmetries of the roots of a polynomial equation, bringing in

group theory and linear algebra.

 

If time permits, we may cover further topics oriented towards number theory or

geometry.

Movement, text, sound, music- these are some of the areas touched upon while developing skills in performance. The emphasis is on building a vocabulary of performance techniques. These techniques can include breathing, movement improvisation, and voice modulation, as well as exercises in awareness and musicality. These ‘tools of performance’ are often tempered by a plethora of contemporary performance outlooks. The emphasis in this most preliminary of Ashoka’s performing arts courses is on the individual as a performing entity. The consciousness of one’s own self vis-à-vis performative potential lays the foundations for the group work so essential to later performing arts courses.  The course work will proceed in a series of ‘etudes’ or studies which will result in small performance ‘moments’ or phrases. Some of the coursework will be based on texts and scripts to be chosen afresh each semester.  Other coursework can be based on non-textual concepts.

Developmental Psychology [PSY-2031] [PSY-2031-1]

Faculty
Annie Baxi [annie.baxi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Developmental Psychology is a systematic approach to study the biopsychosocial dimensions of human development across the lifespan. The course will cover fundamental theories relative to cognitive development, moral development, language development, identity formation etc from the period of the prenatal period to death. During the course, students will engage in key theoretical concepts in human development and their cultural application, critique the idea of normative development and develop a grounded sensibility towards development oriented concerns and challenges. The course will follow a critically reflexive pedagogy, urging students to consistently question developmental givens, introspect on their development and hence develop a nuanced understanding of technical concepts. Pedagogical tools will include a combination of play, reflexive exercises, art work and film clippings. The course intends to  ask the following questions: How do nature and nurture together shape development? How do children shape their own development? In what ways is development continuous, and in what ways is it discontinuous? How does the socio-cultural context influence development? What are the ethical research practices when studying developmental patterns?

Learning Outcomes
  • Develop a thorough understanding of major development theories.
  • Develop a critical approach to linear models of human development.
  • Relate key concepts of the scientific method to research in child development.
  • Identify and illustrate how biological, cognitive and social-emotional processes interact to influence human development.

description:
Statistics and Research Methods II [PSY-2002] [PSY-2002-1]

Faculty
Krishna Venkata Melnattur [krishna.melnattur@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Quantitative psychological data is frequently a bunch of structured numbers. These cannot be interpreted meaningfully until one understands and appreciates how the data came about and what can be properly inferred from the data. In this course, we will focus on quantitative methodology. This course is for students who know the basics of statistical analyses. The aim is to develop a trained eye for sound methodology to better evaluate other scientists’ research, as well as their own. Students will also learn about planning, ethical conduct, and reporting of findings from a survey and experimental study. Along with some of the most widely-used quantitative methods in psychology (e.g., surveys and experiments), students will also understand how these methods are different from alternative methodologies (i.e., qualitative methods, mixed methods).



 

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Understand various quantitative methods that psychologists use to investigate research questions.
  • Plan, design, and conduct a psychometrically-sound survey; formulate hypotheses, test them, analyze the results, interpret them
  • Write report of a survey study to effectively communicate your results
  • Plan, design, and conduct an experimental study; formulate hypotheses, design and conduct an experiment to test the hypotheses, analyze the results, interpret them
  • Write report of an experimental study to effectively communicate your results
  • Understand alternative methodologies available for researchers (qualitative and mixed-method) and when to use them
  • Grasp, analyze, and critique academics research papers in psychology
  • Become literate consumers of scientific information.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Prerequisites: Pass in Statistics and Research Methodology I, or equivalent modules in math, or economics.

Required materials:

Shaughnessy J. J., Zechmeister, E. B., Zechmeister, J. S., & (2012). Essentials of research methods in psychology. (9th ed.) Tata McGraw-Hill.

 

Attendance
Excused absence(s) are not applicable in this course lecture.
Additional excused absence(s) are not applicable for sportspersons in this course lecture.
Additional Comments:

Attendance will be taken within the first five minutes of every class. I expect students to attend all lecture and discussion sessions. All lecture and discussion sessions will count towards attendance. The following rules will apply for absences:

Missing 5 classes: Excused (no grade cut)

Missing 6 classes: One grade cut on the final grade for the course

Missing 8 classes: Two grade cuts on the final grade for the course

Missing 10 or more classes: A ‘Fail’ grade for the course

The five excused absences can be used in case you miss a class due to illness. You do not need to show me a doctor’s note in order to take these five excused absences. However, if illness prevents you from attending class for a longer period of time and you would like more absences excused, you will be asked for documentation from a doctor or nurse practitioner for each of the past absences to determine if that is possible. Additional excused absences are possible only if the past five absences have been due to health reasons and have proper documentation. In previous iterations of the course, we have seen students taking discussion sessions lightly. The discussion sessions are very important, and help consolidate learning from lectures. Please treat discussion sessions on par with lectures.

Participation & Engagement (Class Participation, Attendance, Discussion, Office Hours, or Peer Reviews)5. Attendance: 5%5
Grading Rubric
The final letter grades in this course will be determined as per Relative grading

I will use the relative grading scheme, specifically relative cluster grading. This means I rank order scores and look for "precipitous" drops. These drops form my cut-off scores. Technically A and A- signal categorical differences, but under an absolute grading system, this categorical system is artificially created — a difference of 0.1 points can mean the difference between A and A-. With a relative cluster grading, the categorical differences between letter grades are naturally reflected in the data as the "precipitous drops". Because relative cluster grading is a data-driven technique, there is no fixed rule of how large a cluster can be, or how many grade bins there must be. Occasionally, I might skip a grade bin if the deviation between two adjacent clusters is too large.

Clinical Psychology [PSY-2041] [PSY-2041-1]

Faculty
Pratishtha Petwal [pratishtha.petwal@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This is an advanced course with a focus on enhancing understanding about concepts of psychopathology and various psychological disorders. This will sensitize students to different theories and dynamics of psychopathology. The course presents useful information on history, models, clinical presentations, different classification systems, assessments and interventions available. This course will use an integrative approach towards the study of psychopathology including the interaction of biological, developmental, and social factors. The current course aims to equip psychology students with the basic understanding of clinical psychopathology and clinical formulation rather than treating or diagnosing anyone.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to: 

1. Understand and critically analyze different diagnostic classification systems such as, DSM V and ICD-11.
2. Understand the historical context and causal factors that inform the course and prevalence of various psychological disorders.
3. Understand how empirical research informs our knowledge of psychopathology.
4. Familiarize yourself with the symptoms, causes, formulations, assessment and interventions for the psychological disorders.
5. Construct a formulation-based account of a clinical presentation using the 5Ps framework, in a supervised in-class setting.
6. Read and critically appraise empirical literature in clinical psychology.
7. Apply ethical reasoning to clinical and research scenarios.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Main text: Hooley, J.M., & Nock, M.K. (2025). Psychopathology: A Clinical Science Approach, Global Edition, 19th edition. Pearson.

Reference: Kearney, C. A. &Trull, T. J. (2017). Abnormal Psychology and Life: A dimensional approach, Third edition. Cengage Learning.

Supplementary reading: Hecker, J., & Thorpe, G. (2015). Introduction to Clinical Psychology. Psychology Press. 

Attendance

Additional excused absence(s) are not applicable for sportspersons in this course lecture.

In place of graded attendance, students will complete short reflective writing exercises during selected class sessions. These exercises are designed to consolidate conceptual understanding and to encourage active engagement with material delivered in class.

description:
Clinical Psychology [PSY-2041] [PSY-2041-3]

Faculty
Simi Ghosh [simi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course focuses on understanding the phenomenology (description), etiology (causes), and treatment of abnormal behavior. Major psychological syndromes will be discussed along with the current APA classification system (DSM-5) and other classification systems. Genetic, biological, social, and psychological parameters implicated in the etiology of these syndromes will be introduced. Students will learn the principles of clinical assessment and the 5P model of psychological assessment and case formulation

 

Link to Spring 2025 Sylllabus

Learning Outcomes
  1. Understand the merits and limitations of research methods and assessment techniques for clinical psychology
  2. Learn the basics of critical and analytical skills required to read a journal article on clinical psychology
  3. Understand and be able to describe the current APA classification system (DSM-5) and show appreciation for other classification systems internationally
  4. Understand and be able to describe the major psychological disorders
  5. Describe the genetic, biological, social, and psychological influences on these disorders
  6. Understand the influence of societal, cultural, historical, and environmental influences on these disorders
  7. Appreciate the concept of comorbidity
  8. Discuss mental health services historically, and in today’s USA, and appreciate international differences
  9. Understand ethical issues involved with mental health services
  10. Learn the importance of vocabulary, empathy and nuances in abnormal behavior
  11. Be able to navigate and think through elementary clinical problems in practice
  12. Learn to write an interview questionnaire based on a clinical case study
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

  • Course Readings

    Text: Butcher J.N, Mineka S, Hooley J.M, Kapoor P (2019) Abnormal Psychology (18th ed) Pearson India https://www.amazon.in/dp/9353065593?tag=pearindieduc-21 ( Rs.781 from amazon India for paperback, Rs. 389 for Kindle edition)

    Reference: Nevid, J.S., Rathus, S.A., & Greene, B (2021). Abnormal Psychology in a Changing World (11th ed.) New Jersey: Pearson Higher Education.

Development Economics [ECO-3500] [ECO-3500-1]

Faculty
Compulsory Econ [compulsory.econ@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why are some countries so poor and others so rich? Can governments act to eliminate poverty or must the poor remain poor? What sorts of interventions work and how do we evaluate them? Through this course, you will question the meaning of economic development and identify the factors that affect growth, poverty and inequality. You will engage with contemporary research on markets, institutions, education, health and policy. You will analyse these questions by using both theoretical frameworks as well as empirical evidence based on survey data. In doing so, you will gain an insight into the challenges and constraints faced by developing countries in their quest to improve the quality of human life.

Learning Outcomes
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Pre-requisites: ECO-2101 (Microeconomic Theory I), ECO-2400 (Econometrics), ECO 202

description:
Qualitative Research Methods in Political Science [POL-1030] [POL-1030-1]

Faculty
Dipin Kaur [dipin.kaur@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course will introduce students to qualitative research design, data collection, and analysis. It will focus on a variety of political questions to cover the basic techniques for collecting, interpreting, and writing up qualitative data. The first part of the course is organized around the sequence scholars conventionally follow to conduct qualitative research: find a research question, engage with existing literature, formulate hypotheses, collect material, analyze it, and effectively communicate findings. The second part of the course will familiarize students with various qualitative research methods and analysis tools, including interviews, participant observation, case studies, and archival research using primary sources. In the process, students will (a) reflect on the ethics of conducting qualitative research and (b) get a flavor for some themes/ types of research questions to which such techniques are best suited. In the final part of the course, students will learn how to analyze collected data and develop a research plan on their chosen topic using any one combination of methodologies from the following options: 

1. Participant Observation/ Interview / Oral History (developing interview questions, identifying a diverse portfolio of interviewees, identifying the biases/ positionality of people you are interviewing/ analyzing insights and gaps) 

OR
2. Archival Research and process tracing/ case study (what you find, what is missing, the positionality of the people who wrote the material) 

Based on this data collection, students will write a final paper that formulates a research question, relevant hypotheses, and initial findings.

Multivariable Calculus [MAT-1004] [MAT-1004-1]

Faculty
Pritam Ghosh [pritam.ghosh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces you to the concept of studying and analyzing functions which accept multiple real numbers (variables) as input and spits out either a single real number or an array of real numbers. A concrete example to think of would be the basic example of finding diustance of a point from the origin. We need the spatial coordiates (three inout variables) and then the standard length function spits out the distance (a real number). 

We will take a geoemtric approach to understand and study a plethora of such functions and some applications to real world problems. 

Learning Outcomes

Calculus is the study of approximations and taking limits. Here you will learn how to efficiently estimate multivariable functions and take limits. These will enable us to develop the concepts of continuity, differentiation and integration for multivariable functions. We will also see how these concepts can be used to solve optimisation problems and compte area and volume of complicated geometric objects.

Faculty

Operational Support

Overview

This course aims to support students to create and build organisations that are
ecologically sensitive and socially relevant. In the changing context of the urgent
need to handle climate change, environmental degradation, and increasing social
inequality, the course walks students through opportunities and challenges for
organisations.
The course will draw on cases from a wide variety of settings varying from large
organisations like Patagonia to smaller startups like Skrap and lessons from the
margins -- newspaper vendors, street vendors, traditional arts and crafts -- lessons of
management from the unexplored sector of the informal. Through critical readings,
analysis of videos, and case discussions, participants will engage with the social and
environmental challenges the society is facing.
During field visits, through deeper engagements with organizations and collectives
that have been developing a path of environmentally and socially conscious journeys,
participants will set foot on such paths, by developing the possibilities and potentials
to create more of such paths, not only at a larger scale of building new organizations
but also by incorporating and integrating versatile and pluralistic values and logics of
environmentally and socially conscious decision making.
In-class discussions will be largely based on the cases and readings assigned to the
sessions. This will create a space to learn ways in which collectives and organizations
are being built and, further, shaping environmental and social consciousness.
The course will involve field visits to socially conscious enterprises to give the
students a first-hand experience of what social entrepreneurship looks like in reality.

Quantitative Reasoning and Mathematical Thinking [FC-0306] [FC-0306-3]

Faculty
Sandeep Juneja . [sandeep.juneja@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Mathematical ideas often based on data and analysis play a key role in understanding the world around us and in making rational decisions.  This course will focus on consequential real world problems and discuss the underlying mathematical ideas that illuminate the problem structure and help us make more informed and better decisions.

The questions we consider include the ones that rely on taming uncertainty such as

·      What do income inequality, damage from earthquakes and size of cities have in common?

·      How to estimate and manage supplies at an Ashoka Coffee shop

·      How do fashion stores decide how many clothes to order in a business cycle

·      How tools such as the Monte Carlo method help us measure and control disease spread

·      How to make profitable investments in stock markets

·      The underlying mathematical principles in pricing financial derivatives securities

As well as those that involve problems under certainty assumptions, such as

·      How do utility companies decide how much electricity to generate from various power sources (coal, natural gas, nuclear, solar, wind) hour by hour? 

·      How to estimate a price of a home from data such as square footage, number of bedrooms, location rating, age of the property, and local crime rates.                            

·      How do banks feed historical customer data (income, debt, repayment history) into machine learning models to evaluate a new applicant's risk level and automatically approve or deny lines of credit

·      How can individual rational decisions lead to a collectively terrible outcome?                                                                                       

·      Can a group of men and women be matched in a stable manner so that there is no pair of individuals who would both prefer to leave their assigned partners to be with each other.                                                                                                                                            

·      How Google finds the shortest path from your home town to Ashoka University

Along the way, students will encounter introductory ideas from probability, statistics, optimization, regression, machine learning, game theory, matching theory, and graph algorithms.  By the end of the course, students will be able to recognize mathematical structure in unfamiliar situations and reason carefully with data and uncertainty. The broader aim is to develop a form of intellectual independence: the ability to look beneath the surface of a problem and identify its underlying structure.

Quantitative Reasoning and Mathematical Thinking [FC-0306] [FC-0306-5]

Faculty
Abhishek Khetan [abhishek.khetan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This is a course about how mathematicians think, taught entirely through puzzles.
Each topic opens with a puzzle, a question that is easy to state and tempting to play with, but whose resolution requires a genuine idea, and introduces interesting mathematics.
The students will be active participants rather than passive consumers of a typical "fact of the matter" style of information avalanche.

The course assumes no mathematics beyond basic high school arithmetic.
We do not assume any fondness for mathematics.
On the contrary, the course is designed for those who have so far found mathematics dry, intimidating, or pointless, and aims to change that student's mind.

Following is a rough course outline.

  - Knights. Chess puzzles in which knights jump around on a small board.

  - Logical thinking. Card-flipping tests, prisoners guessing their own hat colors, and islands of truth-tellers and liars teach us what it really means to test a claim of the form "if this, then that," and how much we can deduce from what others do and do not say.

  - Machines with finite memory. We build imaginary machines that read a string of symbols and decide whether to accept it. We learn to reverse- engineer such a machine from its wiring, to combine machines with AND, OR, and NOT, and discuss the machines' limitations.

  - The algebra of yes and no. With only two values and two operations, we build a miniature arithmetic in which logical conditions become equations one can actually solve. The liar-and-truth-teller puzzles, attacked earlier by hand, now become a matter of calculation.

  - Circuits. The same two-value algebra is wired using physical gates. This is the design principle behind every digital chip.

  - Infinity. A frog hops along an endless row of lily pads and a hunter must guarantee a hit.  

  - Permutatonis. We study the act of rearranging things: shuffles of a row of objects, how every shuffle breaks into independent cycles With it we settle the famour Fifteen Puzzle.

A word on what this course is, and is not, about. It is about reasoning, and doing that reasoning properly.
It is not about symbols. The reader will almost never be asked to write down a formula or manipulate the dense notation that mathematics is often, wrongly, identified with.
Where a symbol does appear, it is only a convenient shorthand for something already stated in plain words, and never a prerequisite for following along.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, a student should be able to:

  1. Take a tangled, concrete situation and model it with simple objects, discarding what is not pertinent.

  2. Read and construct careful arguments using the recurring techniques of the course.

  3. Recognize the difference between "I could not do it" and "it cannot be done."

  4. Develop an appreciation for real mathematics.

  5. Impress/torture their friends with clever puzzles.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Detailed, self-contained lecture notes are provided for everything covered, and they include worked examples and practice problems.
They are the primary, and sufficient, resource for the course. No textbook purchase is required.

Grading Rubric

Each student first earns an overall percentage score from the course's assessments. 
The letter grade is then assigned by a hybrid scheme.

  - First, a hard threshold. Any student whose overall score is below 40% fails the course, regardless of how the rest of the class performs. Reaching 40% is the minimum bar for a passing grade, and nothing below it can be rescued by the curve.

  - For every student at or above 40%, the grade is computed in two independent ways. The absolute scheme assigns a grade from fixed, pre-announced score cutoffs, so that a student's grade depends only on their own performance. The relative scheme assigns a grade from the student's standing within the class, so that a uniformly hard examination does not punish the cohort.

  - The student is then awarded whichever of these two grades is the better one.

The F band (below 40%) is exactly the failing threshold described above: no relative adjustment can lift a score under 40% out of an F.

In short: scoring at least 40% is necessary to pass, and above that line the hybrid scheme always reports the more favourable of the absolute and relative outcomes -- a student can only ever benefit from the curve, never lose to it.

Postcolonial Literatures [ENG-3001/ ENG-5301] [ENG-3001/ ENG-5301-1]

Faculty
Vivek Venkitaraman Narayan [v.v.narayan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How did colonialism shape the modern world? What are the ways in which colonial histories continue to inform our contemporary realities? How can we speak of the economic, cultural, and political subordination of the colonized peoples? What does it mean to remain mindful of these legacies as we engage with each other and with works of art and literature? These are some of the questions that inform postcolonial theory. This course reads fiction, nonfiction, and poetry from the Global South to explore the theoretical language and resistant politics of postcolonial theory. Course material includes writing by Edward Said, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Aijaz Ahmed, Benita Parry, Chinua Achebe, Jean Rhys, Homi Bhabha, Frantz Fanon, Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Arundhati Roy, Gloria Anzaldua, JM Coetzee, Eunice de Souza, AK Ramanujan, Zadie Smith, and Arjun Appadurai. How did colonialism shape the modern world? What are the ways in which colonial histories continue to inform our contemporary realities? How can we speak of the economic, cultural, and political subordination of the colonized peoples? What does it mean to remain mindful of these legacies as we engage with each other and with works of art and literature? These are some of the questions that inform postcolonial theory. This course reads fiction, nonfiction, and poetry from the Global South to explore the theoretical language and resistant politics of postcolonial theory. Course material includes writing by Edward Said, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Aijaz Ahmed, Benita Parry, Chinua Achebe, Jean Rhys, Homi Bhabha, Frantz Fanon, Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Arundhati Roy, Gloria Anzaldua, JM Coetzee, Eunice de Souza, AK Ramanujan, Zadie Smith, and Arjun Appadurai.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successfully completing this course, students will be able to:

  • Identify the ongoing legacies of colonialism, and its continuing role in shaping the modern world.  
  • Describe and critically examine a range of postcolonial texts and theories that respond to these colonial legacies.    
  • Situate the emergence of postcolonial theory within its historical context.
  • Engage meaningfully with important themes in postcolonial theory such as colonial modernity, gendered subjectivities, language and identity, violence, and place and voice.
  • Read and analyze literature through the lens of postcolonialism.
  • Develop a critical vocabulary for the legacies of colonialism and an appreciation of the experiences and creative strategies of postcolonial subjects.
  • Demonstrate awareness of the ever-present politics of location; which, put simply, refers to the ways in which who we are and how we say and do what we say and do are always influenced by our access to power and privilege.
  • Interrogate and evaluate the relevance of postcolonial theory in the twenty-first century.

Faculty
Amita Baviskar [amita.baviskar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Any environmental issue is invariably about society and politics.  From global warming to garbage on city streets, nature and culture lie at the centre of competing claims about what should be done.  As Raymond Williams said, “We have mixed our labour with the earth, our forces with its forces too deeply to be able to separate each other out.”  Understanding these processes of ‘socio-nature’ demands a focus on social inequality as well as biological complexity.  This course looks at how biophysical processes in natural landscapes are changed by the cultural geography of capitalism, colonialism, caste and nationalism.  We will analyse environmental crises and explore how collective action can lead to ecological justice.

Learning Outcomes

Course Objectives

*  to appreciate the diversity and complexity of ecosystems

*  to understand the long-term political-economic processes shaping environments

*  to analyse current environmental problems in terms of unequal social causes and impacts

*  to reflect on the connections between personal actions and planetary welfare

*  to develop an interpretive frame that can be applied to understand and address a range of environmental problems

*  to carefully read, critically appraise, and concisely write from a social science perspective

Environmental Studies [FC-0102] [FC-0102-2]

Faculty
Asmita Kabra [asmita.kabra@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course aims to introduce students to a complex, interdisciplinary understanding of environmental issues and challenges, going beyond simplistic discourses of crisis. The pedagogic design is built around ten questions, framed in very simple terms but designed to crack open disciplinary silos to build a multivalent understanding of linked socioecological systems. It exposes students to a diversity of environmental issues, challenges, processes, perspectives, and actors. The objective is to enable students to gain a more nuanced and historicized understanding of the politics of environmental policy and practice.

Learning Outcomes
  • To destabilise simplistic binaries of rural-urban, North-South, environment-development, local-global etc.
  • To foster meaningful dialogue among diverse disciplinary and ideological perspectives
  • To nudge students to think of their own role as embedded actors operating within structural constraints, but with agency to bring about change
  • To understand socio-ecological systems as complex, contingent, and messy 
  • To generate critical hope and action pathways
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course will consist of twelve modules, each lasting approximately a week, with two lecture sessions of 1.5 hours each. Part I of the course walks students through the historical links between environment and development. It traces how these linkages have changed over time and are connected specifically to global geo-politics of the 20th and 21st centuries. Part II focuses on extant environmental solutions - mainstream as well as radical - again teasing out their ontological and epistemological foundations. This interdisciplinary course draws on theoretical insights from political economy, environmental and ecological economics, social anthropology, institutional theory, and cultural and political ecology. Students are expected to prepare in advance by reading short pieces and/or watching films or studying online resources. Classroom time will be devoted to lectures, discussion, and in-class activities, with follow-up readings assigned to dig deeper into the ideas thrown up during class.

Weekly Teaching Plan

  • Week 1: Curtain raiser
  • Week 2: What is the Anthropocene?
  • Week 3: Are there too many people at this party?
  • Week 4: How did we get here?
  • Week 5: How has the world changed since World War II?
  • Week 6: Why is everyone angry?
  • Week 7: Can markets solve the polycrisis?
  • Week 8: Are mainstream solutions working (for everyone)?
  • Week 9: Where do we go from here?
  • Week 10: Whose expertise can we count on?
  • Week 11: Should we go back to living in caves?
  • Week 12: Hope in the Anthropocene

Faculty
Ghazala Shahabuddin [ghazala.shahabuddin@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Overview:

The contemporary world is beset with growing environmental problems. The global focus on economic growth and development has led us onto an unsustainable path: growing scientific evidence now suggests that the Earth may not be able to cope with the demands imposed on it.  This has created an urgent need to critically examine complex environmental issues from a variety of perspectives. It is necessary to inculcate holistic thinking on environmental challenges and their purported solutions, that includes concerns of social and ecological sustainability.  

This course will discuss some of the most current concerns related to the environment, as well as societal responses to them, from a multidisciplinary perspective. Water scarcity, climate change, forest degradation, biological extinction, pollution and agrarian distress are some of the issues that will be studied. This course is intended to familiarise students with environmental problems  and engender a holistic perspective in understanding causes and possible solutions through the lenses of both science and equity. This course will encourage students to synthesize information across a variety of sources.

Practically the course will be taught using a combination of lectures, documentaries, slideshows, guest lectures and in-class group discussions. Discussion on assigned readings will engender critical thinking and debate in class. Students will undertake group projects on current case studies (such as river pollution, tiger tourism etc.). Assessments will be based on in-class tests, essays, group projects and class participation.

 

 

Learning Outcomes
  • The course will create an awareness of, and sensitivity to the complexities of contemporary environmental challenges;
  • Students will learn to analyse environmental issues from a multidisciplinary perspective;
  • Students will learn to think and write analytically about complex issues
  • They will be taught to synthesize knowledge from different sources including scholarly papers, visual media and traditional knowledge.

Overview

This course is meant to introduce students to nature-society dialectics. We will examine the historical, social, and political processes that shape societal relations with the natural environment. The course has three overarching goals. First, it will help students gain an in-depth understanding of some of the pressing environmental issues of our times, such as the agrarian crisis, climate change, disaster and vulnerability, waste, the industrial food system, struggles over water, and neoliberalization of nature, among others. Second, drawing on a variety of theoretical frameworks, including Marxist, feminist, and post-structuralist perspectives, the course will expose students to a breadth of approaches to environmental questions. Finally, through this course, I hope to be able to cultivate a sense of environmental citizenship in students. The course will be taught using a combination of lectures, discussions, films, and group projects.

Faculty
Sumedha Basu [sumedha.basu@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Climate change is one of the biggest challenges of our time—and of the future. To respond to it, we first need to understand its wide-ranging relationships with nature, society and our everyday lives. Through this course, I seek to make these complex interrelationships accessible while building a strong analytical foundation for you. To this end, we will begin with the basics of climate science and the tools we use to study it. From there, we will engage with the different frameworks—both historical and current—that shape how people and governments think about climate change. Informed by these frameworks, we study the three key pillars of response: vulnerability assessment, mitigation, and adaptation.

 We will then explore the social, political, and economic dimensions that shape climate change and, in turn, are shaped by it. We finally examine the implications of these factors on our shared future. We look at alternative frameworks, technologies, and models gaining traction, and finally consider why hope in the era of climate change should be the new politics.

 The course will be taught through:

  • Lectures to introduce core concepts
  • Class discussions on cases and real-life examples
  • Films and documentaries to visualise impacts and solutions
  • Group projects to practice collaboration and problem-solving

 Throughout the course, we will learn about critical thinking, tools to comprehend the underlying layers of the challenge, assess the scope for resistance and create new pathways.

Overview

Course Title: Environmental Studies [FC-0102-6]

Faculty Instructor: Professor A.J. Urfi, an ecologist who specializes in wetland birds. Former Senior Professor and Head of Environmental Studies Department, Delhi University.

Schedule: Wednesday - Friday- 16:40-18:10 

Office Hours: Friday 2-3 PM

The core of environmental studies requires cross-discipline thinking and this course attempts to present broad perspectives on environmental issues from diverse perspectives. As with other FC’s the central point here too is to develop an appreciation of the societal relations with the natural environment, by examining historical, social, political, and ecological processes that shape these relations. In this FC we will first unpack the origins of the ‘environmental movement’ in a broad historical context before we come to the complexities of conflicts over resources, the different stake holders involved and the manner in which people have responded to crisis situations created by environmental destruction. In context of India, the ‘development versus environment protection’ controversy dominated much of our thinking and so this will be covered in fair amount of detail with a discussion of several case studies.  Each module will comprise several classroom interactions, ranging from 2-5, in which the background of the theme under discussion will be laid out and evaluation methods discussed.

 

Learning Outcomes

• An appreciation of the broad historical perspective of the current concern about the environment.

• An appreciation of how seemingly separate events are actually inter-connected and how they impact environment and the human price some people have to pay.

• Students will learn to think about the challenges for the environment movement in India, which has had to balance economic development as well as concerns for environmental protection.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Description:

Module 1: We will make an attempt to place the worldwide concern for the environment in it’s proper historical context, starting the story a few centuries ago. This will involve an overview of colonialism, exploration of the world by Europeans and how some early developments in the Americas triggered off the modern environmental protection drive.

Module 2: In continuation of above we will examine the extinction crisis and examine in some detail some of the major world landmarks in the early history of the environmental movement. We will try to understand how some of the dramatic forms of extinctions impacted people’s response to taking steps to conserve the environment and natural resources. This will be spread out over 2-3 sessions.

Module 3: Over 3-4 different interactions, in this module we will explore different dimensions of conflicts over resources. Important case studies will be discussed in detail in the classroom including the cattle grazing controversy in a wetland and people’s response to cutting forests for commercial purposes.

Module 4: Some relevant concepts will be introduced here and linkages between seemingly unconnected events will be outlined. The human price of environmental destruction, the ramifications of environmental destruction will be discussed.

Module 5: The broad contours of the ‘Environment versus Development’ debate will be laid out with a detailed examination of case studies discussed in the book ‘Temple or Tombs’ by Darryl D Monte. This will involve seminars and assignments.

Environmental Studies [FC-0102] [FC-0102-7]

Faculty
Simon Alexander Burns Brown [simon.brown@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Some of the most pressing issues of our time arise from our impact on the environment. In this course, we will explore questions such as: What obligations, if any, do we have to future generations, other species, or ecosystems, and why?  What does it mean for something to be natural? Does being natural make something good or worth preserving? What does justice look like in a world where development may require environmental destruction—or is this a false dichotomy?  Does responsibility for saving the environment rest with individuals, or with governments, corporations, or social structures—or is this another false dichotomy? How can ordinary citizens think clearly about complex environmental issues when our information environment is polluted by sophisticated campaigns of misinformation and misdirection? Exploring these questions requires drawing on multiple disciplines—philosophy, economics, political science, ecology, atmospheric science, sociology, and more—and we will be especially focused on learning how to draw on these different disciplines to create a coherent and ethical way of looking at and acting in the world.

Learning Outcomes

In this course, you will:

  • gain an understanding of some of the most pressing environmental challenges of our time (including their social and political dimensions) and their policy solutions
  • develop a holistic understanding of the environment around us, including its biophysical and social elements
  • learn to articulate the main claims and strengths and weaknesses of major frameworks in contemporary environmental ethics, and how to apply them to a range of issues 
  • enhance your ability to make informed, environmentally friendly decisions in your life as a responsible citizen, using critical reflection and evidence from multiple disciplines
  • refine your ability in using techniques of analysis, construction, expression, and assessment of logical arguments

Overview

“Is AI really taking jobs away?” is a question that we often get asked by students. While everyone has their own way of answering this question, the answer often revolves around the word ‘creativity’. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs report year after year ranks creativity as the most sought after skill in the job market. This course teaches you exactly that - creative problem solving. The ability to create and innovate isn’t just a skill, it's a mindset. This course will guide you through the process of enhancing your creative abilities, helping you recognize and nurture your innate potential. With hands-on activities and case studies, you’ll learn to generate original ideas and turn them into actionable solutions. Every good solution begins with a well-defined problem. Defining problems and being creative about solving problems has come to be known as design thinking. Design thinking is a human-centered approach to innovation that’s used by some of the world’s leading companies like Apple, Google, and Airbnb. Through this course, you’ll learn how to empathize with users, define problems clearly, ideate, prototype, and test solutions. It’s more than just theory—you’ll walk away with practical skills that can be applied across industries. You will learn design thinking through live action projects. In this project, you will provide consulting services to startups, and use design thinking methodology to solve their problem statements. This is a 13-week course comprising 39 classroom hours and approximately 20 hours of project work, group assignments and book readings. The Mid Term Project and the End Term Project will be team-based submissions.

Overview

Learning Outcomes

Students will learn mathematical tools required for various areas of economics: Microeconomics, Macroeconomics and Econometrics. Topics include (but are not limited to):

Real Analysis
Sequences and limits; continuity; differentiability of functions of one and several variables; implicit and inverse function theorems; convexity and concavity; uniform continuity and compactness results (e.g., Weierstrass’ theorem).

Linear Algebra
Systems of linear equations; rank of a matrix; linear independence and span; bases; matrix algebra; determinants; Cramer’s rule; inverse of a matrix; eigenvalues and eigenvectors; properties and applications in economics.

Differentiation & Optimization
Derivatives, higher-order derivatives, chain rule, directional derivatives; quadratic forms and definiteness; unconstrained optimization (FOC, SOC, local/global optima); constrained optimization with equality and inequality constraints; constraint qualifications; Lagrangian methods; Kuhn–Tucker conditions; Slater’s condition.

Optimization
Homogeneous functions; convex, concave, quasi-convex, and quasi-concave functions; applications in optimization and economic theory; concave programming.

Faculty
Kalyani Chaudhuri [kalyani.chaudhuri@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Experimental economics is one of the most versatile empirical methodologies used across a wide range of economics subfields. By creating carefully controlled environments in the laboratory or the field, experiments allow researchers to precisely measure behavior, test economic theories and hypotheses, and establish causal relationships between variables.

This course introduces students to the foundations and applications of experimental economics through landmark papers in behavioral economics, labor economics, gender economics, decision theory, game theory, and other areas. Alongside these theoretical foundations, the course provides extensive hands-on training in the complete experimental research process—from designing experiments and developing research protocols to implementing studies, managing logistics, collecting data, and conducting statistical analysis and interpretation. Students will also gain practical experience using state-of-the-art software for programming and running economic experiments.

As the capstone component of the course, students will work in teams to replicate a published experimental economics paper. This project will involve programming to develop the user interface, implementing the experiment with real participants, collecting and analyzing the resulting data, and interpreting the findings to produce a complete replication study.

Learning Outcomes
  1. Understand the role of experimental research in testing economic theories, measuring economic variables, and establishing causal effects
  2. Identify and develop hypotheses that can be tested using experimental research design
  3. Understand the logistical and ethical requirements of primary data collection
  4. Program and implement an economic experiment with human participants
  5. Analyze and interpret the experimental data in relation to the hypotheses of the study

description:
Introduction to Indian Politics [POL-1004] [POL-1004-1]

Faculty
Apurva Bamezai [apurva.bamezai@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

India is the world's most populous democracy, its most diverse, and — by many contemporary measures — among its most contested. Since Independence, the country has built a durable set of democratic institutions on foundations that comparative theory expected would not sustain them: a poor, largely rural society; deep cleavages of caste, religion, language, and region; and a state that succeeds spectacularly at some tasks while failing at the most basic. The last decade has intensified a long-running debate. Is Indian democracy eroding under the weight of majoritarian politics, or is it being remade in ways that we are yet to theorise and measure? This course offers a survey of Indian politics designed to give students the vocabulary, the historical grounding, and the analytical tools to think seriously about that question.

 

The course is organised around three parts. The initial  weeks establish the foundations: the animating puzzles of Indian politics, the political-economic settlement of the post-Independence period, and the founding moment of the Constitution. The next few weeks turn to the structures and cleavages that organise political life — institutions, parties and the party system, Hindutva, caste, gender, regional politics and decentralisation. The final few weeks address governance and contemporary politics: state capacity and political economy, elections and voting behaviour, the media and information environment, and the return to the opening debate on democratic erosion.

 

The course is a required core course for the Political Science major and is open to students across the university. It is intended both for students who will go on to specialise in Indian or comparative politics and for students who will not, but who wish to acquire a serious grounding in how the Indian political system works. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyse the institutional architecture of Indian democracy, evaluate competing scholarly explanations for its major puzzles, situate contemporary debates in the longer trajectory since 1947, and learn to construct a written or audio argument about a contemporary Indian political question for a non-academic audience.

 

Learning Outcomes
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

There are no prerequisites for the course. Students are expected to complete approximately 60–70 pages of reading each week and to follow current political developments in India through a national daily newspaper. Prior coursework in political theory, comparative politics, or Indian history is helpful but not required. The course is taught in a large-lecture format with weekly discussion sections led by Teaching Fellows; regular attendance in both is required.
