Introduction to Comparative Politics [POL-1005] [POL-1005-1]

Faculty
Bann Seng Tan [bannseng.tan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces students to the important questions, theories, and fundamental concepts in the field of Comparative Politics, alongside the basic tools necessary for comparative political analysis. It seeks to explore competing theoretical explanations for significant phenomena in world politics, such as the factors driving democratization, democratic breakdown or backsliding, political violence, and the achievement of good governance. We will also examine core debates about the decisive role of political institutions (including presidential versus parliamentary systems, political parties, and electoral systems), the power of states, and the influence of identity in shaping varied political outcomes. These theoretical frameworks are critically examined through an analysis of diverse case studies drawn from across the globe, including Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, and the Middle East, while also considering the United States in a comparative perspective. Ultimately, beyond building knowledge of countries and historical contexts, this course trains students to become critical consumers of political information, proficient in using the scientific method to analyze political life, and skilled in producing sound and well-supported political analysis.

Learning Outcomes

Through the substantive portion of this course, students will 1) identify the major issue-areas in comparative politics, 2) define and demarcate major concepts in comparative politics, and 3) explain the policy predilections of different regime types. Through an emphasis on social scientific methodology, students will 1) understand the importance of methods in political science, and 2) learn about the use of appropriate theories to explain political phenomena.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

courseTitle: History of India II: From c. 200 BCE to 1000 CE
description:
History of India II: From c. 200 BCE to 1000 CE [HIS-2002] [HIS-2002-1]

Faculty
Sanjukta Datta [sanjukta.datta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The history of ancient India covers a vast span of time, roughly between 1.5 million years ago and 1000 CE. So what all was happening in the period since the decline of the Maurya empire in the 3rd century BCE and until the military raids of Mahmud of Ghazni in the early 11th century? This course tracks momentous developments in politics, economy, society, and religion during these centuries, some of which continue to have significant relevance in contemporary times. Divided into three chronological units -- c.200 BCE-300 CE, 300-600 CE, and 600-1000CE – it explores a range of issues such as continuities and changes in the nature of polities and political processes; defining trends in agrarian relations and mercantile matters; consolidation of caste and gender identities, emergence of powerful religious movements and encounters between distinct religious traditions; flowering of regional identities through language and temple architecture; and expanding networks between the subcontinent and other parts of Asia through military campaigns, commercial interests, and cultural exchanges. In this process, the course opens up a dazzling array of literary, archaeological, and visual sources for the study of the pre-modern past until the beginning of the second millennium. 

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students should:

1) Get an overview of the major historical developments in the Indian subcontinent until 1000 CE

2) Be familiar with a range of historical sources 

3) Be able to critically examine historical sources, derive cogent arguments from such cources, and present them through well-structured, clearly written responses

Faculty

Overview

Welcome to the course named, “Electricity and Magnetism in the light of relativity”. This course serves as a gateway into the captivating realm of electromagnetism, exploring its foundational principles and practical applications. We will start with the basic concept of electrostatics and magnetostatics and at the end we will study the relativistic aspects of electrodynamics. At the end of the course, you will have acquired a robust understanding of electromagnetism and electrodynamics, empowering you to analyze and solve a diverse array of problems.

Electrodynamics: Electromotive forces, Ohm law, Faraday’s law, Maxwells equation 

Electrodynamics and relativity:  Einstein postulates, Lorentz transformation, relativistic electrodynamics

The course will focus on why and how political institutions and culture affect economic outcomes and how they are shaped by economic development and policy choices. The goal is to bring students up to date with the current research in the field and develop their understanding to a stage where they can develop and address an original research question. Though the course will begin with some discussion on classical political economy and theoretical concepts in political economy, it will focus on the recent research papers in the field. Economics of Information [ECO-3101] [ECO-3101-1]

Faculty
Suraj Shekhar [suraj.shekhar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Prior knowledge of basic game theory will be assumed. We want to understand outcomes in environments
where some players have more information than others. For example, a car salesman knows more about
the value of the car than a customer, a person buying car insurance knows more than the insurance
provider about their own driving style, a job applicant is more aware of her abilities than the interviewer.
The objective of this course is to understand player incentives and strategies in such environments with
the use of formal economic models. We will highlight the role played by asymmetric information and
study how it changes outcomes compared to an environment where everyone has the same information.
Specific topics include models involving adverse selection, moral hazard, signalling, cheap talk, reputation
and information cascades.

Faculty
Annie Baxi [annie.baxi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course is designed to introduce students to the prominent qualitative research methods in Psychology. Qualitative research facilitates an in-depth and contextual  understanding of  psychological states and processes through systematic analyses of thick descriptive and experiential data. Questions like - What is the lived experience of a psychiatric diagnosis? How are images and symbols in popular media influencing our everyday language and reality? What are the various stages of coping in the aftermath of a trauma? Why are certain stories and myths important in a community? are most suited for a qualitative inquiry. 

The course will begin with a rationale of the various qualitative approaches and their underlying theoretical assumptions. The lectures will include activities designed to give a hands-on-experience of all the major qualitative methods. Throughout the course, students will be encouraged to engage in thinking about and articulating the role of researcher’s subjectivity and social position in qualitative research. 

Learning Outcomes

After completing the course, the student will be able to:

  • - Understand the relevance of the various paradigms in psychological research.
  • - Identify and differentiate between the different methods in qualitative research.
  • - Develop and enhance skills involved in conducting a qualitative interview.
  • - Appreciate the role of Reflexivity and Positionality in the dynamics of qualitative work.
  • - Analyse and interpret data using Thematic Analysis.

Overview

Friendship is an integral part of all our lives – but what makes someone a good friend? Do we have special obligations to our family and to people with whom we closely associate?  Are you certain that you are reading this description? How do you know this isn’t just a dream? How do we come to know anything at all?  We take all kinds of things to be true on a regular basis – but are we really justified in so doing?  Can we be blamed/praised for what we do? Can we say that we have freedom to choose our actions? 

In this course, we'll explore such questions in ethics and politics, epistemology, and metaphysics. Our discussions will be guided by texts drawn from diverse philosophical traditions and time periods, from the 4th century BCE to 2025.  Along the way, you'll develop skills in constructing sustained arguments, considering objections and counter-objections, and making conceptual connections across traditions. The course will demonstrate both the fruitfulness and challenges of philosophical inquiry, and the tools you will acquire here will serve you well beyond the study of philosophy. 

Do not sign up for this course if you find that you cannot read, write, or function without LLMs.

Quantum Mechanics [PHY-3510] [PHY-3510-1]

Faculty
Suratna Das [suratna.das@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Albert Einstein: “God doesn’t play dice [with the universe]”

Niels Bohr: “Einstein, stop telling God what to do!”

 

We are all familiar with the tussle between Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr when it came to Quantum Mechanics: a completely new way of looking at the world of atomic and subatomic particles which started to unravel in the beginning and middle of the last century. In this course, we will learn the very basics of this vast subject, a subject which still causes bewilderment to the greatest of the minds. There’s no well-known physicist in this world who has not pondered over the mind-boggling Quantum Mechanics deeply at some point of time in their life. 

 

The course has been designed in the following way:

 

1. Some historical motivations: Blackbody spectrum: the problem of ultraviolet catastrophe and Planck’s constant, Bohr’s atomic model and de Broglie wavelength, Wave-particle duality: Young’s double slit experiment, Davisson-Germer Experiment, Photoelectric Effect, Atomic spectroscopy.

2. Basics of Quantum Mechanics: Wavefunction, Schrödinger Equation, Interpretation of Wavefunction, Wavefunction normalisation, Wavefunction as a probability amplitude, Principle of superposition, Wavepackets and Uncertainty,  Time evolution of a free wavepacket 

3. Examples: Particle in a 1D potential (Dirac delta, infinite and finite square-well potentials) - bound states and scattering, Tunnelling and quantum mechanical explanation of radioactive decay.

4. Operator method: Hilbert space of states, bra-ket notation, observables as linear operators, Schrodinger equation and unitary evolution, state vector collapse - Born rule, The energy, position and momentum basis - transforming between different bases: Schrodinger and Heisenberg pictures, The harmonic oscillator, angular momentum and spin in Quantum Mechanics, Stern-Gerlach experiment, The hydrogen atom - derivation of its energy levels.

** Some advanced topics: Symmetries and Conservation laws in Quantum Mechanics, Quantum-to-Classical Transition problem (Copenhagen Interpretation, Many-world Interpretation, Decoherence) [These topics will be covered only if time permits]

Learning Outcomes

Quantum Mechanics is the basis of modern science, be it physics, chemistry, biology or computer science. This course will set the basis of other higher level courses that the Physics Major students will credit in future, like Quantum Mechanics II, Physics of Matter and Electronics. By the end of this course, it is expected that students will have a firm foundation in the fundamental concepts of QM, will be familiar with both the state-vector and wave mechanics based approaches, and would have gained the relevant background to explore and understand the manifold applications of QM to explain diverse physical phenomena, be it in Atomic, Molecular, Nuclear, Particle Physics or Quantum Information  or Condensed Matter physics. 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course will closely follow the following text books:

 

1. Lecture notes on Quantum Mechanics: J Greensite (available online)

2. Introduction to Quantum Mechanics: David Griffiths 

3. Principles of Quantum Mechanics: R. Shankar 

 

Other books useful for reference and supplementary reading include: Feynman Lectures on Physics (Vol. III), Modern Quantum Mechanics, by J.J. Sakurai, Quantum Mechanics by Leonard Schiff

Statistical Mechanics [PHY-3610] [PHY-3610-1]

Faculty
Gautam Iqbal Menon [gautam.menon@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces the fundamental principles of statistical mechanics, establishing a microscopic foundation for macroscopic thermal phenomena in physical systems. The question that motivates statistical physics - in simple language - is understanding how we can describe the behaviour of many particles/degrees of freedom using the language of probability, statistics and computation.

Starting with an introduction to probability theory and combinatorics, we will develop the framework of statistical ensembles—specifically the microcanonical, canonical, and grand canonical formulations—alongside the central roles of the partition function and entropy. Students will explore the core ensemble frameworks—microcanonical, canonical, and grand canonical—and learn how to derive thermodynamic potentials, entropy, and the partition function.

The course explores applications across both classical and quantum regimes, emphasizing the statistical behaviour of ideal gases, magnetic materials, and non-interacting systems. A primary focus is placed on quantum statistics, covering Maxwell-Boltzmann, Fermi-Dirac, and Bose-Einstein distributions.  Students will use these statistics to model physical systems including ideal quantum gases, blackbody radiation, phonons in crystal lattices, the Chandrasekhar limit, and the behavior of electrons in metals.

Finally, the course will address a few advanced topics including phase transitions, if there's time.

Core Topics

  1. Foundations of Probability: Random variables, probability distributions (e.g., Gaussian), microstates vs. macrostates, and the statistical definition of entropy.
  2. The Laws of Thermodynamics: Temperature, thermal equilibrium, heat and work, thermodynamic potentials (internal energy, free energy, enthalpy), and Maxwell relations.
  3. Statistical Ensembles: Frameworks for the microcanonical, canonical, and grand canonical ensembles, and the derivation of partition functions.
  4. Classical Gases: The classical ideal gas, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, and the physical significance of chemical potential.
  5. Quantum Statistics and symmetries
  6. Fermi-Dirac Statistics: Ideal Fermi gases, the Fermi surface, and electrons in metals.
  7. Bose-Einstein Statistics: Ideal Bose gases, Bose-Einstein condensation, blackbody radiation (photons), and crystal lattice vibrations (phonons).
  8. Interacting Systems & Phase Transitions: Magnetic systems (such as the Ising model), mean field theory
Learning Outcomes

A deep appreciation of how simple macroscopic (and universal) descriptions emerge from a physical description at the most granular level of many particles/degrees of freedom.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

1. An Introduction to Thermal Physics by Daniel V. Schroeder

2. Statistical Mechanics: Entropy, Order Parameters, and Complexity by James P. Sethna

3. Concepts in Thermal Physics by Stephen J. Blundell and Katherine M. Blundell

4. Thermal Physics by Charles Kittel and Herbert Kroemer

5. Fundamentals of Statistical and Thermal Physics by Frederick Reif

Overview

“Beliefs and practices of religious life; the system of signs we employ to express our thoughts; the monetary system we use to pay debts; the credit instruments we use in commerce…” These are social facts, Emile Durkheim famously wrote in one of the foundational texts of modern sociology. By social facts, Durkheim meant those established patterns of social behavior and interaction that display a degree of continuity and resilience that sets them apart from individual preference and subjective choice, compelling human beings to adapt to and internalize them – and making life difficult for those who do not conform. This course introduces students to the art and science of sociology, defined as the detection, description, and conceptualization of social patterns through empirical observation. As the main 1000-level course for the Sociology-Anthropology major, Sociology and the Making of Concepts introduces students to the six social facts that frame the six core courses in the sociology-anthropology major at Ashoka: Language; Kinship; Religion; Money; State; Stratification.

courseTitle: State, Stateless Societies and Problems of Power
description:
State, Stateless Societies and Problems of Power [SOA-2101] [SOA-2101-1]

Faculty
Mitul Baruah [mitul.baruah@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The question of the state has preoccupied social scientists for a very long time. Much has been discussed and debated about its origins, forms, and relevance, and different theorizations of the state have emerged from across theoretical perspectives. We live at a time when, on the one hand, the forces of neoliberalism seem to want to relegate the state to irrelevance, while on the other, the ongoing genocide in Gaza and conflicts and wars between nation-states challenge the very ideas of “sovereignty” and statehood. The rising authoritarianism and right-wing nationalism pose further challenges to many communities globally, rendering some of them stateless. These are therefore times when the question of the state becomes ever more important. 

What is the state? How are states formed and what forms do they take, when and where? Is the state capitalist? Is the developmental state dead? How does power operate both within a state and between state and society? How does bureaucracy work? Who is a citizen? What does it mean to be stateless? Of what relevance is the state in the age of neoliberal privatization? These are but a few important questions that this course will try to engage with. Drawing on an interdisciplinary body of work, including ethnographies, theoretical texts, and audio-visual materials, this course will expose students to multiple ways of thinking about the state and power in general.

courseTitle: Gift, Commodity and the Exchange of Values
description:
Gift, Commodity and the Exchange of Values [SOA-2102] [SOA-2102-1]

Faculty
Arif Hayat Nairang [arif.nairang@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What kinds of things are gifts and commodities? What does their exchange tell us about the relations between persons and things, between things and things, and between different persons party to an exchange? What gives a thing a sense of value? Are there such things that are useful but that are not up for exchange? What kinds of debts are generated when gifts and commodities are exchanged? Does the clearing of a debt signal the end of a relationship? Is reciprocity a good thing after all? What happens when you refuse a gift? If being creditable is a respectable characteristic, why are creditors typically such villainous characters? Is being indebted a show of strength or sign of weakness? What goes into making a price? What does it really mean for a thing to be priceless? If time is indeed money, is money also in some way a form or measure of time?  

This course is an intensive introduction to the anthropology of exchange through the circulation of gifts and commodities across diverse times and places. We will read a set of classical and contemporary texts that explore the complex processes and relations of gift and commodity exchange and consider the rich and seemingly endless debates that they generate for the discipline and beyond.  

Learning Outcomes
  1. Understand core anthropological concepts of gift and commodity exchange: Students will demonstrate familiarity with foundational theories of exchange, including Mauss's theory of the gift, Marx's analysis of commodity fetishism, and Derrida's concept of the pure gift, and will be able to articulate the key debates these generate within and beyond anthropology.
  2. Analyze the social life of things and the relations they generate: Students will develop the ability to trace how objects, services, and gestures circulate between persons and institutions, and to identify the kinds of value — material, symbolic, moral, and relational — that exchange produces, transfers, or refuses.
  3. Apply ethnographic methods to the study of everyday exchange: Through the exchange diary assignment, students will practice close observation of ordinary giving and taking in their own social worlds, developing skills in description, reflexivity, and the translation of lived experience into analytical insight.
  4. Engage critically with classical and contemporary texts across disciplines: Students will move beyond summary to critically evaluate arguments made by anthropologists, philosophers, historians, and economists, identifying the assumptions, stakes, and limitations of each author's framework.
  5. Connect micro-level exchanges to macro-level historical and political processes: Students will demonstrate the ability to situate specific acts of exchange within broader structures including colonialism, capitalism, caste, and global commodity chains, drawing on ethnographies from South Asia, South America, and Wall Street.
  6. Develop original analytical writing grounded in ethnographic and theoretical engagement: Students will produce written work that moves fluidly between observation and theory, using evidence from their own fieldwork alongside course readings to make original arguments rather than merely applying received frameworks.

Economics of Gender [ECO-3660] [ECO-3660-1]

Faculty
Bipasha Maity [bipasha.maity@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course aims at undertaking an economic analysis of the issues affecting women in the economy. The discrimination faced by women in market scenarios, such as those of labour and credit as well as the impact of globalization on women will be studied. Further, the course will explore issues that women face in non-market situations such as bargaining within the household, marriage and fertility and how market and non-market scenarios interact to in uence women's well-being. Lastly the roles of education, healthcare, property rights, birth control, political franchise and representation in mitigating gender-based inequalities will be studied. Students would be able to understand and appreciate both market and non-market factors that result in or promote gender based inequalities. They would also be able to critically understand why some policies succeed while others may fail to mitigate gender-based inequalities.

Learning Outcomes
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The main textbook for the course is:

Why Gender Matters in Economics. Author: Mukesh Eswaran. Publisher: Princeton University Press, 2014.

A significant part of the course also relies on materials from published papers in academic economics journals. This will be provided by the first week of classes.

Reading Archaeology [HIS-3002] [HIS-3002-1]

Faculty
Sanjukta Datta [sanjukta.datta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Welcome to the world of broken pots, dried bones, buried shipwrecks, and competing claims over antiquities. Conceptualized as an introductory course on the study of material remains, it is divided into two main sections. The first explores fine-tuned methods employed by archaeologists to analyze available data in the reconstruction of the past; the relationship between archaeology and various disciplines such as botany, zoology, chemistry, anthropology, and history; major theoretical turns in the history of archaeology; politics of archaeological practice and key global issues in heritage management; and archaeology in popular culture. The second engages with a scholarly yet unputdownable account of a remarkably preserved archaeological site in Europe. While the first section of the course will be a combination of lectures and class discussions, the second will be based completely on discussions and in-class activities. 

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students should be able to:

1. Get an overview of the basic terms, concepts, and methods used in archaeology

2. Familiarize themselves with the history of archaeology, including some of the key issues in contemporary archeological practice 

3. Savour accessibly written archaeological prose based on rigorous research

Faculty
Arunava Sinha [arunava.sinha@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In this course, students will develop the basic skills of translation by working on a variety of short texts as well as one medium-sized text. The short exercises will be aimed at practising different genres and facets of translation, including prose, poetry, and dialogue. At this stage they will learn about making choices and the elements of the original text that need to be carried over into the translated text. The second half will involve translating a medium-sized text of the student's choice from their mother tongue (or any other language of choice) into English, applying the earlier learnings. The course is aimed at preparing students to translate full-length texts.

Students should have completed the Introduction to Creative Writing Course and Reading For Writers.

First steps towards being a literary translator.

Ecology and Evolution (Lab) [BIO-3012/ ES-3301] [BIO-3012/ ES-3301-1]

Faculty
Shivani [shivani.krishna@ashoka.edu.in ], Imroze Khan [imroze.khan@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Joy Bose [joy.bose@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course offers a hands-on experience to apply concepts from evolutionary biology and ecology theory courses. Students will be introduced to quantitative methods and research processes in ecology and evolution, which include experimental design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, and scientific writing, utilizing both field and laboratory studies. 

Ecological systems are immensely complex due to the diverse and context-dependent interactions among species, shaped by evolutionary processes and resulting in numerous emergent properties. In the course, students learn how real-world ecologists and evolutionary biologists tackle this complexity by beginning with simple assumptions. They will use local plant and animal models to test concepts on population dynamics, competition, resource utilization, foraging behavior, antibiotic resistance, and sexual selection. The course comprises interconnected laboratory modules. Each module aims to revisit some of the concepts introduced in the lectures and also trains students to construct arguments in ecological and evolutionary biology based on the evidence. Thinking analytically and scientific writing are best developed through practice. Thus, actively engaging in writing laboratory reports will serve as a useful tool to improve students’ writing skills. 

Learning Outcomes

Towards the end of this course, students will be able to design experiments, implement appropriate sampling methods for individuals, populations, and communities, and inquire about their diversity and stability. They will be acquainted with potential errors that arise due to observer bias, the significance of blinded methods, and other potential ways to improve the reliability of the data collected.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Reading materials will be provided on a weekly basis for each of the modules.

Attendance
3 excused absence(s) are allowed in this course lecture.
1 additional excused absence(s) are allowed for sportspersons in this course lecture.
Additional Comments: This is a laboratory course that involves live animals and plants; therefore, repeating the modules is not possible. Therefore, the total number of allowed absences cannot exceed 4.

Histories of South Asian Art: From the Earliest Times to the Present [VA-3006/ HIS-3804] [VA-3006/ HIS-3804-1]

Faculty
Mrinalini Sil [mrinalini.sil@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Histories of South Asian Art: From the Earliest Times to the Present

Course Instructor: Mrinalini Sil

What is art, and who is it meant for? What is specifically South Asian about South Asian art? What does it mean to think of South Asia and art as analytical categories? How have artists across history imagined the region we now identify as South Asia? Addressing these questions, this course surveys the visual arts of South Asia from its earliest traces in cave paintings and stone implements to sculpture, painting, illustrated manuscripts, calligraphy, and architecture, spanning prehistory to the late twentieth century. Alongside this chronological framework, the course explores themes across objects, archaeological sites, built environments, religious and political symbols, and institutions of artistic production and display. It examines changing conceptions of image, icon, body, landscape, and portraiture in relation to shifting social and ideological contexts, patronage, markets, material media, and aesthetic practices, while interrogating both South Asia and South Asian art as dynamic rather than fixed art historical categories.

Learning Outcomes

On successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

a) Identify and analyse aspects of works of art and visual images in different material and medium using appropriate vocabulary.

b) Explore the main trends in the development of Art History and Visual Culture of South Asia by accessing the critical essential skills.

c) Evaluate the approaches of artists, art historians, visual anthropologists and curators to the field of South Asian visual arts and culture.

d) Develop the interests for a future training in critical art historical training and art curatorial programme.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Weekly readings will be uploaded and shared with those who choose to pursue the course.

Students are encouraged to engage with materials across disciplines, not limited to art history, and to draw on a range of supplementary resources such as online museum collections, podcasts, films, plays, performance pieces, press reports, newspaper clippings, works of historical fiction, and scholarly blog posts to support their learning.

No prior training in Visual Arts or Art History Required.

courseTitle: Exploring Life in the Neighborhood Lab
description:
Exploring Life in the Neighborhood Lab [BIO-1002/ ES-2301] [BIO-1002/ ES-2301-1]

Faculty
Balaji Chattopadhyay [balaji.chattopadhyay@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Unprecedented loss of biodiversity, anthropogenic activities, exploitation of natural resources, and globalising tendencies in recent decades threaten the balance between the intricate web of life on Earth and the processes that are pivotal to its survival. Although many efforts are being made globally, we are still far from achieving the necessary measures to restore the balance. One of the primary hindrances is the lack of general awareness of how nature drafts the code of life in our neighbourhoods and how various forms of life together respond and form the very basis on which natural forces operate in our backyard, much like a feedback loop. To fill these gaps, this course aims to bring students from various backgrounds— i.e., not limited to Biology only, but also from other sciences, humanities and social sciences— and introduce them to their local ecosystem and the intricacies of biological interactions using some basic and simplified concepts of ecology, evolution, and animal behaviour, followed by field observations as well as laboratory experiments. The course will have many open-ended exercises, encouraging students to develop small questions based on classroom discussions and observing various natural patterns (e.g., diversity of life) and processes (e.g., sexual interactions, prey-predator, disease spread, cannibalism).

Learning Outcomes

Towards the end of this course, we expect students to be more connected to their surroundings, develop an intellectual framework to answer how diverse forms of life coexist, and appreciate the nuanced biological wonders that reside in every pattern and process of the living world. Students will learn to connect bigger ecological phenomena and patterns of animal behaviours with their evolutionary origins. Besides, they will also learn how to build testable hypotheses and design experiments with appropriate sampling, as well as the importance of keeping laboratory notebooks and scientific communication.

Introduction to Neuroscience/ Biological Psychology [PSY-2011/ BIO-2103/ BIO-6103] [PSY-2011/ BIO-2103/ BIO-6103-1]

Faculty
Supriya Ray [supriya.ray@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

“Within this brain of mine, A universe resides, where thoughts like stars align, And reason gently guides.” -Author Unknown.

“I consider that a man's brain originally is like a little empty attic, and you have to stock it with such furniture as you choose. A fool takes in all the lumber of every sort that he comes across, so that the knowledge which might be useful to him gets crowded out..." - Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, A Study in Scarlet

This introductory course provides a broad overview of the fascinating field of neuroscience, exploring the structure, function, development, and disorders of the nervous system. We will delve into the fundamental principles governing neuronal communication, sensory and motor systems, learning and memory, emotion, and higher cognitive functions. This course aims to equip students with a foundational understanding of the brain and its intricate relationship with behavior and cognition. No prior knowledge of neuroscience is required, although a basic understanding of biology and psychology is helpful.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

  • Identify the major structures of the nervous system and their functions.
  • Explain the principles of neuronal signalling, including action potentials and synaptic transmission.
  • Describe the organization and function of sensory systems (e.g., vision, audition, somatosensation).
  • Explain the neural mechanisms underlying motor control and movement.
  • Discuss the biological basis of learning, memory, and plasticity.
  • Describe the neural circuits involved in emotion and motivation.
  • Understand the neural correlates of higher cognitive functions such as language and attention.
  • Gain an introductory understanding of common neurological and psychiatric disorders.
  • Critically evaluate basic neuroscience research findings.
  • Develop an appreciation for the interdisciplinary nature of neuroscience.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Required Textbook:

  • Fundamental Neuroscience (3rd / 4th Ed) by Larry Squire, Floyd Bloom, et al.

Recommended Readings (Optional):

  • Neuroscience (6th Ed) by Dale Purves
  • Biological Psychology (13th Ed) by James W. Kalat
  • Scientific articles and other materials will be shared through Google Classroom.

Microbiology [BIO-2411/ BIO-6411] [BIO-2411/ BIO-6411-1]

Faculty
Laasya Samhita [laasya.samhita@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This microbiology module is designed as an inquiry-based laboratory course. It will investigate antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from multiple angles, incorporating aspects of molecular microbiology, microbial ecology and evolution. The aim is to expose students to how real research stories are built, while simultaneously teaching laboratory tools and techniques such as microbiological methods, PCR, mutagenesis and experimental evolution. Students are expected to participate in generating and evaluating evidence-based data. As a bonus, in cases that yield interesting results, students could also gain the opportunity to further analyse (beyond the class time) and publish their findings, thus gaining valuable research experience. In order to ensure personal attention and hands-on training, the number will be limited to 20 students (groups of 4 x 4 or 4 x 5 at most).

This course has no prerequisites and can be taken up by biology minors for credit. Please note that it is nonetheless a rigorous hands-on lab course that needs substantial time and investment including outside of lab hours. It is intended to give you a flavour for real research work in molecular microbiology and a chance to get your own results (in groups).

Learning Outcomes

 

 

 

 

Learn principles and hands- on execution of the techniques and experimental modules listed below. In the process, students will learn aseptic culture techniques, handling micropipettes and bacterial cultures in a biosafety hood and on the bench and other associated skills.

i)  Document and analyse local environmental AMR using bacterial cultures and antibiotics.

ii) Compare existing clinical with environmental AMR gene data and generate some simple plots (sequence analysis)

iii)  Carry out regular PCR and learn about using PCR for mutagenesis (if time permits, also generate mutants)

iv) Carry out extraction of genomic DNA from bacterial cells

v) Learn and carry out agarose gel electrophoresis

vi) Learn to handle bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) and carry out lysis assays

v) Attempt re-sensitization of antibiotic resistant strains using experimental evolution

Overview

Syllabus: Real vector spaces, subspaces, spanning sets, basis sets, dimension of a

vector space. Solution of a system of linear equations. Row space and column space

of a matrix, rank of a matrix, elementary row and column operations of a matrix. In-

version of square matrices, rank factorization of a matrix. Properties of determinants.

Linear transformations, range and null space of a linear transformation, rank-nullity

theorem. Matrix representation of a linear transformation. Inner product spaces,

normed linear spaces, examples of different normed linear spaces, orthonormal basis

sets. Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, characteristic polynomials. Spectral theorem for real

symmetric matrices. Singular value decomposition.

Learning Outcomes

To be able to do various operations with matrices and use then in some concrete problems.

Introduction to Travel Writing [MS-2000/ CW-2012] [MS-2000/ CW-2012-1]

Faculty
Tisha Srivastav [tisha.srivastav@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

 This course is a contemporary mix of thinking about how we travel, considering travel writing across media formats in India and media writing skills for travel writing. It centres on ideas of travel, a dialogue with decolonization, be they thinkers, historical and contemporary travel accounts on India, or the panorama mode on your smartphone. This course will give you a broad exposure into the kind of travel writing Indians are writing. 

The flow of the classes: Each week, one class will centre on critical thought and practice readings on travel and the other on understanding the fundamentals of media-friendly feature writing.

One guest lecture, documentary screening and field trip is a mandatory part of the course.

No prerequisites.

Learning Outcomes

An introduction to a wealth of textual and visual travel related literary material on India.

Honing your curiosity and observation capacities, you will polish a media writing skill set  to produce a publishing worthy travel account.

Industry linkages

Through writing, reading, communicating and thinking through the question - is there any such thing as an Indian travel voice, you will be encouraged to find your own.

Mihir Vatsa in his book Tales of Hazaribagh looks at many of these tropes as somewhat of an insider.  Mihir Jha (Mihir Vatsa) is a writer and a Ph.D. candidate at the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences, IIT Delhi. Siddharth Pandey is the inaugural joint fellow at the Käte Hamburger Centre ‘global dis:connect’ (Munich) and the International Centre for Advanced Studies: Metamorphosis of the Political’ (New Delhi). Hailing from the Himalayas of North India and evolving into an interdisciplinary academic, artist and writer, much of his work has explored the multifarious interactions between landscape, materiality, imagination and reality. He has a PhD in Fantasy Literature and Craft Studies from the University of Cambridge (UK), where he was based as a Cambridge Commonwealth and Cambridge International Scholar. Post PhD, he has held numerous research fellowships in global history, art history, travel cultures and globalization studies at LMU, Yale Centre for British Art (Yale University), the Paul Mellon Centre for Studies in British Art (London) and twice at the Käte Hamburger Centre. As a landscape photographer and curator, his work has been commissioned by some of the world’s leading museums (including London’s Victoria and Albert and Durham’s The Oriental). Twice a Charles Wallace India Trust Fellow, he was the 2025 Writer-in-Residence at the International Centre Goa (India). His first book Fossil was published as part of a Tasmania-run global arts project ‘Lost Rocks’, and was a finalist for the 2022 Banff Mountain Literature Awards (Canada). His other writings can be found across a host of academic and popular platforms, including the national media such as The Tribune, The Hindu, The Pioneer, The Indian Express, Outlook, Live Wire, Frontline, Scroll.in and The Quint. He is currently working on a narrative history of Shimla, under contract with Hachette India.

Seminar Series in Biological Sciences [BIO-6014] [BIO-6014-1]

Faculty
Laasya Samhita [laasya.samhita@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This seminar series is designed to equip PhD and MSc students in the biological sciences with the essential skills for presenting, critiquing, and discussing scientific literature. This is a mandatory 4-credit course for PhD students (3 hour classes once a week). Students will present papers selected from a pool of papers suggested by the instructors.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Outcomes:

Critically evaluate the structure and organization of a scientific manuscript, identifying the research question, methodology, results, and conclusions.

Assess the strengths and weaknesses of a scientific manuscript, including the validity of its methodology, interpretation of data, and potential limitations.

Write and improve a concise and informative summary of the research question, and key findings from a manuscript.

Formulate well-structured questions during seminars to critically analyze research presented by peers and invited speakers, demonstrating an understanding of scientific concepts.

Develop and deliver a clear and concise scientific presentation that effectively communicates the key findings, strengths, and weaknesses/limitations from a reviewed manuscript, integrating them with existing knowledge in the field.

Overview

Magic, Science, Religion [SOA-2103] [SOA-2103-1]

Faculty
Ravindran S [ravindran.sriramachandran@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What do we mean by magic, science and religion & what are the similarities & differences between them? Are these concepts contradictory or complementary? Are the boundaries between them clear or complicated? And in what ways are they different? How do these core anthropological concepts develop, evolve, and function in the practice of everyday life? This course explores magic, science, and religion not only as systems of explaining and controlling events, and making sense but as illustrative of the theoretical and ontological work that people perform in their everyday life. While magic, science, and religion may seem like stable domains, we examine how the meaning of these social and political categories shifts over time and across contexts, so much so that the difference between them often seems to break down altogether. By focusing on cross-cultural differences, we raise fundamental questions about human nature itself, and the human need/desire to interpret and influence events. Students in this course will learn key debates in social scientific, particularly anthropological, research on magic, science, and religion, and conduct their own original research projects involving first-hand observations of magical, scientific, and religious practices.
The course material is divided into three main sections: 1) Magic and Magical Thinking, 2) Science and Culture, 3) Religion, Ritual and Doubt. We will spend 4 weeks on each section.

Overview

Fourier Analysis, also called Harmonic Analysis, is one of the central areas of mathematics pure and applied. We will study

The course also offers an opportunity to consolidate our understanding of the fundamentals of Real Analysis.

Immunology [BIO-3443/ BIO-6443] [BIO-3443/ BIO-6443-1]

Faculty
Rama Sundari Akondy [rama.akondy@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Immunology is the study of the immune system - a complex network of organs, cells and proteins that protect the body from disease (except when it doesn’t!). It is an evolving field that is difficult to understand and memorize, making it a challenging subject to learn. This course focuses on introducing fundamental concepts of the vertebrate immune system rather than a comprehensive coverage of the subject. UG, ASP and PhD students who want to grasp key concepts of how the immune system works should consider this course. This immunology course can complement student interest / knowledge of cancer therapy, vaccine biology and infectious diseases.

Learning Outcomes
  • Learning Outcomes:
  • After completing this course students will be able to:
  • Identify components of the immune system.
  • Describe how diseased / infected cells are identified
  • Describe the key processes in initiation of an immune response. 
  • Explain how the immune system is able to respond to so many different pathogens, even those that have not been encountered previously.
  • Describe some general and specialized immune mechanisms used to control pathogens.
  • Explain how immune cells move through the body.
  • Describe the fundamental principle behind some common techniques used in immunology research.
  • Describe how the immune system is able to discriminate non-self from self or harmful from harmless.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

It is mandatory that students have a background in basic biology. The immune system uses molecular mechanisms that are a part of cell and molecular biology courses (Introduction to biology II and III), so these are a prerequisite for BIO-3443/6443. We will be using select chapters from Lauren Sompayrac's how the immune system works and Kuby's immunology. Additional reading materials include articles from Scientific American, Resonance or similar journals and will be provided by the instructor.

description:
Arts of our Times (Mediums and Media in Contemporary) [VA-2004] [VA-2004-1]

Faculty
Rakhi Peswani [rakhi.peswani@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Arts of Our Times – Mediums and Materials in Contemporary

VA 2004-1

Gateway Course, Department of Visual Arts (Monsoon 2026)

Faculty Instructor: Rakhi Peswani   

email:  rakhi.peswani@ashoka.edu.in

Schedule: Tuesday, Friday 4:40 - 6:10pm.

Office Hours: Fridays 2pm to 3pm.

The objective of this course is to enable foundational clarity in contemporary artistic practices and its possibilities towards invigorating research. The course is designed to provide students certain potential in observing, co-relating, revising minute reflections into complex questions through varying forms of artistic media and practices.

The course also provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamentals of research through artistic practice through methods and materials. Students will be guided to execute ideas through the media of drawing and sculpture.

One of the defining paradigm of this course is its basis in the practice of artistic forms while simultaneously referring the histories of art practices of  20th C. We will examine various languages of arts to understand the long arc of what is now termed as Contemporary Art.

We will engage experimentation in 2 Dimensional, 3 Dimensional and spatial correlation of ideas. Images will be  developed with critical practices and concepts of aesthetics and politics in the Arts.

Students will develop critical questions, personal or social expressions through a basis in image making practices based in crafting through hands-on production.

Through experiments in various forms of media like graphic drawing, explorations in spatial concepts of text, forms in clay, and explorations in various tenets of sculptural practice, the course will be develop spatial forms to understand the making of installations, site specificity and exhibition making.  

The overarching objective of the course is to enable faith and confidence in visual/ verbal, plastic languages that amalgamate all sense perceptions and to provide certain foundational understanding of language through immediacy and affective potentials.

The course will culminate in a conceptualisation of a project based in a site-specific installation and a public exhibition of all works.

 

Field trip : A field trip to a contemporary artist’s studios will be planned  to visit and understand the methods, positions and vision an artist incorporates in their creative work.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Objectives:

This Course is designed to provide confidence in experimentation with visual material through exploration in various tools and materials to shape artistic vocabulary.

The course also provides contextual survey of 20th C Art through individual artists, languages of art making, various isms of 20th C and the poetic and political dimensions of creative practices.

Framework:

Using perceptual and observational aspects of research, hands-on explorations of different media forms, and fictional routes in placemaking and site specificity, the course will be guided to use drawing and sculpture making- as tools to articulate creative expressions.

Various forms of visual languages will be introduced theoretically and with hands on instructions, to reach beyond the world of words. Students will explore representational and non- representational aspects of 2 dimensional and 3 dimensional media. .

Over the course of 12 weeks, we will delve into making, shaping and expressing with our hands - through materiality of mark-making, line, shapes, forms, spatial expressions as well as materiality of text as concepts.

The course will be heavily based on students’ hands-on explorations, presentations, classroom discussions and immersion in the making of the arts.

Learning Outcomes:

Students after taking this course will gain:

  1. Confidence in experimenting and consolidating the realm of creative practice into everyday engagements.
  2. Confidence in shaping fragmented ideas and reflections into strong visual concepts.
  3. Production of a series of art works for a creative portfolio.
  4. Gaining discursive insights into artmaking and art thinking with various tools of drawing and sculpture.
  5. Awareness of Modern and Contemporary Art and artists, their creative practices and various schools and isms.

 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Course Modules:

Each Module will run for 4 weeks with two classes per week.

 Module 1:

Artistic Agency and the Avantgarde.

(Drawing, Mark-making, Expressionism, Visual art and languages, Arts manifestoes, Abstraction and the non-representational, Arts and affects)

References:

Duchamp, Warhol, Beuys,

Francis Bacon, Antony Gormley, K G Subramanyan

Vivan Sundaram, Bhupen Khakkar, Nalini Malani

Deliverables:

  • Blind Drawings and Partial Blind Drawings – 15
  • Drawing of architectural sites.
  • Manifesto for the Arts of Our Times – group exercise

Module 2: 

Politics and Poetics of New materialism. 

Aesthetics and politics, Sculpture and form, The Found object as image, Materiality of Text, Body as site and sight,  Understanding Installation art -1

References:

  • Vija Celmins, Kiki Smith, Louise Bourgeois, Jenny Holzer,
  • Theaster Gates, Al Enatsui, Ai Wei Wei
  • Anita Dube, Sheela Gowda, Rumanna Hussain
  • Subodh Gupta, Atul Dodiya, Nilima Sheikh,

Deliverables:

  • Series of 5 sculptures from collected trash
  • Text as sculpture from Found material.
  • Mid Term essay – Art and Politics – 1500 words

Module 3:

Ideas and Concepts on Placemaking.

Understanding Installation art -2, Conceptualizing Spaces, Fictional propositions in placemaking. Curating and constituting a pop-up exhibition,

References:

Judy Chicago, Yoko Ono,

James Turrell, Robert Smithson, Christo and Jeanne Claude,

Thomas Hirschhorn, Ernesto Neto, Olafur Eliason,

Anish Kapoor, Nek Chand, Nikhil Chopra

Chemical Basis of Life [BIO-2300/ BIO-6300] [BIO-2300/ BIO-6300-1]

Faculty
Sandeep Ameta [sandeep.ameta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Fundamental chemical principles govern the highly regulated biological systems and their environment. Therefore, to appreciate the complexity of biological systems, we must also examine them from a chemical perspective. This course aims to introduce basic chemistry concepts necessary for studying biological systems. The course is designed to provide students with a framework for understanding the fundamentals of biomolecules, their interactions, and the underlying mechanisms. The course will cover basic chemical concepts (chemical bonds, structures, cellular thermodynamics, cellular reactions, equilibrium, and kinetics) using biological examples to develop a chemical basis for analyzing biological systems. Furthermore, in parallel, we will teach the fundamental building blocks of life (nucleic acids, lipids, carbohydrates, proteins) and the concepts of metabolism.

Learning Outcomes

Within this broad theme, by the end of the course, we aim for students to become familiar with basic chemical concepts relevant to biology. At the end of the course, students should be able to:

1. What are biological molecules made of?

2. Describe the chemical composition and structure of key biological molecules.

3. Analyze how the structure of biomolecules relates to their specific functions within living systems.

4. How do these biomolecules interact, assemble, and get processed in biological systems?

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course content will be prepared from multiple sources and will be sufficient for understanding. However, the following books can be referred to for additional knowledge:

  • Introductory Chemistry, A Foundation by Zumdahl & Decoste
  • Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry by David L. Nelson, Michael M. Cox. Publisher: W. H. Freeman (6th Ed).
  • Biochemistry Voet, D., Voet, J.G. Publisher: Wiley; 3rd Ed.

In addition, lectures, reading material and some notes will also be circulated.

Overview

This course introduces the fundamental concepts of chemistry that are essential for understanding how molecules drive and regulate biological processes. Students will start with the basics of atomic structure and chemical bonding, then explore the key classes of biological molecules, starting with water, followed by macromoleucles - nucleic acids, lipids, carbohydrates, and proteins. The course emphasizes how these molecules collectively define structure and function of a unit of life (cell). Core principles of energy in living systems (thermodynamics), chemical reactions, equilibrium, pH, and reaction kinetics will be discussed in the context of biological examples, helping students connect chemistry to life science.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will develop a foundational understanding of biomolecules, their chemical properties, interactions, and the role of chemistry in governing biological processes.

Students should be able to:

1. Describe the chemical composition and structure of key biological molecules.

2. Explain how biomolecules store, transmit, and process biological information.

3. Analyze how the structure of biomolecules relates to their specific functions within living systems.

Concepts in Organic Chemistry [CHM-1101] [CHM-1101-1]

Faculty
Deepak Asthana [deepak.asthana@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

About the course:

Chemistry teaches the art of creating new molecules, new materials, compounds that never existed. A small modification in chemical structure results in entirely new sets of properties. Bonded atoms form molecule and molecules undergos chemical reaction to form a new molecule. This course offers an introductory level understanding of various processes that take place in organic chemical reactions. Course structure is designed to refresh your chemistry knowledge from your school and to prepare you for your journey towards becoming an expert. It will provide better understanding of all the key concepts that you may require to solve the puzzles of chemical bonding and reactions.

The world of chemistry, and especially organic chemistry, might look scary. However, if fundamental rules and some basic principles are understood, most things start becoming obvious events. Concept of electronegativity, resonance, conjugation, hybridisation, steric effects, and aromaticity are key in explaining the number of complexities found organic chemistry.  

The first question that one might ask is why atoms form molecules, and once they have come close to each other, what keeps them intact. What are the factors that decide the path and the fate of any chemical reaction? The purpose of this course is to make sure that your journey into the realm of organic reactions and all those rule exceptions is more enjoyable!

Course Contents/Topics:

Stereochemistry of simple straight chain and cyclic alkanes

  • Conformational nomenclature: eclipsed, staggered, gauche, syn and anti; dihedral angle, torsion angle
  • Energy barrier of rotation and relative stability of conformers
  • Conformational analysis of ethane, propane, n-butane, and 2-methylbutane; cyclohexane and cyclopentane
  • Geometrical isomerism: cis–trans, syn-anti, and E/Z notations with C.I.P rules.

Organic Acids and Bases

  • Hybridisation, Inductive effects, Hyperconjugation, Mesomeric effects, and Steric effect and their effect on acidity/basicity
  • Concept of pKa and pKaH, effect of structure, substituent and solvent on acidity and basicity; proton sponge

Addition and Elimination Reactions

  • Elimination reactions: formation of alkenes and alkynes; mechanisms, reactivity, regioselectivity and stereoselectivity
  • Addition Reactions of alkenes and alkynes: Mechanism, reactivity, regioselectivity (Markownikoff and anti-Markownikoff addition) and stereoselectivity

Interconversion of functional groups

  • Oxidation of alcohols to form aldehyde/ketone & carboxylic acids
  • Oxidation and reduction of aldehydes to form carboxylic acids & alcohols
  • Conversion of carboxylic acid into acid chlorides, esters, amides and reduction to alcohols

 

Learning Outcomes
  • Students will develop understanding about the factors that make an organic compound acidic or basic. Strength of organic acids and bases will be studied in details.    
  • Electronic and steric factors basically control the behavior of a molecule in any chemical reaction. A clear understanding of electronic and steric effects enables us to predict several chemical properties. 
  • Will study the fact that why some system exists in a particular conformation. What makes a specific geometric arrangement more stable than the other. 
  • Addition and elimination reactions will be studied.
  • Will learn the various oxidation & reduction reactions that lead to inter-conversion of various functional groups such as alcohol to aldehyde or acid etc.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)
  • Organic Chemistry by Jonathan Clayden, Nick Greeves and Stuart Warren.
  • Advanced Organic Chemistry: Part A: Structure and Mechanisms by Francis A. Carey and Richard J. Sundberg.
  • Interested in studying more about atomic orbitals: Principles of Atomic Orbitals by N. N. Greenwood
  • Organic Chemistry by Morrison & Boyd.
  • Organic Chemistry, Vol-1, by I L Finar.

courseTitle: Figure Drawing as Remembering and Reimagining
description:
Figure Drawing as Remembering and Reimagining [VA-2016] [VA-2016-1]

Faculty
Anni Kumari [anni.kumari@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Level of the Course: 2000, 3000

Prerequisites: None

Course Description: In Western academic art education, figurative drawing was until recently considered the foundation, the essential prerequisite for mastering disciplines of painting, sculpture, frescos and murals. Although it is no longer a requisite skill for contemporary artists, a high proportion would still agree that irrespective of whatever material they might choose to work in, they ‘think’ in terms of drawings. Drawing is more than simply a skill in the sense that it offers a path to self-discovery, revealing a cast of minds, an imaginative capacity and a mode of perception.

This course encourages students to re-think and re-imagine the human body beyond a representational image, as an entity with constant trans-mutative possibilities in terms of form, functionality and aesthetics. Through a combination of practice and discourse, the course encourages explorations beyond human anatomy by focusing on the varied manifestations and meanings ascribed to the human figure, vis-à-vis the body, in the context of visual art and beyond.

Students will be introduced to contemporary artistic practices and deliberations on artistic visions, experiences, and wisdom that push the boundaries of accepted notions of ‘high’ art and critique hierarchies of attitude. Tracing the history of figure drawing as a genre that goes back to Classical antiquity to the Italian Renaissance, extending into the 18th century French academia and the 19th century Victorian Era, students will get a broad overview of how the established notion of accuracy and idealized beauty continues to be challenged and reinvented as artists take on a variety of approaches to drawing the human figure. 

The course looks at how the idealized notion of the body is challenged and replaced with bodies that are bruised, grotesque, and out of proportion, with visible stretch marks, skin hair, wrinkles, and pigmentation. How has the conscious shift towards drawing from memory and imagination as opposed to drawing from a live model or from photographic references allowed artists to create works that are often loaded with political commentary and emotive power?

In this course, students have the flexibility to work with various media and materials, enabling them to connect to their own context, concerns, and interests with a sense of immediacy by using the human figure as a trigger.

The frameworks we will be working through the course include:

  • Understanding the various kinds of representations of the human figure from different social and cultural contexts. Locating discursive modes of representation.
  • Probing ideas of beauty, identity, sexuality and gender, through human form.
  • Understanding space-time and memory in the context of the human body and its representation.
  • Exploring the human figure in contemporary drawings under the broad categorizations of the body, self, personal lives, social reality and fictions.
  • Reflecting on processes of overlapping, erasures and incision as acts layered with emotive and intuitive sensibilities.
  • Developing an individual methodology /strategy to figurative drawing.
  • The course will unfold over three modules; each spread over four weeks respectively, and will include both theoretical readings and practical assignments.  

Module 1

The human figure in visual arts:

A historical perspective, a cultural and social perspective.

Representing human body- a repository of concepts.

Overview- Western naturalism through Renaissance, Human form in Egyptian Drawing, Body in Indian miniature painting and folk art.

Basic observational drawings.

Portraiture and history painting.

The renaissance body- Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael, Durer

Representing flesh and desire- Boucher, Ingre, Rubens,

Modernity and Body - Humor, satire and politics of expressing the Body in painting, sculpture. (Manet, van Gogh, Rodin, Daumier,  

Drawing from archival works,

Conceptualising a space for body – Giorgio de Chirico, Piranesi, Escher,  

Module 2:

Body as a biological entity

Anatomy studies, life drawing, studies in biology and medical discourse.

Triumph of realism in representations of body,

Drawing the body- precision in Biology

Structures of form- synthesizing biological and organic material.

Module 3:

The human figure in Contemporary Art

Body as a Phenomenological tool-

Expressionism, Surrealism, Body and Conceptual Art, Feminism, Neo- expressionism, the Popular

Depictions through drawing and photography, - Ana Mandietta, Janine Antoni,

Body as performative tool. - Marina Abramovic, Yoko Ono, Rumana Hussain

Depictions through journaling, everyday bodies – Louise Bourgeois, Chittoprasad, Arpita Singh,

Body as wear and tear, absences, fragmented, diseased – Kiki Smith, Eva Hesse, Anthony Gormley

Body as text and body as material- Jenny Holzer, Nalini Malani, Mithu Sen, Juul Krajer

Body as Monuments of social expressions. – Doh Ho Suh, Kara Walker, William Kentridge

 

 

 

 

Learning Outcomes
  • The course is expected to make students aware of the significant position of the human figure in art, especially in the context of drawing and conceptualization.
  • Some of the key concepts on culture and representation will be explored-  realism, mimesis, illustration, and the role of fantasy and memory in the process of artistic production.
  • Students will learn about fundamental techniques of representation through observation and imaging.
  • Students will learn processes, media, and materials employed by artists, both historically and in contemporary times.

Regime type and War [IR-3011/ POL-3051] [IR-3011/ POL-3051-1]

Faculty
Bann Seng Tan [bannseng.tan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What exactly does regime type (democracy/autocracy) has to do with interstate warfare? It turns out there is a body of literature, known as the Democratic Peace (hereafter DP), that focus on such issues. The DP or the absence of wars between democracies, is one of the more significant findings to have emerged within International Relations scholarship in recent decades. It has consequently attracted significant and critical attention of a large body of scholars and policy-makers alike. In this course we will examine the history of the idea, its main empirical claims, the explanations for it, the auxiliary claims and the criticisms of the research. While the methodological slant will be on quantitative research, we will also examine issues of research design as well as historical case studies as appropriate.

Issue areas that will be covered includes: the Kantian origins of the DP, the dyadic level of analysis, the normative, institutional, and informational explanations of the DP (three sessions), the capitalist peace, the DP as a research program, auxiliary relationships of DP (democracy in war, in covert action and in human rights), criticisms of the DP as well as the challenge of democratization. 

Learning Outcomes

1) Since the course is focused on one topic, the DP, students will acquire substantive knowledge about the major issues in DP research. They should be able to highlight the major works and the arguments made therein. 2) Students should be able to provide a reasoned critique of the major works. This is part of the process of learning to reason in a social scientific manner. 3) Students should gain an exposure to some of the quantitative literature on international conflict. 4) Finally, students should be able to judge the validity of the democratic peace and crucially, justify their judgment.

Faculty
Arpita Das [arpita.das@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In this course, you will develop and rehearse the habits that are essential to the development of a critical mind: reading, writing, speaking, listening and, of course, thinking. In effect, you will learn to ask the 'why' and 'how' questions alongside the 'who' and 'what' queries you have been posing through your school education. You will engage with a variety of source materials and understand how to ask questions that extend and enrich your understanding of situations, texts, institutions and people. You will explore the distinctness of academic research and writing, and participate in an active knowledge community constituted by your peers. By the close of the course, you will have a clearer understanding of what it means to be a scholar in an academic setting, and a keener sense of your own processes of learning, thinking and writing. 

The theme of this ICT course this Monsoon Semester will be Reading the Other. In other words, you will learn to think and write critically with me in the classroom via discussing and reading together about the figure of the 'other'. Examples of the narrative non-fiction works you will reading include James Baldwin, Meena Kandasamy, Nanjala Nyabola, Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar and Sharmila Rege.

The aim is two-fold. To enable you to acquire the skills described at the start of this course overview, with an added understanding of what it means to read works by or about individuals or communities who are outside your own comfort zone. We will also be engaging with popular culture pieces, short films, reels and artworks which will further inform your understanding of the 'other'.

Reading:

1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.

2. Making patterns and connections across texts

3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts

4. Understanding textual context, genre and source material and documenting these via strategic note-making.

Writing

2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing

3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing

4. Using explanatory, narrative and justificatory writing

Thinking

4. Engaging meaningfully with multiple perspectives

4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Overview

The Introduction to Critical Thinking offers different pathways to develop your habits of thinking and communication through reading, writing and research. It considers these as essential habits that can be strengthened through repetition. The aim of this course is to expose you to source materials and themes that will provoke you to think deeply, ask questions that extend and enrich your understanding, and use writing as a means of making sense of the world. By the close of the course, you will have a keener sense of your own challenges and strengths as a writer and student, and a more robust sense of what it means to belong to a knowledge community constituted by your peers.

Learning Outcomes

Reading:

  • 1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.
  • 2. Making patterns and connections across texts
  • 3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts
  • 4. Understanding textual context, genre and source material

Writing:

  • 1. Developing the craft of outlining, revising, editing
  • 2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing
  • 3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing
  • 4.  Producing different kinds of writing (narrative, argumentative etc)

Research

  • 1. Narrowing down a curiosity into a question
  • 2. Identifying credible sources for study
  • 3. Reflecting on  method and organising the research process
  • 4. Handling multiple sources or an archive

Communication

  • 1. Aiming for confidence, clarity, coherence in speaking
  • 2. Practising and harnessing audience engagement 
  • 3. Developing active and respectful listening to others 
  • 4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Introduction to Critical Thinking [CT-0001] [CT-0001-7]

Faculty
Sidharth Singh [sidharth.singh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

We will develop across the length of a semester, a discursive answer to a simple yet fundamental question: what is poetry? The objective of this class is not to simply interpret individual poems (though this will form part of our activity). Instead we will try and determine the ways by which a satisfactory answer to such a question may be figured out at all. The task is one of figuring out a successful definition, and in this process we will devise methods to reliably identify and study the fundamental constituents of any poem. Two such constituents, for example, are language and mind, and so we will explore ideas in the philosophy of these objects to develop an acceptable answer to our question.

As we progress you will learn and practice via exercises, some elementary aspects of logic (such as the meaning of an argument, paraphrasing to clarify and juudge and argument, and the way to describe abstract entities), and decide for yourself whether they are anywhere useful for questions about the nature and philosophy of art. Other fixed aspects of the course include discussions on the philosophy of scientific methods, the nature of human creativity and language; group discussions on the interpretation of poems; and, given this is a writing course, the composition of several essays in response to questions about ideas discussed in class.

You will find that typical academic activities will have to follow naturally for you to develop an answer. These activities include navigating citations and bibliographies; organizing your thoughts by writing essays; and relying on peers for aid and discussion. In large part, however, the trajectory of the course will be decided by collective student effort and the progress made in developing an answer to the stated question. To this end, the syllabus remains flexible and secondary, and is only one means for our progress in discovery and learning. 

Given the nature of the endeavour and the direction this class typically takes, students interested in humanistic disciplines are encouraged to join but so are those who are interested in areas typically allied to the cognitive sciences (biology, computer science, linguistics, mathematics, philosophy, psychology). In any case there are no pre-requisites at all, so regardless of disciplinary leanings, anyone may join and productively engage. 

Learning Outcomes

Reading

1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.

2. Making patterns and connections across texts

3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts

4. Understanding context, genre and source material

Writing 

1. Developing the craft of outlining, revising, editing

2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing

3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing

4. Producing different kinds of writing (narrative, argumentative etc)

Research

1. Narrowing down a curiosity into a question

2. Identifying credible sources for study

3. Reflecting on  method and organising the research process

4. Handling multiple sources or an archive

Communication

1. Aiming for confidence, clarity, coherence in speaking

2. Practising and harnessing audience engagement 

3. Developing active and respectful listening to others 

4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Syllabus

All texts will be provided to students either as print outs in class or as PDFs before class (uploaded to a shared drive). Modules on introductory logic will not be studied via texts. As mentioned above, this is a fairly flexible syllabus with guaranteed additions. But in one way or another, we will be touching on ideas from these following texts.

Essays and Book excerpts:

David Hume- ‘Of the Standard of Taste’

Immanuel Kant – ‘What is Enlightenment’

John Dewey—Art as Experience

Karl Marx – ‘Theses on Feuerbach’/ The German Ideology

Noam Chomsky—What Kind of Creatures Are We?

Samuel Taylor Coleridge—Notes on Shakespeare/Biographia Literaria

Viktor Shklovsky—'Art as Device’

Wilhelm Von Humboldt—Limits of State Action

William Wordsworth- ‘Preface to the Lyrical Ballads’

It will be necessary for students to read some of this material before class. However, in some cases discussions in class should suffice if one cannot read the texts.

Poems:

Mostly selections from Lyrical Ballads, and other English poetry. Since the endeavour of this class is a general explanation of poetry, students are free to suggest poems for everyone to read.

Novel:

Mary Shelley—Frankenstein. Students will have to review this novel for their mid term assignment.
