Introduction to Critical Thinking [CT-0001] [CT-0001-9]

Faculty
Aditya Vikram Shrivastava [aditya.shrivastava@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course has everything to do with 'haunting' - the suspicion and fantasy evoked by strange things. You can expect bereaved mothers, searching daughters, uncanny dreams, lost manifestos, queer photographs, and even the spirits of ancient animals to flit in and out of our classroom. Alongside the ghostly presence, we shall explore repression, absence, and the unspoken in fiction, cinema, essays, and research papers - things that continue to haunt our imagination of the world. This includes readings from literature, philosophy, cultural studies, sociology, and more. While the more seminal essays include Freud’s ‘The Uncanny’ and Mark Fisher’s ‘Depression, Hauntology, and Lost Futures’, we also pick apart everything from Toni Morrison to Shakespeare from the literary, and ‘Haider’ to ‘Tumbbad’ from the cinematic world.

The aim of this course is to expose you to archives and ideas that will provoke you to ask questions that widen and complicate your understanding, and use reading and writing as a means of making sense of the world in critical ways. We will learn how to open up a question in symposia, write in the essay form, trace the archives, read comparatively, and more - a mix of literary and historical orientations. 

You are going to gain a keener sense of your own challenges and strengths as a writer and student, and a more robust sense of what it means to belong to a knowledge community constituted by your peers. 

Learning Outcomes

Reading

1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.

2. Making patterns and connections across texts

3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts

4. Understanding context, genre and source material

Writing 

1. Developing the craft of outlining, revising, editing

2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing

3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing

4. Producing different kinds of writing (narrative, argumentative etc)

Research

1. Narrowing down a curiosity into a question

2. Identifying credible sources for study

3. Reflecting on  method and organising the research process

4. Handling multiple sources or an archive

Communication

1. Aiming for confidence, clarity, coherence in speaking

2. Practising and harnessing audience engagement 

3. Developing active and respectful listening to others 

4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

You do not need to have any specific kind of training in order to do an ICT course. Nor is any ICT course geared towards preparing you specifically for a career in a particular subject or field. Rather, you can expect it to guide you in transition out of how you approached academic work in school to how you might approach it in a university setting, and to sharpen your understanding of what it means to be critical, questioning and deliberate in your approach to the world. 

 

ICT is writing-intensive. You can expect to work on longer assignments (the Mid-Term and the End-Term essays) over multiple rounds of feedback, as well as shorter assignments through the semester. You will also need to rehearse regular habits of reading (of academic texts and wider materials) and responding (to prompts, or given materials). Finally, as the ICT is a small cohort-oriented course, you can expect it to have a strong participation and interaction component, and can expect to work on projects both individually and in collaboration with your coursemates.

Introduction to Critical Thinking [CT-0001] [CT-0001-11]

Faculty
Ishika Saxena [ishika.saxena@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The crux of undergraduate education is to question and unlearn what you know; to take what is obvious, shed it of existing meaning, and add new layers of meaning. 

This iteration of the ICT will build around the theme of 'Justice: Obedience and Disobedience'. We will explore the theme through a myriad of lenses and thematic questions including what is injustice, what are the gaps between law and justice, and what is the work of imagination in thinking about justice. 

The class will offer you different pathways to develop your habits of thinking and communication through reading, writing and research. This ICT will employ material from multiple disciplines to enhance academic reading skills, and will work on writing and research through drafting and feedback. This course aims to teach thinking in two specific ways: to understand assumptions/first principles, and to creatively imagine futures. 

Learning Outcomes

Reading:

1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.

2. Making patterns and connections across texts

3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts

4. Understanding textual context, genre and source material and documenting these via strategic note-making.

Writing 

1. Developing the craft of outlining, revising, editing

2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing

3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing

4. Using explanatory, narrative and justificatory writing

Thinking

1. Practising converting thoughts into words

2. Narrowing down a curiosity or thought into a question

3. Constructing and developing a reasoned argument

4. Engaging meaningfully with multiple perspectives

Speaking-Listening

1. Aiming for confidence, clarity, coherence 

2. Practising and harnessing audience engagement 

3. Developing active and respectful listening to others 

4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Readings for the course will span classical and contemporary understandings and include novels and films. We will explore the theme through multiple disciplines and approaches - sociological, economic, literary, historical, and philosophical. Putting these lenses together we will try to understand the concept of justice and imagine what it could possibly hold. 

No prerequisites are required. This is a reading intensive course. You will be expected to read every week.

Faculty
Pranavesh Subramanian [pranavesh.subramanian@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The Introduction to Critical Thinking offers you different pathways to develop your habits of thinking and communication through reading, writing and research. It considers these as essential habits that can be strengthened through repetition. The aim of this course is to expose you to source materials and themes that aim to examine popular culture in a manner that will provoke you to think deeply, ask questions that extend and enrich your understanding, and use writing as a means of making sense of the world.

This specific course aims to achieve these outcomes through the theme Deconstructing Popular Culture. During the course, you will begin by questioning what it means to study the amorphous term 'culture'. You will be introduced to various material societal concerns, including but not limited to gender, caste, class, ideology, hegemony, globalisation. Over the course, you will examine your encounters with the above concerns through your engagement with popular culture. While the course is currently being formulated, in the past, the following questions have been explored: What does Charli XCX’s album Brat tell us about the economy? How can a game of football be viewed as an ideological exercise? What does a walk around Hauz Khas Village tell us about gentrification? How does Bollywood help create a public imagination of the nation? Through these questions and several others, you will not just establish a critical approach to popular culture, but sharpen your skills of reading, writing and research. 

 

Learning Outcomes

Reading

1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.

2. Making patterns and connections across texts

3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts

4. Understanding context, genre and source material

Writing 

1. Developing the craft of outlining, revising, editing

2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing

3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing

4. Producing different kinds of writing (narrative, argumentative etc)

Research

1. Narrowing down a curiosity into a question

2. Identifying credible sources for study

3. Reflecting on  method and organising the research process

4. Handling multiple sources or an archive

Communication

1. Aiming for confidence, clarity, coherence in speaking

2. Practising and harnessing audience engagement 

3. Developing active and respectful listening to others 

4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

You do not need to have any specific kind of training in order to do an ICT course. Nor is any ICT course geared towards preparing you specifically for a career in a particular subject or field. Rather, you can expect it to guide you in transition out of how you approached academic work in school to how you might approach it in a university setting, and to sharpen your understanding of what it means to be critical, questioning and deliberate in your approach to the world. 

 

ICT is writing-intensive. You can expect to work on longer assignments (the Mid-Term and the End-Term essays) over multiple rounds of feedback, as well as shorter assignments through the semester. You will also need to rehearse regular habits of reading (of academic texts and wider materials) and responding (to prompts, or given materials). Finally, as the ICT is a small cohort-oriented course, you can expect it to have a strong participation and interaction component, and can expect to work on projects both individually and in collaboration with your coursemates.

The Introduction to Critical Thinking offers you different pathways to develop your habits of thinking and communication through reading, writing and research. It considers these as essential habits that can be strengthened through repetition. The aim of this course is to expose you to source materials and themes that will provoke you to think deeply, ask questions that extend and enrich your understanding, and use writing as a means of making sense of the world. By the close of the course, you will have a keener sense of your own challenges and strengths as a writer and student, and a more robust sense of what it means to belong to a knowledge community constituted by your peers.

Learning Outcomes

Reading

1. Breaking down texts into identifiable parts.

2. Making patterns and connections across texts

3. Building reading stamina and the ability to select texts

4. Understanding context, genre and source material
 

Writing 

1. Developing the craft of outlining, revising, editing

2. Applying form, voice, style, tone to affect writing

3. Developing logical, coherent, structured writing

4. Producing different kinds of writing (narrative, argumentative etc)
 

Research

1. Narrowing down a curiosity into a question

2. Identifying credible sources for study

3. Reflecting on  method and organising the research process

4. Handling multiple sources or an archive
 

Communication

1. Aiming for confidence, clarity, coherence in speaking

2. Practising and harnessing audience engagement 

3. Developing active and respectful listening to others 

4. Engaging meaningfully with ongoing discussions

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

You do not need to have any specific kind of training in order to do an ICT course. Nor is any ICT course geared towards preparing you specifically for a career in a particular subject or field. Rather, you can expect it to guide you in transition out of how you approached academic work in school to how you might approach it in a university setting, and to sharpen your understanding of what it means to be critical, questioning and deliberate in your approach to the world. 

 

ICT is writing-intensive. You can expect to work on longer assignments (the Mid-Term and the End-Term essays) over multiple rounds of feedback, as well as shorter assignments through the semester. You will also need to rehearse regular habits of reading (of academic texts and wider materials) and responding (to prompts, or given materials). These will be specified on a weekly basis via Google Classroom. 

 

Finally, as the ICT is a small cohort-oriented course, you can expect it to have a strong participation and interaction component, and can expect to work on projects both individually and in collaboration with your coursemates.

We will then take these tools and apply them to study real-life problems. Graduate Seminar in Literary Theory [ENG-5001] [ENG-5001-1]

Faculty
Huzaifa Omair Siddiqi [huzaifa.siddiqi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Literary theory has become to the study of literature what mathematics is to the study of nature:
indispensable. However, almost none of the theorists that we will read in this course considered
themselves literary theorists. They were phenomenologists, existentialists, linguists, psychoanalysts,
Marxists, structuralists, deconstructionists, feminists, queer theorists, Critical Race and anti-caste
theorists. This diversity of sources for theory means that the study of literature requires a critical
humanist lens which will encompass almost all the human and social sciences. In this course we will
read texts borrowed from multiple disciplines to better understand the object that is the text.

Learning Outcomes

1) To understand the importance of literary theory for literary studies.
2) To introduce students to various theoretical perspectives and make them evaluate their value for
literary study.
3) To develop competence in reading and writing theoretical works.

Econometrics 2 [ECO-6402] [ECO-6402-1]

Faculty
Kanika Mahajan [kanika.mahajan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This is a graduate-level econometrics course focusing on causal identification. The course begins with a discussion of the Rubin-Causal model, and randomized controlled trials – the pinnacle for causal econometric designs. Subsequently, it moves to selection on observable designs, and the use of fixed effects to control for select unobservables. The second half of the course focuses on three key empirical techniques for causal identification: namely differences-in-difference, regression discontinuity designs, matching and instrumental variables. The course will focus mainly on the intuition behind causal identification and applying them in practice. A critical component of the course would be reading empirical academic papers. This would provide students with some context in the application of the empirical methods introduced in class. 

 

Prerequisites: Introductory Econometrics (MA level)

Greene, W.H., Econometric Analysis, (7th edition), Pearson, 2012 (Optional)

Learning Outcomes

This course will focus on both theoretical knowledge as well as implementation of theory through software applications like STATA and real datasets.

Principles of Science [FC-0801] [FC-0801-1]

Faculty
Abhishek Mazumder [abhishek.mazumder@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Biology is often introduced as a tidy catalogue of organisms, organs, and processes—a view of life described from the outside in. This course argues that to truly understand biology, one must first understand its molecules, and that most biological phenomena emerge from the choreography of molecules colliding, binding, folding, and breaking apart. As the course unfolds, students will discover that nearly every major breakthrough and intervention in modern biology—diagnosing disease, designing vaccines, mapping cells, editing genomes—ultimately depends on our ability to read the language of molecules.

Along the way, students will also encounter the stories behind these discoveries. Much of what we now take as settled fact about the molecules of life was once little more than a bold hunch, a smudge on a glass slide that nobody believed, a line in a 1,600-year-old manuscript left unread for centuries, or a rejected grant proposal yellowing in a desk drawer. These are stories of people learning, molecule by molecule, to read life itself. The journey unfolds across three arcs — Seeing, Controlling, and Rewriting — tracing how humans first learned to make the invisible visible, then turned that vision into intervention, and is now beginning to rewrite life itself.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students will appreciate why molecules are the language in which biology is written and will leave with a curiosity-driven understanding of how living systems are seen, controlled, and rewritten at the molecular level. They will engage with the stories — scientific, historical, and human — behind major discoveries in modern biology, and develop the critical-thinking habits needed to weigh evidence, ask better questions, and recognise both the promise and the responsibility that come with this field.

Principles of Science [FC-0801] [FC-0801-3]

Faculty
Sanjay Jain [sanjay.jain@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Title: Playing Scientist: From Laws to Life

Is the universe simply obeying rules, or is it making them up as it goes along? All matter and radiation that we observe in the universe seems to obey certain fundamental physical laws. Nevertheless, on the surface of the Earth the same matter has organized itself into complex structures and living things that enjoy the freedom of creating new kinds of structure and life. In fact the living world is best described by new kinds of emergent principles that are quite different from fundamental physical laws.

How can one reconcile the creative abilities of the living world with physical laws that the matter it is made of obeys? This leads to one of the oldest questions human beings have ever asked: how did life originate? It is a mystery which lies at the intersection of physics, chemistry, biology, and the earth sciences.

The course is organized as a three-act intellectual journey, moving from the simplicity of physical laws, to the complexity of the living world, to the twilight zone in between where life originates.

Act I.  Laws, symmetry and hidden rules: The universe is full of regularities we call laws of nature. We open by asking what a law actually is, how we determine what qualifies as a law, and how scientists go about discovering these hidden patterns in the first place. We explore how simple, deterministic rules can give rise to structural order and symmetry, and how they can just as easily give rise to chaos and randomness.

Act II.  The wonder that is life: Nature is also an astonishing tapestry of diversity and complexity. Here, we shift our gaze to the biological world: how a tiny planet in a vast universe plays host to an incredible, sprawling variety of life. We explore the scale of this diversity, from the intricate machinery of a single cell to the entire biosphere. We examine how a different kind of principle -- Darwinian evolution -- acts as a unifying idea for making sense of this diversity.

Act III.  The transition – the origin of life: Somewhere between order and chaos, life finds room to exist. What mechanisms can steer inanimate matter to produce the organized complexity that is life? This is where the course turns to the origin of life problem and the question of whether we are alone in the universe.

Throughout this course wherever possible, ideas will be taught through play and examples (games, hands-on demonstrations, and simulations) before moving to formal definitions.

Topics Covered

I. Laws

  • The nature of scientific laws: What is a scientific law and how do scientists uncover patterns hidden within nature?
  • Update rules and cellular automata: Understanding physical laws of classical systems, like Newton's laws of motion, as local update rules. Cellular automata as simple dynamical systems in space and time.
  • Symmetry and order: Periodic tilings (geometric patterns that repeat).  Aperiodicity and Penrose tilings (patterns that never repeat). Connection to irrational numbers, quasicrystals, and the Fibonacci sequence.
  • The edge of order: A brief look into how deterministic rules can lead toward asymmetry, disorder, and chaotic dynamics.

II. Life

  • The rarity of life: Reflecting on the uniqueness of Earth as a planet with life nestled within a vast, inanimate universe.
  • The staggering diversity: The variety of physical, chemical, and biological adaptations across ecosystems in the biosphere. The diversity of flora and fauna.
  • The complexity of life: Exploring the extraordinary complexity embedded within a single living cell compared to traditional physical systems. Genes and proteins. Multicellular organisms.
  • Order within diversity: Unity of life on Earth at the molecular level. Evidence for common descent; evolution. Growth of populations. The idea of evolution by natural selection.

III. The Transition

  • The prebiotic Earth: Conditions on the early planet and what made it a candidate cradle for life.
  • Atoms to networks: Molecules, chemical reactions, replicators and autocatalytic sets, the foundational chemistry that life had to be built from.
  • Puzzles and hypotheses: How might complexity arise? Leading scientific frameworks and experiments simulating prebiotic processes. 
  • The cosmic horizon: Estimating the probability of life arising, Fermi's paradox, and the search for life beyond Earth.
Learning Outcomes
  • Students will acquire knowledge of aspects of physics, chemistry, biology, and mathematics, viewing them not as separate subjects, but as part of mankind’s integrated attempt to understand nature.
  • They will develop an intuitive understanding of how scientific laws are discovered through induction, evidence, observation and revision, rather than received as finished facts.
  • Students will appreciate the complexity and diversity of life forms as well as their underlying unity at the molecular level.
  • They will appreciate why the origin of life remains one of science's most exciting puzzles.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Pre-requisites

Mathematics up to Class X in school. Mathematics will run throughout the course. Familiar mathematical concepts will be reviewed and new concepts will be taught within the course.

References and Materials

A short list of gateway readings before the course begins, simply to spark curiosity and give students a feel for what lies ahead:

  • Sagan, Carl. Cosmos. New York. Random House, 1985. Chapter 1 The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean; Chapter 2 One Voice in the Cosmic Fugue.
  • Gleick, James. Chaos: Making a New Science. New York: Viking Penguin, 1987. Prologue; Chapter 1 The Butterfly Effect.
  • Wilson, Edward O. The Future of Life. New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 2002. Chapter 1 To the Ends of the Earth.
  • Kauffman, Stuart. At Home in the Universe. New York: Oxford University Press, 1995. Chapter 2 The Origins of Life. 

Companion readings and web resources tied to specific classes, along with optional rabbit holes (more advanced readings) for students who wish to go further on their own, will be provided as the course progresses, alongside selected short fiction relevant to the topics covered.

Overview

This course concerns the nature of Time and the important role it plays in our lives. It introduces the concept of age and time in the context of Physics and Astronomy- how Time is measured, its connection with Space, and why it moves in one direction, as well as the way Time is perceived in biological systems. Through this course we would be like to bring to the students our current understanding about the scale and age of the Universe, and how this knowledge has evolved; how biological systems including human body maintain temporal patterns; the impact of climate change and ecological damage on biological time and the evolution of survival strategies that require the understanding of past, present and future.

The course will start with a general introduction and historical perspective to the concept of time in our day-to-day life and in physics and in biology. We shall discuss the history of measurement of time and invention of clocks. Without involving much mathematics, the course will help students derive relationship between speed of light and time, space-time continuum, age of the universe, stars, earth etc. We would then follow concept of time in biology in the context of birth-growth-ageing-death. Seasonal variations in morphological and life-history traits as measurement of time, mechanism of timekeeping - biological clocks, circadian rhythms. We will also discuss the evolutionary time and the important concepts pertaining to our understanding of this such as generation time of different living beings. The course ends with discussions on human cognition and the concept of time: conceptual understanding of past, present and future.

The course is taught through lectures, discussions, flip-the-classroom mode (students making presentations on various related topics), reading books/watching movies and writing assignments.

Learning Outcomes

1.     Our current understanding about the scale and age of the Universe, and how this knowledge has evolved.

2.     Understanding how Astronomers and Geologists measure time and age, and how reliable these measurements are.

3.     Appreciation for different scales of time in biology: from timescales of biomolecules to the evolutionary timescale.

4.    Understanding of interdependencies in biological timescales.

Principles of Science [FC-0801] [FC-0801-5]

Faculty
Sujan Kumar Sengupta [sujan.sengupta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Planet Earth: Its status in the Universe, potential threats and the ultimate fate.

    A formidable combination of astronomical and geological conditions has made it possible for the Earth to harbour life on it. But there are many catastrophic events in the space that may destroy life, even the planet which in the vast cosmic arena appears as a mote of dust suspended in a beam of sunlight and floating in the vast emptiness of space.  Search for extra-terrestrial life has taught us an important lesson that our world, mother Earth is an extremely rare place in our galaxy and possibly the only planet that has the required astrophysical and geological conditions for harbouring life. Even if there are other planets similar to the Earth wherein life may exist, the number of such planets in the vast galaxy is extremely small and so we are alone at least within a radius of few hundreds of light years. 

    This course will unfold the fact that our home, the planet Earth is so special yet so vulnerable, so crowded yet so lonely, so common yet so unique, so insignificant yet so great! 

        The following topics will be covered in the whole course: 

    (i)   Our address in the Universe, the boundary of the solar system, the solar neighbourhood and the hierarchy in the structure of the                              visible Universe. A brief history of the solar planets.  

   (ii)   Birth of the Sun and its planets including the Earth. We are made of star dust – the origin of heavy elements including carbon- the building block of organic molecules. 

  (iii)   The Solar family – Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto and the other dwarf planets. Moons of the solar planets. 

  (iv)   Planet Earth – its evolving geology and the atmosphere. The Oceans- where has so much water come from? The ecological system.   

   (v)   Life is a puzzle: Definition of life- its main functions: metabolism, replication and evolution by natural selection.  Origin of life on the Earth. The Extremophiles  

  (vi)   The potential threats to the Earth – Astronomical, Geological and Man-made threats. Extinction of life in the past. 

 (vii)  The natural protection for life – The extremely rare combination of astronomical and geological coincidences that has enabled   life on the Earth to survive and evolve.  

(viii)   Are we alone? Search for extra-terrestrial bio-signature and techno-signature. 

  (ix)  The evolution of the Sun – from a faint young star to a red giant and a changing environment of the Earth – from habitable to    uninhabitable planet. 

   (x)  The death of the Sun and the fate of its planets.         

Learning Outcomes

Basic knowledge and understanding on the formation of the Sun and the Solar system alongwith the planet Earth; Earth's evolution and ecology; Origin, evolution and extinction of life; Search for Extra-terrestrial life; Future of planet Earth and life on it.

(3) Pale Blue Dot : A Vision of the Human Future in Space by Carl Sagan , Ballantine Books Inc, NY

(4) Worlds Beyond Our Own : The Search for Habitable Planets by Sujan Sengupta, Springer International

Somak Raychaudhury [somak.raychaudhury@ashoka.edu.in], Gautam Basu [gautam.basu@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Deconstructing Discoveries

Almost all high school graduates have studied science. However, the science they encounter is typically presented as a body of established knowledge—the products of science—rather than the processes through which discoveries and inventions are made. As a result, students often learn scientific facts in isolation, with little appreciation of the scientists behind the discoveries, the processes that led to them, or the important roles played by society, funding agencies, and research institutions in shaping the course of scientific inquiry.

The aim of this course is to introduce students to how science is actually done. It will examine how scientific discoveries and inventions are made; how society—including governments and the media—responds to them; how scientific recognition and prizes are awarded (or sometimes not awarded); and how the practice of science has evolved from the work of isolated individuals to Big Science, in which large international teams collaborate to address complex problems. Drawing on examples from biology, chemistry, astronomy, and physics, the course will demonstrate how observations, experiments, and discoveries have advanced our understanding of nature while illustrating the scientific method in practice. It will also foster an appreciation of scientific temper and examine the scientific basis of some of the major global challenges facing humanity today, including epidemics, climate change, and environmental pollution.

The course will be conducted through a combination of lectures, readings, discussions, and student seminars on topics assigned by the instructors. Students will also interview practicing scientists after reading selected papers from the primary scientific literature, participate in hands-on activities (such as constructing a double-helical DNA model and performing experiments with a simple pendulum), and stage scenes from the play Oxygen by Carl Djerassi and Roald Hoffmann to explore the human, historical, and social dimensions of scientific discovery.

Learning Outcomes

At the end of the course, it is expected that students are expected to learn and better appreciate:

1. the process of Science as a human pursuit, albeit special, that operates with tacit support from Society;

2. how observations and discoveries help us gain insight into Nature, and lead to advances in knowledge;

3. the far-reaching implications of the inventions and discoveries, often serendipitous, and beyond what the discoverer ever imagined;

 4. how by understanding nature through incremental and intermittent processes, Science gains a better understanding of the scientific process itself, and updates its goals and methods.

Literature and the World [FC-0701] [FC-0701-2]

Faculty
Jonathan Gil Harris [jgharris@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This class begins with the premise that every story is a migrant.  A story migrates in a variety of ways – from the teller to the audience or reader; but also from reader to reader, place to place, and culture to culture, as the story gets told and retold (or written and rewritten) over space and time. 

We live in a capitalist age when ideas of private property have subtly colonized how we think about stories.  It is assumed that a story is always BY someone, and is therefore their possession.  But if stories migrate, can a single author really claim full ownership of the story she has written?  How is every story a re-imagining of another story, or many stories, that have become before?

The notion that a story is an author’s private intellectual property also inhibits how we read.  Readers become potential trespassers; they must pay the price of admission, and then act respectfully when they enter the property, making sure not to damage or alter it.  If you are a student of literature, it’s likely that the command to respect an author’s private property will be accompanied by the assumption that the objective of literary analysis is simply to understand what the author intended, and to submit to that deferentially.  But if stories migrate from teller to reader, and from reader to reader and culture to culture, maybe the act of reading should not be thought of just as a respectful encounter with an author’s private property.  Every act of reading instead becomes a creative re-imagining of the story, in conversation with new potential readers and audiences. 

If stories are migrants, then they are no longer individual property by authors who command their readers.  They are collective artefacts that invite us to respond creatively and re-imagine them anew.

If you doubt what I am saying, think this.  Do any two readers respond exactly the same way to a story?  Each reader, when asked about a story and what it meant, will retell it slightly differently.  Recognizing that reading is a form of creative re-imagining is one of this course’s most important themes.

As stories migrate across space, time, and languages, they are re-imagined by the world across many genres and media – poems, plays, novels, essays, films, graphic novels.  These re-imaginings might prove that, in literature, there is nothing original under the sun.  Yet how literature reimagines earlier stories also tells us a lot about the extraordinarily diverse ways in which different cultures have understood the world: relations between men and women, relations between diverse ethnicities and religions, the nature of political and social power, humans’ relations to the animal and plant world, the agonies and ecstasies of love, and the nature of imagination itself. 

How, for example, is a Roman re-imagining of an old Greek story about an Asian witch re-imagined by an English playwright in an “American” drama that has itself been re-imagined in very different ways by writers and artists from the Caribbean, Sierra Leone, Mauritius, and Samoa?  How is a Roman re-imagining of a Babylonian (ie Iraqi) love story reworked by the same English playwright in a Greek mythic tale with an Asian subtext that gets in turn re-imagined by a Bombay director in Hindi, Punjabi, Urdu and English as well as by an English graphic novelist in a reworking of an American comic-book hero’s saga based on a character from a German short story?  And how is an antique Persian story about an African migrant re-imagined in an Arab novel and then re-imagined by the same English playwright, whose play is then diversely re-imagined by a Sudanese novelist and a Hindi film-maker from Uttar Pradesh?

Overview

What is liberal arts education? Is it identified with particular subjects, or a certain style of teaching and learning? This course will offer an introduction to liberal arts education as it might be practiced in a literature classroom for non-specialists, including students who may major in any subject at Ashoka – a be it literature, economics, or biology. Our focus will be on English as a world language, and particularly one of global literature. How did the British Empire shape a global terrain of colonial modernity? How did that modernity merge with Anglo-American globalization of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries? How did this create the English-speaking and English-reading worlds, and how did it turn English into a

language of world literature? We will examine the transnational trajectory of this diverse and diffuse body of writing, including work from spaces with vastly different histories – the colonies in sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean and South Asia, and the hard-to-classify context of South Africa.

Literature and the World [FC-0701] [FC-0701-4]

Faculty
Vivek Venkitaraman Narayan [v.v.narayan@ashoka.edu.in]
Teaching Fellow
Fuzaila Khan [fuzaila.khan_tf@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Literature lives in a strange place where the word meets the world: here, the fantastical can seem familiar and the mundane may seem bizarre. The act of reading allows us to imagine the strange worlds of others as if we lived in them, and, equally, to reimagine our everyday worlds as if we viewed them through unfamiliar eyes. This imaginative encounter with otherness—other people, other perspectives, other places, and other worlds—lies at the heart of the literary experience. 

In South Asia, the literary encounter with otherness is inextricable from the worldly encounters of caste. The aesthetics of caste inform our literary sensibilities, the social experiences of caste frame the world we inhabit, and the everyday performances of caste shape our bodies. In short, the encounters that create our aesthetic, social, and embodied experiences—between the word and the world, between the self and the other, and between the real and the imagined—are all entangled with caste.   

This course will examine the relationship between literature and the world by focussing on the aesthetic, social, and embodied experiences of caste. We will ask: What can caste and literature tell us about each other? What do the intersections of caste and literature tell us about the world? How does our experience of the world inform and inflect our responses to literary representations of caste? And, perhaps most important, how will this kind of literary experience help us inhabit the world? We will read fiction, nonfiction, poems, and plays to explore what literature can reveal about others, ourselves, and a world organized by caste.

Great Books [FC-0601] [FC-0601-1]

Faculty
Arpita Das [arpita.das@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Memoirs by women that act as political beacons are the focus of this course. Each one is a stellar example of the genre we know as narrative non-fiction, and each one has been cited and referred to by generations of scholars, practitioners, activists, and students for whom equity and social justice are of importance. Over time, these memoirs have taken on a talismanic importance and yet, they age well with the times and remain supremely relevant. Is that something to celebrate in terms of the prescience of the texts themselves, or to lament in terms of how the world does not seem to become a more equitable place even over the decades since these texts were read for the first time. 

The texts we will be reading: Karukku by Bama; The Prisons We Broke by Baby Kamble; Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal by Jeanette Winterson; 'Memories of an un-Palestinian story, in a can of tuna' by Susan Abulhawa; Our Words, Our Stories by A. Revathi. 

The final project which accounts for 50% of the course will be a group creative project based on any theme in the books we have read together during the semester and can take the form of a podcast, original song, short film, comic book, art installation, live performance, broadsheet or zine.

Learning Outcomes

Studying texts from different cultures, chronologies, disciplines, and languages, the Great Books course introduces students to multiple ways of thinking and being in the world. As the semester progresses, students are encouraged to ask questions of the books or fragments of books they are reading. The intent is to familiarise students with how to engage with texts and not be intimidated by them, and in so doing, opening a door for students, inviting them into new landscapes of ideas, narratives, arguments, and experiences.

Overview

This course seeks to reflect on care and love both conceptually and experientially. What does it mean to love and care for oneself and for others? What allows us to love and care? What prevents us from caring and loving ourselves and others? What forces—personal, interpersonal, or collective and communal—regulate, prescribe and even prohibit experiences and expressions of love.

Our primary goal in the course is to work towards developing a critical and comprehensive language around understanding care and love as the basis for any and all configurations of relationalities that both make and unmake our senses of being in the world. Beginning our journey with selections from The Symposium by Plato, verses from the Gatha Sattasai, and poetry from the Akam repertoire of Sangam literature, we will make our way through more contemporary iterations and meditations on caring and loving such as, Roland Barthes’ A Lover’s Discourse and Ocean Vuong’s On Earth We Are Briefly Gorgeous. All along the way we will be reflecting on and attempting to problematize “traditional” and “normative” structures within which care and love are usually understood and experienced.

Learning Outcomes

To understand representations of caring and loving in literature and culture.

To contemplate and reflect on caring and loving experientially and critically.

To develop a critical lexicon for addressing the ethics of caring and loving.

Overview

Love and Other Literary Moods: the Great Books Challenge in the Age of AI 

We will read select books (and extracts) from a wide range of themes and ask ourselves what makes them great.

Specifically, we will examine the dominant mood the text evokes – its “rasa” – and how it acts in concert with other elements to craft the specific version of the book that goes out into the world and is recognized as “great”. Over the first eight/ nine weeks, we will closely read a wide range of texts, both fiction and non-fiction, in and out of class. In the final four weeks of the course, each student will – as a part of a group or individually – work on a project that will seek to bring in a new mood or invent a new rasa, alongside a “great” book/ short story/ cycle of poems of their choice. Audacious experiments are not only allowed but encouraged!    

Through the weeks we spend together, reading and writing, we will also consciously - and consistently - situate ourselves in the present. We will pose to ourselves honestly - and intuitively - meta-questions, such as: WHY should we read great texts at all in the age of AI, when summaries are available in the blink of an eye and seem to give us everything we need? Is a great text one where the summary misses the mood? And, finally, the mother of all key questions: WHAT'S SO GREAT ABOUT GREAT BOOKS? 

Learning Outcomes

You will learn to read critically and closely; you will examine the idea of "great" and you will also learn to push back against its canonical frames; you will write short essays, present your own findings to your peers and defend your own position, with evidence, nuance and grace. 

You will have opportunities to connect the idea of Great Books to your chosen discipline, and develop a radical canon of your own if you like. 

You will be evaluated through the semester.

The class will be dialogic in nature; there will be a mid-term exam and end-term exam; in-class assessments; and an end-term presentation (and write-up).   

THE CLASS IS SCREEN-FREE AND TECHNOLOGY-FREE. You will have to keep your phones and laptops away for most of the class (unless a specific learning requirement needs you to use screens.)

Faculty

Overview

Taught by Justin McCarthy

This course guides students through a multiplicity of performance practices existing on the subcontinent. These practices include the locally specific, the socially specific, the traditional, the hereditary, the rural, the nomadic, the urban, the pan-Indian, as well as those practices with discernible connections to performance conventions beyond the specifically Indian context. An important premise of this course is that music, dance and theatre are three strands of an intertwined whole. Their closely related cultural, social and aesthetic histories will constitute the core material to be studied. While acknowledging a cultural corpus often possessing obvious mutual affinities, this course will give pride of place to the wide varieties of performance practices found in India and the divergent histories accompanying them.  Though mainly academic, the course can contain performance elements depending on the students’ inclinations and their performative relationship to the material being studied.

There is no prerequisite for this course.

This course is mandatory for all students wanting to pursue  a minor in performing arts.

Faculty
Abir Bashir Bazaz [abir.bazaz@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What is faith? What is the difference between faith and religion? What does faith mean in ‘a secular age’? And what is the relation of faith to belief, trust and wonder? Can a thinking of faith transform our understanding of the political? What is at stake in the relation between the question of faith and the question of literature? These are some of the questions that will guide our thinking on the question of faith in literature and cinema. We will be reading literary texts by Fyodor Dostoyevsky, Mikhail Bulgakov, Jens Peter Jacobsen, Flannery O'Connor, J.M.Coetzee, Shusako Endo and David Foster Wallace. We will also be reading key philosophical and theoretical reflections on the question of faith by Blaise Pascal, Soren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger, and Jacques Derrida. We will also be screening and discussing films by Terrence Malick, Robert Bresson, Krzysztof Kieslowski, Wim Wenders and Abbas Kiarostami.

Overview

NOTE - Registration is open only to 3rd year students. 

This course aims to teach students the basic concepts of Cell Biology and Genetics. In the first module (by Sandeep Ameta), students will be taught the concepts and experiments for forward genetics by subjecting microorganisms to harsh environmental conditions and observing the phenotypes. The second module complements the first module by focusing on reverse genetics using the classic eukaryotic model system – Drosophila. The third module will introduce the genetic model system - Caenorhabditis elegans and its advantage in feeding based RNAi screens to uncover molecular mechanisms driving cellular processes.

Learning Outcomes

The course will provide students with a basic understanding and hands-on experience in handling, manipulating, and investigating cell-biology problems using genetic tools. Importantly, this is a discovery-based course, students will not simply replicate known results, but instead actively participate in generating new knowledge. The goal is to stimulate students’ interest in life sciences through inquiry-based learning. In the process, students will also advance their understanding of the field more broadly.

Understanding Structure and Function [BIO-3006/ BIO-6006] [BIO-3006/ BIO-6006-1]

Faculty
Dilip Kumar [dilip.kumar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why water boils at 100°C and methane at -161°C; why blood is red, and grass is green; how sunlight makes plants grow and how living organisms have been able to evolve into ever more complex forms- the answers to all these problems have come from structural analysis. –Max Perutz

Have you ever visited a key maker? You must have seen lots of premade keys with unique shapes and sizes. However, only certain keys might work for a particular lock. But what makes a particular key functional for one lock but not for others? It entirely depends on the structural complementarity of lock and key. Similarly, in Biology, thousands of such keys for specific locks mediate numerous biological functions based on their shapes, features, and their interactions with the surroundings. This course will discuss how these biological keys or biomolecules are structured for their specific functions. Through this course, we will be asking some of these questions. We will also be visiting various biophysical techniques that are used to measure and visualize biomolecular interactions.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Outcomes: At the end of the course, the students will have clarity and understanding of the role of structure in the functions of biological macromolecules. The precise learning outcomes

of this course will be:

1. Students will be able to understand the basic chemistry behind the biological functioning of macromolecules.

2. We will also be discussing published research articles on related topics. This course will enable students to interpret the research articles and frame relevant questions related to the topic.

3. Through active participation, students will also enhance their communication and presentation skills.

 

Weekly learning outcomes:

W1: Basics of biomolecular interactions and how structure leads to function.

W2-W3: Details of building blocks of proteins

W4-W6: Structure and chemistry of lipids, carbohydrates, and Nucleic acids, and Mid-term presentation by PhD students

W7-W11: Methods for macromolecular structure determination and interaction analysis

W12: Macromolecular interactions and Paper presentations by PhD students in the last class of the semester

This module will be mostly based on research papers and reviews. The following books can be referred. In addition, reading material in the form of papers and notes will be circulated.

• Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry- 6th Ed. David L Nelson, Michael M Cox

• Molecular Biology of the Cell- Bruce Alberts, Alexander Johnson, Julian Lewis, Martin Raff, Keith Roberts, Peter Walter

Online resources: Atlas of the Bacterial and Archaeal Cell Structure (Catherine M. Oikonomou & Grant J. Jensen)

description:
Introduction to Biology II: Cell Biology [BIO-2214] [BIO-2214-1]

Faculty
Anup Padmanabhan [anup.padmanabhan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Cells are the fundamental unit of life. It carries out all (well… almost all!) the physiological processes essential for its survival and propagation. Within the cell, each of these processes is accomplished by molecular-machines. What are these processes and how do these mini machines carry out cellular functions? How do these cellular machines know the right place and the right time to carry out appropriate functions?

Learning Outcomes

In this introductory Cell Biology course, essential processes at the cellular level will be explored to understand how molecular machines carry out these processes.

The primary focus of this course will be on eukaryotic cells.  There are 3 lectures on prokaryotic cell biology to draw comparisons between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cellular processes to appreciate their similarities and distinctness.

By the end of this course,

The participant is expected to have a good conceptual grasp of basic cellular mechanisms, the molecular machinery involved, and their functional regulation within a cell.

Through detailed discussions on cell biology methods and classical cell biology experiments, the participants should be able to read and interpret experimental data and appreciate the role of controls and able to design cell biology experiments to test hypotheses.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Prerequisites: There are no mandatory prerequisites for this course. Prior exposure to Biology at the Class 11–12 level may be beneficial, but it is not required. In previous offerings, many students without a high-school biology background have performed exceptionally well in the course. Success ultimately depends on a student's curiosity, aptitude, commitment, and willingness to engage deeply with the material.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials):

Molecular Biology of the Cell – Bruce Alberts

Molecular Cell Biology – Lodish and Baltimore

Essential Cell Biology

iBiology.org talks on relevant topics.

The sequence of topics covered in this course may not necessarily follow the order presented in the prescribed textbook. Participants are expected to consult the textbook and other reference materials after each class to review and reinforce the concepts discussed during the sessions.

Overview

The primary focus of this course is to introduce students to the Itihāsa/Purāṇic and simple belles-lettres (kāvya) traditions through the reading of original Sanskrit texts. The course is designed to help students strengthen and expand their knowledge of Sanskrit vocabulary, grammar, and syntax while developing confidence in reading continuous Sanskrit passages.

As the main reading text, students will study the Kādambarīkathāsāra of Abhinanda, a accessible work that provides an excellent entry point into classical Sanskrit narrative style. Through close reading, translation, and grammatical analysis, students will become more familiar with the structures, idioms, and literary features of Sanskrit prose and narrative poetry.

The course will also review and discuss grammatical topics that have not yet been fully covered in previous Sanskrit classes. For this purpose, students will use Madhav Deshpande’s Saṃskṛta-Subodhinī: A Sanskrit Primer as a supporting reference.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students are expected to have:

  • the ability to read selected Classical Sanskrit texts with the help of dictionaries and grammatical tools;
  • a sound working knowledge of Classical Sanskrit grammar and syntax;
  • the ability to translate simple narrative passages from Sanskrit into English;
  • improved confidence in correct Sanskrit pronunciation and recitation.

      2. Recommended Reading

Faculty

Overview

This is the required writing course for all SOA PhD students.

This course is designed to hone your skills as an academic writer, particularly a professional academic writer in the field of anthropology. Centrally, the course takes as its major assumption the fact that you are all already writers. Our task, then, is to think critically about writing, to challenge assumptions about what constitutes “good” writing, to deconstruct writing for its rhetorical practices, and, crucially, to establish our own personal practices for planning, starting, and refining our own writing. This class is thus built around writing, re-writing, peer review, and structured revision. 

We will learn to write in several distinct academic genres: literature reviews, abstracts, personal statements, and book reviews. Learning the formal conventions of each of these practical forms of writing brings you into conversations with other anthropologists so you can easily share your thoughts and ideas across the world, while also working to develop your own writing voice.

Concepts, Contemporaneity and the Social [SOA-6101] [SOA-6101-1]

Faculty
Arif Hayat Nairang [arif.nairang@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How can anthropology or sociology help us understand our contemporary social worlds and what can such an understanding tell us about being human, a condition fundamentally marked by contingency, and which constitutes the cornerstone of anthropological inquiry. This course puts together a toolkit of concepts, including Language, Culture, Social, and Power which have continued to shape knowledge-making in Sociology and Anthropology, allowing anthropologists and sociologists to, presumably, access the perspective of the “other”, interpret socio-cultural phenomenon, and produce evidence of how social life is inflected by power. The goal is to put together a conversation on, first, how meaning is assigned, and second, how sites of meaning making are not simply cultural or social sites but encounters with a multiplicity or an overwhelming complexity that refuses/exceeds/disavows existing vocabularies or orders. The aim is for every participant, or say participant-observer, to look for such an encounter in their work with the hope that it refuses to abide by what they know of the world and calls forth an engagement with the possible for new concepts and terms to understand a world that is not of our own making and where we are always struggling to come of age. 

Learning Outcomes
  1. Develop a critical command of foundational concepts in sociocultural anthropology and sociology — Students will demonstrate a nuanced understanding of core theoretical concepts — language, the social, culture, and power — tracing their genealogies, internal tensions, and ongoing relevance for contemporary anthropological and sociological inquiry.
  2. Engage in close reading of canonical and challenging theoretical texts — Through weekly reading responses, students will practice rigorous analytical reading across a range of difficult texts — from Saussure and Lacan to Foucault, Fanon, and Ambedkar — developing the capacity to identify arguments, trace conceptual moves, and situate texts within broader theoretical conversations.
  3. Identify and articulate moments where existing concepts exceed or fail their objects — Students will develop the ability to recognize in their own and others' work those encounters with social reality that resist available vocabularies, and to use such moments as productive sites for conceptual experimentation and the development of new analytic terms.
  4. Situate their own research within broader theoretical conversations — Through the mid-term presentation, students will demonstrate the ability to bring course concepts into dialogue with their own dissertation projects, identifying the theoretical stakes of their research questions and the conceptual resources available to address them.
  5. Produce original theoretical writing at the level of doctoral scholarship — The final paper will demonstrate students' capacity to develop a sustained, original argument that engages seriously with at least three theoretical traditions covered in the course, moving beyond summary or application toward genuine conceptual contribution.
  6. Participate as scholar-interlocutors in a seminar community — Students will contribute to the intellectual life of the seminar through prepared, substantive participation in discussion, responding generously and critically to one another's ideas, and treating the seminar as a site of collective inquiry rather than individual performance.

Probability and Statistics [MAT-2020/ CS-1209/ PHY-1208] [MAT-2020/ CS-1209/ PHY-1208-1]

Faculty
Debapratim Banerjee [debapratim.banerjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This is a first course in probability theory where the students are expected to learn the foundations, basic concepts of probability theory and be able to solve problems. We shall also discuss some preliminary concepts and foundations of statistics. This course is the first step to take future advanced courses in probability and statistics.

Learning Outcomes

Frequency and axiomatic definition of probability, random experiments with equally likely finite outcomes, Inclusion exclusion principle. General finite sample spaces, infinite sample spaces.  Concept of probability spaces and construction of probability measures. Conditional probability, Bayes theorem, Independence of events. Random variable (discrete), probability mass function and distribution function. Examples: Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Geometric distributions. Expectation and variance of a random variable, sum law and product law of expectation, moment generating functions. Random vector (discrete), joint distribution, Marginal distributions, joint moment generating functions, covariance, Multinomial distributions. Continuous random variables, density functions, distribution functions, expectation, variance, moment generating function, example: uniform, normal, and exponential. Continuous random vector, joint density function, joint distribution function, conditional density, example: multivariate normal. 

Inequalities: Markov, Chebyshev. Weak variant of law of large numbers, Central Limit Theorem (without proof). 

Descriptive statistics, Distribution of sampling statistics, Parameter Estimation and Hypothesis testing basics.

Simple linear regression with one regressor (only if time permits).

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

 Students are expected to have a strong background in permutation and combination and calculus. Hence, they should be comfortable with the course materials of Mathematics in 10+2 standard and MAT 1000: Calculus. Following books are in the reading list:

1. S. M. Ross: First Course in Probability, Pearson.

2. S. M. Ross: Introduction to Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists

Financial Markets and Institutions [FIN-3002/ ECO-3207] [FIN-3002/ ECO-3207-1]

Faculty
S K Shanthi [sk.shanthi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The main emphasis of this course is to develop the perspectives of a practicing finance professional. This course will enable students to understand the role of financial markets and institutions in shaping the economic and business environment of the nation. With the help of some simplifying frameworks and models, the students will be equipped to develop a series of applications of principles from finance and economics that explore the connection between the firm, financial markets, financial institutions and the broader economy. The financial markets studied will include money markets, bond markets, insurance markets, stock markets and currency markets. Students will study the role of financial institutions (intermediation and innovation) played by central banks, commercial banks, investment banks, insurance companies and mutual funds in facilitating the flow of funds in the economy. Keynesian IS-LM theory and the loanable funds theory provide the theoretical background for the course and help students develop simple analytical frameworks to study the interaction of individuals, firms, governments, markets and the aggregate economy. The students will also understand the role of regulation in the overall functioning of financial markets and institutions in the economy.

Learning Outcomes

Upon finishing the course, students are expected to 

  • know the drivers of the term structure of interest rates. 
  • explain how investment banks and mutual funds operate.
  • How money markets, stock markets and bond markets work 
  • discuss the stock valuation based on fundamental analysis. 
  • read a bank’s balance sheet and discuss how risks are managed in banks. 
  • know the role and impact of the Central bank as the main regulator in the domestic and international currency markets.
  • grasp the fundamentals of regulatory practices in the stock markets and the insurance markets.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Urban Economics [ECO-3605] [ECO-3605-1]

Faculty
Lalit Hemant Contractor [lalit.contractor@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The decision of where to locate is essential for both business and individuals. It determines the profits of firms through the cost of inputs, market size, the level of competition, and the policy environment they face. It also determines job opportunities, schooling, and other amenities accessible to individuals. In turn, firm and individual decisions aggregate to determine the performance of cities and regions. This course studies business and individual location decisions
and how they determine the main economic forces that lead to the existence and performance of cities and regional
agglomerations. 

The course starts by developing a simple theory of cities and its implications for density, city size, firm productivity,
and housing prices. We will study the internal structure of cities, and how to evaluate the effect of new infrastructure or policy on land and housing values and overall welfare. We shall consider evidence on the impact of cities on firm and worker productivity, urban amenities, and congestion. We then consider regional spatial development and more local aspects such as urban transportation, housing policy and urban fiscal policy. Finally, the course will analyze cities in the developing world, and conclude with recent innovations in urban economics.

Learning Outcomes

At the end of the course, students should:
• Understand the forces (agglomeration economies) that underpin the formation of cities

• Understand the notion of spatial equilibrium, applied to models about the internal structure of cities as well as systems of cities in a region

  • Evaluate the effects of policies like rent control and understand outcomes like neighbourhood segregation
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course will be based on the exposition in the following textbooks. However,
lecture notes and slides shall be sufficient to answer homework and exam questions.
In addition, I shall draw upon selected book chapters and papers.

2. Sieg, Holger (2020). Urban Economics and Fiscal Policy; Princeton University Press
Additional Reading: books, papers and miscellaneous materials
I recommend the following books for an engaging non-technical survey of the themes
and concerns of Urban Economics:
1. Glaeser, Edward L. (2011). Triumph of the City; Pan Macmillan India
2. Moretti, Enrico (2012). The new geography of jobs. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt
3. Glaeser, Edward L. and David Cutler (2021). Survival of the City: Living and
Thriving in an Age of Isolation. Penguin Press/Basic Books

Organizational Economics [ECO-3107] [ECO-3107-1]

Faculty
Ayush Pant [ayush.pant@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces the world of organizations observed through an economist's lens. Organizations exist because the price system and complete contracts cannot solve every collective-action problem. Firms, governments, nonprofits, platforms, teams, and supply chains therefore rely on non-market methods of organizing: ownership, authority, hierarchy, culture, incentives, mission, monitoring, relational contracts, and technology.

The updated course is organized around a single question: How do organizations govern collective action when information is dispersed, incentives are misaligned, and complete contracts are unavailable?

The course is not a management-advice course. It is a course in economic diagnosis: identifying the players, their information, incentives, decision rights, contracts, norms, feasible redesigns, and causal mechansims at play within organizations. We will use formal models and empirical papers to understand modern organizational problems: outsourcing, government contracting, management practices, work-from-home, generative AI at work, delegation to bureaucrats, leadership, culture, harassment monitoring, discrimination, politics at work, and mission-driven organizations.

Children’s Literature [ENG-4330] [ENG-4330-1]

Faculty
Geetanjali Chanda [geetanjali.chanda@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What we read as children forms who we become and provides our first world view. This course provides an opportunity to critically assess the stories that shaped our understanding of morals, culture, and values, as well as those we will impart to future generations. In this discussion-oriented interactive course, we will read and review children’s books, examine the purposes of visual literacy, and write reviews on specific authors and illustrators. We will write our own children’s book to gauge all that we have learnt.

This course aims to examine how the books children read shape their outlook and emotional development. We will study the historical, creative, nurturing, emotional, and educational aspects of these forms of literature and their impact on us later in life. We will also consider why a study of children’s literature is important, and how it impacts pedagogies for children across borders.

            We will examine the views of multiple theoretical thinkers and texts in conjunction with actual children's literature. We will ask the important but often overlooked questions about this particular genre, mainly focusing on Indian and Western children’s literature. The purpose is not so much to compare these two cultural offerings, but to give us a taste of both. 

            We shall consider popular stories for children up to 12 years old, including Amar Chitra Katha, Matilda, The Little Prince, Feluda and Mulan. At the same time, we will also study theoretical thinkers such as Jack Zipes, Seth Lerer, Paulo Freire, and Bruno Bettelheim to help us navigate the complex field of children’s literature in relation to issues of culture, religion, difference, gender, and sexuality.

We will unpack the didactic intent as well as the pleasure principle that might have prompted the writers. Authorial intent is, however, only one part of our study; the other part is to see how children and parents receive these stories. Children’s literature creates moral as well as national frameworks that help acculturate young people. In examining the genre of children’s literature, we will consider various sub-genres such as picture books, fairy tales, fables, and chapter books. 

Learning Outcomes

Learn the importance of children's literature.

Examine visuals and texts in children's literature. 

Write, illustrate and critique your own childrens book. 

Learn how to peer review  the work of your classmates.

courseTitle: Visual and Material Cultures of the Himalayas
description:
Visual and Material Cultures of the Himalayas [VA-2006/ SOA-2215/ MS-3098] [VA-2006/ SOA-2215/ MS-3098-1]

Faculty
Latika Gupta [latika.gupta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Level: 1000/ 2000/ 3000

Prerequisites: None

This course focuses on the Western Himalayas to understand how visual and material cultures are intrinsically connected with the idea of ‘place’, which in the case of the Western Tibetan plateau has been the subject of desire, curiosity and fear in equal measure. We will study how places, cultures and people in the Western Himalayan borderlands are constructed through representations — visual and written — both by ‘outsiders’ as well as local communities from the 19th century until today. At the heart of our enquiries will be the importance of places as ‘contact zones’ and the centrality of 'things' in the construction and telling of histories from multiple perspectives.

We will read travel accounts from the 19th century onwards and a contemporary novel, critically examine the emergence of colonial displays of cultures through the Great Exhibitions and the persistence of this model in contemporary times; we will do a deep dive into colonial and contemporary photography, watch films and look at representations in popular culture. We will also examine the recent museum-making impulse in the Western Himalayas through case studies of a range of museums situated in these borderlands — war memorial museums; community museums of conflict and of trade route artefacts; and museums in Buddhist monasteries to understand the relationship between heritage and religion, the impact of the movement of things from sacred sites to ‘secular’ museums, and to ask how a politics of remembrance may manifest in cultural production. The course will conclude with an introduction to Tibetan culture-in-exile through contemporary art, poetry, writing and films. The course includes field visits to a Tibetan exile settlement and the National Museum in Delhi

Some of the questions we will explore include: What are the processes through which cultures are constructed in colonial and contemporary times, and what impact does this have on communities and people? How did the field of Himalayan Art emerge? Where do we ‘locate’ this field; which geographical areas and religions are made emblematic of this discipline; which cultures are excluded and why? How were museum collections of Himalayan objects built and in what historical circumstances? How are sacred objects of use segregated into categories of art and ethnography? What curatorial strategies are used to reconstruct the auras of objects? Understanding our affective relationships to things and the many complex lives that objects traverse through time and geographies, will be central to this course.

Utilising interdisciplinary methodologies from history, visual anthropology, material culture studies and museology, students will engage with critical questions about historiography, ethics of representation in imaging places and people; the socio-political processes that inform the writing of histories, and the entanglements of politics and culture in the formation of regional and national identities. By the end of the semester, we will have constructed a visual and material culture led history of the Western Tibetan plateau, via writing, image-making, institutions and the political imperatives that shaped each of these forms, and the resultant impact in contemporary times.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Outcomes:

By the end of the course, students:

  • will be familiar with the broad field of visual and material cultures in the Western Himalayas in Tibet, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh, and the colonial histories of the western and eastern Himalayan borderlands.
  • will acquire the critical tools interrogate the nature and impact of representation of regions, religions, cultures and communities through images and written texts.
  • will be conversant with critical questions around heritage, the politics of museums and the role of tradition in the construction of contemporary cultural identities.
  • will learn about major international museums and collections of Himalayan art and be able to critically analyze the framing of objects as art or ethnography, and questions of provenance research and object displays.
  • will be able to analyse and 'read' images and texts, with a focus on meaning making through vocabularies and terminologies, and apply this critical thinking in a curatorial project.

Faculty
Nirajan Kafle [nirajan.kafle@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Elementary Sanskrit II is the second part of a three-course series focusing on Sanskrit Grammar. By completing this course, students will grasp essential principles, enabling them to interpret and understand Classical Sanskrit texts more effectively. The emphasis on foundational skills ensures a solid understanding of the language's intricacies and better engagement with classical Sanskrit literature.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of Elementary Sanskrit II, students will be able to:

  • Demonstrate a clear command of intermediate Sanskrit grammar, including the formation and usage of noun stems ending in consonants and a range of verbal forms.
  • Accurately recognize and construct key grammatical forms, such as present active participles, past imperfect participles, gerundives, and the conditional mood.
  • Understand and apply syntactic structures, including compound formations (samāsa), locative and genitive absolutes, and the use of demonstrative pronouns (इदम् and अदस्).
  • Conjugate and employ secondary verbal roots and desiderative verbs within accurate grammatical contexts.
  • Parse and translate Sanskrit sentences by identifying grammatical elements and applying rules of agreement, case usage, and verb conjugation.
  • Build the grammatical foundation necessary for reading Classical Sanskrit texts, with increasing independence and accuracy.

Faculty
Abheek Barua [abheek.barua@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why does the US have the lead in AI? What do vests and bank loans have in common? What is money and what does the Reserve Bank of India do? What does deglobalization mean and what do tariffs and controls on immigration by Western countries have to do with it? What is a budget and why do economists spend so much time worrying about government budgets? Is the Sensex a correct gauge of how the Indian economy is doing? Why are countries afraid of “Japanification”? What is China’s “ mayor economy”?

This course addresses a diverse range of issues in economics and public policy in a non-technical way. It emphasizes the intuition behind complex economic ideas and also explores the connections of economics with other disciplines – psychology, philosophy, finance, sociology and political science—for example. Finally, it  explores India specific problems such as the risk of a middle-income trap. The aim is to blend an understanding of current issues with the history of ideas to leave students with a quick but comprehensive idea of the science and art of economics.

 The course will use a diverse set of resources – short videos, excerpts from Yale and MIT open learning course, blogs and a simple textbook written by Nobel Laureate Paul Krugman.

Faculty
Arun Mohan Sukumar [arun.sukumar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course puts the I in EPS. Few social, political, or economic movements can be understood in isolation from their international context. Their triggers may be local, but the ideas, people, money, and technologies that mobilise them travel. We will therefore read economy, politics, and society in comparative perspective, unearthing shared intellectual undercurrents and the material impact of watershed events across time and geography. We will pay particular attention to global markets as shapers of political and social developments.

Rather than starting with theory, the course is organised around ebbs and flows in societies.  We will connect social upheaval to disruption in markets, understand the role coercion plays in international political economy, ground the origins of economic life in religion and dogma, and frame technology as a vehicle for political engineering. When we do go through canonical texts, it will mostly be to understand societies in convulsion: Luther's Europe, Smith's Scotland, Meiji Japan, Weimar Germany, Mao's China and Malviya’s Benares for example. Technology will play a starring role in this course -- and although you are not expected to have a legal background, we will occasionally analyse legal texts both as an instrument of powerful interests and a resistance tool for social movements.

This is a reading-intensive course with 40% of the grade earmarked for classroom discussions. No laptops allowed in class.

Overview

This course introduces students to seminal writings on the intertwined trajectories of economy, politics, and society in the Indian subcontinent during the emergence of modernity. It traces the evolution of modern South Asia from 1818 to 1947, examining key social, political, and economic transformations under colonial rule.

We will explore major figures who engaged with — and shaped — the political and social struggles of the period, alongside critical debates on religious reform, women’s roles, caste hierarchies, communalism, and nation formation. Special attention will be given to the complexity of colonial governance, economic change, and social contestations.

Students will engage with a range of primary texts — including autobiographies, speeches, political treatises, ethnographies, and literary fiction — to analyze how ideas of economy, politics, and society were debated and reimagined in colonial South Asia.
