Faculty
Surajkumar Dnyandeo Thube [surajkumar.thube@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Does Caste Still Matter in India Today?

“Democracy in India is a top-dressing on an Indian soil which is essentially undemocratic.” These words by Dr. Ambedkar in the Annihilation of Caste continue to compel us to critically reflect upon the myriad hurdles that have kept India away from fully realizing its democratic potential. For Ambedkar, one of the main social cleavages that resisted notions of equality and social justice was the pervasive phenomenon of caste in India. Achieving political freedom, as Ambedkar presciently reminded everyone, was no guarantee for realizing social freedom. Seven decades after India’s independence, how deeply entrenched is this social idea of democracy in India today? More specifically, how do we understand the role of caste in the chequered story of India’s democracy? Should caste only be understood as a pernicious form of social hierarchy or can it also be seen as an entity that has shaped the rise of ‘lower-caste’ identity assertion and led to the socio-economic upliftment of marginalized sections?

This course will introduce students to debates and discussions around why, how and in what ways caste shapes different facets of everyday life in contemporary India. With a thematic focus around politics, society and economy, this course will offer varied perspectives to meaningfully approach a deceptively simple question – ‘Does Caste Still Matter in India?’. The course will be divided into 3 categories. The first section will deal with how caste became politicized after 1947 by focusing on the rise of caste-based political parties and social movements in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. The second section will introduce students to how caste continues to operate as a form of social hierarchy through seemingly egalitarian spheres of food, music, sport and educational institutions. The final section will focus on the complex role caste plays in the Indian economy by dealing with conceptual issues like ‘caste and class’, along with thematic issues like caste-based discrimination in labour markets, the gig economy, the question of Dalit capitalism, among others. This course will encourage students to think critically about these issues in relation to how the story of Indian democracy has unfolded over the years. It will provoke students to think of caste as the ‘undemocratic soil’ of a rapidly urbanizing India, and not treat it as a past relic or as a phenomenon that rears its ugly head only among rural, ‘backward communities’ and in underdeveloped regions of India.

Economy, Politics and Society [FC-0412] [FC-0412-5]

Faculty
Uday Chandra [uday.chandra@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What makes a society just, prosperous, and worth living in? Questions of the common good cannot be answered by economics, political science, sociology, philosophy, or environmental studies alone. They require us to move between moral ideas, empirical realities, institutional arrangements, and lived experience.

This foundation course examines how states, markets, communities, and other institutions organize collective life. We shall study how societies produce order, distribute resources, manage conflict, define belonging, respond to inequality, and confront environmental and technological change. Rather than treating states and markets as separate or opposing spheres, the course asks how they are historically constituted, socially embedded, and politically contested.

Students will learn to read across social science disciplines, reconstruct arguments, interpret evidence, and exercise judgment when reasonable people disagree. The aim is not to provide a single theory of the common good, but to develop the intellectual habits needed to think carefully about competing values, institutional choices, and their consequences.

Overview

In this class, we examine the big questions: how are we connected? How do we come to live the lives we do, surrounded by other people? How do we depend on others, and how do such relations of interdependence give rise to the systems of economy that we know as normal? We use serious social theorists as well as real life examples to consider the conditions of living in our world. 

Throughout the semester, you will be challenged to reconsider your received ideas about the structures that shape your life, asking: what accounts for the similarities that make us feel like a part of society? Why are we different from one another? How does inequality come about? How are our most cherished ideas – about the nature of families, or the trajectory of modern progress – complicated by empirically examining the economic, political, and social world around us?

Students will be able to discuss and evaluate claims on "society," "economy," and "politics." They will be equipped to question and critique scholarly and popular writings on social norms, inequality, capitalism, economic growth, families, modernity, and related themes.

Economy, Politics and Society [FC-0412] [FC-0412-7]

Faculty
Nitish Kashyap [nitish.kashyap@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How does an economy shape the society it sits inside, its politics, its culture, its institutions, and even its most intimate human arrangements? This course builds a working framework for reading any politico-economic system. We begin with the foundational insight that economies are not natural facts but social constructions: they are built through institutions, legitimized through ideology, and reproduced through the everyday habits and beliefs of ordinary people. From that foundation, we trace the historical arc of capitalism — from its origins through imperialism and industrial labour, to its transformation via financialization and the welfare state, to its current mutations in platform monopoly and digital extraction. Running alongside this economic history is a second strand: the story of how political power is organized in capitalist societies, how business captures the state, how international institutions transmit a particular economic ideology across the globe, and where the cracks in democratic governance are appearing. The course closes with the question that all of this is building toward: what does the system do to people, to their emotions, their relationships, their sense of hope and meaning and where is it headed?

No prior background in economics, politics, or sociology is required. 

Learning Outcomes

Students shall be able to

1. Read any economic system diagnostically, applying frameworks from political economy, economic sociology, and institutional analysis to identify who wrote the rules, who benefits from them feeling natural, and who pays the cost of that arrangement.

2. Trace the relationship between economic organisation and social life — understanding how capitalism's successive phases have shaped family structures, political institutions, emotional life, and the distribution of hope across populations.

3. Critically evaluate the claims made by markets, states, and multilateral institutions — distinguishing between evidence-based policy and ideological mandate, and recognising where democratic governance has been captured by concentrated economic power.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

I shall share the readings as we progress through the course. The course shall be divided into 5 units focusing on reading a system, evolution of capitalist regime, social contract (labour, welfare, financialization), business and politics, and platform economies and exhaustion of hope. I shall circulate a pre-course survey form to seek your responses and might modify the emphasis in some units while doing the course.

Faculty
Pritam Ghosh [pritam.ghosh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This is a Calculus course inteded to review and strengthen your understanding of a fundamental pillar of mathematics. The course differs from your usual school level calculus course in the sense that we will not follow a "memorise a formula and learn hpw to apply it" type of approach. Deductive logic will our primary tool here and you will the "how and why" behind various ideas studied in Calculus.

Students who wish to study Mathematics, Physics, Computer Science, Economics and BIology in the future will all benefit from this course. 

 

Learning Outcomes

You will re-learn the basics of Calculus from the perspective of a university level student. The central idea of calculus is taking limits and making approximations. All other concepts such as continuity, differentiation, Integration, Infinite series etc follow from the basic ideas of approximation and limits. 

These concepts are taught using a formalised framework and we will learn how to read and write elementary "proofs" using deductive logic.

Apparitions of Macbeth [ENG-4203] [ENG-4203-1]

Faculty
Jonathan Gil Harris [jgharris@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Macbeth stands unsurpassed among Shakespeare’s works for its capacity to frighten.  It is not just that it features scary Witches who predict the future in riddles, or a murderous tyrant who strikes terror into every corner of his kingdom.  Much of the power of the play derives from its staging of eerie, unsettling apparitions – a floating dagger, a bloody ghost, a series of visions that emerge from a cauldron.  Even the name of the play has acquired a legendary apparitional power: merely to mention it in a playhouse is supposed to conjure unspeakably bad luck.  What is behind the play’s ability to scare the heck out of us?  This seminar will scrutinize Macbeth and its terrifying apparitions.  As we will see, these apparitions are not just plot points or theatrical special effects.  They are also emblematic of the spectral power of matter to conjure untimely possibilities and impossibilities – to make us feel, as Lady Macbeth says, “the future in the instant.”  We will consider how Macbeth’s apparitions have eerily predicted subsequent apparitions of the play, in theory (Sigmund Freud’s account of psychological attachment, Terry Eagleton’s analysis of capitalist reification, Michel Serres’s imagining of human-non-human assemblages) and in cinema (Polanski’s Macbeth, Kurosawa’s Throne of Blood, Bhardwaj’s Maqbool, Jayaraj’s Veeram).  In the process, we will treat the “apparitional” as a theoretical lens that helps us think about the temporalities of political conflicts involving tradition and modernity, indigeneity and cosmopolitanism, globalisation and planetary turmoil, violent tyranny and resistance.

Faculty
Deepak Asthana [deepak.asthana@ashoka.edu.in], Munmun Ghosh [munmun.ghosh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The industrial revolution would not have happened if sufficient energy supply was not there. It is not wrong to say that development of any country depends upon the availability of energy resources. Globally, the demand for energy has been growing rapidly. Conventionally, fossil fuel, which includes coal, oil and natural gas, have been our major sources of energy. However, as it takes millions of years to form these, we have only a limited number of resources left. Soon we will run out of it. Additionally, excessive use of fossil fuel has caused severe damage to our environment and human health. To ensure the energy demands are met and to prevent the climate change threatening our survival, we have to find alternate energy sources that are greener in nature.

Broadly, energy sources can be categorized in two groups: Nonrenewable and Renewable types.

Renewable energy sources are obtained from natural sources such as sunlight, water or wind, etc. Renewable energy reduces the overall emissions and therefore plays a crucial role in addressing current climate change and pollution issues. In this course we will discuss all the forms of energy sources including fossil fuel to atomic or nuclear energy, hydropower, rechargeable batteries, solar power, hydrogen as fuel and fuel cells. Course is designed to suit anyone who has interest in understanding the underlying scientific concept, pros and cons, and chemistry behind rechargeable batteries and hydrogen production.        

1- Need for sustainable Energy

  • Understanding the energy crisis
  • Analysing energy consumption
  • Discussion about SDG criteria

2- Conventional energy sources: Fossil Fuel

  • What are fossil fuels
  • Our dependency on fossil fuels
  • Availability of fossil fuels

3- Renewable Energy

  • Introduction to renewable energy
  • Biofuel
  • Solar cell technology and its recycling issue
  • Geothermal energy

  • wind power and turbines, hydropower and oceanic currents

    biomass and biological energy sources

      Hydrogen as Fuel

  • Production of hydrogen
  • Basics of Electrolysis and Water splitting
  • Fuel cell
  • Demonstration
  • Issue with Hydrogen storage

4- Rechargeable Batteries

  • Galvanic cell, coin cell
  • Redox flow battery
  • Principle behind Li-ion batteries
  • Na-Battery: Alternative to Li-battery
  • Recycling of batteries

5- Nuclear Energy and Policy

  • Principle of nuclear energy (Fission vs fusion-based reactors)
  • National and International policy of nuclear energy
  • Thorium based nuclear energy (guest lecture)
  • Technical challenges in Fusion-based energy
  • Pros and cons of nuclear power
Learning Outcomes

Knowledge of renewable energy, fossil fuels in addressing climate change and global energy equity.

Solving energy challenges beyond Chemistry: interdisciplinary approaches.

How to practice sustainability in energy research and in life

Overview

Faculty:

Alok Bhattacharya  alok.bhattacharya@ashoka .edu.in   Office AC05 Rm 415 (TSB building)

This course prepares you to start your life as a researcher. A researcher needs to learn how to initiate a research project, plan the research project, execute the plan and finally write up the findings in order to disseminate the results. In the process, the researchers have to follow certain rules, guidelines including statutory requirements. There are due processes that also guide how the research results are written up and who all get credits for the work. The course will be a participatory one involving discussions and case studies.

Evaluation: Assignments and no examination

Learning Outcomes

Topics to be covered:

What is Science

How to read and critique a scientific paper

Source of error in results

Design of a research project or a grant

General Principles of Ethics

Ethics in scientific research

Regulatory guidelines and rules in scientific research

Publication ethics 1

Publication ethics 2

Fostering fairness in lab microenvironment, whistle blowing, lab gossip, detecting and responding to disputes at the lab bench and in lab meetings.

Reading for Writing [CW-1005] [CW-1005-1]

Faculty
Adam Klein [adam.klein@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

 Communication is wider and more varied now than at any time in history and our expanded field of expressive modalities are both indiscriminate and proliferating. Immersed in a world of texts, a torrent of rediscovered and newly translated writings, we are more permeated by language and images than ever. Formerly marginal writings are at the center of our considerations, and the distinctions between visual and linguistic signs have been torn away. So, what and how should a writer read? With openness, anticipation, awe? Or with reserve, a quarrel with sensibility, technique, execution? We’ll read broadly for starters.

Over this course, we’ll encounter novellas, short stories, creative nonfiction, as well as works that combine text and image. We’ll consider the use of photographs in W.G. Sebald’s stories and follow Sophie Calle’s photo-text wanderings in Suite Vénitienne. We’ll revisit this same idiosyncratic artist in Grégoire Bouillier’s strange, comic memoir The Mystery Guest. We’ll read three vivid experiments in form: Vladimir Nabokov’s Pale Fire and Ann Carson’s Autobiography of Red, and Justin Torres’s Blackouts.

In an age of deep-fakes, consciousness machines, and social networks fully entwined with our social lives, considerations of formal strategies for writers abound. We’ll enter the mind-bending stories of Jorge Luis Borges and Alain Robbe-Grillet and Clarice Lispector. Finally, we’ll explore two pioneers in feminist sci-fi James Tiptree Jr. AKA Alice Sheldon and Joanna Russ; the philosophical horror of Brian Evenson; and the "strange stories" of Elizbeth Hand. 

Marcel Duchamp wrote, Water writes always in plural, and in this course, we’ll dip our toes into multiple streams. We’ll consider how, by allowing ourselves to read new forms of writing, we can open our practice and ourselves up to new ways of thinking and writing.

Readings are subject to change. 

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the semester:

Students will encounter a wide variety of approaches to narrative that deploy various formal options including the use of intermedia, fragmentation, appropriation, and other organizational or text-generating strategies. They will produce new work in response to the work they encounter. Students will learn to assess the strengths of these works and will reflect on their learning and development as writers and readers.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

ASSESSMENT

Writers are going to encounter more feedback on their work than most people ever do in their professional lives. My responses are intended to help you reach other readers, to provide you options and models of others’ work and processes. It is my hope that the artistic strategies you encounter in the class may help you to see writing connected to other forms of storytelling, and to consciously avail yourself of new methods. Writing will ultimately be a pact with yourself, and so I prefer to assess grades as collaboratively as possible while adhering to institutional requirements.

1. Each of you will submit three response papers of 1,500 / 2,000 words (two prior to the mid-term, and one three weeks prior to the last week of class). You may take any of the writings you encounter and create your own responses in a way that emulates or deploys a strategy found in the work we’ve studied. Plagiarism will not be tolerated. Plagiarized or AI-generated assignments will not be credited and cannot be made up. They will result in a 0 for the assignment.

Visual Storytelling [VA-2010/ MS-1081] [VA-2010/ MS-1081-1]

Faculty
Vishwajyoti Ghosh [vishwajyoti.ghosh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

VISUAL STORYTELLING: MAKING COMICS, ZINES, PICTURE BOOKS AND PHOTO ESSAYS

Why tell stories visually

As the world’s reading engagement is rapidly shrinking into a palm sized mobile, the engagement with the visual is rapidly becoming the new language, with the binaries between the texts and visuals fading away. In these times visual storytelling is making a strong space for itself in every form of information or content. Be it journalism, health information, economics or plain fiction, the visual approach is now here to stay, in an age where the best of storytelling, poetry, journalism or reportage are now visually led.

What this course is about

In sync with the time’s media or information dissemination, it is important to learn and practice visual storytelling as both a language and a medium that can be incorporated in one’s individual academic discipline. This approach can help the students in articulating their learnings, research and storytelling in multi-disciplinary formats that is much required in today’s realm of information & content, where visual storytelling is an alternate and a popular form of information, opinion and communication.
This course seeks to engage with this fast-moving genre of visual storytelling through zines, picture books, photo essays, animations, comics and graphic narratives with a research led and inter-disciplinary approach, in sync with the student’s core area of interest or discipline.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES

The semester will be a sequential flow from the history of visual documentation and articulation to the modern practices of photo zines, graphic novels, mobile cartoons, comic strips and now visual narratives on the mobile to a practice- based approach.

In the fast-moving visual world, students will learn to negotiate between the visuals and the written word in the process of crafting their individual narratives. The students will also explore and practice the modes and methods of visual storytelling through their chosen styles and influences. The expected outcome for the students will be practice based learning to develop their visual storytelling language, exploring the fluid connections between fact and fiction.

COURSE DELIVERABLES: Every student will be expected to develop, produce multiple research-based short visual stories and graphic narratives/ comics, picture books, photo essays and visual zines or any other output of their choice.

Learning Outcomes

LEARNING OUTCOMES

The preliminary module of this course of 2 weeks will be a curated overview of the published, popular and the prevalent and emerging forms of visual storytelling in the world of graphic narratives and visuals. The idea would be exploring the diversity of practice across the globe and the processes involved in the making. The core idea here will be to discuss the forms and works to bring new practice-based influences and ideas, their working process and explore the architecture of visual storytelling in these works.

Weeks 1-2: Discuss works of art, graphic novels, cartoons, comic strips and create short narratives.

This will be a presentation and discussion-based approach discussing the presented works in detail and the stories behind making many of these works. The idea will be to discuss the journey of the works from the intent to execution and the struggles and transformations that make the narrative in the final output. For example, Van Gogh’s study of the peasantry, the sketch book notes leading to the potato eaters or Somenath Hore’s diaries documenting the Tebhaga movement or Marjane Satrapi’s background story behind the making of Persepolis or Chris Ware’s documentation of the American Midwest or Joe Sacco’s Footnotes from Gaza are some of the well-articulated stories in the making of these works.

Weeks 3-5: Ideate, research, explore graphic storytelling ideas and create micro books, zines etc.

This will be followed by 3 weeks to ideate, research, explore ideas of student’s interest in their areas of discipline followed by field work, data collection and research on the ground. This will include visual data collection, interviews, recording, documentation and conceptualizing the idea based on the research.

This will lead to create micro books, zines etc.

Documentation of the research will be followed to process and distill the findings to create the core conceptual idea and be presented in the studio sessions for the benefit of collective brainstorming and discussions. These discussions with fellow classmates will led to an inter-disciplinary ideation and conceptualization, moving closer to shape and sharpen the core project ideas of the students. The students will also be expected to share the processing of their research findings along with their influences and inspirations.

Weeks 6-7: Exploring possibilities of form, conceptualization, layout, architecture etc. and presentation of a final project idea followed by discussion on similar ideas & influences.

Moving on from research the course will discuss the working process of creating a visual narrative using multiple influences of form and genres. This will include detailed discussions on the various possibilities of the form i.e. different forms that can be explored -doodle narratives, popular comics, mobile based narratives, photo comics, design, layouts, page architecture, typography, sequential storytelling and the work process involved in each, enabling the students to make informed choices in sync with their ideas.

Week 8: Presentation of a final project idea followed by discussion on similar ideas & influences

The following week the students will be expected to present their ideas and preliminary drafts as scribbles/ sketches with fellow batchmates, followed by open discussions, suggestions and ideation to evolve a clear understanding to flesh out the final narrative.

Each student/ project will be further exposed to similar works through display and in-depth discussions on influences and ideas related to the project to lend a visual and storytelling perspective, enabling the practitioner to take one’s work further.

Besides creating multiple micro narratives through the semester, finally, the semester will move to its last weeks to create a bigger multi-page graphic narrative.

Weeks 9-14: Final completion with a mid-level presentation in week 11.

A mid-level draft presentation will be shared in the studio to display the work in progress after 2 weeks then followed by the final 4 weeks or the end of the semester, ready for display, presentation and production. Studio presence in these weeks will be a must.

OUTPUT PARTICIPATION: Though the output will be individual, the process of production will be based on field research, short studio collaborations and conversations and work-in-progress presentations at regular intervals as discussed above.

PREREQUISITES

Basic drawing/ sketching, mobile photography, basic research skills and writing.

Political Philosophy and Public Policy [POL-3084/ PHI-3810] [POL-3084/ PHI-3810-1]

Faculty
Bastian Steuwer [bastian.steuwer@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Public policy requires value judgments. Cases in which we only need to know “what works” are rare. The choice between different policies requires us to trade off different values or trade off benefits to some against burdens to others. Some social scientists therefore seek to describe their task more modestly. The task of social policy as a discipline is to measure, at least estimate, the outcomes or effectiveness of a policy proposal. But even this modest task involves value judgments. How should we measure welfare? Or health? Or poverty? Or inequality? In this course we will connect political philosophy with public policy. Political philosophy is concerned with reasoning about value judgments.

Each week we will connect one debate in political philosophy with a debate in public policy. The public policy debates are often examples. Philosophical debates on inequality, for instance, bear on many policy questions. However, for this course it helps to focus our discussion by looking at one policy case in particular. There will be student presentations on the policy cases and we will work together to draw the connections between the political philosophy material and the social policy debate in India.

The course is intended for two groups of students. First, it is intended for students interested in entering public policy. This means students interested in working for policy-oriented NGOs, think tanks, IAS, public interested spirited litigation, political parties, and so on. The course shall help students sensitize about value questions as they arise in public policy. At the end of the course, students shall be able to identify implicit value questions and reason about them critically. The second group of students are students interested in political philosophy and political theory. Many courses in political theory are, well, theoretical. This course seeks to apply and make relevant debates in political philosophy for real-world concerns. Students interested in political theory can benefit from this applied focus.

Learning Outcomes
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

In the course well will draw on political philosophy/theory as well as economics and law. Basic knowledge of political theory, political or moral philosophy is highly recommended as evidenced by completion of Western Political Thought I, Introduction to Political Theory, or an equivalent course in political theory and/or philosophy. Students without such prior courses should approach me with a short description of their background before registration. Prior knowledge of economics and/or law is helpful but not required.

description:
Introduction to the Study of China [CHI-2001/ HIS-2804/ IR-2038] [CHI-2001/ HIS-2804/ IR-2038-1]

Faculty
Eloise Wright [eloise.wright@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What is China? Who counts as Chinese? What is China’s place in the modern world? These contentious questions have been continually debated both inside and outside China, with more and more urgency. This course will introduce students to a variety of approaches to the interdisciplinary study of the societies and peoples that have been called ‘Chinese,’ both past and present. We will read works by historians, anthropologists, political scientists, sociologists, and other commentators to explore when and by whom these questions have been asked, and how they have been answered. We will examine what the study of China has meant for different kinds of audiences, and how those perspectives have evolved across time and disciplines. Therefore, we will also pay special attention to how ‘China’ has been explained to academic and popular audiences by non-Chinese commentators. As a deeply heterogenous cultural formation that has transformed and been transformed by other cultures and systems, we will consider what is distinctive, or not, about the study of “China” in our time and our region.

This semester, the topical focus for the class is ‘food’, structured around four themes: movement, labour, identity, and ritual.

This course is the core course for the China Studies minor. It is offered in Monsoon semester only.

Learning Outcomes

Think critically about the concept of ‘China’ in long-term historical perspective.

Be able to identify multiple alternative sources through which to learn about China, and analyse their strengths and weaknesses.

Identify common tropes in written and visual primary source material related to China.

Analyse the arguments and sources used by scholars in different disciplines writing about China.

Overview

Tentative context coverage: Integrated Chinese level 1 part 1 Lesson 0-4.1

Lessons 0 through 4.1 of Integrated Chinese introduce students to the very foundations of Mandarin Chinese, guiding them from basic greetings to self-introductions, family descriptions, and discussing dates and time.

The preliminary Lesson 0 focuses on building a strong foundation in pronunciation, tones, and pinyin. Students learn essential greetings like nǐ hǎo and zàijiàn, classroom expressions, and numbers from 0 to 10. This stage emphasizes oral practice, tone recognition, and simple character writing, preparing learners for communication in the classroom setting.

In Lesson 1, students move into formal greetings and introductions. They practice asking and answering questions about names using polite structures such as qǐng wèn (“May I ask…”) and nǐ guì xìng? (“What is your surname?”). They learn to use shì (“to be”) and jiào (“to be called”) to introduce themselves and others. Cultural insights, such as the order of Chinese names and the importance of politeness, are integrated to help students understand not just the language but also social etiquette.

Lesson 2 expands into the topic of family. Students acquire vocabulary for family members—bàba, māma, gēge, mèimei, etc.—and learn to use the measure word gè when talking about people. The verbs yǒu (“to have”) and méiyǒu (“not to have”) are introduced, as well as yes/no questions with ma and question words like shéi (“who”). This lesson highlights the cultural significance of family in Chinese society while encouraging students to describe their own families, often through activities such as drawing family trees or sharing information about their household.

By Lesson 3, students are ready to discuss dates, time, and age. They learn how to count beyond 10, how to express days, months, and years, and how to talk about birthdays using shēngrì. Time expressions like jīntiān (today), míngtiān (tomorrow), and zuótiān (yesterday) are introduced, along with age expressions using suì. Students also learn about sentence order in Chinese, especially the placement of time words before the verb. Cultural notes in this lesson include how dates are written in Chinese (year → month → day) and the role of both the solar and lunar calendars in daily life.

In lesson 4, students will be introduced hobbies (ài hào) in Mandarin. They will be equipped with the ability to: Ask someone what they like to do? Talk about your their hobbies. Respond simply and politely. Key Question Patterns such as: 你喜歡做什麼? / 你有什麼愛好? / 你喜歡+activities嗎?

By the end of Lesson 4.1, students will have a working ability to:

Greet others and exchange names politely.

Introduce their family members.

Ask and answer questions about dates, time, and age.

Read, write, and recognize around fifty basic characters.

These first four units establish the essential foundation of communication, character literacy, and cultural understanding that the rest of the textbook builds upon.

Discussing about personal hobbies, and ask about others’. The first step to deepen the content of conversation.

Learning Outcomes

After completing Lessons 0–4.1, students will have developed the foundational skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing needed for basic interpersonal communication in Mandarin. They will be able to greet others, introduce themselves and their families, and talk about dates, time, and age, while also beginning to read and write approximately 70 essential characters.

In addition to the textbook content, the instructor will supplement lessons with extra vocabulary and cultural knowledge, with the aim of preparing students for the TOCFL Novice level. This ensures learners not only master the material within the book but also expand their practical language use beyond the classroom setting.

courseTitle: Militants or Freedom Fighters? Armed Conflicts in India
description:
Militants or Freedom Fighters? Armed Conflicts in India [POL-2091] [POL-2091-1]

Faculty
Kaustav Dhar Chakrabarti [kaustav.chakrabarti@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

“One person’s freedom fighter is another person’s terrorist” is a common expression that sums up the complexity of armed conflicts around the world. How should we understand the state’s claim to sovereignty when it clashes with some of our most cherished beliefs in the right to self-determination? This course will approach the question through the lens of theories in political science while being grounded in the empirical realities of armed conflicts across India. The course does not take a normative position on these conflicts – we will not assume that armed groups are ‘unlawful’, neither will we valorise them. We will treat armed conflicts as a political phenomenon of interest, and I invite you to use the course to sharpen and test your prior views.

The course will cover four major themes on armed conflicts (or civil wars). Each module will expose you to important theoretical debates, which will juxtapose with case studies from across India. We will begin with establishing a solid conceptual foundation – What are armed conflicts? How are they different from other forms of organised violence? Next, we will examine the causes of armed conflicts. Are conflicts rooted in political and economic grievances? Or should we blame self-interested rebel leaders who are driven by personal ambition and (mis)led by outsiders? We will then ‘apply’ those theories to case studies of Kashmir, Naxal, and Punjab conflicts.

In the second module, we will study how combat, or war-fighting in civil wars differs from conventional interstate war. We will contrast canonical political science accounts of violence with counterinsurgency doctrines of India and US. We will explore how counterinsurgency practitioners view the effect, both positive and negative, of violence and examine empirical studies that scrutinise those views. We will also study other aspects of counterinsurgency that are clubbed under the rubric of ‘hearts and minds’ and look at the role of development programs and electoral politics.

The third module covers arguably the core of guerrilla warfare – armed groups’ relations with the community. The course will introduce you to classical treatise by revolutionary icons - Mao, Guevara, and the Irish Republican Army. We will then examine how armed groups mobilise support and recruit cadre, and the methods that they adopt to solicit the community’s support. 

The fourth module refocuses our gaze on armed groups and identify two key factors that negatively impact rebel groups’ behaviour toward the community - group fragmentation and external support. What happens when armed groups splinter into factions? When do they ‘turn renegade’ and collaborate with the state? What happens when an armed group receives massive support from external factors – foreign bases in inaccessible forests of Myanmar, support from China and Pakistan.

The course culminates with the important topic of conflict resolution where we explore different ways in which civil wars come to an end - military victory and peace deals, but also ‘live and let live’ tacit ceasefire arrangements.  

Learning Outcomes

The goals of the course are threefold. By the end of the course, students should have an overview of some of the major debates in the political science of civil war, especially those that are pertinent to India. In addition, the course will familiarise students with major civil wars (or ‘insurgencies’) in India through detailed case studies. Finally, the course will reinforce the department’s continuous training in analytical thinking. It will bolster students’ ability to distinguish between different theoretical explanations, evaluate the merit of competing arguments made in the literature, and communicate their arguments clearly in written form. 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Please refer to readings from the previous iteration of the course. Expect some modifications (but not many) for the Monsoon 2026 iteration of the course. 

Class 1: Introductions, Greetings, Review of Syllabus. 

Reading and Writing Resources (optional) 

Humphreys, Macartan. Excerpts from Comparative Politics Field Seminar I, Columbia University, 2013

Farrell, Henry. Good Writing in Political Science: An Undergraduate Student’s Short Illustrated Primer, 2010

Edwards, Paul. How to Read a Book, v5.0. School of Information, University of Michigan

MODULE 1: Concepts, Definitions and Causes

What are civil wars, or armed conflicts? How are they different from other forms of organized violence? What are armed groups? What are the causes of armed conflict? Are conflicts rooted in political and economic grievances? Or should we blame self-interested leaders? 

Class 2: What are Civil Wars? 

How does political science define civil wars? If I show you an example, will you be able to tell if it is a civil war or another form of organized violence? What are the major themes in the scholarship of civil wars? Can you identify gaps?  

Kalyvas, Stathis N. 2006. The Logic of Violence in Civil War. Cambridge; New York: Cambridge University Press. (pages 16-31)

Galula, David. 2006. Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice. Westport, CT: Praeger Security International. (pages 1-10)

Staniland, Paul. 2012. “States, Insurgents, and Wartime Political Orders.” Perspectives on Politics 10 (02): (pages 244-246, start reading from ‘Concepts and Outcomes..”) 

Tarrow, Sidney. 2007. “Inside Insurgencies: Politics and Violence in an Age of Civil War.” Perspectives on Politics 5 (03): (pages 587-600, read till end of section I). 

Class 3: What Causes Civil Wars to Take Place? 

What are the causes of civil wars? Can you identify explanations that you can confidently dismiss, or explanations that appear particularly relevant to India? 

Wimmer, Andreas. 2013. Waves of War: Nationalism, State Formation, and Ethnic Exclusion in the Modern World. Cambridge England ; New York: Cambridge University Press. Read Chapter 5 - Ethnic Politics and Armed Conflict pp 143-173

Class 4: Case Study of the Kashmir Conflict 

Ganguly, Sumit. “Explaining the Kashmir Insurgency: Political Mobilization and Institutional Decay,” International Security, Vol. 21, No. 2 (Autumn, 1996), pp. 76-107

Varshney, Ashutosh. 1991. “India, Pakistan, and Kashmir: Antinomies of Nationalism.” Asian Survey 31 (11): 997–1019.

Optional Reading 

Staniland, Paul. 2013. “Kashmir since 2003: Counterinsurgency and the Paradox of ‘Normalcy.’” Asian Survey 53 (5): 931–57.

Class 5: Case Study of Punjab Conflict 

What led one of the more prosperous and well-connected regions in the country to experience civil war, a phenomenon associated with poverty and poor connectivity?

 We will read sections from Mark Tully and Satish Jabob’s classic Amritsar, and Mallika Kaur’s soon to be classic, Faith, Gender and Activism in the Punjab Conflict. The readings exceed 35 pages, but the prose is beautifully crafted and makes for quick reading. If you like good writing, read the entire chapters; but I have suggested trimmed selections to cram everything around 45 pages. 

1.     Tully, Mark, and Satish Jacob. 1985. Amritsar: Mrs Gandhi’s Last Battle. J. Cape. [Chapter 3: The Grievances of the Sikhs] 16 pages

2.     Kaur, Mallika. 2020. Faith, Gender, and Activism in the Punjab Conflict: The Wheat Fields Still Whisper. 1st ed. 2019 edition. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan. [Chapter 8: Guavas and Gaslighting, read pages 223-228] 6 pages

3.     Kaur, Mallika. 2020. Faith, Gender, and Activism in the Punjab Conflict: The Wheat Fields Still Whisper. 1st ed. 2019 edition. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan. [Chapter 9: Glasnost] 23 pages.

Class 6: Case Study of the Naxal Conflict 

Mukherjee, Shivaji. 2021. Colonial Institutions and Civil War: Indirect Rule and Maoist Insurgency in India. Cambridge; New York, NY: Cambridge University Press. [Read Chapter 1: Colonial Institutions and Civil War] 

Optional

Sundar, Nandini. 2008. Subalterns and Sovereigns: An Anthropological History of Bastar. 2nd edition. New Delhi: OUP India. [Introduction]

Kennedy, Jonathan. 2014. “Gangsters or Gandhians? The Political Sociology of the Maoist Insurgency in India.” India Review 13 (3): 212–34. 

MODULE 2: Civil War and and Repertoires of State Response 

How is war-fighting or combat in civil wars different from conventional interstate wars? What makes civil wars particularly violent toward civilians? Overview of how states respond through counterinsurgency and ‘hearts and minds’ state-building activities. Examination of whether violence generates negative consequences. 

Class 7: ‘The Logic of Violence’

 Two big questions - What drives the actions of states and armed groups during civil wars? Why are civil wars so violent toward civilians? We read the seminal Logic of Violence in Civil Wars by Kalyvas. The book's theory itself is divided into four chapters. I have curated sections from different works of Kalyvas to provide a full account in around 40 pages. 

Kalyvas, Stathis N. 2006. The Logic of Violence in Civil War. Cambridge University Press. May 2006. (pages pages 89-106, 118-132) 

Kalyvas, Stathis N. 2008. “Promises and Pitfalls of an Emerging Research Program: The Microdynamics of Civil War.” In Order, Conflict, and Violence, edited by Ian Shapiro, Stathis N. Kalyvas, and Tarek Masoud, 397–421. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Pages 405-414 

Lynn, John A. 2005. “Patterns of Insurgency and Counterinsurgency.” MILITARY REVIEW, 6. (pages 22-25, read the section ‘Basic Model of Insurgency/ Counterinsurgency’)

Kilcullen, David J. 2005. “Countering Global Insurgency.” Journal of Strategic Studies 28 (4): 597–617.  (read the section ‘Competing Paradigms – Terrorism and Insurgency’, pages 604-606) 

Please do the readings in the order that I suggest below. 

1. Start with Kalyvas 2012 (pages 660-661, section "The Control Collaboration Model"). This is a one page summary of the argument. 

2. Read Kalyvas 2006 (pages 89-106, section 4.2 to 4.4). This identifies the problem of separating armed groups from ordinary civilians and explains how the community's compliance is generated.  

3. Read Kalyvas 2008 (pages 405-414, begin reading from the sub-title "Omitted Variable Bias"). This is a longer summary of the theory of selective violence. It will familiarise you with the argument that the threat of violence produces community's collaboration.  

4. Read Kalyvas 2006; (pages 118-132, section 5.3 and 5.4). This adds more detail to the previous reading. 

Put together, the four readings will give you a sufficient picture of Kalyvas's argument that is otherwise spread over 100 pages in the book. Don't think about organizing the readings or think about how they speak to each other. Instead, think about the four readings as different accounts of the same argument. 

In addition, supplement Kalyvas with two perspectives from military practitioners. If you are really pressed for time, you can skip these, but I urge you to read them, since it'll enhance your understanding of how guerrilla wars are fought. 

Lynn 2005 (pages 22-25, section "Basic Model of Insurgency/Counterinsurgency"). Ask yourself - is Kalyvas saying the same thing with more bells and whistles?

Kilcullen 2005. (pages 604-606, section "competing paradigms - Terrorism and Insurgency). 

Class 8: Counterinsurgency Doctrine 

Canon of Western (and Indian)- Counterinsurgency Doctrine. We will compare Kalyvas’s ‘logic of violence’ with case studies of how India and the United States understand the nature of civil war and the way to respond to the threat. Two declassified doctrines of the US and Indian military provide an opportunity to carry out this comparison. We will read the selections of the doctrine with their academic criticisms.

US Army/Marine Corps. 2007. Counterinsurgency: FM 3-24. Boulder, Colo: Paladin Press. (see selections below)

Isaac, Jeffrey et. al. 2008. “The New U.S. Army/Marine Corps Counterinsurgency Field Manual as Political Science and Political Praxis.” Perspectives on Politics 6 (02). 

Army Training Command (ARTRAC). 2006. Doctrine for Sub Conventional Operations, Shimla: ARTRAC 

Ahmed, Ali. Revision of the DSCO: Human Rights to the Fore. IDSA Policy Brief. 

Read selections in the following order.  Just to be sure, sections that I have crossed out in the uploaded documents are not to be read.  

 First, read US Army/Marine Corps Counterinsurgency Field Manual (pages 1-1; 1-5 to 1-8) for state’s understanding of civil wars, and pages 1-19 to 1-25; 1-26 to 1-27; 1-28 to 1-29 for state’s understanding of counterinsurgency. 

Second, read reviews of the US doctrine by Stephen Biddle and Stathis Kalyvas in Isaac, Jeffrey et. al. 2008 (pages 347-353). 

Third, read the Indian Army’s Doctrine of Sub-Conventional Operations (pages 8-13, 16-23, and 38-39). 

Fourth, read a review by military officer turned scholar Ali Ahmed (pages 3-6, start from ‘doctrinal dissonance’) where he offers a human rights based review of the doctrine. 

Class 9: Does Violence Incur Negative Consequences?   

Counterinsurgency ‘Hearts and Minds’: Beyond Violence 

Kalyvas tells us that coercion prevails over persuasion, as a result of the strategic nature of the contest between a state and an armed group. On the other hand, COIN doctrines espouse restraint and call for winning ‘hearts and minds’. We extend our understanding of the motivation of armed actors and the consequences of coercion. 

Lyall, Jason, Graeme Blair, and Koseuke Imai. 2013. “Explaining Support for Combatants during Wartime: A Survey Experiment in Afghanistan.” American Political Science Review 107 (04): 679–705.

Sambanis, N., J. Schulhofer-Wohl, and M. Shayo. 2012. “Parochialism as a Central Challenge in Counterinsurgency.” Science 336 (6083): 805–8.

Class 10: Role of Electoral Politics and Parties  

Chandra, Kanchan, and Omar García-Ponce. 2019. “Why Ethnic Subaltern-Led Parties Crowd Out Armed Organizations: Explaining Maoist Violence in India.” World Politics 71(2): 367–416.

Optional Readings 

Kohli, Atul. 1997. “Can Democracies Accommodate Ethnic Nationalism? Rise and Decline of Self-Determination Movements in India.” The Journal of Asian Studies 56 (2): 325.

Lacina, Bethany. 2009. “The Problem of Political Stability in Northeast India: Local Ethnic Autocracy and the Rule of Law.” Asian Survey 49 (6): 998–1020. 

Class 11: What is the Role of Development in Civil Wars? 

 Dasgupta, Aditya, Kishore Gawande, and Devesh Kapur. 2017. “(When) Do AntiPoverty Programs Reduce Violence? India’s Rural Employment Guarantee and Maoist Conflict.” International Organization 71 (3): 605–632

 

MODULE 3: GUERRILLA WAR 

Revolutionary ideologues call for guerrilla war as people’s war. How do they generate support from the community? Do all communities respond alike to armed groups’ call for support? Who supports armed groups? Who joins armed groups? What makes some communities more capable of extending support than others? 

 

Class 12: How do Armed Groups Fight: Canons of Guerrilla Warfare 

What do some of the most iconic thinkers of guerrilla war (or ‘revolutionary war’) think about civil wars? How do they distinguish irregular war from conventional war, and how do they envision defeating a superior adversary? 

 

Zedong, Mao. 1937. On Guerrilla Warfare. University of Illinois Press. (pages 41-57,102-114) 

General Headquarters Irish Republican Army. 1956. Handbook for Volunteers of the Irish Republican Army (chapters 2,3,4,6. They add to 7 pages)

Guevara Ernesto. 1961. Guerrilla Warfare (pages 7-14) 

 

Class 13: Support Through the Strategy of Persuasion   

Mao, Che, and the IRA call for armed groups to generate support from the community. Is this strategy always superior from the perspective of the goal of meeting the larger goal of the movement? What are the pros and cons of the strategy of persuasion? When is this strategy likely to be fruitful? 

Begin with Stewart and Liou who outline the relative strengths of both coercion and persuasion. Then, read Mampilly, and focus on ‘Gramscian balance’, skimming the rest. Finish with Weinstein.   

Stewart, Megan A., and Yu-Ming Liou. 2016. “Do Good Borders Make Good Rebels? Territorial Control and Civilian Casualties.” The Journal of Politics 79 (1): 284–301. [read pages 285-286, look at markings in the uploaded document] 

Mampilly, Zachariah Cherian. 2012. Rebel Rulers: Insurgent Governance and Civilian Life During War. Cornell University Press [pages 50-58]

Weinstein, Jeremy M. 2006. Inside Rebellion: The Politics of Insurgent Violence. Cambridge University Press. [Chapter 5: Governance] [skim]

Nguyen Van Thieu. 1982. Our Strategy for Guerrilla War. In  Chaliand Gérard  (ed) Guerrilla Strategies: An Historical Anthology from the Long March to Afghanistan

 

Optional Readings

Wood, Elisabeth Jean. 2003. “Insurgent Collective Action and Civil War in El Salvador.” Cambridge Core. Cambridge University Press. August 2003. [Chapter 4]

Petersen, Roger Dale. 2001. Resistance and Rebellion: Lessons from Eastern Europe. Cambridge; New York: Cambridge University Press. [Chapters 1 and 2]

 

Class 14:  : Mobilisation - Who Joins Armed Groups? Why?  

Key Questions 

Who Fights? What are the correlates of recruitment into armed groups? 

What are the reasons or motivations that prompt individuals to join armed groups? 

What are the processes through which individuals join armed groups? 

Are individuals who join armed groups different from those who support them from outside? 

Readings 

Humphreys, Macartan, and Jeremy M. Weinstein. 2008. “Who Fights? The Determinants of Participation in Civil War.” American Journal of Political Science 52(2): 436–55. Read for substance, skim the technical sections on statistics. 

Parkinson, Sarah Elizabeth. 2013. “Organizing Rebellion: Rethinking High-Risk Mobilization and Social Networks in War.” American Political Science Review 107(3): 418–32.

Tezcür, Güneş Murat. 2016. “Ordinary People, Extraordinary Risks: Participation in an Ethnic Rebellion.” American Political Science Review 110(02): 247–64. Read abstract and introduction to get the gist of the argument. 

 

Further readings for future research 

Petersen, Roger Dale. 2001. Resistance and Rebellion: Lessons from Eastern Europe.

Cambridge: Cambridge University Press

Gates,  Scott.  2002.  “Recruitment  and  Allegiance:  The  Microfoundations  of  Rebellion.”

Journal  of  Conflict  Resolution  46  (1):  111–130.

Eck, Kristine. 2014. “Coercion in Rebel Recruitment.” Security Studies 23: 364-398. 

Eck, Kristine. 2018. “Recruitment and Violence in Nepal’s Civil War: Microstudies under the Microscope.” Asian Survey 58(2): 261-280.

 

Class 15: Community Collective Action – Dense Social Ties and Armed Group-Community Ties 

Key Questions 

What is/are the difference(s) between individual level unit of analysis and community level unit of analysis?

What is the difference between bonding ties and bridging ties? 

What kind of social networks come to the aid of armed groups? 

What are the mechanisms through which social networks aid armed groups? 

Reading 

Sarbahi, Anoop. 2021. “The Structure of Religion, Ethnicity, and Insurgent Mobilization: Evidence from India.” World Politics 73 (1): 82–127. 

Further readings for future research

Staniland, Paul. 2012. “Organizing Insurgency: Networks, Resources, and Rebellion in South Asia.” International Security 37 (1): 142–77.  

Rubin, Michael A. 2020. “Rebel Territorial Control and Civilian Collective Action in Civil War: Evidence from the Communist Insurgency in the Philippines.” Journal of Conflict Resolution 64(2–3): 459–89.

 

MODULE 4: ARMED GROUPS REDUX

Mao and Guevera lay out a blueprint of revolutionary war and paint the revolutionary guerrilla as a social reformer who patiently wins over the community to fight against the stronger state. Do revolutionary practitioners remain true to theory? In this module, we examine some factors that influence the behaviour of armed groups, especially their treatment of community members - access to external sources of funding, splintering, and collaboration with the state.

 

Class 16: External Support and Consequences on Behaviour Toward Community Members 

Toft, Monica Duffy, and Yuri M. Zhukov. 2015. “Islamists and Nationalists: Rebel Motivation and Counterinsurgency in Russia’s North Caucasus.” American Political Science Review 109 (2): 222–38. 

Salehyan, Idean, David Siroky, and Reed M. Wood. 2014. “External Rebel Sponsorship and Civilian Abuse: A Principal-Agent Analysis of Wartime Atrocities.” International Organization 68 (3): 633–61.

 

Class 17: Armed Group Fragmentation and Fratricide 

Two articles that explain why armed groups splinter into rival factions and the dynamics of factional violence. In the following class, we will take up the related topic of how some armed groups switch sides and ally with the state.  

 

1. McLauchlin, Theodore, and Wendy Pearlman. 2012. “Out-Group Conflict, In-Group Unity? Exploring the Effect of Repression on Intramovement Cooperation.” The Journal of Conflict Resolution 56 (1): 41–66.

2. Pischedda, Costantino. 2018. “Wars within Wars: Why Windows of Opportunity and Vulnerability Cause Inter-Rebel Fighting in Internal Conflicts.” International Security 43 (1): 138–76.

 

Class 18: Fragmentation and Armed group-State Collaboration

We extend the discussion of conflict among armed groups to a related question - why do armed groups ‘flip’ and collaborate with the state.  

 

1. Staniland, Paul. 2012. “Between a Rock and a Hard Place: Insurgent Fratricide, Ethnic Defection, and the Rise of Pro-State Paramilitaries.” Journal of Conflict Resolution 56 (1): 16–40.

2. Staniland, Paul. 2017. “Armed Politics and the Study of Intrastate Conflict.” Journal of Peace Research 54 (4): 459–67. 

 

MODULE 5: CASE STUDIES, GENDER. CONFLICT TERMINATION

 

Class 19: Nagaland 

The story of Nagaland and Mizoram have similar beginnings, but take different trajectories at the turn of Partition. Read for – state violence, guerrilla war, fratricidal violence, and peace-making both with India and among armed factions. 

Wouters, Jelle J. P. 2018. In the Shadows of Naga Insurgency: Tribes, State, and Violence in  India’s Northeast. Oxford University Press. (Chapter 4)

Chakrabarti, Kaustav. 2021. Underground Governance: Rules-Based Order by Armed Groups in Northeast India [dissertation, Brown University]. (Chapter 4, selections)

Sundar, Nandini. 2011. “Interning Insurgent Populations: The Buried Histories of Indian Democracy,” no. 6: 11. [repeat reading, revise your notes from the Mizoram reading]

The readings are more voluminous than I could have liked, but many sections can be skimmed, and the time that it takes to read will be less than the number of pages would otherwise suggest. Jelle Wouters is one of my favourite writers and a role model for beautiful prose. He shows two faces of the state in Nagaland - one that is coercive and the other that is developmental. Skim his engagement with anthropology theory and read for content that shows the state’s two dimensions. Follow it with a chapter from my dissertation (pages 6-34, begin from ‘Summary of Evidence’ and read till end of Section 3). The chapter shows how factional conflict is different from state-armed group conflict. Case studies of Dimapur and Kohima also show both ‘tribalism’ at play and armed group-community ties. Skim the sections on governance and focus on factional conflict and armed group-community ties. Revise your notes for the Sundar article that you have read for Mizoram. 

 

Class 20: Mizoram 

Mizoram is a remarkable case study of both war and peace, which makes its relative absence in scholarly debates all the more perplexing.

Pachuau, Joy L. K., and Willem van Schendel. 2015. The Camera as Witness. Cambridge University Press.

Sundar, Nandini. 2011. “Interning Insurgent Populations: The Buried Histories of Indian Democracy,” no. 6: 11.

Jafa, Vijendra Singh. 2001. “Counterinsurgency Warfare The Use & Abuse of Military Force.” South Asia Terrorism Portal.

Lalrawnliana. 2014. Freedom Struggle in Mizoram. Aizawl: self-published.

Start with Chapter 17 of Pachuau and van Schendel. Prof Pachuau who teaches at JNU and is herself from Mizoram presents a history of Mizo society through photographs. This chapter will ‘show’ details of civil war. Follow it by reading Nandini Sundar’s oral history of civil war in both Mizoram and Nagaland, where she focuses on the strategy of grouping, or forced displacement of village communities into internment camps.

Two accompanying articles provide primary source evidence. Read Jafa’s (another IAS officer who continues to be hugely admired, as I found out, in Mizoram) recollection of a candid conversation with a military officer who questioned the morality of his actions (pages 10-12, start with the highlighted part). Do not miss selections from a memoir of Lalrawnliana, a former commander of the Mizo Army that captures vivid details of guerrilla warfare and the role of the community.   

Class 21: Assam 

Baruah, Sanjib. 2005. Durable Disorder: Understanding the Politics of Northeast India. New Delhi; New York: OUP India. Chapter 7: The Indian State and ULFA

Baruah, Sanjib. 2005. Durable Disorder: Understanding the Politics of Northeast India. New Delhi; New York: OUP India. Chapter 8: Twenty-Five Years Later: A Diminished Democracy 

Mahanta, Nani Gopal. 2013. Confronting the State: ULFA’s Quest for Sovereignty. New Delhi: Sage Publications. Chapter 5, read pages 144-145

 

Class 22: Civil War and Gender 

Trigger Warning: Anubha Bhonsle’s case study has details of sexual violence against  Manorama, a young women from Manipur whose death prompted Irom Sharmila to a 16-year long hunger strike to demand the repel of the Armed Forces Special Powers Act. If you feel that reading this might cause you discomfort, please skip the first few pages and begin from page 112 - ‘At the Nupi Samaj, a prominent Meira Paibi group….’ 

 

Theory 

Bakken, Ingrid Vik, and Halvard Buhaug. 2021. “Civil War and Female Empowerment.” Journal of Conflict Resolution 65(5): 982–1009. [Read pages 982-990 and 1000-1003] 

 

Case Studies 

Meitei community: Bhonsle, Anubha. 2016. Mother, Where’s My Country?: Looking for Light in the Darkness of Manipur. Latest Edition. New Delhi, India: Speaking Tiger Publishing Private Limited. [Read Chapter 8 ‘Indian Army, Rape Us!’, pages 108-121] 

Naga Community: Manchanda, Rita. 2005. Naga Women Making a Difference: Peace Building in Northeastern India. Women Waging Peace Policy Commission. [Read Part Two: Women’s Contributions to the Peace Process. Pages 12-27] 

Kuki/Zomi Community: Sharma, G Amarjit. 2018. “Politics of the Informal: Women’s Associational Life and Public Space in the Hills of Manipur.” Economic and Political Weekly 53(8): 48–55.

 

Class 23: Kashmir 

Hasnain, Syed Ata. 2012. Kashmir: Analysing “Heart is My Weapon” Doctrine. South Asian Idea 

"Everyone Lives in Fear" Patterns of Impunity in Jammu and Kashmir. 2006.  Human Rights Watch. Vol 18, No 11(C). See selections below 

 

The Human Rights Watch report is extensive and voluminous. To keep the reading manageable, read the summary and key recommendations (pages 1-11). Then move to Section V and Section VI. The two sections provide a glimpse into the nature of violence carried out by state and armed groups. We will try to compare them. 

 In Section V, read the introduction to the section, and introduction to sub-parts A, B, C and D. In each sub-part, read a couple of examples. Do the same for Section VI.  

 

Class 24: Civil War Resolution/Termination 

How do conflicts end? What explains the successful transition to peace in Mizoram, a two-decade long ceasefire without conflict resolution in Nagaland, and continued hostility in Manipur?  

Walter, Barbara F. 1997. “The Critical Barrier to Civil War Settlement.” International

Organization 51 (3):

Jafa, V.S. “Mizoram Contours of Non-Military Intervention.” Faultlines. Available online  

 https://www.satp.org/satporgtp/publication/faultlines/volume4/Fault4-JafaF1.htm.

Mahadevan, Prem. 2008. “A Model for 21st Century Counter-Terrorism? -.”Faultlines  Vol 19. Available online - 

https://www.satp.org/satporgtp/publication/faultlines/volume19/article1.htm.

 Begin by reading Walter’s famous 1997 article about commitment problem as a major barrier toward conflict resolution. Follow it with contrasting case studies of military approaches to conflict termination in Punjab (Mahadevan, read only the Conclusion) and political negotiations in Mizoram (Jafa, read the last section ‘Towards Peace and Settlement’). Note that both case studies are drawn from South Asia Terrorism Portal, which has a reputation of celebrating militaristic strategies.

No readings!!

courseTitle: Real and Imagined Journeys: Tibet Through Imperial Eyes
description:
Real and Imagined Journeys: Tibet Through Imperial Eyes [HIS-3522/ CHI-3202/ ENG-3460] [HIS-3522/ CHI-3202/ ENG-3460-1]

Faculty
Sayantani Mukherjee [sayantani.mukherjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Real and Imagined Journeys: Tibet through Imperial Eyes

HIS-3522/CHI-3202/ENG-3460

Monsoon 2026

Tuesdays & Thursdays 10.10-11.40 am

Sayantani Mukherjee – sayantani.mukherjee@ashoka.edu.in – AC02-339

In this class, we will investigate some of the ways in which the knowledge of particular geographical and cultural spaces in the trans-Himalayan regions was constructed over the course of time. Our aim will be to examine two central issues: the production of knowledge and historical memory in, and about Tibet, within the context of entwined British and Chinese colonial and imperial forces, as well as the agency of those engaged in such productions.  

We will look at Indian, Chinese, Tibetan, and British travelers and travelogues in the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth centuries to ask; what is the relationship between articulations of an individual or communitarian knowledge of the land—and the routes through which it may be traversed—and the development of cartography and ethnography as coercive disciplines within an imperial imaginary? Highlighting the phenomenological connection between the physical experiences of travel and abstracted knowledge about colonial spaces, we will look at the linkages between the landscape, the space, the traveller, and the audience of the account. Questions of power and violence will be uncovered in reading through unique relationships of intimacy—the traveller and the landscape, and the audience to the experience of travel—between “colonial” agents and “colonised” space. The asymmetrical relations of prerogative and access: who is allowed to travel, who can be called an explorer, what particular efforts distinguish scientific and sacral knowledge. These questions are never more acute than when travellers embody processes of knowledge production, step-by-meticulous-step.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Objectives:

Read intertextually and understand literary productions as artefacts of historical and social construction.

Summarize academic monographs in South and East Asian studies and introduce salient points in

             notes and in speech.

Be able to draw connections between works to gain an overview of scholarly and historiographical debates.

Be able to trace theoretical or methodological trends across multiple empirical contexts.

Learn the skills of co-writing and co-presenting to gain a sense of how cooperative work can integrate intellectual property as well as collective clarity.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Requirements and Expectations:        

Assessment & Assignments:

40% - Regular participation in class discussions (including group essay discussions)

20% - Mapwork

20% - Flash essays (x6, best of 4)

20% - Group essay and discussion

Attendance, Participation and Discussion Étiquette:

I will not take attendance in each class meeting, however, participation in weekly class discussions is a mandatory part of your grade and is necessary for succeeding in the course. If you have circumstances that might affect attendance at a specific class meeting, please let me know ahead of time whenever possible. Flexibility is especially important since Covid is still with us. To protect your privacy, please do not describe any medical situations to me; just inform me that the situation exists and be prepared to provide a doctor’s note if requested.

Participation is part of your grade, and should be based on attentive reading, listening, and preparation. Always keep an open mind and be respectful of your classmates and your instructor regardless of what you wish to say, or whether you agree with what has already been said. Being respectful also means that (1) if you have not completed a particular reading, please refrain from commenting on it (2) in the normal course of discussion, if you have just spoken, you should refrain from speaking again until others who wish to contribute have done so (3) contributions to discussion should be based on the readings, lectures, and discussion questions, and should aim to improve our collective understanding of them. In general, please avoid unstructured/unsupported reflections as well as topics that are beyond the scope of the course.

Mapwork

We will be dedicating a few classes over the course of the semester to understand the production of (Tibetan) space through the medium of maps. Mapwork will range from short quizzes to close reading maps to plotting route surveys. No additional preparation will be required if you have been regularly attending classes. Classes with a mapwork component will be indicated on the syllabus, these dates are not negotiable.

Flash essays

Over the course of the semester, you will be required to write six short essays in response to a prompt provided in class. You will receive a PASS or FAIL grade for each essay. As long as you receive a pass for at least four of your six essays, you will receive the full twenty points of this grade component. If only three of your essays pass, you will receive fifteen points towards your final grade. If only two pass, you will receive ten points. If only one passes, you will get five points. If none pass, you will receive zero points for this component. In the event that all six of your essays receive a pass, extra credit up to five points will be considered.

All these essays will be hand-written in notebooks provided in class, and the dates will not be announced beforehand. No additional preparation will be required if you have been regularly attending classes.

Group essay

Over the course of the semester, the entire class will work on one single long-form essay as your final exam. The format will be discussed in class, and we will discuss the progress of the essay through regularly scheduled check-ins during class time. These check-ins are indicated on the syllabus and count towards your participation grade.

The essay will be awarded one final grade out of twenty points. Every single student will receive the same number of points for this grade component. The use of any generative AI for this essay will result in zero points for this assignment for everyone.

Intellectual Integrity, Plagiarism, and AI Policy

The intellectual venture in which we are all engaged requires of faculty and students alike the highest level of personal and academic integrity. As members of an academic community, each one of us bears the responsibility to participate in scholarly discourse and research in a manner characterized by intellectual honesty and scholarly integrity.

 

Scholarship, by its very nature, is an iterative process, with ideas and insights building one upon the other. Collaborative scholarship requires the study of other scholars’ work, the free discussion of such work, and the explicit acknowledgement of those ideas in any work that inform our own. This exchange of ideas relies upon a mutual trust that sources, opinions, facts, and insights will be properly noted and carefully credited. In practical terms, this means that, as students, you must be responsible for the full citations of others’ ideas in all of your research papers and projects, and you must always submit your own work and not that of another student, scholar, or internet agent.

 

While the use of generative AI and LLMs may have already become a part of your academic process, remember that AI isn’t merely problematic but technology which actively reshapes and intensifies the worst tendencies of knowledge relations. AI is a form of computation and it is also an apparatus that configures and patchworks concepts, policies, institutions and subjectivities to force out a certain kind of end product. This is not simply a nasty application of an otherwise productive technology. At base AI and LLMs are no more than forms of statistical pattern finding, which means that the end product is fake knowledge and fake text, even when it appears to be “accurate”. Because such technology relies on abstracting away all specific context in order to create generalisations that can be applied to anything, the end product is very easy to identify and mark down. If you are using AI to formulate your points of view, your analysis and arguments, or for other parts of the generative process including formulating style and voice, then be aware that you are simply cheating yourself of the opportunity to develop original insights. If you use AI you are not imbibing or producing analysis or knowledge, it will reflect in your work and earn you an automatic fail for that assignment. 

 

This classroom should constitute a form of mutual and relational accountability, where we learn from each other rather than prioritise reductive automation. Any breach of this intellectual responsibility and the goal of community learning is a breach of faith with the rest of our academic community. It undermines our shared intellectual culture, and it will not be tolerated in this class.

description:
Physics of the Universe [PHY-2850/ AST-2850] [PHY-2850/ AST-2850-1]

Faculty
Terizhandur Rajagopalan Seshadri [terizhandur.seshadri@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course will introduce the students to the contents of the universe and the physical processes that occur in them.  It will describe how, starting from the big bang, the universe expanded to its present size, what forces it experienced, the nature of dark matter and dark energy, how galaxies, stars and planets formed, the origin and properties of compact objects such as neutron stars and black holes and the predicted future course of evolution of the universe.  The prime role of General Theory of Relativity in many of these processes will be highlighted.

Syllabus:

(1) Contents of the Universe from Stars/Galaxies to largest scales
(2) The smooth expanding Universe: Hubble law-redshift-Newtonian cosmology-Dark matter, Dark energy
(3) The Hot Universe: Big bang-Thermal history-Nucleosynthesis-Atom formation-Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation-Puzzles in cosmology-inflation-seed fluctuations-sound waves
(4) Structuring the universe: gravitational instability-spherical collapse-galaxy formation-dark ages-21 cm line-reionization-lyman alpha clouds-galaxies
(5) Gas in galaxies-atomic and molecular probes-formation of stars and planets-stellar structure and evolution-end state of stars.
 

Learning Outcomes

The student will develop appreciation of the many exciting phenomena that go on in the universe and learn how to understand them using only the basic laws of Physics.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

1. The Physical Universe, Frank H. Shu, University Science Books
2. Foundations of Astrophysics, Barbara M. Ryden and Bradley M. Peterson, Cambridge University Press
3. An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics, B.W. Carroll and D.A. Ostlie, Cambridge University Press
4. Astrophysical Concepts, M. Harwit, Springer
5. IGNOU PHE-15 Study Material

Faculty
Hao Yu Lu [hao.lu@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This curriculum track bridges the transition from exploring personal lifestyle preferences to managing active social relationships and executing functional tasks in academic environments. Through intensive study of complex sentence structures, students master social planning, polite professional arrangements, and performance evaluation. 

Lesson 4, Dialogue 2 – Hobbies: Let's Play Ball 

This segment introduces active social coordinating, focusing on how to extend invitations, suggest activities, and gracefully handle counter-proposals or rejections when making weekend plans.

Core Grammar & Vocabulary Highlights

Key Vocabulary: Yesterday (昨天), so/therefore (所以), foreign country (外國), to treat/invite someone (請客), in that case/then (那).

Grammar Forms:

The Conjunction那 / 那麼 (nà / nàme; then, in that case): Initiating a response based on a prior statement.

去 (qù; to go) + Action: Structural pattern for expressing localized intention (e.g.,我們去看電影 / Let's go see a movie).

Soliciting Agreement with好嗎 (hǎo ma): Appending tags to sentences to seek soft compliance or consensus.

Lesson 5 – Visiting Friends

This unit navigates the linguistic and cultural protocol of visiting a friend’s home. Students explore standard hospitality exchanges, offering and accepting beverages, and describing surroundings.

Core Grammar & Vocabulary Highlights

Key Expressions: "Who is it?" (誰呀？), "Please come in" (請進), "Nice to meet you" (認識你很高興).

Grammar Forms:

The Particle 了 (le): Introduction to its basic use indicating a completed action or a change of state within a narrative sequence.

The Adverb 才 (cái; not until): Expressing that an action happened later than expected.

Special Review: Keeping It Casual (Lessons 1-5) – A synthesis module analyzing conversational shortcuts and high-frequency colloquialisms.

Lesson 6 – Making Appointments

  This unit covers functional, real-world communication strategies via telephone and messaging networks. Students learn to coordinate meeting times, request assistance, and interact politely with institutional authorities.

Core Grammar & Vocabulary Highlights

Key Vocabulary: To make a phone call (打電話), teacher (老師), availability (時間), test (考試), problem (問題}).

Grammar Forms:

Prepositional 給 (gěi): Targeting the recipient of an action (e.g.,給我打電話 / call me).

Modal Verbs要 (yào) & 想 (xiǎng): Differentiating obligations, concrete future plans, and desires.

Lesson 7 – Studying Chinese

This unit centers on academic self-reflection and communication in an educational setting. Students develop the vocabulary required to review class performance, talk about test results, and deCore Grammar & Vocabulary Highlights

Key Vocabulary: Exam考), character (漢字), grammar (語法), slow (慢), fast (快), to prepare (預習).

Grammar Forms:

Descriptive Complements using 得(de): Evaluating how an action is or was performed (e.g., $\text{寫字寫得很好}$ / writes characters very well).

The Adverb 就 (jiù): Indicating that an action happened earlier or more smoothly than anticipated.

Learning Outcomes

By completing this module of the Integrated Chinese (4th Edition) curriculum, covering Lesson 4, Dialogue 2 through Lesson 7, you will reach a proficiency level equivalent to TOCFL Band A (Level 1), ACTFL Novice-High. Over the course of these lessons, you will acquire approximately 120–140 high-frequency words and achieve mastery in reading and writing about 90–110 unique characters, bolstered by the understanding of roughly 15–20 essential semantic radicals. Pedagogically, this curriculum enables you to perform several real-world communication tasks, including navigating social negotiations and invitations, observing proper hospitality etiquette as both a guest and a host, and managing professional interactions such as scheduling appointments with instructors over the phone. Additionally, you will develop the ability to conduct academic self-reflection, using descriptive complements to critique and discuss your own language learning habits and exam performance.

Overview

The “Designing Your Life” process has evolved through rigorous research at
Stanford’s Design Your Life Lab (d.life). This Lab teaches courses, offers programs,
and conducts research that applies Design Thinking’s innovation principles to life,
education, and career challenges. Building on their success and under the guidance of
Stanford’s Studio team, over 300+ universities have adopted the programme
including Harvard, Yale, Cornell, Dartmouth, and Northwestern, among others.

The "Designing Your Life" framework uses design thinking as the scaffolding of Life
Design. It draws on the tenets of Behavioural Science, Positive Psychology,
Philosophy, and other fields to design your life and future. The framework enables
one to gain agency and be generative, productive, and proactive.

A creative and generative framework that aims to address ambiguity is more
important now than ever. An extensive amount of research has shown that the youth
of today, more often than not, feel uncertain about their future.

This course is for students — For any and every student looking to approach and
think about their future more intentionally. The course will benefit students seeking
clarity regarding their future aspirations and those currently facing any stress about
their way forward in life.

The course is offered under a license through Stanford-trained Life Design Educator,
Certified Instructor, and Coach, Navyug Mohnot.
