courseTitle: On Photography: Histories, Theories, and Practices
description:
On Photography: Histories, Theories, and Practices [VA-3018/ MS-2239/ SOA-3106] [VA-3018/ MS-2239/ SOA-3106-1]

Faculty
Rakhi Peswani [rakhi.peswani@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

On Photography – Histories, Theories, Practice 

VA 3018-1/ MS-2239/ SOA-3106-1

(Monsoon 2026)

Course Faculty Instructor: Rakhi Peswani

 Email: rakhi.peswani@ashoka.edu.in

Course Pre-requisites for students: Curiosity and interest in photography history and/or practices. Any VA practice courses whether elective or gateway, preferred.

Schedule: Tuesday and Friday – 3pm to 4:30 pm.

Office Hours: Tuesdays, 2-3pm

This course will bring together image making histories, concerns, theories and practices, based on photographic techniques and technologies.

The course will comprehensively introduce proto-photographic methods to trace the various technologies that came together in the invention of modern Photography. We will re-trace modern and contemporary material as well as some nineteenth and twentieth century cultural reactions, theoretical formulations in the histories of photographic image-forms.

Considering its interdisciplinary nature, the media of photography will be introduced and explored through its social and cultural histories, important theoretical underpinnings, contemporary usage as well as creative possibilities, bringing in perspectives from Art History, Visual Culture, and Visual Anthropology.

The course will be led with exercises and assignments in artistic practice of the form.

 

Field trip : One exciting field trip will be planned to Museo Camera, and perhaps a photo studio, in Gurugram.

Learning Outcomes

 

  1. Students will learn hands-on techniques from what makes a camera to what calls for a good image.
  2. To recognize and locate photographic image-making language as a nuanced process with historical and theoretical underpinnings.
  3. To frame (reading) and craft (making) photographic practices from the discourse of technique, technology, aesthetics and as a sign.
  4. To discern and gain confidence in situating and making of photographic images.
  5. To discern the historical, political and cultural implications of Photography.

 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Each module will be for a month (will run for 8 sessions). All three modules provide a comprehensive overview of Photography with path-breaking readings on the field.

 Students seeking to audit the course must consider two out of the three assignments.

Module 1: Proto-photography techniques and histories:

This module will emphasize on the early techniques and technologies that led to the invention of the photographic camera as we know it.

Various histories of image making will be excavated to understand the concepts of photography.

This module will also delve into the interdisciplinary nature of photography, the relation of art and science, the inherent quality of photo(light) sensitivity, differences in technique and  technology, and the  impact photography had in shaping global modernity.  

Proto-photography and various techniques of image making:

  1. Fading of a color or a surface due to light as reaction or creation of an image due to light sensitivity.
  2. Camera Obscura
  3. Camera Lucida
  4. Proto-photographic methods and image making in oil painting- development of Single Point (Linear) Perspective.
  5. Linear perspective and development of photography
  6. Tableaux Vivant for painting- history painting, Caravaggio and baroque light.
  7. Shroud of Turin and the ‘miraculous’ image form.

Readings:

  1. Mike Ware- Proto Photography and the Shroud of Turin
  2. Peter Galassi – Before Photography

Artists’ references:

  1. Single Point Perspective:   Some paintings, drawings and images of Masaccio, Giotto, Durer, Raphael, Caravaggio,

  2. Cyanotype and Daguerreotype: Anna Atkins, Henry Talbot- Cyanotypes. Louise Daguerre.

Workshop: Hands on Cyanotype workshop

Practice exercise:

Practice Workshop - Making Cyanotype images.

1 day- 3 hours. VA studio.

Assignment 1: create 4-5 image forms using any one or two proto-photographic methods introduced in class. 

The assignment will be based on experimenting and producing images with the aid of tools that seemingly appear familiar or simplistic.

Use some or any of the methods as tools to create 4-5 images and reflect (write an essay) on the experience, technique the outcome of the images, especially considering what are the significant markers of making images in such ways? what kind of aesthetic attitude or aesthetic form does such a method entail? 

Alternate assignment  – Cyanotype workshop exploring photo-chemicals and sun exposures to create image forms.

(Considerations of Dark room, safe light, 2 D and 3D image forms, imagination and image creation.)

 

Module 2: Photography as Representation and as Reproduction

This module will explore early and mid 20th C photography, through its defining features of reproduction and representation.

Both these tropes will be explored to understand how photographic images played a role in the political, social, cultural shaping of individuality, modernity, urbanism, and nationalism. 

Readings:

  1. Walter Benjamin (1931) - Little History of Photography
  2. Walter Benjamin (1936) – The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction

Artists References:

Louise Dagguere, Edward Muybridge, Henry talbot, Karl Blossfeldt, David Octavius Hill, Julia Margaret Cameron, Victor Hugo, Felix Nadar., August Sander, Man Ray, Laslo Moholy Nagy,  Sasha Stone, Henri Cartier Bresson, Eugene Atget, Raghu Rai,

Practice exercise:

Assignment 2: Making a Photo Essay- Or a photographic Folio based on a chosen theme.

Representation, Reproduction, Sequentiality and Narration 

Using some of the most basic aspects of photographic form, representation and reproduction, construct a sequential arrangement of photo images that shape a narrative of your choosing. 

Early Photography had its claim in indexicality- a 'true' 'impression' of an object or event that has existed in front of the camera lens. While photographic images stand for real/truth of an image, ie, 'this exists' in a moment in time, it is also a framing device; it is an apparatus that lends itself to re-presentation and reproduction of an image. 

While a still image captures the fleeting momentary aspect of a world we live in, it represents this moment in specific ways. It reproduces this moment, frames it and imbues it with the subjectivity of the photographer. 

It is this aspect of photography that this assignment explores, especially in relation to early photographic folios, albums and other incunabula as Walter Benjamin points out to us.

Note:  Sequentiality and Repetition could be utilised to hold certain directorial vision or poetic aspects to the narrative. Also you could utilise the inherent qualities of a photograph- that a photograph manages to capture a fleeting moment of a second (shutter speeds), as well as varying qualities of light (aperture);  it captures certain frames that human eye cannot capture, including a point of view where human eye may not be able to reach.) 

 

Module 3: Photography and Identities

This module will address the complex lines of the real and the fictional in relation to photographic images. The two readings will address the forms and formations of identity and the political nature of representation, distribution and circulation of photographic images.

The module will emphasise on aspects of photography that spill into the amateur, the cinematic, and the everyday. Its ubiquitous aspects will be explored through various lenses.

The practice exercise will be a way to address the complex space of creating meanings and identities through photographs.

  • Tableaux Vivant and Photography.    
  • Photography and Anthropology,
  • Archival Practices and Photography.

Artists References:

Hippolyte Bayard,  Marcel Duchamp, Homai Vyarawalla, Helmut Newton, N. Pushpamala, Cindy Sherman, Sheba Chachi, Annie Leibovitz, Robert Mapplethorpe, Jitish Kallat

Readings:

  •               Christopher Pinney  (1997) - Camera Indica          Chapter- Chamber of Dreams
  •               Susan Sontag   (1973) - On Photography          Chapter- On Melancholy

Practice exercise:

Assignment 3: Shifting from the premise of photography as that representing a reality, create a series of images that provide a convincing impression of a construction/ a framing/ or a fictitious real of a tableau. Use lights, props, models, or any required additional elements to create a ‘subject’ of description through photography.

Bibliography of further readings

Additional reading:

  • Roland Barthes (1980)-  Camera Lucida- Reflections on Photography
  • Christopher Pinney (2004): Photos of the Gods : The Printed Image and Political Struggle in India
  • Susan Sontag (1977)-  On Photography
  • John Berger (1972) – Ways of Seeing
  •  Aileen Blaney and Chinar Shah (2018): Photography in India from archives to Contemporary Practice

Faculty
Dipankar Bhattacharya [dipankar.bhattacharya@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course will introduce general techniques of data analysis and of drawing inference from multi-attribute, multi-mesenger data.  Specific examples from Astronomy will be used, but the underlying methods will have applicability in a wide variety of domains.

Syllabus:

Brief overview of different electromagnetic bands and the instruments employed for astronomical data collection.  Ground vs Space based astronomy. Inference from data, role and techniqes of model fitting.  Temporal, spectral and direct/indirect imaging data will be treated in an unified framework.

Types of data - Image data, Spectral data, Temporal data, Interferometry data, Event data.
Principles of reduction of different data types. Calibration requirements.  Background estimation and removal. Error estimates.  Elements of Fourier analysis.

Astronomical data and metadata formats:  The FITS standard.  Viewing, writing and manipulating FITS files.  The AstroPy package.

Hands-on analysis of data including introduction to packages:

Optical: IRAF
Measuring the optical magnitude of a star. Estimating the surface brightness profile of a galaxy. Reduction of a one-dimensional spectrum - wavelength calibration, line identification, continuum subtraction, line profile fitting and radial velocity measurement.

X-ray/Gamma-ray: HEASOFT
Binning of event data to create image, spectrum and light curve.  Response Matrix and Auxiliary Response Files.  Orbital motion of a space-based observatory and charged particle background.
Temporal analysis of Crab pulsar data - barycentric correction, power spectral estimation, epoch folding, phase tracking.  Estimation of spin and spin-down rate.  Transient detection: GRB

Radio interferometry: friendlyVRI, CASA
Creation of an image from visibility data, snapshot vs earth rotation synthesis.  Spectral channels and data cubes.  Local Standard of Rest correction.

Gravitational Waves
Matched filtering through a burst segment and parameter estimation.

Learning Outcomes

This course is intended to familiarise the students with the analysis of multi-messenger astronomical data at different wavebands, including optical, X-ray, radio and gravitational waves.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Recommended Reading:
1. Observational Astronomy (2nd ed): D. Scott Bimey, Guillermo Gonzalez and David Oesper, Cambridge University Press
3. Essential Radio Astronomy: James A. Condon and Scott A. Ransom, Princeton University Press
5. Handbook of X-ray astronomy, ed. K. Arnaud, R. Smith and A. Siemiginowska, Cambridge University Press
7. General Relativity and Gravitational Waves: Essentials of Theory and Practice: Sanjeev Dhurandhar and Sanjit Mitra, Springer
8. Basics of Fourier Analysis for High Energy Astronomy: T. Belloni and D. Bhattacharya, Handbook of X-ray and Gamma-Ray Astronomy, Springer [arXiv: 2203.04106]

Pre-requisites:  This course is intended to familiarise the students with the analysis of multi-messenger astronomical data at different wavebands, including optical, X-ray, radio and gravitational waves.  General knowledge about astronomical sources and various types of radiation is essential.   Working knowledge of linux operating system, python programming and conda environment will be required.

- W.B. Yeats

Invasions, conflicts, persistant warfare, How does one make sense of it all? Does theory make the world go round or is it ideas, interests, and institutions? How do those ideas, interests, and institutions all change with the passage of time? Does war emerge from threats or does peace come with allies/alliances? Do we live in a world of anarchy or cooperation? Does a state’s perception impact its behaviour? And if so can this behaviour be understood to better explain and predict how the international system works? This course aims to use theory as a way to understand the world and the ways in which it shifts and turns in times of peace and war. It seeks to adopt different lenses to see which one works best (and in what context) to understand state behaviour in an interconnected world; and in doing so hopes to find new ways of understanding not just how we got here, but also where we might go next.

Foreign Policy Analysis [IR-2050] [IR-2050-1]

Faculty
Quintijn Benjamin Kat [quintijn.kat@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

As a discipline, IR is initially taught in terms of grand theories—realism, liberalism, constructivism, Marxism—which try to explain in one fell swoop the entirety of international politics. Foreign Policy Analysis is much more granular because it examines how policymakers decide. As you will learn, actual decision-making is always messier than what grand theories imply. So, from the grand and the ‘macro’, we look on the domestic, state, organizational, and personal levels to understand the multitude of factors that affect a country’s foreign policy. To do this, we make use of various conceptual lenses: theories of rational choice and alternatives to rational choice, individual/group psychology, emotions, culture/identity, and more.

So, what are the kind of questions that this class will help you think about? Perhaps questions such as ‘Why did the United States respond to the discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba with a blockade rather than any other possible response?’, ‘Why do state leaders sometimes choose policy options with a high risk of failure while less risky options are available?’, ‘How did domestic politics impact US-Iranian relations in the early twenty-first century?’, ‘How did Nehru’s experience of colonial subjugation shape his ideas of non-alignment?’, ‘What are the effects of social media on foreign policy?’, and ‘Can small states be successful in their foreign policy and, if yes, under what conditions?’. These are just some examples. The main objective of the course is to introduce you to the many approaches one can take when trying to understand, explain, and analyse foreign policy processes and decision-making.

Learning Outcomes
  • A basic understanding of Foreign Policy Analysis and how it converges with and diverges from systemic IR theory.
  • Familiarity with several theories and core concepts of Foreign Policy Analysis.
  • Ability to distinguish between different levels of analysis and how each of these entails varying approaches to research.
  • Ability to question rhetorical justifications for prominent foreign policy decisions that may not explain them adequately.
  • Ability to apply a Foreign Policy Analysis theoretical framework to a case of choice or to write a critique of such a theoretical framework.

Computational Astrophysics and Geophysics [PHY-4830/ PHY-6830/ AST-4830] [PHY-4830/ PHY-6830/ AST-4830-1]

Faculty
Dipankar Bhattacharya [dipankar.bhattacharya@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Computational modelling is an essential tool in Astrophysics and Geophysics.  Comprehension of diverse physical effects including fluid and gas flow under gravity, heat and radiation transport, oscillations and seismology, formation of structures in the universe etc is being developed through computations.  This course will introduce the students to some of the basic techniques to perform such computational modelling.    At the heart of the mathematical description of these problems are partial differential equations (PDEs).  Several common methods used to solve PDEs will be discussed, with application examples drawn from Astrophysical and Geophysical settings.   Statistical moelling through Mone-Carlo methods and methods of inference from data will also be discussed.

The following is an outline of the syllabus:

1. Ordinary and Partial differential equations; Different discretization schemes - Finite difference, Finite Volume and Finite element methods; Euler, Crank-Nicholson and Runge-Kutta integration schemes. Fourier Transforms and Spectral Methods.
2. Applications to the structure and oscillations of stellar and planetary bodies, dynamic, thermal and radiative processes in diffuse material, Geophysical heat and material transport.
3. N-body simulations and formation of structure in the universe 
4. Bayesian inference from observed data. Basic Monte Carlo and MCMC techniques.
Learning Outcomes

1. Learn to formulate physical problems in a computational setting
2. Learn various algorithms for solving problems described by differential equations, their pros and cons and domain of applicability.
3. Experience hands-on the application of numerical techniques to astrophysical and geophysical problems
4. Learn methods to draw statistical inference from data

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Prerequisites:

Coding ability in any one programming language such as Python, C, C++ or FORTRAN.   Familiarity with differential and integral calculus. Basic knowledge of classical mechanics and thermodynamics.  Basic plotting and visualisation techniques.  Working knowledge of Linear Algebra and Root finding methods.

Recommended Reading:

1. Numerical Recipes: The Art of Scientific Computing -  by W.H. Press, S.A. Teukolsky, W.T. Vetterling and B.P. Flannery, Cambridge University Press, http://numerical.recipes
2. Finite Volume Methods for Hyperbolic Problems - by Randall J. Leveque, Cambridge University Press
3. Numerical Solutions of Partial Differential Equations - by K.W. Morton and D.F. Mayers, Cambridge University Press
4. Partial Differential Equations for Scientists and Engineers - by Stanley F. Farlow, Dover Publications
5. Lecture Notes on Computational Geophysics by A.P. van den Berg: http:// www.geo.uu.nl/~berg/compgeoph/lecturenotes.pdf
6. Data Analysis: A Bayesian Tutorial by D.S. Sivia and J. Skilling, Oxford University Press

Overview

The main aim of this course to introduce the fundamental concepts of General Theory of Relativity and then extends its application to Modern Cosmology.

1. Brief review of Special Theory of Relativity

2. The Equivalence Principle and motivation to General Theory of Relativity

History Sleuths [HIS-3527/ ENG-3910/ MS-3335] [HIS-3527/ ENG-3910/ MS-3335-1]

Faculty
Aparna Vaidik [aparna.vaidik@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Ever fancied yourself as Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple, Mr. Thorndyke, Karamchand, Feluda or as a crime scene investigator – Gil Grissom or Fox Mulder or even James Bond? A reconstruction of the crime scene, a search for and evaluation of evidence, serializing events before and after the commission of crime, and coming up with a narrative of how and why a crime was committed are all part of a detective's workday. A historian’s practice of their craft is much the same. The whodunit in our case takes the form of collection and evaluation of several different kinds of evidence that are etched in time – archival, oral, material, experiential, digital, and psychic. The evidence may speak volumes or may be silent or scattered or fragmented; or it can be absent like Hansel’s breadcrumbs that were eaten by the birds; and on some days the Houdini historian even makes evidence appear where people believe there was none. After all, a historian, much like our literary detectives, combines the skills of a huntsman, a conjurer, a forensic scientist, and a ventriloquist. This course takes you on an adventurous journey into the world of history sleuthing where you will learn to hunt for clues, closely read them, and learn to narrativize them.

Learning Outcomes

Learning objectives:

1.     Learning historian’s craft: How does a historian go about piecing together the past? What is the relationship between evidence and narration? Historical thinking trains us to question what we know: That is, it forces us to ask how do we know what we know. By doing this it helps establish the connection between evidence and conclusion and differentiate between an assertion and an argument. 

2.  Learning How to Narrativize: By learning to formulate a narrative, you will learn to look for sources, understand the relationship between evidence and narration, to establish the connection between evidence and conclusion; and to differentiate between an assertion and an argument. 

3. Learning history through literature: History and Literature are both narrative forms with common origins. Literature also provides an important doorway for studying our past.

Faculty
Sanjiva Prasad [sanjiva.prasad@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This introductory course offers a foundation in computational thinking as a powerful, structured approach to problem-solving. It is built around one uncompromising standard: correctness. Students will explore the core principles of computation and gain familiarity with key subdisciplines in the field.Working both with and without code, students will learn to design, analyze, and refine solutions with attention to correctness, clarity, and style. The course is anchored in two fundamental computational models: the functional model, which treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions, and the imperative model, which views it as a sequence of state-changing instructions. More details are available on the course webpage.

Learning Outcomes

1. Algorithmic Thinking: Develop the ability to analyze and design algorithms as systematic problem-solving approaches, with an emphasis on precision and efficiency.  

2. Program Correctness and Design: Understand the theoretical principles of program correctness, as well as design principles that emphasize clarity, structure, and style in solutions.  

3. Computational Models: Explore computation through two core paradigms, the functional model (evaluation of mathematical functions) and the imperative model (state manipulation via sequences of instructions).  

4. Practical Coding Skills: Gain hands-on experience coding in OCaml, with opportunities to explore other languages such as Python, Rust, Java, and Datalog.

5. Foundational Disciplinary Topics: Acquire an introductory understanding of subfields such as information theory, cryptography, compiler design, databases, numerical algorithms, quantitative modeling, and machine learning.

description:
Empires, Nomads and Barbarians [HIS-3538] [HIS-3538-1]

Faculty
Upinder Singh [upinder.singh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Did ancient India have a political tradition analogous to Greek democracy or the SPQR slogan of the Roman republic? What are the differences between ideas of empire in ancient India and China? How did the Achaemenid empire of Iran change world history? Was Alexander’s invasion of India an episode of little historical consequence? In what ways did Chandragupta and Ashoka interact with their Hellenistic contemporaries? What lies behind Pliny’s complaint of a drain of Roman gold to India? What impact did the Bactrian Greeks, Scythians, Parthians and Kushanas have on Indian history? What does the Begram treasure tell us about the centrality of Central Asia and Afghanistan in the ancient world? How did Gupta kings deal with the threat posed by the Hunas and Sasanids? Why is it that in spite of a long history of varied, vibrant interactions with the world, Sanskrit texts display a disdain for foreigners, describing them as mlechhas or barbarians? -- This course answers these and many other questions by viewing the history of the Indian subcontinent within global and comparative frames. It uses primary sources -- textual, archaeological, epigraphic, numismatic and visual – to explore the intricate networks of political, economic, religious, intellectual and artistic interaction across the Afro-Eurasian world. Touching on anthropological and historical debates related to states, empires, nomads, frontiers and borderlands, the course explores how cultural others become ‘barbarians,’ what happens when ‘barbarians’ become rulers, and the cultural synthesis that can emerge from war and political conflict.

Learning Outcomes

Students will understand the interconnections between different parts of the ancient world, and the value of a comparative historical perspective.

description:
Law and Lawyerly Thinking: An Introduction for Entrepreneurs and Beyond [ENT-2039] [ENT-2039-1]

Faculty
Nikhil Sud [nikhil.sud@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

So you don’t want to be a lawyer. Or maybe you do. Who knows, and who cares, because either way, a general understanding of key legal concepts – and the ability to think like a lawyer – will add invaluably to your arsenal as you step out into the real world. This knowledge and skillset will make you a distinctly sharper leader in the business world, because legal issues routinely – and increasingly – strike at the heart of business risks and opportunities, and are integral to overall corporate strategy. And so not just lawyers but a wide range of business executives (including C-suite executives) and their advisors routinely work on legal issues alongside lawyers. Legal roles are increasingly business roles, and vice versa. Therefore, the knowledge and skills this course provides will make you a sharper entrepreneur, or a sharper business executive, or a sharper consultant to businesses across sectors. But that’s not all. The benefits extend to countless roles even beyond the business world: you’ll be a sharper problem-solver regardless of field. To this end, the course will explore key concepts across several fundamental areas of law including issues involving goods and services; tort law; constitutional law; criminal law; administrative law; competition law; intellectual property law; evidence law; and legal procedure – each of which is applicable across a wide range of professional fields. The course will explore these concepts in two jurisdictions: India and the U.S. The course will also introduce students to thinking (and related) skills fundamental to not just the legal profession but also to the many professional roles (discussed above) that require frequent engagement with the law or with lawyers. These skills include: crafting and interpreting legal positions and instruments; analyzing and applying a case; textual interpretation more broadly; analytical writing; persuasive writing; persuasive verbal argument; and highly analytical thinking with unrelenting precision, agility, and creativity.

This course offers an introduction to war and strategy in international politics. Faculty
Munmun Ghosh [munmun.ghosh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

1. Atomic Structure

Recapitulation of Bohr’s theory, atomic spectrum of hydrogen atom. its limitations Wave mechanics: de Broglie equation, Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle and its significance.

Quantum numbers and their significance, Radial and angular wave functions for hydrogen atom. Radial and angular distribution curves. Shapes of s, p, d orbitals.

Pauli’s Exclusion Principle, Hund’s rule of maximum multiplicity, aufbau principle and its limitations. Electronic configuration

2 class (3 hrs)

2. Chemical Bonding:

Ionic bond: General characteristics, types of ions, size effects, radius ratio rule and its limitations.

Covalent bond: Lewis structure, Valence Bond theory, Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory (VSEPR)

Energetics of hybridization, Bent’s rule,

Molecular orbital theory. Molecular orbital diagrams of diatomic and simple polyatomic molecules N2, O2, C2, B2, F2, CO, NO, and their ions; HCl (idea of s-p mixing and orbital interaction to be given).

Covalent character in ionic compounds, polarizing power and polarizability. Fajan’s rules and consequences of polarization.

Ionic characters in covalent compounds: Bond moment and dipole moment.

6 class (9 hrs)

3 Chemical Periodicity:

Brief discussion of the following properties of the elements, with reference to s & p-block and the trends shown:

Effective nuclear charge, shielding or screening effect, Slater rules, variation of effective nuclear charge in periodic table.

Atomic and ionic radii

Ionization enthalpy, Successive ionization enthalpies and factors affecting ionization enthalpy and trends in groups and periods.

Electron gain enthalpy and trends in groups and periods.

Electronegativity, Pauling’s/ Allred Rochow’s scales. Variation of electronegativity with bond order, partial charge, hybridization, group electronegativity.

2 class (3 hrs)

4. Acids & Bases

Arrhenius & Protonic Theory of Acid & Bases,

Strength of acids & bases, General trends in periodic table, superacids, pH scale, Buffer solution, Acid-Base titration, Choice of Indicators

2 class (3 hrs)

5. Coordination Chemistry:

IUPAC nomenclature of coordination compounds, isomerism in coordination compounds.

Stereochemistry of complexes with 4 and 6 coordination numbers.

Bonding in Coordination Complex

Reaction Mechanism

CFT (Crystal Field theory)

10 class (15 hrs)

6. Magnetism

Magnetic properties of complexes

Zeeman interaction

2 class (3 hrs)

basic understanding of metals.

atomic structure, electronic configuration

Acidity & basicity

periodic table, periodic trends

Inorganic complexes/ Coordination of complexes

reaction of coordination complexes

Colour and magnetism in complexes

courseTitle: Archive Fever: Representation, Affect, and Historian's Craft
description:
Archive Fever: Representation, Affect, and Historian's Craft [HIS-6500] [HIS-6500-1]

Faculty
Aparna Vaidik [aparna.vaidik@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Description

History as an academic discipline traces back its genealogy to European Enlightenment, a philosophical movement in 17th and 18th century Europe identified with the Age of Reason. The institutionalization and professionalization of History followed in the 19th century. History as a discipline came to be conceived of as a rigorous science based on evidence. Since that time, notwithstanding the intellectual and ideological orientation of a historian, historical inquiry has been premised on gathering and interpretation of evidence. However, the postmodernist critique shook the foundational ideas of the discipline. It questioned the objectivity and stability of historical facts, the historians’ narratives and their epistemic truth. The consequent disciplinary churn led to a  rethinking of the idea of archive and the referential paradigm of the historian’s craft.  This course explores the questions that came to fore in what has come to be known as the ‘archival turn’ in History. These include: Is archive simply a physical repository of historical materials or an idea or a storehouse of memories and dreams? What role does power and privilege play in the creation and one’s access to an archive?  What distortions or accretions does time create in the archival objects? What are the layers of narratives that an archive embodies? What does it visibilize or silence? In what way does the historian's subjectivity and desires mediate their work in the archives? How does one work with archival artifacts - against the grain or along the grain? What is the difference between an extractive and ethnographic approach to the archives? Can the archives be queered? What are the ethics of working with an archive? This course engages with the conceptual writings on archives and seeks to train students in working with different kinds of archival material. The class format will be a combination of discussions on a set of thematic readings and workshops with archival materials.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Objectives

1.     Learning historian’s craft: What is a historian’s relationship with their archive? How does a historian go about piecing together the past? What is the relationship between evidence and narration?

2.     Historical thinking trains us to question what we know: That is, it forces us to ask how we know what we know. By doing this it helps establish the connection between evidence and conclusion and differentiate between an assertion and an argument. 

3.     Learning about limitations of the discipline: History is a way of studying the past but not all past is history. The historian needs a variety of tools to construct the past. Knowing about the strengths and limitations of those tools is part of historical practice.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Course Requirements

I. Discussion Participation: (50% of your course grade) Please come prepared for the class discussions. This class is weighted heavily toward personal reading and discussion. Therefore, speaking and sharing ideas will contribute to your participation grade. Please also keep in mind that the assignments will not make up for absence at discussion or lectures. It has two components:

a. Attendance: (constitutes 10% of discussion participation grade) Attending the classes is mandatory. You have three grace absences which include family emergencies, period leave, mental health days. Please use them only if you must. Other than these two grace absences, each absence will lead to loss of the attendance grade. More than 5 absences (please note whether un/excused) will be an automatic fail for the entire course. Please honor this policy and not inundate my inbox with medical notes or emails with long explanations for absences. 

b. Facilitating Class Discussion: (10% of your discussion participation grade) You can choose any one segment to facilitate the class discussion

II. Research Essay: (50% of your course grade) You are expected to write a 3,500-5,000 word research essay using primary sources. It is an essay that you work on throughout the semester:

10 October ‘26 - Submission of Primary Sources 

13 October ‘26 - Office hour check-in. Come prepared to discuss the primary sources you would be working with. Please sign-up.

13 November ‘26 - Submission of First Complete Draft - the draft has to be ready for peer-review, complete with title, a thesis, footnotes and bibliography. 

17 November ‘26 - Office hour check-in - Come prepared to discuss the Draft Please sign-up

17-22 November ‘26- Peer Review  - You are expected to grade the First Draft of two of your peers. 

23 November ‘26 - Presentation

15 Dec ‘26 - Final Submission

Academic Honesty and Plagiarism

You are required to uphold academic honesty in all aspects of this course. As faculty, I too am obligated to uphold the Honor System, and will report all suspected cases of academic dishonesty. Think for yourself, do your own work, and cite sources properly.

AI Policy: Writing is Thinking. It is also hard. Becoming a critical and imaginative thinker is the reason you have come to the University. An indiscriminate use of AI amounts to letting it rob you of your voice, your agency and your creativity. I am interested in how you think, not how ChatGPT thinks. While it is okay to use AI for editing your essay but NOT for summarizing your readings, for coming up with talking points or for writing your essay. You are expected to disclose AI use transparently—whether in text, images or visualizations or for editing.



Grade Appeals

You are always welcome to discuss a paper, but if you want the grade reconsidered, you must first submit a two-paragraph written appeal in which you evaluate your paper in each of the four criteria: thesis, organization, evidence, and style. Remember that a grade does not reflect  process (it does not measure whether you worked hard) and it certainly does not reflect a value judgment about you as a person. A grade constitutes an evaluation of the quality and analytical rigor of the thesis, organization, evidence, and style of a single piece of work, so ensure that your written appeal addresses your finished paper in terms of those criteria rather than time and effort expended on it. Appeals must be submitted in hard copy no later than one week after graded papers are returned in class.

International History [IR-1010] [IR-1010-1]

Faculty
Nayan Ranjan Chanda [nayan.chanda@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In this course, we will analyze the major events of the Cold War through the
prism of three analytical lenses: interests, individuals, and ideology. We will
attempt to evaluate the extent to which each of these factors, either singly, or
in combination, affected decision making on inter-state relations during the
decades of the Cold War and in the post-Cold War decades.
Secondly, the course will also highlight how the progression of the Cold War
decades also witnessed the making of deeper inter-connections across the
globe. For example, we will consider how the distant developments of the
Cold War were also of relevance in shaping India’s position in the world.
Furthermore, we will examine how the developments of the Cold War were
equally shaped, not just by the superpowers, but also by smaller, poorer, and
recently decolonized countries. The course will also show the role trade and
technology played in sparking a new Cold War between the superpowers.
Enabling an evaluation of why developments unfolded in the way that they did
during the Cold War, therefore, the course
will show how the appraisal of events from more than a single point of view, is
necessary to understand the impact of the Cold War more fully on present day
international politics.
Finally, we will also explore the newer directions of the historiography on the
Cold War, including the ways in which its debates influenced popular culture
and the international perceptions of technological aid. Ultimately, we will ask,
in what ways can our analysis of the Cold War help us in shaping our present
day understanding of the conduct of international affairs in the present?

Learning Outcomes

This elass will equip students to study international relations by providing essential context, analytical framework and a deeper understanding of the forces that shape today's global affairs.

Art and Craft of Sound [MS-3041] [MS-3041-1]

Faculty
Gaurav Chintamani [gaurav.chintamani@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Overview:

Of all the senses we possess, hearing cannot be voluntarily turned off. Sound — as music, sound design, sound art, or spoken word — can construct, amplify, and direct engagement, often subliminally. This course deconstructs sound through three lenses: its Nature (physics and perception), its Behaviour (interaction with space and medium), and its Interaction (how selective processing and manipulation shape a listener's interpretation). We then move through the levels of intervention available in pre- and post-production via the DAW, building toward techniques applicable across podcasting, audiobooks, music production, sound design, and sound art.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Outcomes:

  • Build a strong foundation in the key components of sound, including the ability to visualise and interpret how sound interacts with different acoustic environments.
  • Identify the skills necessary to record and manipulate audio, using post-production techniques to process and tweak audio for coherence and continuity in program material.
  • Make informed choices on recording equipment and technique, navigate DAWs, and work with multitrack audio; engage with sound using processing tools, with a focus on emotional contour and context.
  • Create an audio-driven story or podcast — including licensed stock music and SFX — or a piece of music, and render it to industry-standard specifications so it translates across playback systems.

Microbiome and Health [BIO-3457/ BIO-6457] [BIO-3457/ BIO-6457-1]

Faculty
Kavita Agarwal [kavita.agarwal@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course offers an engaging introduction to the world of the human microbiome and its growing significance in health and disease. We move beyond popular terms like probiotics and good bacteria to explore the microbiome as a dynamic and context-dependent system. Beginning with core concepts in microbiology, students will gain the essential background to understand microbial life, diversity, and interactions within the human body. You'll examine how microbial communities interact with each other and with the host, ranging from beneficial to pathogenic relationships, and how these shifts influence disease outcomes.

Throughout the course, we will:

  • Explore distinct microbial ecosystems across the human body—oral, gut, and vaginal microbiomes—and their roles in maintaining or disrupting health
  • Investigate the concept of microbiome dysbiosis and its contribution to site-specific and systemic diseases
  • Analyze how therapies such as antibiotics and probiotics affect microbial communities, and how microbiome-informed treatments are emerging
  • Study polymicrobial interactions, microbial cross-talk, and mechanisms like colonization resistance

The course will also introduce students to key experimental and clinical methodologies used in microbiome research—such as sequencing technologies (NGS), in vitro models, and study designs (cross-sectional vs. longitudinal)—and how these approaches influence findings and interpretations. An important emphasis of this course is on developing critical reading and analytical skills. Through guided discussions of primary research papers and reviews, students will learn how microbiome studies are designed and interpreted, how to evaluate the strength of scientific evidence, and how to thoughtfully engage with emerging ideas and controversies in mcirobiome research. Assignments and projects will connect scientific concepts with real-world applications, including evaluating the claims and evidence behind consumer products like probiotics and hygiene products targeting microbiota.
By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess microbiome research and appreciate its relevance in clinical practice, public health, and everyday life—all while gaining insight into one of the most rapidly evolving areas of biomedical science.

Learning Outcomes

After completing this course students should:
1. Understand the biology, diversity, and utility of microorganisms.
2. Explain what the microbiome is.
3. Describe how microbiota benefits the human body.
4. Explain how changes in microbiome are associated with adverse health outcomes.
5. Describe how microbiota targeting therapies work and what are the current challenges related to microbiome research.

In addition, by reading and evaluating relevant articles, students will become familiar with approaches used to solve research problems concerning microorganisms.

courseTitle: Demystifying Investments: Private Equity and Venture Capital
description:
Demystifying Investments: Private Equity and Venture Capital [ENT-2034] [ENT-2034-1]

Faculty
Sridhar Sethuraman [sridhar.sethuram@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Institutional capital has played a transformative role in emerging markets such as India, enabling entrepreneurs to build businesses that address some of society's most pressing challenges while creating significant economic value. From grants and angel investments to venture capital, private equity, and public markets, the journey of capital mirrors the journey of enterprise itself.

This course examines how investors identify opportunities, assess risk, support entrepreneurs, and create value across different stages of a firm's evolution. Through a series of cases drawn from sectors such as fintech, real estate, social enterprises, healthcare, and technology, students will explore the realities of investing in rapidly evolving markets. The course combines analytical frameworks with practitioner insights from investors and entrepreneurs who have built, funded, and scaled successful ventures.

At a deeper level, however, this course is not merely about investing in companies. It is about learning to think like both an entrepreneur and an investor. Regardless of one's profession or career path, every individual allocates scarce resources under uncertainty. The most important of these resources is not money but time. The same principles used to evaluate investments—opportunity cost, risk, compounding, resilience, and adaptability—apply equally to decisions about careers, relationships, and life.

Students will be encouraged to view their own professional journeys through the lens of enterprise evolution. Early career choices often resemble startup investing, requiring experimentation, risk-taking, and learning. Mid-career transitions resemble growth-stage investing, demanding focus, scale, and disciplined execution. Later stages require the stewardship and adaptability expected of mature enterprises operating in competitive environments.

While the course focuses primarily on private and unlisted investments, its broader objective is to develop a mindset rather than mastery of a specific asset class. By the end of the course, students should be better able to:

• Recognize the limits of their knowledge and develop intellectual humility.

• Identify the few critical factors that determine success in complex situations.

• Build mental models for continuous learning and decision-making under uncertainty.

• Understand the role of fear, failure, and resilience in both investing and entrepreneurship.

• Apply investment thinking to life and career choices, not merely financial decisions.

Ultimately, the course seeks to help students become better allocators of capital, time, and effort—three resources that determine success in business and in life.

Learning Outcomes

This course is designed as an overview, not a foundational finance course, and does not require any prior finance coursework. Success in the course depends largely on practical common sense, intellectual curiosity, and the ability to apply critical thinking. In fact, in previous editions, students from non-finance or non-economics backgrounds have often excelled and gained significant value from the material, sometimes outperforming the average.

We make sufficient arrangements (by means of external resources, remedial classes from TA & group leaders) to enable non-fin- eco students to self-learn basic concepts like NPV, IRR and cash flows within the first 4 sessions of the course.

The course offers:

Insights into the mindset, decision-making frameworks, and journey of investors in unlisted assets, from startups to listed entities (covering Grants, Seed funding, Venture Capital, Private Equity, and Listed Companies) within emerging companies in India.

Diverse perspectives from investors at different stages of a company's growth.

Exploration of real-life investor decisions and what drives them to invest in particular entrepreneurs.

Discussion on the key factors that shape unlisted investments.

Tools and knowledge to help students identify opportunities and make well-informed decisions from an institutional investor’s standpoint.

If time allows, the course will also present the entrepreneur’s perspective at each of these stages.

Target Participants:

Students aspiring for careers in investment management (VC/PE/Family Office/ AIFs firms) or investment banks

Understand nuances of how investor firms evaluate investments and their reasons for seeking out certain entrepreneurs.

Students aspiring for careers in consulting firms esp. MBB

Since a large share of consulting and advisory work today originates from private equity–backed or listed companies, understand how investors actually drive strategic and operational decisions inside firms. Participants learn how PE and growth investors influence priorities such as capital allocation, cost structures, expansion strategy, professionalization of management, M&A, and exit readiness.

Students aspiring to join start-ups or PE funded enterprises and/or to be entrepreneurs,

An insight into the mind set of decision maps of private investors and actions that they may face in their entrepreneurial journey.

Others

Institutional capital is increasingly shaping which sectors grow, which firms scale, and which roles get disproportionate opportunities and rewards. Understanding how PE and growth investors allocate capital and drive value creation will therefore have a direct bearing on your own career choices as a working professional. This perspective enables students to make more informed decisions about which sectors to enter, which types of firms to join, and how to interpret the strategic and operational priorities set by top management.

Faculty
Rajendra Bhatia [rajendra.bhatia@ashoka.edu.in]
Teaching Fellow
Pritam Chandra [pritam.chandra_tf@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The key concepts of Mathematical Analysis are limits and continuity. In our first Calculus course we learn about sequences and series of real numbers, and about the behaviour (continuity, differentiaion, integration) of a (single) function. In this course we first revisit these concepts from a little more rigorous point of view, and then go on to study sequences and series of functions. Thus whereas Calculus is the study of one function, Real Analysis is the study of infinitely many functions together. This course is the foundation for a major part of mathematics. Topics like Probability, Stochastic Processes, Differential Equations, Measure and Integration, Fourier Aalysis, Functional Analysis all go further with ideas picked up in this course.

This course also trains the student to understand and write precise and rigorous proofs and to recognise economy and elegance of mathematical arguments.

It is essential that the student has a thorough grasp of what was taught in the Calculus course. Many new concepts have to be picked up quickly in this course. Students can help themselves by revising their Calculus course before they come to this course. In addition they could make themselves familiar with the language of metric spaces (the very basic notions and examples).

Learning Outcomes

Understanding of convergence, continuity, limiting processes, sequences and series of functions.

Ability to understand and to write out formal proofs.

Appreciation of beauty, economy and elegance in mathematics.

 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

It is absolutely essential to have a good grasp of Calculus.

The recommended text for this course is K. A. Ross, Elementary Analysis.

You could also look at the books by W. Rudin, Terence Tao, R. Bartle and D. Sherbert

At some point early in the course the concept of metric space is introduced. While the concept is easy and natural, it worries students just because it is new. You can help yourself by reading about it (from one of the books mentioned above or from any source in the web).

Faculty

Overview

The objective of this course is to provide UG and PhD students with a comprehensive foundation in nanoscience and nanotechnology, starting with the fundamental quantum mechanics and structural, thermal, and optical properties to define materials at the nanoscale. It aims to familiarize students with diverse nanoscale fabrication techniques, including both bottom-up approaches like chemical synthesis and top-down methods such as lithography. Furthermore, the course is designed to cover advanced characterization tools and explore the practical applications of nanomaterials in modern therapeutics and diagnostics.

 

Course contents:

1- Introduction or nanoscience and nanotechnology

  • Applications, special properties of nanomaterials namely structural, thermal, electrical, magnetic, optical,
  • challenges of nanoscience and nanotechnology
  •  Basic quantum mechanics, Fundamental of nanomaterials, Crystal bonding, structure, band theory and density of states at nanoscale

2- Nanoscale fabrication

  • Bottom-Up approach: Chemical synthesis, Self-assembly, Sol-Gel technique, Electro deposition,
  • Top-down approach: Lithography (Photolithography, Electron beam lithography) sputtering, Thermal and Electron beam evaporation, molecular beam epitaxy.

 3-Characterization techniques:

  • Atomic structure: X-ray and Neutron diffraction, X-ray and UV spectroscopy
  • Size, shape, and surface area: Electron microscope, Transmission electron microscope, atomic force microscope, scanning probe microscope.

4- The era of Carbon nanostructures & 2D Materials:

  • Carbon nanotube: Structure of nanotubes, synthesis of nanotubes, applications
  • Graphene-based materials
  • MoS2, MXenes

5- Nanomaterials in Therapeutics and Diagnostics

  • Definition and scope of nanomedicine
  • Rational for using nanomaterials in medicine
  • Nanoparticles for drug delivery, photothermal therapy
  • Iron oxide nanoparticles in magnetic hyperthermia
  • Nanoparticles-enhanced CT and PET imaging
  • Nano-biosensors for biomarker detection

 

Books followed:

  • Nanostructures and nanotechnology by Douglas Natelson
  • Introduction to Nanoscience and Nanotechnology by Charles P. Poole, Frank J Owens
  • Nanoscience and Nanotechnology in Engineering by Vijay. Vardhan, A. S. Pillai, D. Mukherjee, M. Dwivedi, L. Chen
  • Introduction to Nanoscience and Nanotechnology by K. K. Chattopadhyay and A. N. Banerjee
  • Nanotechnology: principals and practice by S. K. Kulkarni
  • Nanoparticles: A Boon to Drug Delivery, Therapeutics, Diagnostics and Imaging. Nanomedicine. NBM. Parveen, S., Misra, R., and S. K. Sahoo.
  • Nanobiotechnology II, Wiley-VCH. Mirkin, C.A. and Niemeyer, C. M. (ISBN: 978-3-527-61037-2)

Upon completion of the course, students will be able to analyze the unique physical properties and challenges associated with nanotechnology.

Students are expected to understand the synthesis and structural characteristics of advanced materials like carbon nanotubes, graphene, and MXenes.

Advanced chemistry laboratory [CHM-3613/ CHM-4408/ CHM-6613] [CHM-3613/ CHM-4408/ CHM-6613-1]

Faculty
Vidya Dnyaneshwar Avasare [vidya.avasare@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The Advanced Chemistry Laboratory course provides an intensive, multi-disciplinary research experience designed to bridge advanced theoretical frameworks with contemporary synthetic and analytical strategies. Moving far beyond traditional, recipe-driven procedures, this curriculum emphasizes structural design, molecular architecture, and sustainable laboratory methodologies.

The course is structurally anchored around four core pillars of modern chemical research:

Nanotechnology & Macromolecular Materials: Exploring quantum confinement and collective electronic motion via size-tunable gold nanoparticles, alongside dynamic covalent chemistry (DCC) via the bottom-up assembly of porous Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs).

Organometallic Functionalization & Bio-orthogonal Linkages: Transitioning from the fundamental aromaticity of sandwich complexes such as ferrocene to advanced, target-oriented coupling via copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne "click" cycloadditions.

Green Chemistry & Sustainable Synthesis: Mitigating environmental impact and eliminating toxic solvent matrices through solid-state mechanochemistry (grinding/milling) and neat thermal reactions to construct fluorescent heterocycles (coumarins) and functional porphyrin macrocycles.

Advanced Coordination Chemistry: Systematically isolating homoleptic iron architectures to map how subtle alterations in ligand-field strength and oxidation states fundamentally govern macroscopic optical anomalies, electron-transfer kinetics, and magnetic configurations.

Through this rigorous curriculum, students will transition from structured laboratory learners into independent investigators capable of handling highly complex reactions, interpreting data, and fine-tuning reaction protocols with a fundamental understanding. 

Learning Outcomes

The pedagogical targets of this laboratory course are to:

Train Students in Advanced Synthetic Modalities: Provide mastery over modern synthetic paradigms including mechanochemical macrocyclization, dynamic covalent framework assembly, multi-step organometallic functionalization, and air-sensitive coordination chemistry.

Embed Green Chemistry Metrics: Quantitatively demonstrate the principles of sustainable molecular design by prioritizing high atom-economy reactions, eliminating volatile organic compounds (VOCs) via solvent-free pathways, and replacing precious metals with earth-abundant iron systems.

Develop Fluency in Electronic Spectroscopy and Data Interpretation: Deliver hands-on operational and interpretative expertise in UV-Vis absorption and steady-state fluorescence spectroscopy, and analytical data and physical properties to structure correlations.

Correlate Molecular Structure with Physical Anomalies: Drive students to fundamentally decode macroscopic variables such as shifting luminescent profiles, visual solution color flips, and magnetic attraction

Cultivate Collaborative Big-Data Analytics: Implement a cooperative "jigsaw" laboratory framework wherein student teams optimize distinct electronic derivatives and pool their spectroscopic data to chart comprehensive periodic and substituent trends.

Upon successful completion of this laboratory module, students will be able to:

1. Advanced Materials & Organometallic Synthesis

Synthesize and control monodisperse colloidal gold nanoparticles, intentionally tuning particle-size regimes to visually dictate the Surface Plasmon Resonance (λmax) absorption peaks.

Construct an ordered, porous Covalent Organic Framework (COF) via a reversible Schiff-base condensation, verifying framework integration by monitoring the conversion of carbonyl (C=O) linkages to imine (C=N) joints via FT-IR.

Execute a multi-step organometallic functionalization sequence to convert a stable ferrocene core to ethynylferrocene and successfully link it to an organic target via a Copper-Catalyzed Azide-Alkyne Cycloaddition (CuAAC) "click" reaction.

2. Green Chemistry & Substituent Analysis

Apply solvent-free, neat thermal methods and solid-supported mechanochemical techniques to bypass corrosive liquid-acid matrices in the generation of coumarins and tetraarylporphyrins.

Synthesize a series of core-substituted metalloporphyrins and systematically map the electronic influences of electron-donating groups (EDGs) and electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) using the Hammett principle.

Quantitatively calculate optical Stokes shifts across structurally varied heterocycles using steady-state emission and absorption profiles.

3. Magnetochemistry & Coordination Theory

Isolate and stabilize highly oxidation-prone divalent transition-metal states (e.g., Fe2+) in aqueous media using precise oxygen exclusion and chemical buffering strategies.

Measure and calculate the effective magnetic moments (μeff) of transition-metal complexes with a magnetic susceptibility balance, using the data to determine high-spin versus low-spin ground states and to map spin-state crossovers induced by strong π-backbonding.

Differentiate and rationalize the intense optical color profiles of Metal-to-Ligand (MLCT) and Ligand-to-Metal (LMCT) Charge Transfer transitions compared with weak, spin-forbidden d-d electronic transitions.

Identify structural symmetries and spatial anomalies, such as the Jahn-Teller distortion in high-spin d4 complexes.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

In addition to the fundamental reference books, the students should consult the following references.

A) Advanced Laboratory Manuals (Practical Techniques)

These manuals offer rigorous reference protocols for handling air-sensitive compounds, running column chromatography, and setting up green chemical reactions.

Microscale Inorganic Chemistry: A Comprehensive Laboratory Experience by Zvi Szafran, Ronald M. Pike, and Mona M. Singh.

Application: Excellent resource for small-scale coordination chemistry and oxygen-exclusion tricks without using high-end Schlenk lines.

Green Organic Chemistry Strategies, Tools, and Laboratory Experiments by Albert S. Matlack.

Application: Provides the educational philosophy behind the solvent-free and mechanochemical setups used in Experiments 4 and 5.

The Chemist's Companion: A Handbook of Practical Data, Techniques, and References by Arnold J. Gordon and Richard A. Ford.

Application: A timeless bench-top guide for crystallization solvents, TLC optimization, and structural characterization values.

B) Literature reports:

Reading the original papers or related high-impact articles helps not only to learn how to write lab reports in a standard journal format, but also to learn the philosophy and logic of research.

1: Nano & Materials (Exps 1 & 2)

Gold Nanoparticles: Bastús, N. G., Comenge, J., & Puntes, V. (2011). Kinetically Controlled Seeded Growth Synthesis of Citrate-Stabilized Gold Nanoparticles of Versatile Size and High Monodispersity. Langmuir, 27(17), 11098–11105.

Covalent Organic Frameworks: Segura, J. L., Royuela, M. J., & Mar Ramos, M. (2016). Post-synthetic modification of covalent organic frameworks. Chemical Society Reviews, 45(20), 5635–5671. (Great for understanding how imine bonds assemble dynamically).

2: Organometallics & Green Synthesis (Exps 3, 4, & 5)

Click Chemistry: Rostovtsev, V. V., Green, L. G., Fokin, V. V., & Sharpless, K. B. (2002). A Stepwise Huisgen Cycloaddition Process: Copper(I)-Catalyzed Regioselective "Ligation" of Azides and Terminal Alkynes. Angewandte Chemie International Edition, 41(14), 2596–2599. (The pioneering paper on the click reaction).

Green Porphyrins: Warner, M. G., & Hutchison, J. E. (2005). Green synthesis of organic macrocycles: Solvent-free porphyrin synthesis. Green Chemistry, 7(5), 366–370.

 3: Coordination Chemistry & Spectroscopy (Exp 6)

Iron Complexes: Structural data and magnetic behavior can be referenced against standard entries in the Journal of Chemical Education regarding the Evans Balance method, such as: Crawford, T. H., & Swanson, R. (1971). Magnetic susceptibility studies in the advanced undergraduate laboratory. Journal of Chemical Education, 48(6), 382.

Synthetic Biology [BIO-3455/ BIO-6455] [BIO-3455/ BIO-6455-1]

Faculty
Sandeep Ameta [sandeep.ameta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Biological systems are complex but function like a well-controlled machine that can be engineered for societal benefit. This course aims to introduce students to the exciting field of synthetic biology to teach them how biological systems can be reprogrammed using a synthetic and systems approach. The course is divided into three modules (M). M1: Tools of Synthetic Biology, which will cover understanding synthetic availabilities (DNA, RNA, peptides) to manipulation tools (regulators, expression systems). M2: Implementation in the Regulation of Biological Systems. It will cover the basics of gene network organization, regulation, artificial/synthetic networks, and gene circuits. M3: Synthetic Cells and Evolving Systems. This module will cover the work around Minimal Cell Research (Minimal cell/Craig Ventor) and bottom-up approaches (Origins of Life Perspective).

This course is designed to be interdisciplinary, and all the concepts required for understanding will be taught in the class. However, a basic understanding of Molecular Biology, Cell Biology, and Biochemistry will be really helpful.

Learning Outcomes

At the end of this course, the students should be familiarized with the following ideas and concepts:

  • Basic principles and tools of synthetic biology.
  • Designing and analyzing gene networks and gene circuits.
  • State of the field and achievements of synthetic biology

Faculty
Sneha Bakshi [sneha.bakshi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course will focus on pricing. We will cover the theory of price determination, in different market structures like monopoly, oligopoly, and competitive markets, between different demand segments in the form of price discrimination, and the idea of price collusion. We will also look at a behavioral economics approach to pricing, discounts and promotions; and at the particulars of pricing in some specific industries. And we will explore price as a policy instrument: to correct market failures and to create markets where none exist to improve resource allocation, and to provide support or incentive for target products, suppliers or consumers.

Learning Outcomes

The first part of this course aims to enable students to understand the considerations on which pricing decisions are theoretically based in various types of markets, and to learn how to apply them to different industries, cases, and problems. The second part of the course will help students get familiar with the use of price as a policy instrument and help them explore and analyze how governments and institutions do this to improve upon non-existent and incomplete markets.

In essence, food is a way of fulfilling a biological need—nutrition—within an ecologically and culturally defined context.  At the same time, it is a medium for expressing one’s sense of self in relation to a changing world of ideas and institutions.  This course examines the political ecology of food from the farm to the plate, looking at the connections between the well-being of land-based resources and human and non-human living beings.  It provides an understanding of changing agrarian systems and how access to food intersects with existing structures of social inequality.  It explores how ethics and emotions, science and religion, nature and culture, shape contemporary food systems.

Learning Outcomes

Course Objectives

*  to appreciate the diversity and complexity of food ecologies and ideologies

*  to understand the long-term political-economic processes shaping food practices

*  to analyse contemporary food practices in terms of unequal social causes and impacts

*  to reflect on the connections between personal action and planetary welfare

*  to develop an interpretive frame that can be applied to understand and address issues around food justice and sustainability

*  to carefully read, critically appraise, and concisely write from a social science perspective.

Data Structures and Algorithms [CS-2212] [CS-2212-1]

Faculty
Aalok Dhaval Thakkar [thakkar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Niklaus Wirth titled his 1976 book Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs, an equation as close to a definition of our discipline as we are likely to get. Computing is, in no small part, the art of choosing well between these intertwined halves. But the equation, taken at face value, is misleading in its symmetry. It suggests that the two summands are independent contributions, to be developed in parallel and combined at the end. They are not. The choice of data structure is, more often than not, the choice of algorithm in disguise: settle the representation, and the procedure is half-written before you have begun.

This course begins from that unity. Data structures and algorithms are not two subjects placed side by side, but two perspectives on the same act of thought: the organization of information and the transformations that organization permits.

From there, we turn to a disunity: the separation of interface (what a thing does, its purpose) from implementation (what a thing is, its form). This separation is arguably the most revolutionary idea in software engineering. It is what makes large-scale systems possible, what lets us write modular code, reason about one component without holding the rest of the program in our heads, and swap a library for a better one without rewriting the programs that depend on it. The distinction builds on Introduction to Computer Science, where we looked at specifications through pre- and post-conditions. A specification is a contract between a piece of code and its user: the interface states the promise, the implementation keeps it. A discipline that holds these two apart rigorously is a discipline that can build things too large for any single mind to grasp. This separation also gives us the right way to define correctness for a data structure: an implementation is correct when it is faithful to its interface, when the contract is kept.

Finally, we will look at efficiency. Efficiency is never absolute; it is a negotiation among competing costs: time against space, worst case against expected case, the cost of building a structure against the cost of querying it. We will examine different implementations of the same interface and compare them along several axes, including time, memory, ease of design, ease of understanding, and ease of reasoning about correctness. Learning to navigate this space of choices is one of the central intellectual habits this course aims to build.

These three goals, namely unity, separation, and tradeoff, will be pursued through a sequence of structures of increasing subtlety: the linear (lists, arrays, dynamic arrays and the amortized analysis they invite); the hierarchical (abstract data types, binary and balanced search trees, heaps both eager and lazy); the probabilistic (hashing and its theory, skip lists); the string-oriented (tries and range queries); and the relational (graphs and their fundamental traversals). At its core, this course will show you how data can be represented and transformed. It will give you a way of thinking precisely about computation, and hand you the epistemological tools of a computer scientist: the discipline of separating what from how, the habit of analysing before believing, the instinct to ask not whether a thing works but at what cost, and, in the end, the strange and durable pleasure of thinking like one.

A note on languages. I will use OCaml throughout. Its type system makes abstract data types literally abstract, and its blend of functional and imperative styles lets us discuss the tradeoff between sharing and mutation without ideology. That said, the concepts in this course are language-independent, and students are welcome to implement their programs in any of: Python, C, C++, Java, OCaml, or Rust. Each teaches something different about the same structure.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  1. Separation of Interface and Implementation. Specify a data structure as an interface, give multiple implementations of it, and establish correctness as fidelity of the implementation to the interface.
  2. Efficiency and Tradeoffs. Analyze data structures along axes of time, space, worst case, and expected case using asymptotic, amortized, and probabilistic methods, and defend a choice of implementation in context.
  3. Algorithmic Thinking. Identify the structural features of a problem that admit an efficient solution, design an algorithm that leverages them, and prove its correctness and complexity.
  4. Programming. Implement the data structures and algorithms of the course in a programming language, and verify their behavior through testing and empirical measurement.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course does not follow a single textbook. The following six works will be drawn on throughout the semester.

  1. Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, and Clifford Stein. Introduction to Algorithms.4th ed., MIT Press, 2022.
  2. Donald E. Knuth. The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1: Fundamental Algorithms. 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1997. 
  3. Donald E. Knuth. The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 3: Sorting and Searching. 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1998.
  4. Chris Okasaki. Purely Functional Data Structures. Cambridge University Press, 1998. 
  5. Robert Sedgewick and Kevin Wayne. Algorithms. 4th ed., Addison-Wesley, 2011.
  6. Niklaus Wirth. Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs. Prentice-Hall, 1976.

courseTitle: Anthropology of Religion: Animism, Hylozoism, Panpsychism, Techno-Sacramentalism
description:
Anthropology of Religion: Animism, Hylozoism, Panpsychism, Techno-Sacramentalism [SOA-3150/ SOA-6125] [SOA-3150/ SOA-6125-1]

Faculty
Harish Naraindas [harish.naraindas@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What is religion in the anthropological canon? Why has religion been addressed, either tacitly or explicitly, in conjunction with magic and science? Are magic, religion and science (MRS hereafter) epochal moments in mankind’s evolutionary ascent, or are they coeval in time? How has anthropology, starting with Tylor, Frazer, Durkheim and Malinowski, attempted to come to terms with it? Does the religious history of these European thinkers, with the Reformation as a watershed, have a bearing on why they have been addressed together? Or were they led to invoke the category of magic through a colonial encounter with cultures – which the New World Encyclopaedia charmingly calls “newly contacted societies'' – that they designated primitive, which in fact is the title – Primitive Culture – of Edward Tylor’s celebrated work of 1871. The work where Tylor christens such cultures as animistic, thus setting in motion the formal study of religion through the concept of animism: a concept that inaugurates and virtually sets in stone the distinction between Us and Them, or between European and non-European cultures, or between the European past and its present, or between an enchanted, pre-modern and primitive world, and presumably a disenchanted, secular and modern world. It is through the concept of animism, along with its cognate concepts of hylozoism and panpsychism, that this course will trace the genealogy of the study of religion and interrogate its consequences. We will, after running through the canon from Tylor to Evans Pritchard, examine contemporary but “conventional” ethnographies in “primitive” or “polytheistic” settings such as Vitebsky’s “Dialogues with the Dead” in Orissa, or Sax’s religion, affliction and healing in the Himalayas. We will then examine Kalpana Ram’s “Fertile Disorder”, and her “provocation of the modern”, that at once extends and attempts to call this trajectory into question. We will pursue this questioning by turning to witchcraft in post-war Germany, and then turn to the fusion of MRS through “techno-sacramentalism” in twenty-first century German Hospitals. We will then, through Keith Thomas’ work, mark the presumed decline of animism and magic, not in primitive cultures but in European Catholicism, through the assiduous work of the Protestants who presumably bequeathed to us the modern idea of Religion. We will end the course by asking – through the “animistic turn” and Jason Storm’s work – whether the supposed exit of animism, which presumably inaugurates European modernity and sets it apart from the non-European world, spawning in the bargain ethnographic objects and explanatory moves, is indeed true, and, if not, how are we to rethink the future of not only religion as an object of enquiry, but of our very disciplines and their founding premises? Finally, the coda to the course, if time permits, will examine not only the religious roots of the world’s most powerful democracy, but show how the Puritans and Presbyterians in particular provided the theological and conceptual blueprint for its Constitution.
