courseTitle: Foundations of Modern China: The Qing Dynasty in World History
description:
Foundations of Modern China: The Qing Dynasty in World History [CHI-3205/ HIS-3535] [CHI-3205/ HIS-3535-1]

Faculty
Sayantani Mukherjee [sayantani.mukherjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

CHI-3205/ HIS-3535

Foundations of Modern China I: The Qing Dynasty in World History

Monsoon 2026

Tuesdays & Thursdays 11.50-1.20 pm

AC-04-LR-404

Sayantani Mukherjee – sayantani.mukherjee@ashoka.edu.in – AC02-339

Modern China is among the world’s two largest countries by population, two largest by economy, and its fourth largest by geographical size. As a state, it follows centuries of imperial dynasties whose complex legacies it sometimes claims and sometimes rejects. In the last two hundred years, China has experienced some of the most dramatic social and cultural transformations and some of the most violent conflicts of any region of the world. As it was incorporated into an international system dominated by Europe and the United States, it became an integral part of global history in new ways and, increasingly, a shaper of that history. Often imagined as a monolith, it is in fact deeply heterogeneous, home to multiple languages and ethnicities, countless local traditions, millions of adherents of major world religions, and sizable foreign communities. Today, China is the site of crucial questions concerning geopolitics, the environment, global health, and human rights. At the same time, it has inherited and continues to produce immense bodies of art and literature, distinctive belief systems and intellectual movements, and delicious food. In these and other capacities, it also informs the identities of millions of people of Chinese ancestry living around the world.

            This course examines the Qing Dynasty (1644-1912) and the early days of the Republic of China. It makes reference to Tibetan, Taiwanese, diasporic Chinese, and global histories as well. It offers systematic coverage of Qing expansion and crisis, Qing culture, encounters with Asia and the West, the emergence of nationalism, and the transition out of the dynastic state. In the process, it gives special attention to questions of race and ethnicity, gender, frontiers, global connections, and nation-building. Instead of a chronological overview of the Qing era, this class will deal with historical processes between 1644-1912 through the four themes of statecraft, agriculture and commerce, ethnicity, and gender. This course design emphasizes historical thinking skills (e.g. understanding causation, contingency, agency, anachronism, meaning, and so on) and highlights the voices of historical figures, both powerful and ordinary, through translated primary sources. No prior knowledge is required.

Learning Outcomes

Course Objectives

This course has two objectives. One is to develop productive familiarity with some of the most representative themes, questions, and sources associated with the study of Qing history. The other is to cultivate the ability to ask historical questions in an intellectually responsible and rigorous way. We will focus on skills of critical thinking, reading, and writing (including textual, contextual, conceptual, comparative, and synthetic analysis), as well as habits of reasonable, respectful, and inclusive discussion. By the end of this class you should be able to:

Summarize academic monographs in East Asian studies and introduce salient points in notes and in speech.

Draw connections between works to gain an overview of scholarly and historiographical debates in the study of Qing China.

Trace theoretical or methodological trends across multiple empirical contexts.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Requirements and Expectations:       

 

Assessment & Assignments:

40% - Participation

10% - Map quizzes (x2)

20% - 科舉 (Imperial exams x4)

20% - 奏折 (Palace memorials x6, best of 4)

Attendance, Participation and Discussion Étiquette:

I will not take attendance in each class meeting, however, participation in weekly class discussions is a mandatory part of your grade and is necessary for succeeding in the course. If you have circumstances that might affect attendance at a specific class meeting, please let me know ahead of time whenever possible. To protect your privacy, please do not describe any medical situations to me; just inform me that the situation exists and be prepared to provide a doctor’s note if requested.

Participation counts for a total of forty points of your final grade, and should be based on attentive reading, listening, and preparation. Always keep an open mind and be respectful of your classmates and your instructor regardless of what you wish to say, or whether you agree with what has already been said. Being respectful also means that (1) if you have not completed a particular reading, please refrain from commenting on it (2) in the normal course of discussion, if you have just spoken, you should refrain from speaking again until others who wish to contribute have done so (3) contributions to discussion should be based on the readings, lectures, and discussion questions, and should aim to improve our collective understanding of them. In general, please avoid unstructured/unsupported reflections as well as topics that are beyond the scope of the course.

Map Quizzes

There will be two in-class map quizzes, the format will be discussed in class. The dates for both quizzes are indicated in the syllabus and are not negotiable. No additional preparation will be required if you have been regularly attending classes. Each quiz will count for a maximum of five points, for a total of ten points for this component.

Imperial Examinations

In order to become the top scholars of your group, you will each write four levels of imperial exams, as generations of aspirants did in the civil service exams held in Qing-era China. You will either PASS or FAIL each level.

Each exam will involve an in-class hand-written essay in response to a prompt provided in class. All exam dates will be indicated in the syllabus. These dates are not negotiable. No additional preparation will be required if you have been regularly attending classes.

On the first examination date, all of you will write the preliminary exam 童試tongshi. If you pass this level and earn the 秀才xiucai degree, you will be inducted into the ranks of the local gentry and may move on to the next level. On the date of the next exam, all xiucai scholars will write the provincial-level or the 鄉試 xiangshi examinations. Anyone who did not pass the preliminary level will repeat the tongshi exam. Those of you who pass the provincial level will be granted the 舉人juren degree and become eligible for government appointments at the provincial level. On the date of the third exam, all juren scholars will write the 會試 huishi or metropolitan-level exams. All those still at the xuicai rank will repeat the provincial-level, and those without any degrees will repeat the preliminary exam. If you pass the huishi, you will earn the 貢士gongshi degree and become eligible for appointment in the major Qing cities. On the date of the fourth and final exam, all gongshi scholars will write the palace level 殿試 dianshi exams. All juren holders will repeat the huishi level, and so on. If you pass the palace level and earn the 進士jinshi degree, you will be eligible for direct appointment to important posts throughout the empire, receiving great fame and the entire twenty points for this component.

Your final grade for this component will depend on how many levels you have passed. If you pass all four levels, you will receive the full twenty points for this component. If you pass three levels, (i.e. juren rank) you will receive fifteen points. If you pass two levels (huishi), you will receive ten points. If you pass one level only (xiucai), you will receive five points. If you do not pass any levels, you will receive zero points for this component.

Palace Memorials

As and when crises arise in the imperial lands, as responsible members of the educated classes you may petition the imperial throne for help. You will have six opportunities to write a short memorial to the palace stating the nature of the crisis and your case for aid. Your petitions may be ACCEPTED or REJECTED. As long as at least four of your six petitions are accepted, you will receive the full twenty points of this grade component. If only three of your memorials are accepted, you will receive fifteen points towards your final grade. If only two are accepted, you will receive ten points. If only one is accepted, you will get five points. If none are accepted, you will receive zero points for this component. In the event that all six of your petitions are accepted, extra credit up to five points will be considered.

As is the nature of crises, these may arise at any time in any class over the course of the semester. Each memorial will be hand-written in class, and no additional preparation will be required if you have been regularly attending classes.

Oral report

You will be required to make three oral reports in class in response to a set of pre-circulated themes.

If you have a topic of particular interest that you would like to make an oral presentation on, you may discuss it beforehand with me in office hours. The format of these presentations will be discussed in class. The highest number of points you can get for each report is five points, and only your best two presentations will count towards your final grade. No additional preparation will be required if you have been regularly attending classes.

Intellectual Integrity, Plagiarism, and AI Policy

The intellectual venture in which we are all engaged requires of faculty and students alike the highest level of personal and academic integrity. As members of an academic community, each one of us bears the responsibility to participate in scholarly discourse and research in a manner characterized by intellectual honesty and scholarly integrity.

 

Scholarship, by its very nature, is an iterative process, with ideas and insights building one upon the other. Collaborative scholarship requires the study of other scholars’ work, the free discussion of such work, and the explicit acknowledgement of those ideas in any work that inform our own. This exchange of ideas relies upon a mutual trust that sources, opinions, facts, and insights will be properly noted and carefully credited. In practical terms, this means that, as students, you must be responsible for the full citations of others’ ideas in all of your research papers and projects, and you must always submit your own work and not that of another student, scholar, or internet agent.

 

While the use of generative AI and LLMs may have already become a part of your academic process, remember that AI isn’t merely problematic but technology which actively reshapes and intensifies the worst tendencies of knowledge relations. AI is a form of computation and it is also an apparatus that configures and patchworks concepts, policies, institutions and subjectivities to force out a certain kind of end product. This is not simply a nasty application of an otherwise productive technology. At base AI and LLMs are no more than forms of statistical pattern finding, which means that the end product is fake knowledge and fake text, even when it appears to be “accurate”. Because such technology relies on abstracting away all specific context in order to create generalisations that can be applied to anything, the end product is very easy to identify and mark down. If you are using AI to formulate your points of view, your analysis and arguments, or for other parts of the generative process including formulating style and voice, then be aware that you are simply cheating yourself of the opportunity to develop original insights. If you use AI you are not imbibing or producing analysis or knowledge, it will reflect in your work and earn you an automatic fail for that assignment. 

 

This classroom should constitute a form of mutual and relational accountability, where we learn from each other rather than prioritise reductive automation. Any breach of this intellectual responsibility and the goal of community learning is a breach of faith with the rest of our academic community. It undermines our shared intellectual culture, and it will not be tolerated in this class.

Faculty

Overview

The course examines a range of topics at the intersection of culture and psychology. How culture influences the lives of people across the world, their feelings, thoughts, and behaviours, is explored to better understand one another. Both cultures that are overrepresented and underrepresented in psychological research are covered.

Learning Outcomes

The goals of the course are to help you:

  1. Increase cultural competence, including knowledge about different cultures and the thought, feeling, and behavior patterns that are common in these cultures. 
  2. Improve written and oral communication skills. 
  3. Understand and identify credible versus non-credible sources.
  4. Connect concepts covered in this course to those covered in other related courses (e.g., Clinical, Cognitive, Developmental, Social Psychology, etc.).

description:
Understanding audio visual production [MS-1567] [MS-1567-1]

Faculty
Natasha Badhwar [natasha.badhwar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course offers practical training to students in audio and video production and visual literacy at an introductory level. Through a series of viewings of historical, contemporary and student films, students learn to understand storytelling formats and tools of audio visual communication.
Working on film projects, students are introduced to the basics of project development and organization, working with the camera, conducting interviews, using light and sound, and post-production techniques. The course develops analytical, rhetorical, visual, as well as a range of practical skills, including collaboration and communication skills as students work in groups as well as individually to create multiple video projects through the semester.

Students receive basic training in professional video production as well as use of smartphones to make effective video films, including documentary, trailer, music video and personal films. Special emphasis is paid to composition, light and texture in photography and its affective impact on the viewer. The use of movement, sound and transition techniques in editing will be observed and put into practice.

Through a series of practical exercises, students learn low-budget production methodologies including basic studio production - and the many open-source software tools and platforms that can facilitate video production.

Learning Outcomes

Students will become familiar with the basic components of audio-visual production and the technologies that have enabled them.

They will learn about the power and resonance of audio-visual expression through guided exercises in components of photography, videography and video editing.

Digitality: Ethnographic Approaches [MS-3090/ SOA-3152] [MS-3090/ SOA-3152-1]

Faculty
Chitralekha Dhamija [chitralekha@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Ethnography provides an irreplaceable lens to study the lived relationships of human life and cultures with digital technologies, and their constitutive linkages with what it means to be human. While the idea of the digital may be used to refer to binary connections, the computational, electronic, or anything that is internet mediated, ethnographers are interested in the imbrications of these technologies in everyday life and the consequences of the digital for the human condition- in online worlds and in their entanglements with lived realities in physical places. Ethnographic approaches in other words help us explore human interactions with digital devices, the making of human connections in cyberspace, coproduction of notions of the real and the virtual, or the conditions of living and being in a digital culture- that might be called `digitality’. We will examine possibilities of these human engagements in diverse sites and contexts. 

The course will be taught over three sections. 

We first chart some of the conceptual dilemmas in the terrain. In what ways has/ may the digital mediate human life and culture? In an age of techno-feudalism and artificial intelligence, are these mediations and their consequences paradigmatically different than in the past? What does it mean to `ethnographically’ approach or attempt to understand `digitality’?

The second section engages with methodological contestations that ethnographers of digitality often grapple with. These include existent questions of power, subjectivity, or reflexivity in ethnography in general, but also those that address specific dilemmas in digital ethnography. What does it mean to do `digital ethnography’? What may be its analytic advantage to study sociality or politics? Can virtual worlds be studied on their own terms- without ethnographic engagement in the physical worlds that actors in digital places also belong to? What does it mean to conduct multi-sited or multi-timed fieldwork on specific congeries of media practices, forms and agents? How does ethnography help us approach closer towards understandings of digital media in everyday life that is ‘non-media-centric’? Can the study of media beyond media content, as part of the sensory, embodied and affective routines of everyday life, help us arrive at thicker understandings of the possible role of media in social life and change? 

Finally, we engage with a range of generative ethnographic studies of lived histories and vernacular cultures of digital media, exploring local meanings to digital genres of work, homing, dating, gaming, protest, blogging, hacking or memes for instance, but also their intersections with existent localities of class, caste, disability, gender and sexuality etc. 

Learning Outcomes

Students will, via this rough trajectory, acquire:  

Theoretical grasp and methodological acquaintance with the conceptual terrain and contestations around understandings of `digitality’ and `ethnography’

Ethnographic possibilities and problems 

Seminal studies in different contexts and localities

Economic Forecasting and Analysis [ECO-3402/ MAT-4203] [ECO-3402/ MAT-4203-1]

Faculty
Piyali Banerjee [piyali.banerjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces students to time-series forecasting and analysis, focusing on the latest tools in time-series econometrics to enable them to make informed judgments across various types of data. This course is beneficial for forecasting business time series, such as sales and expenditures, and macroeconomic time series, such as GDP, interest rates, and inflation.
The course will introduce some of the basics of time-series econometrics before moving on to the main topics in forecasting. You will learn ways to examine and prepare data before forecasting. Various useful techniques will be taught to improve forecasting precision. Time series topics will include linear regression, ARIMA models, Box–Jenkins models, reduced form VAR models, ARCH–GARCH models, and unit root models. description:
Venture Design Lab [ENT-4012] [ENT-4012-1]

Faculty
Srikant Sastri [srikant.sastri@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Venture Design (& Innovation) Lab

India is in the midst of a entrepreneuship boom. Tens of thousands of new startups each year. Bigger companies in corporate sector are also embracing innovation and intrapreneurship to stay relevant and succeed in a fast-changing world. To succeed, innovation needs to be rooted in customer-centricity. Without excessive fixation on technology & valuation. Paying attention to customers, revenues & long-term scalability.

This hands-on bootcamp course intertwines theory & practice so that students learn key concepts of new venture design, and implement them with customer-centricity. On the one hand, students with entrepreneurial dreams would be well equipped to pursue that path (‘The Founder Track’). On the other hand, students who want to work in the corporate sector will have the confidence to be successful intrapreneurs driving innovation in these larger companies (‘The Intrapreneur Track’). This course also aims to prepare students with the right balance of hard and soft skills.

Students opting for ‘The Founder Track’ will experience the full journey from an Idea to a MVP (Minimum Viable Product), while those in ‘The Intrapreneur Track’ (‘Corporate Innovation’ track) will experience how a Pilot(PoC) Design can be built with alignment to a company’s corporate strategy. In both cases, the focus will be on creating sustainable, scalable ventures with tech as key enabler. Learn to navigate this journey will provide a valuable skill for aspiring entrepreneurs, and also highly prized by consulting firms & other recruiters.

Use of AI will be strongly encouraged at all stages during this course. Students may use no-Code & AI tools to quickly build and test functional MVPs & pilot projects. Gen-AI can be used for faster market sizing, to pre-test customer interviews, to finesse the customer personas, and to stress-test some of your ideas.

Each class session, a ‘hard’ or ‘soft’ startup concept “(“theory”) will introduced in the class. Students will then (working in groups) execute that concept (“practical”) in the weeks to come. A simulated ‘game’ will be used across the 13 classes to provide these groups an experiential, and enhanced view of the progress they are making.

Learning Outcomes

This course is designed to:

  • Expose students to all the key concepts and steps involved in designing & building a new venture, whether a start-up, or as a new unit in a big company
  • Bridge Strategy & Execution: Demonstrate the ability to move from a high-level ‘Problem Statement’ to a tangible ‘MVP’ or ‘Pilot project’ that can deliver results
  • Provide hands-on experience of venture development in a near-real environment
  • Building a Resilient Temperament: Develop the ‘mental muscle’ to navigate through the endless cycles of highs and lows in new venture creation.
  • Develop Storytelling & Influence skills: Master the art of pitching ideas to stakeholders, whether investors or a corporate board of directors.

The key takeaways for the students will be:

  • Master the “0 to 1” Lifecycle: Learn to navigate this high-ambiguity phase, a valuable skill for aspiring entrepreneurs, and also highly prized by consulting firms & other recruiters.
  • Become well-versed in key concepts like problem identification, ideation, customer development, MVP, business models, defensibility, and go-to-market strategy.
  • Gain hands-on experience of development all the way through to creating and testing a MVP or Pilot project.
  • Leave this course with a portfolio (a 90-sec video, a pitch deck, a prototype) that proves you can build from "0 to 1".
  • Learn life-skills like teamwork, real-time iterations, overcoming roadblocks, and storytelling.
  • Begin to appreciate the need to take a reflective and well-balanced approach to venture creation, rather than get carried away by hype.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Prerequisites

This elective course is ideally for students who are in their 2nd/3rd/4th year of UG, and have already taken some Entrepreneurship courses. But others are welcome, too.

A requirement during the course is that students must be part of a project group (3-4 students per group, depending on class size). During the first class, the instructor will facilitate the process of group formation.

Each group should ideally comprise a set of people with complementary skill sets. A team must have at least one person who’s able to use AI tools to build simple prototypes ( e.g. website/app/chatbot), and one person with digital marketing skills.

Required Texts and Readings

The main required readings are mentioned in the detailed course plan and will be shared timely with the students on Google Classroom along with other relevant AV and reading material.

2 additional excused absence(s) are allowed for sportspersons in this course lecture.

Pedagogy

●     Class Structure: The course consists of 13 sessions, each lasting 180 minutes. Students are expected to actively contribute in class, and especially their group work. Groups should also expect to spend time outside (before/after) the class to ensure rapid progress ( this would entail 2-3 hours of work each week).

Class format: Classroom sessions will feature a mix of concepts, several case-lets, a simulated ‘game’, and industry stories. Some classes are likely to feature a case-study and/or  guest speaker

●      Assignment Submissions: Students will work in groups of 3-4 and submit one group assignment midway through the course. The final submission at the end of the course will be a comprehensive one, and in four parts- group video, group presentation, group submission, and an individual submission

●      Fireside Chats: Many of the classes will feature guest speakers- virtual or sometimes, in person.  These guest sessions will be for 45 minutes; they may start with a short presentation followed a fireside chat format, led by pre-assigned student groups. The student host panel will pre-curate the questions, focusing on the key learning outcomes for the session.

Faculty
Partha Pratim Das [partha.das@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces students to structured design practices in computer science, bridging foundational knowledge in data structures, algorithms, and systems with the real-world challenges of software development. It emphasizes hands-on experience in designing, implementing, testing, and maintaining software systems through iterative project work.

Students will engage with the full software development lifecycle - from requirement analysis and modelling (using UML) to implementation (primarily in C/C++ as well as mixed languages), testing, debugging, and deployment. Alongside, they will explore essential tools and techniques, including version control (Git), build automation, documentation systems (LaTeX, Doxygen), and issue tracking.

The course also introduces emerging AI-based development tools that aid in coding, debugging, and maintenance. The projects will be completed individually or in small teams, encouraging collaboration, reuse of code, and design thinking. In the end, students will be equipped with the mindset and skills to approach software engineering tasks in a methodical and efficient way, preparing them for academic and industry-level software projects.

Learning Outcomes

This course familiarizes students with the design and development of software projects in collaborative mode, building on their learning of data structures, algorithms, systems, and other core CS courses. The students work individually or in small groups, start with a descriptive specification of the projects, and take them through the entire software development lifecycle.

By the end of this course, the students will learn:

  1. To handle software development life cycles comprising multiple stages like
    • Problem specification and requirement analysis
    • Software modelling (in UML) and design specification (with classes and interfaces)
    • Software implementation (coding) and debugging
    • Software testing and feedback analysis
  2. To use various common software tools for
    • Modelling & Design
    • IDE for Coding & Debugging
    • Documentation
    • Test planning & Testing
    • Issue Management
    • Version Control
  3. To use AI tools for software development, debugging, and maintenance
  4. To use and reuse libraries, to deploy & configure software, etc. 
  5. To deploy software systems on a cloud platform (AWS, Azure) and configure APIs, Databases, Static Storage, etc.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

It is necessary to have completed the following courses before attending this one. These are pre-requisites on AMS:

  1. Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA)
  2. Computer Organization and Systems (COS)

In addition, it is expected that the students attending this course have

  1. Strong familiarity of Database Management Systems (DBMS). While students will be permitted to attend this course without DBMS too, they will need to go through additional reading and discussion sessions to catch up on the concepts of relational databases and SQL.
  2. Good familiarity with handling on concurrency (as is typical in Operating Systems). Students not having these, would need to work additionally to catch up on the concepts of processes, threads, mutual exclusion, critical section, semaphore, etc. and programming with POSIX (or some similar thread models).
  3. Prior experience in programming in C and C++. Familiarity with Python, GUI design, and Web Development would be useful. Students not having these, would need to work additionally to catch up on these.
  4. Good familiarity with AI, ML, and LLMs. Students not having these, would need to work additionally to catch up on these, especially GenAI for coding.

description:
Artificial Intelligence [CS-4440] [CS-4440-1]

Faculty
Lipika Dey [lipika.dey@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Artificial Intelligence (AI) stands at the intersection of philosophy, logic, computation, and cognition - shaping the future of how people and machines interact with each other.  This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the core concepts and methodologies that define the field of AI. Beginning with the philosophical foundations of designing  intelligent agents that can perceive, reason, and act, the course will then delve into how knowledge is represented for reasoning with it. It will include logic-based systems, ontologies, and knowledge graphs. The course will then move over to discuss uncertainty, which is a key challenge in real-world. Different kinds of frameworks like Bayesian networks, probabilistic inference, and causal reasoning will be discussed. Foundational concepts of reinforcement learning and decision theory will be discussed to reveal how intelligent systems are designed to make choices under uncertainty and conflicting objectives. The course will conclude with discussions on Trustable AI examining fairness, transparency, accountability, and ethical concerns in AI systems.

Topics to be covered
1. Introduction - Philosophy of AI, Intelligent Agents
2. Problem Solving - Uninformed Search, Heuristic search, Adversarial search, Constraint
satisfaction problems
3. Knowledge Representation - Logic and reasoning, Ontology and knowledge graphs
4. Handling Uncertainty - Bayesian Networks, Learning and Inference over Bayesian
Networks, Introduction to Causality

5. Learning - Learning probabilistic models, Knowledge-driven learning, Reinforcement
Learning

6. Decision Theory - Simple and Complex Decision-making

7. Agentic AI frameworks for building autonomous systems

8. Trustable AI

Learning Outcomes

1. Learn about representing real world problems as AI problems
2. Learn to apply AI techniques for problem solving

3. Learn Logic and reasoning
3. Judge applicability of AI techniques for solving real world problems
4. Is knowledgeable about the needs to make AI systems trustable

description:
Methodological Approaches to Understanding Media [MS-4026] [MS-4026-1]

Faculty
Chitralekha Dhamija [chitralekha@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How should we try to understand the media? There are several established methods that are employed frequently by scholars interested in questions of media and mediation: textual analysis, content analysis, critical discourse analysis, political economy, media history, media ethnography, digital ethnography, visual ethnography, among others. But how do we know which of them, if any, are right for our project? Towards this process/ possibility of knowing, we must of course first get to the heart of what each of these `methods’ involve, not just in their modes of examination, but in their epistemic promise. Do they help us understand media histories, its texts and shifting discourses, its rapidly evolving technologies, or do they help us get closer to the meanings that human actors ascribe to their mediations? To understand which methods might help our research, we must know what we seek to understand: in our other words- we must be clear about our research question. The methods we employ will depend on the question/s that we seek (some) answers to. A good place to begin this journey might be to delve into questions of what it means to `understand’- or to put it simply, what happens in human understanding. 

 

Learning Outcomes

Over the course of this semester, we will:

Examine the epistemic dilemmas involved in thinking about `evidence’ and understanding `understandings’  

Discuss the diverse methods that scholars have employed to understand media and its relationships with social worlds – including media history; textual analysis; critical discourse analysis; political economy; media ethnography; digital ethnography; visual ethnography

Think deeply about the research question/s that actually matters to us

Formulate a sharp research problem

Identify which methodological approach/es would best address the problem we seek answers to

Formulate a cogent research proposal that productively employs those approach/es to address our research problem

description:

Faculty
Dipyaman Ganguly [dipyaman.ganguly@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course aims to offer the students with a synoptic view on the conceptual and mechanistic understanding of ‘diseases’, defined as ‘deviation from healthy homeostasis’, in the context of multicellular organisms in general and humans in particular. The course will start with a brief history of how human contemplation on ‘deviation from health’ came by, followed by discussion on basic mechanistic understanding of diseases at different scales across organisms. Discussion on specific disease contexts will majorly involve the animal kingdom, especially mammals. At the end the course will offer a preliminary introduction to recent efforts at seeing diseases through the lens of evolution.

Learning Outcomes

An understanding of emergence of human knowledge on diseases and mechanisms.

A synoptic understanding of disease mechanisms as deviations from health.

Connecting disease outcomes with deviations in molecular, cellular and tissue-specific functions.

An understanding on potential evolutionary underpinning of disease biology.

description:
India: A Short History of English News [MS-2116] [MS-2116-1]

Faculty
Tisha Srivastav [tisha.srivastav@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

 This is a media literacy course on news in the English language and focuses on the Indian news landscape only. It introduces its unique trajectory in each decade, some broad tendencies and several landmark events. With key highlights in coverage over a 80-year period, this includes the earliest reception of Ambedkar in news cartoons of the 1930s to a generation of freedom fighters writing columns in newspapers to the formation of The Working Journalists Act to the Emergency. Here we deep dive through the many original papers available of Emergency era English newspaper editors at Ashoka University’s HDFC Archive of Contemporary India. The course goes on to introduce students to the culture of news video magazines of the 80s, the TV news industry programming priorities and ends on social media in early to mid2000s.

As a general course on becoming literate about how news works and its coverage has evolved, it is significantly different from the newswriting and reporting course, also offered once a year by the Media Studies department. 

No prerequisites.

Learning Outcomes

Knowing India’s unique news history, without needing to become a journalist.

Receiving a journalism history primer and tools to understand and analyse news. 

Become news literate.

This course will prepare you to have options for courses coming in the Spring semester of the upcoming academic year.

Mobility and Power in Eurasia, 800-1800 [HIS-3100/ SOA-3157/ POL-3119] [HIS-3100/ SOA-3157/ POL-3119-1]

Faculty
Pratyay Nath [pratyay.nath@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why did kings travel? What has historically been the relationships between places, spaces, mobilities, and immobilities? What did the lavish tents and travelling households of rulers look like? How would military campaigns, hunting expeditions, and religious pilgrimage constantly intersect in the course of royal travel? These are some of the questions this course investigates. It is a course in world history, that offers a social understanding of mobility from the perspective of the political elite. Drawing upon the new field of mobility studies, it analyses the workings of mobility as a form of royal power, aristocratic lifestyle, and state governance in Eurasian history. Temporally, we will focus on the medieval and early modern periods (800-1800). Spatially, we will look at England, Europe, the Ottoman Empire, Iran, South Asia, China, and Central Asia. We will study journeys, roads, routes, as well as the camps and gardens as conduits and nodes in elite travel. We will explore the social world of the mobile encampment, the logistical roles of mobile human and nonhuman labour, and the myriad political, recreational, and performative functions of royal journeys. We will unravel the thrill, theatrics, and politics of the royal hunt. We will finish by studying how the advent of modernity impacted the politics of royal mobility.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will gather an understanding of 

  • how to think about mobility politically, socially, and historically,
  • the importance of mobility as a means of exercise of power, and
  • the social dimensions of worlds on the move.

courseTitle: (De)Constructing the International: An Introduction to International Political Sociology
description:
(De)Constructing the International: An Introduction to International Political Sociology [IR-3033] [IR-3033-1]

Faculty
Natallia Khaniejo [natallia.khaniejo@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How does one break up the international, political, and the social? Is the international apolitical or is the individual/social only rooted in the local? How do these levels of analysis carve up the international system into discrete parts? Does the analysis that emerges out of this segmentation still hold weight in an increasingly interdependent and interconnected world? IR scholars have long contended with the difficulty of segregating levels of analysis but what happens when the lines between the micro, meso, and macro structures end up breaking down? This course attempts to deconstruct conventional understandings of "the international" in International Relations (IR) by looking at the construction of taken for granted concepts like anarchy, security, migration, knowledge, and power. In doing so the course seeks to re-examine the ontological and epistemic foundations of what is being named and by whom to explore how global politics is shaped by a complex interplay of social forces, power relations, and contested meanings.

Pre-Requisites: Intro to IR + 1 2000 level IR course

Kanti Prasad Bajpai [kanti.bajpai@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course deals with key issues in traditional security. Traditional security here is used to describe the state and other actors’ use of coercion, by the use or threat of use of violence. War is the greatest form of coercion, so we will begin by asking what is war and can war ever be “just”. From there, we will learn about the conduct of war in the modern age – land war, naval war, and air war. We go on to consider nuclear weapons and their role in preventing war by means of deterrence. What is nuclear deterrence and deterrence more broadly? Do nuclear weapons promote stability between rival countries and is nuclear proliferation therefore a good thing? Next, we deal with the impact of the newest technologies on the conduct of war – cyber, drones, robots, AI. We will end with the use of violence by non-state actors in insurgencies and terrorism. How do non-state actors coerce, and how do states respond by counter-coercion but also by other means? Finally, we will analyze the likelihood of mainland China attacking Taiwan and how the defence of the island can be constructed. An attack on Taiwan would have serious consequences not just for the two parties involved but also for all of Asia and the international system.

Student assessment will consist of three in-class tests of 90 minutes each. The weightage for each test is 30%, 40%, and 30% respectively.

SUMMARY OF THE COURSE STRUCTURE

Week 1            Course Introduction; and What is Security?

Week 2            What is War, and Can War Be Just?

Week 3            Land Warfare

Week 4            Naval Warfare

Week 5            First Test; and Air Warfare

Week 6            Nuclear Weapons and Deterrence

Midterm break

Week 7            Nuclear Proliferation and Stability

Week 8            New Technologies and Security: AI, Drones, and Cyber

Week 9            Second Test; and India’s Wars

Week 10          Terrorism

Week 11          Insurgency

Week 12          India’s Counterterrorism and Counterterrorism

Week 13          Future War – Taiwan; and Third Test

Learning Outcomes

This course is aimed to help students:

Get an overview of traditional security challenges

Understand key concepts, theories, and debates in security studies about the logics of coercion and organized violence

Think about how concepts, theories, and debates in security studies can help us understand contemporary challenges internationally and in India.

description:
Bewitched: Marginality, Perception, Insurrection [SOA-3158] [SOA-3158-1]

Faculty
Deepak Mehta [deepak.mehta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

SOA 3158-1

Bewitched: Marginality, Perception, Insurrection

Why are people accused of witchcraft and sorcery? What makes a neighbour, a relative, a healer, or a stranger appear dangerous? Across different societies, witchcraft has offered anthropology one of its most powerful ways of thinking about fear, misfortune, social tension, and the limits of explanation. This course introduces students to major anthropological debates on witchcraft and magic, from classic distinctions between so-called primitive and modern societies to accounts of colonial resistance, cultural authenticity, gendered violence, and capitalist transformation. We will ask how witchcraft becomes a language for naming what otherwise appears inexplicable, and how accusations of witchcraft expose hidden conflicts within kinship, inheritance, intimacy, domestic life, and political order. We will also learn of how the mystical and nocturnal side of power is played out on the bodies of those accused as witches.

At the centre of the course is the figure of the witch: feared and needed, intimate and alien, vulnerable and powerful. In other words, the witch is simultaneously abject and sovereign, unsettling conventional distinctions between inside and outside, victim and aggressor, reason and fear. Rather than treating witchcraft as an archaic remnant of a belief system or symbolic reversal of the normal, we will examine how the figure of the witch reveals deeper instabilities in culture, law, kinship, gender, and everyday life. Students will explore why the witch so often appears at moments of crisis, when communities struggle to make sense of violence, inequality, illness, death, or rapid social change. By following both female and male figures of the witch, we will consider how witchcraft makes visible what a society tries to deny, contain, or cast out.

The course concludes by turning the question back onto anthropology itself. If witchcraft disturbs the boundaries between truth and accusation, knowledge and fear, the familiar and the strange, then how does anthropology write about such disturbance without taming it too quickly? Does the anthropologist herself become a ‘parlour savage?’ We will examine ethnographic accounts that reveal the discipline’s own desire to explain, order, and domesticate what may resist explanation. In doing so, the course invites students to ask not only what witchcraft means, but what it teaches us about perception, power, and the unstable grounds of knowledge itself.

Learning Outcomes

We will learn of how the effects and affects of marginality open a window to social stability and order.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

I will share an extensive reading list two weeks before our first class. For those interested in the course, the following readings are indicators of the content of what we will address in class.

1. E.E. Evans-Pritchard: Witchcraft, Oraclces and Magic Among the Azande

2. Peter Geschiere: The Modernity of Witchcraft

3. Julien Bonhomme: The Sex Thieves

3. James Siegel: Naming the Witch

4. Jeanne Favret-Saada: Deadly Words

Reading Ethnographies [SOA-3160] [SOA-3160-1]

Faculty
Deepak Mehta [deepak.mehta@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Reading Ethnographies

How do we understand the making of anthropological texts and what is the purchase of ethnography in this understanding? In focusing on ethnography (literally, the writing of an ethnos) the course will provide a picture of fieldwork as a ‘collaborative exploration of a shared human field’, where anthropologists explore a ‘living textuality’ in the words of Boyarin (reference given below). This picture emerges from a dialogue between the analyst and the field showing how contexts are malleable and often fungible. A second theme of the course shows how reading practices are colored by the position of the reader as much as they are by the force of the ‘field’. Indeed, reading and the field are never static, even though the writing up of fieldwork orders and disciplines this mobility. A final theme of the course will explore how documentary practices are etched within relations of power, the various ways in which interpretive communities read such documents to seek gain or restitution.

The course is planned as a series of readings, six sets in all. Students will be distributed across these sets. We will be especially attentive to a comparison between the readings. In the latter half of the semester students will be encouraged to observe, through participant observation, the environs of the university. This will provide us with an initial understanding of how ethnographic texts are produced.

Learning Outcomes

Students will learn to focus on granular detail in the writing of academic texts.

Organic Chemistry [CHM-2012/ CHM-4012] [CHM-2012/ CHM-4012-1]

Faculty
Vidya Dnyaneshwar Avasare [vidya.avasare@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Organic Chemistry (CHM-4012/2012-1) is an advanced, 4-credit course designed to deepen students' structural and mechanistic understanding of organic molecules. The curriculum bridges foundational concepts with advanced synthetic strategy by focusing heavily on how reactions occur, why they happen, and how to prove their pathways.  The course is divided into four core topics:

 Organic Reaction Mechanisms & Kinetics: Investigating how reactions proceed using physical organic chemistry tools like the Hammett equation (Linear Free Energy Relationships), kinetic isotope effects, and experimental techniques (trapping intermediates, crossover experiments, and isotope labeling).  

Reactive Intermediates: Analyzing the generation, stability, and reactivity of highly reactive species including carbocations, carbanions, free radicals, carbenes, nitrenes, and benzynes.  

Neighboring Group Participation (NGP): Exploring anchimeric assistance in SN1 and SN2 nucleophilic displacement reactions, mediated by heteroatom lone pairs, alkenes, cycloalkanes, and aromatic rings.

 Rearrangement Reactions: Masterminding the mechanisms, migratory aptitudes, and structural shifts behind free radical, electrophilic, electrocyclic, and acid-catalyzed rearrangements, alongside ring expansions and contractions.  

Backed by seminal textbooks of organic chemistry such as Clayden, March, and Carey & Sundberg, this course not only equips chemistry students with the analytical toolkit needed to decipher complex organic systems but also deepens their understanding for advanced research. Furthermore, this course may be useful in preparing for the national-level examinations for PhD admissions.

Learning Outcomes

Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to:

Explain the stability and reactivity of the reactive intermediates and their significance in the stereochemical outcomes 

Predict Reactions: Design and predict the outcomes of advanced chemical reactions and synthetic strategies.

Analyze Mechanisms: Use rate laws, kinetic data, and experiments (like isotope labeling or trapping intermediates) to understand and prove how a reaction happens.

Understand Rearrangements & NGP: Explain how molecules rearrange their structures and how neighboring groups assist in reactions to provide surprising results.

Solve Complex Problems: Think independently to solve advanced chemistry problems and communicate your ideas clearly.

Organic Chemistry (Arun Bahl)

Advanced Organic Chemistry (Jerry March)

description:
Gaming and Cognition [PSY-4022] [PSY-4022-1]

Faculty
Robin Sharma [robin.sharma@ashoka.edu.in], Nandini Chatterjee Singh . [nandini.singh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Vision/Philosophy/Purpose

Digital gaming is the delivery of interactive learning and  entertainment experiences delivered through interactive digital formats. Gaming or play is a powerful cognitive tool since it promotes and stimulates activities like attention, motivation, reward, creativity and memory and social interaction. Consequently, digital game design is influenced by  an understanding of cognition. In recent years, research has shown that well-designed digital games can enhance cognitive abilities like attention, visuospatial skills, and working memory.  This course will provide an introduction to cognitive processes that influence game mechanics and followed by an application of this to learning. We will reflect on a range of guiding questions critical to game design in the context of learning and training. The course will adopt an interactive teaching-learning methodology with a mix of lectures and hands-on activities.

The course will be structured in four parts - 

In the first part students will be introduced to the concepts of perception, attention, memory examples of cognitive processes that are important for game design.

This part will cover how aspects of cognition are captured in digital games. Students will be introduced to critical theories like cognitive load theory and situated cognition.

It will cover how digital games are different from tabletop games, board games, and other analog games from the perspective of cognitive science.

The second part will introduce game mechanics and game elements. We will also discuss how both these aspects enhance engagement, cognitive flow and emotion

This part will introduce students to the role of learning theories in educational game design.

It will describe several aspects of a game (e.g., narrative, rewards, penalties).

The difference between gamification and game-based learning.

In part 3, we will discuss how well-designed digital games have emerged as  powerful tools for learning. Students will be introduced to theories from educational psychology and the learning sciences and how they can inform educational game design. Using examples, features of good and bad educational games will be explored.

To identify distinctive features of good educational games.

How multiple aspects of learning can be integrated into games

In the fourth and final part of the course students will be divided into groups where they will undertake a project to study and evaluate a game for its learning potential. 

Groups will be tasked to create an “educational game design document” of an existing game of their choice. A repository of educational games will be provided for reference.

Learning Outcomes

Students will be able to:

Develop their knowledge of the cognitive theories central to educational game design.

Recognise that games have the potential to be playgrounds for learning and assessing cognitive and social-emotional skills.

Understand that games can build knowledge, induce emotions, and attitudes towards academic and non-academic content.

Identify the emotional foundations and features of games that can aid in learning.

Non Fiction Workshop [CW-3060] [CW-3060-1]

Faculty
Adam Klein [adam.klein@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The field of nonfiction writing or writing at least theoretically based in fact, in “real” or reported experience, has never been as vast or wildly engaging as it is today. Cutting across the essay form, biography, memoir, diary, travel and anthropological writing, oral histories, philosophy, environmental and science writing, how-to and how-not-to books, the works we call nonfiction can enlarge the world or reduce it to the size of a cell. Nonfiction can act authoritatively or destabilize our ideas of what constitutes proof or reliability. In all its sub-genres, nonfiction can consider or call for, even if it’s unable to render, justice. It may rouse passion or equanimity or seduce with both small and large revelations. This course will introduce students to the variety, language, and posture of many of these works, beginning with those that first address how we read and write (Virginia Woolf, Mary Ruefle, Joan Didion), followed by those that explore the technologies that undergird our sense of the “real,” from the photograph (Susan Sontag) to physics (Benjamin Labatut) to neuroscience (Oliver Sacks). We’ll explore the ethics of crime reporting (Janet Malcolm), and writings on place and politics (Ryszard Kapuściński, Svetlana Alexievich). We won’t leave out writing on race (James Baldwin, Hilton Als) or on love and art and secrets (Sarah Manguso, Maggie Nelson). And finally, we’ll delve into podcast journalism and other interdisciplinary conveyances of the “true story.” Students will produce original works utilizing examples drawn from our syllabus.

Readings are subject to change.

Learning Outcomes

Students will encounter a wide variety of approaches to nonfiction narrative that deploy various formal options including the use of reports, personl anecdote, appropriation, and other organizational or text-generating strategies.

Students will produce new work in response to the work they encounter. 

Through class discussion and analysis, we will assess the strengths of these works and consider the decisions authors take in the organization and genesis of the work.

Using journaling, students will reflect on their learning and development as writers and readers.

Research Design Workshop [IR-2068] [IR-2068-1]

Faculty
Dipin Kaur [dipin.kaur@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course is designed as a set of collaborative sessions to help you along your thesis journey and impart to you the skills to conduct, write, read, and appropriately critique research. We will use your thesis proposals as a starting point and, from there, combine your research interests with elements of effective research writing. Throughout the course, you will learn how to identify a research question, develop testable hypotheses, and develop an empirical plan of action. We will also go over a lot of the basics, such as: What is the best software for note-taking? How to manage citations and references? Along with that, we will learn how to do specific tasks such as writing a literature review, finessing your writing, and finding your own voice. As part of this plan, you will (a) briefly survey the various methods of data collection and analysis prevalent in IR research (historical and archival analysis, conducting interviews, discourse analysis, reading regression tables) and (b) interface with faculty experts on the subject/ and your supervisors on the dissertation. By the end of this course, you will hopefully have a good handle over some foundational aspects of your thesis that you will present in front of the faculty and your colleagues at the end of the semester and take into Spring 2027.

courseTitle: Critical reading and scientific writing in biological sciences
description:
Critical reading and scientific writing in biological sciences [BIO-4605] [BIO-4605-1]

Faculty
Deblina Raychaudhuri [deblina.raychaudhuri@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course offers students the opportunity to engage deeply with academic literature while preparing for research. In this course students will be introduced to the essential skills of scientific reading, critical analysis and academic writing. Students will learn to develop effective literature search strategies, use citation management tools and critically evaluate research papers. Through literature exploration, guided discussions and concept mapping, students will synthesize existing knowledge and construct a well-structured literature review on a topic aligned with their thesis work. They will also discuss and present key research papers within their chosen area of study. Each class will be of 3 hours duration, consisting of 1.5 hours of instruction followed by 1.5 hours of hands-on exercises and practical application by the students.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course students will be expected to be able to:

a) Perform targeted literature searches to identify relevant papers of interest using appropriate databases and tools, including Boolean operators, filters, MeSH terms, and citation tracking.

b) Begin building and organizing reference libraries with basic annotations on their chosen topic of interest, using a reference manager such as Zotero.

c) Develop skills to critically read and discuss scientific papers, identify key themes and gaps, and distinguish between well-designed and flawed studies.

d) Create an initial concept map linking selected research findings around a central question, using the references they have gathered.

e) Draft a short, structured literature review based on their collected materials.

f) Create effective presentation slides and practice presenting their work, while engaging in constructive peer discussions and exchanging meaningful feedback.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Students will be guided to read review articles from Nature Reviews, Trends, Annual Review series as well as original seminal studies.

description:
Biostatistics and Bioinformatics [BIO-3005/ BIO-6009] [BIO-3005/ BIO-6009-1]

Faculty
Kedar Nath Natarajan [kedar.natarajan@ashoka.edu.in], Tanmoy Roychowdhury [tanmoy.roychowdhury@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This undergraduate course introduces students to the foundational concepts and tools of bioinformatics and biostatistics, equipping them with skills to analyse and interpret biological data. With the growth of genomics, biomedical research, and computational biology, students will explore how biological data (e.g., DNA, RNA and Protein sequences) can be analyzed; as well as understanding statistical principle and methods. This course aims to equip students with the basic knowledge about different types of data, concept of probability, hypothesis testing, and how to analyze data. The major emphasis of the course is to be able to analyze data using the approaches being taught in the class.

Course Outline

Week 1: Introduction to biology, genomics, biological data, databases, and data mining

Week 2 & 3: Principles of sequence alignment and hands-on session

Week 4: Principles of phylogenetic analysis

Week 5: Homologs, motifs and structural analysis

Week 6: Descriptive statistics, concept of probability, and probability distribution

Week 7: Hypothesis testing: one sample inference

Week 8: Hypothesis testing: two sample inference

Week 9: ANOVA

Week 10: Non-parametric statistics

Week 11: Correlation & Regression

Week 12: Final Semester evaluation

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Understand and explain the core principles of biostatistics and bioinformatics relevant to biological research.

Use bioinformatics databases and tools (e.g., NCBI, BLAST, Ensembl, UniProt) to access, retrieve, and analyse molecular biology data.

Conduct basic computational analyses including sequence alignment, gene annotation, and clustering.

Interpret and communicate the results of data analyses in a biological context, with appropriate visualizations and scientific reasoning.

Apply statistical methods such as descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression to biological data.

Assess suitability of statistical tests for underlying data distributions in biological data.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

No prerequisite courses required for joining course. Students are expected to know basic familarity with molecular biology, biochemistry concepts such as Cellular domains (Eukaryotes vs Prokaryotes), Biomolecules (DNA, RNA, Proteins and modifications), Central Dogma, genome metrics and broad applications (Genomics, Transcriptomics, Proteomics)

Optional reading material (will be added soon)

QuickStart Molecular Biology: An Introductory Course for Mathematicians, Physicists, and Engineers (Philip N. Benfey, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press)

Essential Cell Biology (Bruce Alberts, et al., W. W. Norton & Company)

An Introduction to Bioinformatics Algorithms (Neil C. Jones and Pavel A. Pevzner, MIT Press)

John H. McDonald, Third Edition. Handbook of Biological Statistics. Sparky House Publishing.

Quinn & Keough (2002) Experimental design and data analysis for biologists. Cambridge University Press.

courseTitle: Art and Ecology in the Wake of Climate Change
description:
Art and Ecology in the Wake of Climate Change [VA-2066/ ES-2038] [VA-2066/ ES-2038-1]

Faculty
Srinivas Adiya Mopidevi [srinivas.mopidevi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces the students to the history of art’s relationship with ecology. It argues that art has always had ecological considerations in its materiality and meaning. Beginning from Indigenous art practices that have always been in sync with the flows of nature, the course will delve into diverse movements from the 1960s, such as Land Art, Earth Art, Environmental Art, Bio-art, and community-based practices. The course also maps the shifts in artistic methodologies in the wake of climate change, where creative practice is a catalyst to educate the larger public about the shifting planetary realities. In its part-theoretical and part-practical approach, the course will include ‘material literacy’ sessions and workshops to unpack the potentiality of art in addressing ongoing concerns of climate adaptation and sustainability. 

 

Course Modules

Art and Ecology - An Overview 

The introductory module offers the students a comprehensive entry into the field of art and its particular relationship with ecology. This will encompass examples of early cave painting, Indigenous art practices, and movements such as Romanticism, Impressionism, Earth Art, and Land and Environmental Art. It will also speak about how contemporary art forges a multifaceted approach to addressing the planet's current ecological realities. 

Ravi Agarwal, Latika Gupta Ed., Art & Ecology, Marg - A Magazine of the Arts, Mumbai, Vol.71, No.3 2020. https://marg-art.org/product/UHJvZHVjdDo1Mjc3

Andrew Brown, Art & Ecology Now, Thames & Hudson, London, 2014

Alan C. Braddock, Implication: Theory and Practice in Ecocritical Art History, Yale University Press, New Haven, 2023.  

T.J. Demos,  Against the Anthropocene - Visual Culture and Environment Today, Sternberg Press, 2017. https://www.sternberg-press.com/product /against -the- anthropocene-visual-culture-and-environment-today/

Sugata Ray, Venugopal Maddipati Ed., Water Histories of South Asia: The Materiality of Liquescence, Routledge India, 2021.

Folk and Tribal / Indigenous / Aboriginal Cultural Practices

This module will discuss how the art practices of  Folk and Tribal, Indigenous, and Aboriginal communities have been responding to land and nature through art. It will draw examples from South Asia, Aboriginal Australia, and some First Nations in the United States. It will also discuss the limitations of art historical discourses that often see these living and contemporary practices relegated to tradition.  

Jyotindra Jain, Other Masters: Five Contemporary Folk and Tribal Artists of India, Crafts Museum and The Handicrafts and Handlooms Exports Corporation of India Ltd,  New Delhi, 1998.

Jyotindra Jain, Painted Myths of Creation: Art and Ritual of an Indian Tribe, Lalit Kala Akademi, 1984. 

Annapurna Garimella, Vernacular in the Contemporary, Exhibition Publications, Devi Art Foundation, New Delhi, 2010 - 11 https://deviartfoundation.org/exhibitions/vernacular-in-the-contemporary/

Forge Project, https://forgeproject.com/

Marie Geissler, Dreaming the Land: Aboriginal Art from Remote Australia, Thames & Hudson, 2023.   

“Visualizing Ecology: Adivasi Art and the Politics of Representation” – curated writing from Museum of Art & Photography (MAP) Bangalore https://map-india.org/understanding-adivasi-artists-in-the-contemporary-context/      

‘Pedagogy of the Land’ - Shantiniketan and Beyond

Since its inception in the early 20th Century, Shantiniketan has been committed to the ethos of ‘land’ and its embodied knowledge. Drawing from the artistic and pedagogic methods of the ‘Bengal School of Art,’ this module will delve into the ecological considerations in the practices of Abanindranath Tagore, Rabindranath Tagore, Nandalal Bose, Ramkinkar Baij, Benod Behari Mukherjee, Sanchayan Ghosh, among others. 

R. Siva Kumar – Santiniketan: The Making of a Contextual Modernism https://www.academia.edu/42665455/Santiniketan_The_making_of_A_Contextual_Modernism_with_Notes

Aida Yuen Wong, Landscapes of Nandalal Bose (1882–1966): Japanism, Nationalism and Populism in Modern India, in Brij Tankha Ed., Okakura Tenshin and Pan-Asianism, Brill, 2009.

Shukla Sawant, Cultivating a Taste for Nature: Tagore's Landscape Paintings, Vol. 52, No. 19, 2017, pp.57-63. https://www.jstor.org/stable/26695612.

Art Practice as Pedagogy: Anudev Manoharan & Sanchayan Ghosh, https://hakara.in/anudev-manoharan/.

K G Subramanyan, The ‘Phenomenon’ ​​of Abanindranath Tagore, Critical Collective ​​https://criticalcollective.in/ArtistInner2.aspx?Aid=279&Eid=970.

Santhal Family: positions around an Indian sculpture, Anshuman Dasgupta, Monika Szewczyk, Grant Watson Ed., Museum van Hedendaagse Kunst Antwerpen (MuHKA), 2008.

Land Art, Earth, and Environmental Art 

This module will specifically discuss the movements of the 1960s with a range of artists from the West engaging with land and environment as sites of artistic practice. These include Christo, Robert Smithson, Nancy Holt, and James Turell. While some worked with found elements as material, others tried to reinvent the landscapes through spatial and architectural interventions. The discussion will also reflect on the gaze of these artists on the landscapes they were working with.

description:
Empire, Colony, Subject: A Genealogy of Ideas [POL-2136] [POL-2136-1]

Faculty
Adam Woodhouse [adam.woodhouse@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course allows students to trace the development of three concepts –– empire, colony and the imperial subject –– which were central to sustaining intellectually Western imperial practices, broadly understood, from Roman antiquity to the close of the early modern period (c. 100 BCE–c. 1800). The course follows a genealogical approach –– it focuses on a series of historical ruptures when these concepts were formed, contested and refashioned: the Roman military and political conquest of the Mediterranean region; the emergence of the early modern European sovereign state and its imperial expansion; European colonial encounters with indigenous peoples in the Americas; anti-colonial revolution in the Atlantic world. We will study the employment of the concepts in the works of, among other thinkers, Cicero, Niccolò Machiavelli, Francisco de Vitoria, John Locke and Toussaint L’Ouverture. We will also read work by contemporary political theorists and international relations scholars who draw resources from the pre-modern materials while trying to make sense of global politics today.

Machiavelli and Global Political Theory [POL-3133] [POL-3133-1]

Faculty
Adam Woodhouse [adam.woodhouse@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course allows students to engage closely with the political thought of Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), both within its own distinctive intellectual context of the European Renaissance, and with respect to modern and contemporary global political theory. We will study in detail Machiavelli’s two masterworks of political theory: The Prince (c. 1513) and the Discourses (c. 1518). While doing so, we will examine Machiavelli’s treatment of some topics relevant to a global history of political thought: the nature and origins of the state; the differences between monarchical and popular government; political corruption and its possible remedies; class conflict; civil freedom; slavery; imperialism. To appreciate the distinctiveness of Machiavelli’s interventions, we will read his texts alongside some other influential works of Renaissance political thought, and some of the major writers from Greco-Roman antiquity who supplied the linguistic and conceptual basis for Renaissance intellectual culture. The course then turns to consider some areas of modern and contemporary global politics and political theory in light of Machiavelli’s thought, including Communism, Fascism, republicanism, international relations theory and postcolonialism.

Faculty
Devesh Roy [devesh.roy@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Agri-food systems and economic development: Monsoon 2026- Ashoka University

Course Description

In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), agri-food systems can be instrumental in not only reducing poverty and hunger but also ensuring sustainable food security and nutrition; healthy populations and environment; efficient use of resources, and resilience to shocks and crises. Agri-food systems are critical also as sources of economic growth and development. Agri food system mandate dilution of the binary where there is difference between agriculture, manufacturing and services. The objective of this course is to introduce students to the concept of agri-food systems, their role in economic development, why and how they should/could be transformed to be sustainable, resilient, and inclusive in providing livelihoods and nutritious, safe, accessible, affordable, and sufficient food for current and future generations. The course will focus on topics such as role of agri-food system in growth and development, global trends in food demand and supply with concomitant nutrition transition; trade as a system for agri-food sector inclusive of global value chains that remains under researched, the roles of organizations, institutions, policy and technology and the broad food environment, as well as shocks and crises (such as climate change and COVID-19) on agri-food systems, and will highlight national, regional and global level opportunities and challenges for LMICs to transform their agri-food systems into one that produces sufficient, affordable, accessible, culturally acceptable, safe and nutritious food for all its citizens. The course will look at global and Indian policy transitions and how agrifood systems play a disproportionate role in economic integration and development pathways. Towards this significant attention will be paid to policy landscapes and political economy related to agri-food systems. The course will involve significant empirical focus using global and Indian data assessed analytically.  In addition to providing the theoretical frameworks and the latest literature on each topic, we may feature an invited guest speaker from the field, and where appropriate will feature to make the topics and working thereon more relatable and accessible to those who may want to work in this field. All these themes will be presented and discussed with an equity and social justice lens.  In each class students will have opportunities to present, discuss or debate the topics, and in a few of the classes, experts from the field from within Ashoka or outside may be invited to share their points of view and discuss opportunities and challenges of working in their fields.

Classical Mechanics [PHY-2210/ MAT-3210] [PHY-2210/ MAT-3210-1]

Faculty
Gautam Iqbal Menon [gautam.menon@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

 

MP1 is a pre-requisite for this course

Many of the core concepts of modern physics can be traced back to their origins in classical mechanics, developed by Newton, Lagrange, Hamilton and others. The terminology developed here will find use in many other and more advanced areas of physics, such as quantum mechanics (Hamiltonian, phase space), quantum field theory (Lagrangians, symmetries), statistical physics (ergodicity, chaos) and so on. Classical mechanics is also indispensable in astronomy and astrophysics. 

This is the course to gain the right intuition for these ideas and to build up a strong framework for understanding physics at a higher level.

It begins by formulating  the laws of motion and the dynamical equations as differential equations which need to be integrated to find the solutions of mechanical problems. Conservation laws and constraints will be discussed, with central force motion and the harmonic oscillator playing an important role

The second part of the course deals with Analytical Mechanics: We begin with the idea of generalised coordinates and then move from Newtonian to Lagrangian dynamics. The variational principle is then introduced as a unified way of dealing with diverse physical problems. 

Lagrange’s equations will be derived and the transition to the Hamiltonian form of dynamics will be made, introducing the concept of phase space - a notion of special importance in statistical mechanics.  Subsequently, the Poisson bracket formulation will be discussed. 

Detailed Course Outline

  1. Space and Time, Force and Inertia, Inertial frames, Newton’s Laws, equations of motion, Galilean transformations as symmetries - principle of relativity
  2. Work- energy theorem, kinetic and potential energy. rotational motion: torque, angular momentum and moment of inertia
  3. Harmonic Oscillator: simple, damped and driven oscillators
  4. Many particle systems: energy, momentum and angular momentum - their conservation laws and use in solving dynamical problems
  5. Constraints, generalised coordinates and configuration space, the transition from Newtonian to Lagrangian Mechanics, ignorable coordinates.
  6. The Principle of Least Action: motivation, Fermat’s principle of least time, the brachistochrone problem, general formulation and Euler-Lagrange equations of motion
  7. Symmetries and conservation laws - Noether’s theorem.
  8. Law of Gravitation, Kepler’s Laws and Planetary Orbits: motion in a Central force. LRL vector and its use in deriving the orbit equation
  9. The Legendre transform and Hamiltonian function, Hamilton’s equations of motion, phase space, Liouville’s theorem, Poisson brackets and connections to quantum mechanics.
  10. Non-Inertial frames of reference, effects of acceleration and gravity, the principle of equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass as the foundation of the general theory of relativity.
  11. Simple dynamical systems
Learning Outcomes

A panoramic view of the ideas behind classical mechanics, problem solving abilities, and a good preparation for advanced courses that use these ideas

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Recommended preparatory/supplementary reading: Feynman lectures on Physics Vol. 1, upto chapter 21

  1. Marion and Thornton, Classical Dynamics of particles and systems [Cengage]
  2. R. Douglas Gregory, Classical Mechanics [CUP]. These two texts cover most of the lectured material at essentially the same level.
  3. Landau and Lifshitz, Mechanics [Elsevier]

Discrete Mathematics [CS-1110/ MAT-2203] [CS-1110/ MAT-2203-1]

Faculty
Abhishek Khetan [abhishek.khetan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course provides an introduction to discrete mathematics, the foundational language of computer science. Unlike continuous mathematics, discrete mathematics focuses on distinct objects such as finite sets, integers, and networks. Our objectives are to develop rigorous reasoning skills—including precise definitions and proof-writing—and to apply these concepts through algorithmic implementation.

The curriculum is structured into three primary areas:

  - Foundations: Sets, functions (injections, surjections, bijections), and relations (equivalence, partitions, and orders).
  - Graph Theory: Core concepts including subgraphs, trees, connectivity, Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs, matchings, and coloring.
  - Number Theory: Divisibility, the Euclidean algorithm, primes, modular arithmetic, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

A central theme of the course is the development of algorithms. We will move beyond theoretical proofs to explore practical computational methods, such as breadth-first search, the augmenting-path algorithm, and the Miller-Rabin primality test. Whenever possible, abstract concepts will be motivated by complex puzzles and real-world applications.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, a student should be able to:

  1. read and construct rigorous proofs using the standard techniques (direct proof, contradiction, induction, extremality, the pigeonhole principle, counting arguments).

  2. work fluently with the basic language of mathematics (sets, functions, and relations) and use it to model problems precisely.

  3. reason about graphs and trees, recognise the standard structural notions, and apply the central theorems of a first course in graph theory.

  4. carry out the core computations of elementary number theory (gcds, modular inverses, solving congruences) and explain why the underlying algorithms are correct).

  5. translate a mathematical theorem into an algorithm, and reason informally about whether that algorithm terminates and is correct.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Comfort with high-school algebra and a willingness to engage with proofs.
No prior programming experience is assumed, though students who can write a little code will find it rewarding to implement the algorithms we discuss.

Detailed lecture notes will be provided for everything covered in class, and these notes will include practice problems. They are the primary resource for the course.

For supplementary reading:

  - Douglas B. West, Introduction to Graph Theory (graph theory)
  - David M. Burton, Elementary Number Theory (number theory)
