Grading Rubric

Each student first earns an overall percentage score from the course's assessments. The letter grade is then assigned by a hybrid scheme, designed so that no student is ever penalized by it:

  - First, a hard threshold. Any student whose overall score is below 40% fails the course, regardless of how the rest of the class performs. Reaching 40% is the minimum bar for a passing grade, and nothing below it can be rescued by the curve.

  - For every student at or above 40%, the grade is computed in two independent ways. The absolute scheme assigns a grade from fixed, pre-announced score cutoffs, so that a student's grade depends only on their own performance. The relative scheme assigns a grade from the student's standing within the class, so that a uniformly hard examination does not punish the cohort.

  - The student is then awarded whichever of these two grades is the better one.

      D-        0.7        40 -  44
      F         0.0         0 -  39

The F band (below 40%) is exactly the failing threshold described above: no relative adjustment can lift a score under 40% out of an F.

In short: scoring at least 40% is necessary to pass, and above that line the hybrid scheme always reports the more favourable of the absolute and relative outcomes -- a student can only ever benefit from the curve, never lose to it.

Financial Modeling and Valuation [ENT-2047] [ENT-2047-1]

Faculty
Tushar Ramesh Jaruhar [tushar.jaruhar@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Imagine being able to predict the success or failure of a billion-dollar investment, accurately value a fast-growing startup, or structure a multi-million-dollar acquisition deal—this is the power of Financial Modelling and Valuation. These skills are the backbone of investment banking, private equity, trading, and mergers & acquisitions (M&A). Mastering them can open doors to some of the most lucrative and competitive careers in finance. Financial modelling has played a crucial role in some of the biggest financial decisions in history. Take, for example, the acquisition of WhatsApp by Facebook in 2014—valued at $19 billion. This deal was largely justified based on predictive financial models that projected WhatsApp’s user growth, revenue potential, and future market dominance. Similarly, Tesla’s rise to a trillion-dollar company has been driven by detailed financial models that forecasted its profitability and long-term sustainability in the electric vehicle market. India has also witnessed several high-profile deals driven by financial modelling. The acquisition of Flipkart by Walmart in 2018 for $16 billion was one of the largest e-commerce deals in the world, justified using detailed valuation models that accounted for customer growth, logistics expansion, and competitive positioning. Similarly, Reliance Jio’s rapid rise was underpinned by extensive financial modelling that projected subscriber acquisition, ARPU (Average Revenue Per User), and network expansion costs, ultimately leading to investments from global firms like Facebook and Google. For entrepreneurs, mastering financial modelling and valuation is not just about crunching numbers; it’s about understanding the story behind the numbers—why businesses succeed or fail, how markets react to financial decisions, and what makes a deal profitable. Whether you’re analyzing a company's stock, structuring a leveraged buyout, or forecasting revenues for an M&A deal, these tools help turn complex financial data into actionable insights.

Overview

This 13-week course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practices of Operations Management (OM), with a particular focus on entrepreneurial and small business contexts. Designed for students pursuing a minor in Entrepreneurship, the course explores how well-designed operations strategies can drive business success by enhancing efficiency, improving quality, and enabling scalable growth.

Students will examine core OM topics such as process design, capacity planning, supply chain management, inventory control, quality management, and lean operations. Special attention is given to how these concepts apply uniquely in resource-constrained startup environments and early-stage ventures.

Using real-world case studies, simulations, and hands-on exercises, students will learn to diagnose operational challenges, apply analytical tools, and design practical solutions that align with business goals. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically assess operational performance, make data-informed decisions, and contribute to the sustainable growth of entrepreneurial ventures.

For students interested in launching or working within a new business venture, this course offers vital insights into how efficient operations serve as the backbone of sustainable growth. It demystifies core functions such as supply chain setup, production planning, quality control, and service delivery—all crucial to delivering value to customers and maintaining a competitive edge. Students will learn to identify bottlenecks, manage limited resources, and scale operations strategically—skills especially critical in early-stage and high-growth businesses. By mastering these tools and frameworks, students will be better equipped to design and manage operations that are not only efficient and resilient but also aligned with the dynamic needs of entrepreneurial ventures.

Learning Outcomes

Learning Objectives

- Understand the scope and strategic importance of operations management

- Analyze and design efficient business processes

- Apply lean thinking, capacity planning, and quality management tools

- Use operations tools and techniques to support entrepreneurship and innovation

- Design sustainable, scalable, and ethical operations strategies

description:
Visual configurations of the Body, Gender and Identity in Indian Manuscript Paintings (1100-1900) [VA-2830/ HIS-2807] [VA-2830/ HIS-2807-1]

Faculty
Priyani Roy Choudhury [priyani.choudhury@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Laur attempts to climb up to Chanda's bed chamber, Laur-Chanda, Rylands Collection, University of Manchester. c.1570.

This course uses gender as a critical category of analysis to explore pre- and early modern manuscript paintings in South Asia. It focuses on the evolving artistic styles, cultural and literary norms, and the articulation of gendered selves within them. It offers a critical interrogation of the depiction of the human body, identity markers, and power dynamics in these paintings. Through thematic and visual analysis, students will examine how manuscript paintings portrayed bodies, social and spatial relationships, and power structures. The diverse collection of illustrated manuscripts from various cultural backgrounds spanning eight centuries will be studied to understand the adaptation of visual language and narrative traditions. Students will explore how textual and oral traditions influenced visual and poetic representations, shaping artistic and literary expressions over time. For a detailed overview of the course along with descriptions of each course module, please refer to the attachment.

There will be one museum visit.  

 

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

Learn how to “read” and analyse visual images.

Understand the stylistic development of manuscript painting in South Asia between 1100 and 1900, and identify and differentiate between various historical and regional styles.

Critically examine how visual articulations of the body in manuscript paintings construct and communicate ideas of gender and identity within their historical and cultural contexts.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Essential and suggested readings for the theoretical framework*, museum visit**, and course modules will be uploaded and shared with those who choose to pursue the course.

* The theoretical framework  will provide students with a critical appraisal of Visual Studies research methodologies that incorporate gender studies discourses, particularly in the historical context of South Asia and Iran. Key concepts like ‘gender,’ ‘body,’ ‘identity,’ and other related discursive categories emerging from the diverse historical, socio-cultural, and aesthetic contexts of the course will be introduced.

** There will be one Museum Visit to the National Museum.

This twelve week course of lectures studies the dynamic and dissonance in India-China relations since the founding of the modern republics. Overview

Myth: “This course is heavy on tech.  Expertise/interest in tech is necessary.”

Reality: Not at all.  Tech is just the context.  The course is about policy issues on the internet platforms we all use constantly – issues that affect us all, such as privacy; censorship; competition and choice; and others.

This course (cross-listed with Political Science and with International Relations) will draw from the first-hand experience of a seasoned global tech lawyer and policy practitioner to explore the following questions: around the world, how are businesses, governments, and others thinking about new “rules” for the internet – and how should they be thinking, and how can one help shape this thinking? The course will explore emerging law and policy issues in the context of the internet and technology – in India and key foreign contexts including the U.S. and Europe. Given the increasingly pervasive nature of the internet and technology, these issues bring new and critical implications for a wide variety of professionals and businesses including but not only startups and other entrepreneurial initiatives; for society at large; and for the roles that businesses can play in society. These issues also transcend national boundaries, and routinely reflect and influence complex interactions between different nations. The course will address issues including data privacy; free speech and content moderation; competition; Artificial Intelligence; and others – and also distill practical skills and insights that cut across the various substantive issues discussed in the course. In doing so, the course will help prepare students to navigate, critically evaluate, and shape tech law and policy as part of the business world and more broadly – in India and globally – drawing from the instructor’s first-hand leadership experience in crafting and executing innovative, high-impact strategies in the field.

Faculty
Debapratim Banerjee [debapratim.banerjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

$\sigma$-algebras of sets, Monotone Class Theorem, probability and $\sigma$-finite measures, construction of general

measure, measurable sets, example of a non-measurable set on R at a very basic level.

integration, Fatou’s Lemma, Monotone and Dominated Convergence Theorems. Product measures, Fubini’s theorem. A review of concepts and results from basic discrete and continuous probability. Distribution Functions of Probability Measures on R, Borel-Cantelli Lemma, Weak and Strong Laws of Large

Numbers in i.i.d. case, various Modes of Convergence, Characteristic Functions, Uniqueness/Inversion/Levy

Learning Outcomes

Measures are the basic building block of probability theory. In this course at the beginning, the students should learn how measures are defined formally. They should understand what do we mean by measurable sets and measurable random variables. They should know how measure theory generalizes Riemann integral and how discrete and continuous random variables all come under the common umbrella of measure theory. In the later part, they should understand the convergence of random variables, notion of almost sure, probability and weak convergences along with L^{P} spaces. The proof of central limit theorem will also be done. If time permits, I shall do the proof of strong law of large numbers.

description:
Graduate Algebra I [MAT-5001/ MAT-4104] [MAT-5001/ MAT-4104-1]

Faculty
Conjeeveram Srirangachari Rajan [cs.rajan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The language, concepts and techniques of homological algebra play a fundamental role in modern mathematics.

The course is an introduction to homological algebra via examples, coupled with a review of the associated mathematics. 

We will start with the homological version of Cauchy's theorem on complex analysis. 

Next, we will consider the converse to Galois' theorem on solvability by radicals. We will review Galois theory, 

especially over positive characteristics.  This will introduce us to some basic group cohomology. 

The third motivating example will be Mittag-Leffler's theorem on the existence of meromorphic functions on the complex plane with given 

principal parts at a discrete set of points. This will give us a chance to introduce sheaves. 

We will then move on to considering homological properties of topological spaces, defining and examining the various homology and 

cohomology theories. 

At some point of time, it is possible that  I will try to talk about Weil conjectures. 

We will review the course at regular intervals, allowing us to figure out a way to understand the use of homological methods in modern mathematics.

Learning Outcomes

Review of complex analysis, Galois theory. 

Introduction to algebraic topology. 

Introduction to homological methods in mathematics. 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

A desire to learn mathematics and ready to put in the required effort. 

Basic algebra,  linear algebra, complex analysis, field theory, etc.

courseTitle: Shaping the India Way: Foreign policy institutions, sites and forces
description:
Shaping the India Way: Foreign policy institutions, sites and forces [IR-2061/ POL-2139] [IR-2061/ POL-2139-1]

Faculty
Constantino Cristovam Hermanns Xavier [constantino.xavier@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

As a rising power India is deepening and expanding its ties with the rest of the world across different domains, from climate and technology to trade and security, culture and sports. There is a growing and diverse flow of goods, capital, people and ideas moving across India’s territorial borders amidst an uncertain, fractious geopolitical order. India’s foreign economic and security policies are also assuming electoral salience at home, as well as a growing extra-territorial dimension, including a 30-million strong diaspora. India now aims to be a “voice of the Global South,” reform multilateral institutions and host the 2036 Olympics. Whether it is artificial intelligence, health, outer space or the Internet, Indian officials are now increasingly involved – or expected to be present -- at the global “high tables” setting new global standards and regulations. This increasingly complex, fast-paced international environment is posing new challenges for India to define and pursue its interests abroad.

Yet while we know much about the rising ambition, expanding scope and accelerating pace of India’s international engagements in recent years, there is less knowledge about the growing number of institutions, sites and forces that shape its foreign policy behaviour. This course introduces students to the broader yet also less visible ecosystem in which Indian foreign policy is made or “begins” at home: What traditional and new organizations are involved in defining India’s international posture? What are the main institutional sites and locations of decision-making, at different levels of government and across the country, from New Delhi to border regions? How do different domestic, non-governmental forces and actors shape the ideas and interests that drive India’s international engagements?

The course is divided in three parts, focused on specialized readings, class discussions and different types of oral and written assignments to map the different institutions, sites and forces that shape the India way of diplomacy. The first part (state institutions) explores the traditional, state-centric perspective including the role of different ministries and the bureaucracy, the armed forces, intelligence organizations, the parliament and regional states. The second part (non-state forces) examines the non-state perspective, including the role of political parties, the private sector, civil society organizations, media and think tanks. The third part (transnational sites or spaces) examines transnational or immaterial issue areas where institutions and forces come into play between the domestic and the international, such as borderlands, the environment, space and cyberspace.

The course thus connects the study of India’s foreign policy state institutions to the rising number of new non-governmental forces that shape foreign policy in an increasingly complex range of transnational issue areas. This is critical to understand the changing role of the Indian state in a changing international order, marked by geopolitical competition and multiple power transitions.

Learning Outcomes

By tracking these different levels of analysis, focused on case studies across time and space, we  will also assess how this environment has changed in recent years, reflecting issues of Indian state capacity, policy coordination, organizational change and accountability that are rarely studied in Indian IR. This will help students to a) familiarize themselves with both old and new institutions, sites and forces that are shaping Indian foreign policy, b) connect (or apply) theoretical concepts and learnings from foreign policy analysis, international political economy, transnationalism and historical institutionalism to the case of India, and c) develop insights and analytical skills that are required for most public policy professionals focused on India. government, think tanks, private sector or multilateral institutions.

Global Politics and Football [POL-3122/ IR-3036] [POL-3122/ IR-3036-1]

Faculty
Surajkumar Dnyandeo Thube [surajkumar.thube@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Global Politics and Football

In his book The Ball Is Round: A Global History of Football, David Goldblatt argues that football is the most globally recognised cultural phenomenon. Perhaps no other sport manages to generate and capture the euphoric sense of collective joy along with shades of profound dismay and dejection as much as football. It also allows the game to serve as a playful conduit to the cultural and political intricacies of a particular country. Instead of envisioning football merely as a source of mass entertainment, it allows one to map the unfolding socio-political ramifications through what can be termed as the 'raw appeal of the game'. The course will explore the intimacy of football and politics.

Some of the prominent themes that will be covered in the course are: political origins of football, political ideologies and football, intermeshing of religion, culture and the State, political fandom and identity formations, football as a means of gender emancipation, racism in football, and the political economy of football in the contemporary period. The course will begin in the late 19th century and extend to the present time. It will cover these themes and issues from various political perspectives, highlighting personalities, football clubs, and passionate football countries across the globe. It will introduce football as one of the most potent cultural media to express myriad political sentiments. The course will seek to address questions, which include, but are not limited to: Why and how does football provide a unique framework to understand 20th-century global politics? How has football been used both as a tool of propaganda and as a medium of radical resistance? Is it possible to extricate the element of entertainment from the reprehensible aspects of racism and violence it ends up promoting? Why and how does faith in football supplement instead of contradicting the faith of religious beliefs? How does modern-day ‘sportswashing’ alter the mass perception of the basic raw appeal of the game? 

The course is directed towards students who are eager to learn more about international politics through the lens of football. It is also meant for students who wish to view football as a gateway to get introduced to global politics. Lastly, it is also for those who want to marry their passion for playing and watching football to the notion of understanding how sports are never only about entertainment, as they actively shape individual lives and societies. Even for students who are indifferent to the game, the course will allow them a unique vantage point to comprehend issues that have defined global politics since the early 20th century.

Cryptography [CS-3621/ MAT-3214] [CS-3621/ MAT-3214-1]

Faculty
Mahabir Prasad Jhanwar [mahavir.jhawar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Coverage:

Symmetric key cryptography: Symmetric Key Encryption, Pseudorandom number generators (PRG), Pseudorandom functions (PRF), Stream cipher, Block cipher, Modes of Operation, Security definitions for Encryption, Message integrity, Message authentication codes, Hash Functions.

Public key cryptography: Diffie-Hellman key exchange, Discrete logarithm problem and its variants. Public key encryption (PKE), security definition. ElGamal  PKE. Factoring and RSA problem. RSA PKE. Digital Signature. RSA and DSA signature schemes. Elliptic curves and ECDSA signature scheme. 

Efficient cryptographic operations and cryptanalysis algorithms: Modular arithmetic, modular inverse, modular exponents, prime number generation, picking generators for cyclic groups. Algorithms for discrete logarithm and factoring. 

Cryptography Applications: Public key infrastructure (PKI), Brief Introduction to TLS.

Advanced Cryptography Concepts (if time permits): Commitment Schemes, Secret Sharing, Oblivious Transfer, Zero knowledge Proofs, Multiparty Computation.

Course Outline:

Confidentiality/privacy of communication, symmetric-key encryption (SKE); basic security definition

Toy SKEs: shift cipher, affine cipher, substitution cipher

Exhaustive key search attack, large key space being necessary but not sufficient

Advanced security definitions for SKE

Computational vs Unconditional/Information theoretic Security 

Basics of Information theoretic security

Design of SKE with indistinguishability security (ind-security)

Pseudo random generator (PRG), PRG $\implies$ SKE with ind-security

Design of SKE with ind-cpa security

Pseudo random function (PRF), PRF $\implies$ SKE with ind-cpa security

Stream cipher, Block cipher, Modes of operation

Pseudo random permutation (PRP)

Construction framework: Substitution-permutation network (SPN)

Advanced encryption standard (AES)

Message Integrity, Message authentication codes (MAC), MAC security 

Construction of MACs from PRF, ECBC-MAC

Hash function, security, random-oracle construction

Merkle-Demgard construction for hash functions

MAC from hash function, HMAC

SKE with Ind-cca security 

Privacy + integrity: encrypt and authenticate; authenticate then encrypt; encrypt then authenticate 

Key exchange; Diffie-Hellman key exchange 

Discrete logarithm problem (DLP), Computational Diffie-Hellman (CDH) problem 

Algorithms for DLP

Public-key encryption (PKE) scheme, security definitions

ElGamal PKE, Ind-cpa security proof of ElGamal, Decision Diffie-Hellman Problem

Efficient algorithms for ElGamal components

RSA PKE

Efficient algorithms for RSA components

Digital Signature scheme, security definitions

RSA signature, Schnorr signature, DSA scheme

Public key infrastructure (PKI)

Transport layer security (TLS)

 

Learning Outcomes

Privacy, secrecy, and security are central to our emerging “information society”, and cryptography is a key technology for achieving them; it is also a fascinating field of study in its own right. This course serves as an introduction to modern cryptography.

Students will first understand the foundational goals of cryptography - confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity - and learn how to rigorously formalize these goals through precise security definitions. They will study key cryptographic primitives - encryption, hash/MACs, and digital signatures - as tools to achieve these goals.

They will explore the conceptual and historical progression of encryption: beginning with symmetric-key encryption, advancing to key exchange, and culminating in public-key encryption (PKE). Students will also understand why combining symmetric and public-key techniques, as in real-world protocols like TLS, offers both efficiency and security for secure internet communication.

Throughout the course, students will appreciate the role of mathematical hardness assumptions (like factoring and discrete log) in securing cryptographic systems, and how security proofs reduce cryptographic security to these underlying problems. They will also gain hands-on experience implementing core cryptographic primitives and applying them to build real-world applications where security is paramount.

Decolonisation: An International History [IR-2074] [IR-2074-1]

Faculty
Pallavi Raghavan [pallavi.raghavan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In this course, we consider the different motivations that accompany the internationalist behavior of decolonized states, and whether these should constitute a separate set of categories from the norms that otherwise govern the developed world.

To begin with, we examine how the term ‘Decolonization’ is defined, along its implications for how the internationalist behavior of states is to be judged. Subsequently, we will examine how this is connected to processes of state monopolization over violence, anxieties over territoriality, and the tensions involved in creating a unanimously agreed to ‘national’ identity in different parts of the Global South.

The concluding set of readings in this course will explore how the tensions of shaping the ‘national’ are also present in governing the ‘international’. We explore how the process of constructing an argument about “Decolonization” also entails a conversation between competing worldviews. We will explore how these tensions are present in the shaping of Foreign Policy as well as “Worldmaking” and develop a fuller analysis about how these also constitute a tussle over the definitions of international norms themselves.

Learning Outcomes

*To understand the ways in which colonialism is present in contemporary international order

*To understand the way in which the contemporary international order itself is a construct, subject to change, contestation or even rejection

*To understand the commonalities of nation building challenges faced by the post colonial leadership in large parts of the Global South.

Corporate Finance [ENT-1021] [ENT-1021-1]

Faculty
Vandana Gupta [vandana.gupta@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The objective of this course is to explain the role of finance in an organization and enable students to analyze the relationship between strategic decision-making and corporate financing decisions. Beginning with the premise that the financial objective of a business organization is to increase the value of the firm, the course deals with the key issues that contribute to shareholder value, including capital budgeting or investment decisions; capital structure and sources of funding, or the financing decision, how companies can return value to shareholders via the dividend and other "payback" strategies that are the dividend function, and short-term investment decisions, that is working capital management as also financial risk management. By an in-depth understanding of the financial issues faced by companies, together, these concepts make up the essential building blocks for a career in finance. As students progress, they will delve deeper into asset valuation, covering a broad spectrum of asset classes. The course provides detailed instruction on how to value bonds and equities, teaching participants to evaluate key factors like bond yields, bond pricing, and yield curves. For equity valuation, students will explore various methodologies, including discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis and relative valuation methods. The course emphasizes the distinction between enterprise value and equity value, helping students understand how to think critically about a company’s financial worth from different perspectives. The section on risk management introduces students to the use of derivatives—such as interest rate swaps, foreign exchange contracts, and commodity derivatives—as tools to hedge financial risks and protect companies from adverse market movements. In addition, the course includes an in-depth analysis of mergers and acquisitions (M&A), focusing on how these corporate deals can create or destroy value for companies. Students will learn to analyze M&A transactions using tools such as earnings per share (EPS) accretion/dilution analysis, leverage analysis, and shareholder impact assessments. By building M&A models in Excel, students will gain a practical understanding of how these deals are structured and evaluated in the corporate world. This course lays the foundation for those looking to advance their career in a range of professions, including investment banking, equity research analyst, credit analyst, consulting, general management, and CFO track jobs within a corporate.

Learning Outcomes

The course is designed with the following specific objectives and learning outcomes: • Understanding the Objective of Corporate Finance: Students will understand the role of finance in an organization and how corporate finance decisions contribute to shareholder value. They will examine the role of financial management, agency problems, and the relationship between managerial decisions and firm value. • Time Value of Money and Financial Asset Valuation: Students will learn to use present value and future value techniques for financial decision-making. They will value bonds at premium, discount, and par, calculate yield to maturity, and apply dividend growth and free cash flow approaches to equity valuation. • Risk, Return, and CAPM: Students will acquire basic knowledge of risk and return, portfolio diversification, systematic and unsystematic risk, beta estimation, determinants of beta, and the Capital Asset Pricing Model. This will enable students to estimate expected returns and cost of equity. • Capital Budgeting and Investment Appraisal: This objective emphasizes on financial appraisal of investment proposals for firms using NPV, IRR, discounted payback, payback period, and profitability index. They will learn to evaluate independent and mutually exclusive projects, replacement decisions, and capital rationing situations. • Cost of Capital and Financing Decisions: Acquire the knowledge to study the cost implications of alternative sources of funding. They will estimate cost of debt, cost of equity, cost of retained earnings, and combine these into WACC. They will also appreciate the link between investment decisions and financing decisions. • Capital Structure and Leverage: To analyze operating and financial leverage, EBIT-EPS analysis, capital structure theories, financial distress, and Modigliani-Miller propositions. Learning to evaluate how financing choices influence firm risk and value. • Dividend Policy and Payout Decisions: Students will understand dividend payment decisions, different types of dividends, bonus issues, stock splits, repurchase of shares, and the implications of payout policy for shareholders. • Manage Risk with Derivatives: Learn how to mitigate financial risks through the use of derivatives, such as interest rate swaps, foreign exchange contracts, and commodity derivatives. Assess how changes in interest rates, currency fluctuations, and commodity prices can affect a company’s financial performance and apply hedging strategies accordingly. • Evaluate Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A): Acquire the skills to analyze and model the financial impact of mergers and acquisitions. Conduct detailed assessments of EPS accretion/dilution, leverage effects, and shareholder dilution, and understand the strategic rationale behind corporate M&A transactions. Develop and interpret comprehensive M&A models using Excel for real-world application.

courseTitle: "Who Speaks for the “Wounded” Earth? Fiction, Nature, and Gender in India"
description:
"Who Speaks for the “Wounded” Earth? Fiction, Nature, and Gender in India" [CT-2355] [CT-2355-1]

Faculty
Debadrita Saha [debadrita.saha_phd23@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

When a forest is destroyed, who mourns it, and in what language? This course begins with a simple but unsettling observation: in India, the history of ecological violence and the history of gendered oppression have the same roots. They originate in colonial and caste-based hierarchies that treated both land and feminine bodies as resources to be owned, exploited, and controlled. Reading prose fiction, poetry, and essays by 21st-century Indian women writers writing in the wake of liberalisation, amongst them Anuradha Roy, Kavery Nambisan, Anita Nair, Mitra Phukan, Sumana Roy, Temsula Ao, and Meena Kandasamy, we will examine how writing about nature, land, and ecological crisis is also always writing about gender, caste, and colonial history. To do so, we will draw on key texts in ecofeminist and postcolonial criticism as lenses for reading and critiquing rather than as isolated conceptual ends in themselves. In the classroom, I would like you all to perceive this course as an invitation to embark on a different odyssey of higher education: to read, to write, and to think differently about land, body, and belonging in contemporary India.

Learning Outcomes

This course is designed to help you:

  • familiarise yourself with an important and understudied body of 21st-century Indian women's writing in English, spanning the novel, poetry, and the essay.
  • develop the skills of close reading, such as attending carefully to language, form, and structure as carriers of meaning and argument.
  • build and sustain an academic argument by bringing primary texts into conversation with theoretical frameworks.
  • compose a clear, well-evidenced academic essay through iterative writing, revision, and peer discussion.
  • think critically about the relationship between ecological violence, gender, caste, and colonial history in contemporary India.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Suggested Secondary Readings (tentative):

Agarwal, Bina. “The Gender and Environment Debate: Lessons from India.” Feminist Studies, vol. 18, no. 1, 1992, pp. 119–58, https://doi.org/10.2307/3178217.

Baviskar, Amita. "Red in Tooth and Claw?: Searching for Class in Struggles over Nature". Social Movements in India: Poverty, Power, and Politics, edited by Raka Ray and Mary Katzenstein, Rowman & Littlefield, 2005, pp. 161-179.

Mukherjee, Upamanyu Pablo. Postcolonial Environments: Nature, Culture and the Contemporary Indian Novel in English. Palgrave Macmillan, 2010. 

Nixon, Rob. Slow Violence and Environmentalism of the Poor. Harvard UP, 2011. 

Ortner, Sherry B. "Is female to male as nature is to culture?" Woman, Culture, and Society, edited by M. Z. Rosaldo and L. Lamphere, Stanford UP, 1974, pp. 68-87.

courseTitle: Dystopian Novel and Phenomenology of Religion
description:
Dystopian Novel and Phenomenology of Religion [CT-2345] [CT-2345-1]

Faculty
Junaid Farooq [junaid.farooq_phd23@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What does dystopian fiction know that theology and philosophy cannot say outright? This course asks a significant question: dystopian fiction keeps reaching for religious language, messianic metaphors, parodic scripture, engineered prophecy, eschatological thought, long after its imagined societies claim to have left God and religion behind. That recurrence is not incidental borrowing; it is the genre doing its own distinct kind of thinking about what happens when the human search for ultimate meaning is denied a transcendental object. Reading specific sections from the works of Mary Shelley, H.G Wells, Yevgeny Zamyatin, Aldous Huxley, George Orwell, Ray Bradbury, Frank Herbert, Jose Saramago, Kurt Vonnegurt, Ursula Kroeber Le Guin, and a non-Western dystopian work chosen in consultation with students, we will ask what each novel is arguing, in narrative as well as in an argumentative form. Whether the crisis of the subject under totalitarian control is the same crisis phenomenologists identify in modernity at large, or whether fiction, through character, plot, and the slow unfolding of a lived world, reaches a kind of understanding that philosophical and theological prose cannot reach on its own. To pursue these questions, we will draw from the phenomenology of religion (Rudolf Otto, Mircea Eliade, Martin Heidegger, Walter Benjamin, Jean-Luc Marion, Jean-Louis Chrétien, Jean-Luc Nancy, Claude Romano, Jacque Derrida, Nader El-Bizri and Hasan Hanafi) and the theory of political messianism (J.L.Talmon, Eric Voegelin, Jacob Taubes, Gil Anidjar, Michael Lowy, Emilio Gentile, Michael Burleigh) as means for reading rather than as ends in themselves. The theoretical framework will be read as inherent conversation the novels demand and not a set of frameworks the novels merely illustrate. This course is, above all, an invitation: to take dystopian fiction seriously as a form of inquiry into the sacred, the political, and the limits of phenomenology.

 

Central Question

How does dystopian fiction stage the logic of political messianism, the promise of secular salvation through absolute political order, historical necessity, and collective submission, and what does the protagonist's phenomenological “awakening” reveal about whether messianic politics can ever truly deliver redemption, or whether it must, by its very structure, perpetually defer the sacred it claims to have already realized?

Learning Outcomes
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Dermot Moran, Introduction to Phenomenology, Routledge, 1999.

Brandon Simonson, ed., Theology, Religion, and Dystopia, Bloomsbury, 2022

Adam Stock, Modern Dystopian Fiction and Political Thought Narratives of World Politics, Routledge, 2019

Monica Duffy Toft, God’s Century: Resurgent Religion and Global Politics, W. W. Norton & Co Inc., 2011

Wittgenstein’s Riddles [ENG-4459] [ENG-4459-1]

Faculty
Eesha Kumar [eesha.kumar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Ludwig Wittgenstein is commonly regarded as one of the most important philosophers of the 20th century; but he has also been described as an anti-philosopher. While Wittgenstein has enduring legacies in several fields (ordinary language philosophy, literary fiction, literary criticism, the interdisciplinary study of pain, formal logic, mathematics, religious studies, anthropology), rarely can any one of these accommodate the heterodox range of his writings. Despite having legions of devoted commentators, his primary texts remain sibylline and obscure, without obvious precedents or peers. 

This graduate seminar will center the methodological question of how to “read” Wittgenstein—and, more generally, how to “read.” The theme of riddling (etymologically linked with reading) will guide us through his texts, as we we take an atypical path that starts with the 1929 Lecture on Ethics, goes back to the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), and leaps forward to the posthumous Philosophical Investigations. We will also spend some time with his journals, diaries, and other fragmentary writings to consider the question of genre in relation to philosophy. Other methodological concerns will include the significance of translation and biography. 

In addition to primary texts (in translation), students in this course will be introduced to several schools of secondary literature on Wittgenstein, and can elect to pursue one “stream” for a sustained engagement in their presentations and final papers.

courseTitle: Small Town in Hindi Cinema and Literature
description:
Small Town in Hindi Cinema and Literature [ENG-3420] [ENG-3420-1]

Faculty
Rita Kothari [rita.kothari@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course is focused upon an under-theorized spatiality called the “small town.” The term “small town” is transitional, in the sense that it may refer to what were once rural hinterlands that have now become urbanized. It may also refer to the new configuration at the edge of existing cities that develop into their own entities, neither rural nor fully city-like. One of the key themes that underlies the small town is aspiration and mobility. But small town also destabilizes the metropolis, which is always seen as the sign of futurity. How does one move between an understanding that is not simply recursive to parochialism and regional hegemony? We will employ the lens of language, caste, sexuality, family and modernity  to understand the phenomenon of the small town. By combining literature and cinema and putting them in conversation, the course would make theoretical interventions in this under-studied subject.

courseTitle: Studies in World Literature: Myth, Literature, and Africa in the World
description:
Studies in World Literature: Myth, Literature, and Africa in the World [ENG-2354] [ENG-2354-1]

Faculty
S Satish Kumar [s.kumar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course seeks to explore the ostensible tensions that have historically existed and continue to do so, between what Chinua Achebe famously described as “An Image of Africa” and the plural experiential realities of the peoples and nationalities across Continental Africa. We will be working towards a sense of Afrocentric literary and cultural historiographies starting with perceptions of “Africa” and “Africans”. Beginning around “late antiquity”, through the Enlightenment and leading into the colonial enterprise, such “images” of “Africa” have not only dominated a Eurocentric imagination, but also formed the basis for the subjugation and despoliation of African peoples. Through readings of African mythologies, oratures and early colonial literatures, this course seeks to both problematize and deconstruct dominant Eurocentric discourses about “Africa” that continue to endure in our “global” imaginations.

courseTitle: The Theory of Corporate Finance and Banking
description:
The Theory of Corporate Finance and Banking [FIN-3555/ FIN-4555] [FIN-3555/ FIN-4555-1]

Faculty
Kaushalendra Kishore [kaushalendra.kishore@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In a perfect world, all projects that create value should receive financing. But in the real world, they do not. In this course, we will first learn about the various economic frictions that prevent firms and entrepreneurs from receiving financing, and how they can be mitigated. We will learn that at the heart of the problem are various information and contracting frictions such as moral hazard and adverse selection. The course examines the foundations of corporate finance, including capital structure, corporate governance, information asymmetries, agency problems, incentive design, and the role of contracts.

As several banking crises, including the global financial crisis (GFC) of 2008, have highlighted, banks matter. But why did the GFC occur? Who was responsible: the shareholders of the banks, the CEOs of the banks, the traders, or regulators? Designing appropriate regulation to prevent the crisis requires knowing exactly where the problem was. If the problem was the perverse incentives of the traders, then increasing bank capital requirements may not solve the problem. The second half of the course will introduce you to key ideas in modern banking theory, along with some related empirical research. Our emphasis will be on banks both as a major source of corporate finance for non-financial firms and as firms making financial decisions in their own right. We will learn why banks are important and what role they play in the economy, and also discuss ideas related to banking crises, financial stability, and regulation.

We will extensively use the tools of game theory and solve a lot of models. While most of these model and not very mathematically complicated, they will be economically rich. The tools learnt in this course also have extensive applications in the fields of labour economics and organisation design, which will not be covered.

Learning Outcomes

The goal of this course is to teach the students about various agency frictions and modelling techniques so that they learn the theory of corporate finance and also become capable of reading more advanced papers in corporate finance. In the second part of the course, the students will learn about the role banks play in the economy and the reasons and consequences of banking and financial crises, along with how regulators try to maintain financial stability.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Prerequisites: ECO 2102 & ECO 2201

There will be no single required textbook for the course. Recommended books include:

The Theory of Corporate Finance by Jean Tirole.

Microeconomics of Banking (2nd Edition) by Xavier Freixas and Jean-Charles Rochet.

Contemporary Financial Intermediation (3rd Edition) by Stuart I. Greenbaum, Anjan V. Thakor and Arnoud W.A. Boot.

Economics of Money, Banking and Financial Markets (11th edition) by Frederic S. Mishkin

Principles of Corporate Finance (14th Edition) by Richard A. Brealey, Stewart C. Myers, Franklin Allen, Alex Edmans and Pitabas Mohanty

Corporate Finance (6th Edition) by Jonathan Berk and Peter DeMarzo

Microeconomics (1-Yr MA) [ECO-5004] [ECO-5004-1]

Faculty
Sumit Goel [sumit.goel@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces the major concepts and tools of microeconomics. Broadly, microeco-
nomics is a study of institutions in terms of how they allocate scarce resources. We begin by

discussing why designing good institutions is fundamentally challenging. Much of the course
then focuses on one particularly important institution, the market mechanism. We will study
how consumers and producers interact to jointly determine the prices and allocation of goods,
and discuss conditions under which markets promote an efficient allocation of resources, as
well as sources of market failure where they may lead to inefficient outcomes. Towards the

end, we will briefly discuss game theory, and see how it provides a useful framework for eval-
uating institutions in a variety of other contexts.

Overview

This course equips students with the econometric methods essential for causal inference and program evaluation. The curriculum covers the fundamentals of linear regression and its extensions, experimental methods (including an overview of randomized controlled trials), and key quasi-experimental techniques (such as instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and regression discontinuity design). Additionally, students will gain hands-on experience applying these concepts using STATA through application-based problem sets and assignments.

Financial Institutions (1-Yr MA) [ECO-5008] [ECO-5008-1]

Faculty
Abheek Barua [abheek.barua@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course will serve as an introduction to financial markets and institutions and leave students with both an analytical framework to understand them as well as an appreciation of “ real world” financial markets and institutional structures. The broad topics covered in the course will be:

Section1

An introduction to asset classes and their markets.

The reasons for the existence of financial institutions

Problems of asymmetric information and solutions

Case studies on the problems of microlending, the transaction cost revolution (Zerodha and Robin Hood), regulatory failure and the Enron case, assessing Adani group’s debt financed expansion

Section2

Approaches to valuation

The ‘ fair value’ idea and cash flow discounting

Interest rates, yields and risk premia

The term structure of yields and their interpretation

The notion of bond “duration”. How to “ trade duration”?

Section 3

Seminal ideas in investment – the Markovitz Frontier and the Sharpe ratio

How does one use financial theory to explain Warren Buffet’s success?

The Fama French Factor model

Alpha and Beta and their application to the real world finance

Section 4

Central banking – how is money created. The RBI’s balance sheet

The LAF corridor and transmission of monetary policy

The zero bound problem, quantitative easing and the notion of negative interest rates

The nominal anchor idea and ways to establish it.

Central bank targets – inflation targeting versus alternatives

Should the central bank deflate asset bubbles

Case study on the RBI’s response to the taper tantrum

A quick review of India money and bond markets

Section 5

Financial crises

Causes, impact and remedies

Markers of macroeconomic stress.

Section 6

The changing approach to financial regulation

A quick introduction to Basel norms

Regulatory failure and India’s twin balance sheet problem

Section7

Residual topics

The international financial system

Exchange rate models and markets for managing external risk

The course will leave students with a broad understanding of financial markets and the various institutions that constitute the financial system. While international examples will be used, the emphasis will be on exploring the Indian financial structure.

description:
Reading in Parts: Seminar in Ninetenth-Century Literature [ENG-4385] [ENG-4385-1]

Faculty
Mandakini Dubey [mandakini.dubey@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course asks you to travel out of your skin, in a manner of speaking, and explore a new -- or rather, an old -- mode of reading.

What might it mean to read like Victorians? Unlike us, Victorian readers were not likely to consume the great nineteenth-century novels that Henry James famously described as "large loose baggy monsters" in linear fashion, marching regimentally from beginning to end. Rather, they moved between texts that were in circulation, in parts, all in the semi-public sphere of serialised publication. How might such a practice of reading rupture our understanding of texts as singular, bounded, and individual, and what does that do for our work as literary critics and theorists? We will explore, together, the connections and intersections that open up through a more partial, in-between approach to reading. 

The primary genre we explore in this course is the Victorian novel, but that will come with a suitably high number of exceptions and digressions as we try and replicate some aspects of the nineteenth-century culture of reading. Expect to read novels by George Eliot, Charles Dickens, Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay, Elizabeth Gaskell, and others; poetry by Alfred Tennyson and Elizabeth Barrett Browning; and journalistic, scientific, and ethnographic writings. We will dip in and out of periodicals (including those that circulated in the British metropolis or in the colonies, as well as those that were aimed at women), and we will allow our conversations to both tunnel into these texts through close reading and swoop among them and beyond them as we think intertextually and historically. This will be a screen-free classroom; you are expected to have physical copies of the readings (including a coursepack).

Microeconomics of Artificial Intelligence [ECO-3552/ ECO-4552] [ECO-3552/ ECO-4552-1]

Faculty
Abhinash Borah [abhinash.borah@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course develops a microeconomic analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) and situates it within the broader data economy. Its organizing idea is that recent advances in AI are best understood not as a new form of intelligence but as a dramatic fall in the cost of prediction. Treating AI as a “prediction machine” lets us bring the standard toolkit of microeconomics—decision-making under uncertainty, the theory of the firm, pricing, and market structure—to bear on questions that otherwise seem to belong to computer science. The payoff is a disciplined account of where AI creates value, who captures it, and when and why it is adopted. 

The primary unit of analysis is the individual decision. Cheaper, better prediction changes decisions, and the value of AI is inherited from the value of the decisions it improves. We begin with the classical benchmark of a rational agent choosing under uncertainty, but a central theme of the course is that this benchmark is not enough. Because real decision-makers face cognitive and informational constraints, much of AI’s economic impact runs through boundedly rational behavior: the rules people fall back on, the information they choose not to acquire, and the attention they cannot spread everywhere at once. Understanding when prediction substitutes for these coping devices, and when it complements them, is the key to the microeconomics of AI. 

On the demand side, we study how a lower cost of information reshapes optimal behavior, shifting agents away from rigid, one-size-fits-all rules toward flexible, state-contingent decisions. In the process, prediction can substitute for traditional risk-management tools such as insurance and buffer stocks. We then turn to human judgment—knowing what a good outcome is worth—as the critical complement to machine prediction. The prediction–judgment distinction lets us analyze automation: when it pays to automate a narrow task rather than delegate an entire decision, and why capturing value from AI typically forces a firm to redesign its organization and internal incentives. Each of these margins is, ultimately, a driver of adoption. 

On the supply side, we integrate the perspective of the data economy and treat data as a distinctive economic asset—nonrivalled, and valuable precisely because it reduces uncertainty. We examine where training and input data come from, why users may share or withhold it, and why they may even behave strategically toward the systems that learn from them. A data feedback loop, in turn, can convert an early advantage into durable market power. Bringing demand and supply together yields a theory of AI pricing: how providers price prediction in light of the user’s judgment, and how that judgment evolves through experience and experimentation to support “AI-as-a-Service” subscription models. Pricing and adoption then play out together in competitive markets, under monopoly, and in bilateral negotiation. Adoption becomes a market outcome: providers set prices in anticipation of who will take up AI, and each firm’s adoption alters the payoff to adoption by the rest.

A goal of the course is to connect the micro analysis to its macroeconomic counterparts. The decision-theoretic core of the prediction-machine framework often aligns with the aggregate analysis of the data economy: how data-driven predictions feed into aggregate dynamics, how strategic “forecasting the forecasts of others” shapes prices and volatility, how the feedback loop concentrates production, and how data should be measured and valued. Where these links hold, we draw the macroeconomic consequences out explicitly, so that students see the same forces at work at the level of the firm and of the economy.

The course also confronts the debate over whether AI is in a financial bubble. Building on the treatment of data as an asset, a dedicated unit asks how the economic value of data and prediction should be measured, why that value is so hard to pin down, and how these fundamentals square with what we see in current AI markets—markets marked by extraordinary valuations, heavy capital expenditure, and circular financing. The aim is to give students the tools to reason about valuation and speculation for themselves, not to adjudicate the debate.

The final part turns to welfare and policy. We weigh the antitrust concerns raised by data-driven market power and algorithmic collusion, the design and limits of privacy regulation, and the intellectual-property questions posed by training data. We also assess the systemic risks of misinformation, algorithmic bias, and discrimination. The part closes with a more speculative discussion on the behavioral, social, and macroeconomic consequences of widespread AI adoption—and with what, if anything, policy can do to steer them.

description:
Competitive Strategy [ECO-3551/ ECO-4551] [ECO-3551/ ECO-4551-1]

Faculty
Saish Vijay Nevrekar [saish.nevrekar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why did India's telecom price war end with three survivors instead of ten? When does moving first --- building capacity, setting a standard, signing a long-term contract --- confer an advantage, and when does it invite ruin? How much of the value a firm creates can it actually capture in negotiations with suppliers, buyers, and partners? And how should a firm bid when it knows less than its rivals?

This course develops the economics of competitive strategy: a rigorous toolkit for analyzing markets in which each firm's fortunes depend on what its rivals do. Where introductory economics studies firms that take the market as given, this course studies firms that shape it --- by committing, threatening, signaling, bargaining, and bidding.

We build the game-theoretic apparatus from the ground up --- dominance, equilibrium, credible commitment, strategic behavior under incomplete information --- and put each tool to work on the central problems of strategy: rivalry in prices and quantities, product positioning, entry and entry deterrence, sustaining cooperation among rivals, negotiation and value capture, competing when rivals' costs or intentions are unknown, and bidding in auctions and procurement contests. Models are developed formally and then applied to real market episodes, with particular attention to Indian markets (telecom pricing, airline capacity, spectrum auctions).

description:
Magnetism and Magnetic Materials: An Experimental Approach [PHY-4060/ PHY-6060] [PHY-4060/ PHY-6060-1]

Faculty
Susmita Saha [susmita.saha@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Overview

This course provides undergraduate students with early exposure to advanced experimental techniques in materials science, with a focus on magnetism.

It combines theoretical understanding with hands-on laboratory training.

By integrating solid-state physics concepts with practical experience in fabrication and characterization, the course bridges the gap between theory and experiment.

Course Objectives

To introduce the fundamental principles of modern experimental techniques.

To provide hands-on experience in the fabrication of metallic thin films and nanostructures.

To study structural properties using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Atomic force microscope (AFM), and Field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM).

To investigate magnetic properties using Magneto optical Kerr effect microscope (MOKE).

To explore magnetization dynamics using Ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) techniques.

Course Structure

Theory

Introduction to magnetic materials: domains, anisotropy, and exchange interactions.

Overview of bulk vs thin-film magnetism.

Introduction to characterization techniques: XRD, FESEM, AFM, MOKE, FMR, and sputtering methods.

Experiment

Sample Fabrication

Training in thin-film deposition using direct current/radio frequency (DC/RF) sputtering, Fabrication of metallic magnetic thin films (Co, Ni, Fe), Understanding the influence of growth parameters on material properties.

Introduction to electrochemical deposition for grow nano structures such as nanowires, Optimize the growth parameters for Electrodeposition techniques

Structural Characterization

Use XRD to atomic structure of the thin film and nanostructure.

Calculate the crystal size estimation using the Scherrer formula.

Surface morphology, thickness and roughness analysis using FESEM and AFM.

Correlation between fabrication conditions and structural properties.

Magnetic Characterization

Measurement of magnetic hysteresis (M–H loops) using MOKE.

Determination of coercivity (Hc) and remanence (Mr).

Study of magnetization dynamics in the GHz frequency range using FMR.

Estimation of the Gilbert damping parameter.

Learning Outcomes

Wil get exposure to advance experimental techniques.

References :

Nanostructures and Nanotechnology by Douglas Natelson

Introduction to Solid state Physics by Kittel

Solid State Physics by Ashcroft and Mermin

Magnetization Oscillations and waves by Melkov and Gurevich

Magnetism and Magnetic Materials by JMD Coey

Quantum Mechanics 3 [PHY-4530/ PHY-6530] [PHY-4530/ PHY-6530-1]

Faculty
Somendra Mohan Bhattacharjee [somendra.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Quantum mechanics is far more than solving the Schrödinger equation for isolated particles. This course explores how the same principles explain phenomena ranging from scattering and the formation of energy bands in solids to graphene and other forms of collective quantum matter. A central theme is that a remarkably wide range of physical phenomena can still be understood within the wavefunction formalism, even when the relevant wavefunctions describe many interacting particles rather than a single particle. Along the way, students will encounter powerful concepts such as relativistic quantum mechanics, second quantization, and the renormalization group—ideas that lie at the heart of modern physics, especially condensed matter physics and emerging quantum technologies. Bridging the gap between standard undergraduate quantum mechanics and contemporary research, the course provides both the conceptual framework and the mathematical tools needed for advanced study in physics.

Learning Outcomes

On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

  Apply quantum mechanics to phenomena such as scattering,  relativistic particles, magnets.
  Explain how collective quantum phenomena emerge from microscopic principles, with examples including graphene, quantum magnets, and superconductivity.
  Use the basic language and methods of many-body quantum physics.
  Appreciate the role of the renormalization group as a unifying concept in modern physics.
   Develop the conceptual foundation required for advanced study in condensed matter and quantum physics.

Faculty
Geetanjali Chanda [geetanjali.chanda@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Description
 

Bombay cinema, affectionately called “Bollywood” has become the background music to our lives, whether as innocent entertainment or ‘time pass’. However, we often overlook Bollywood’s serious intent and strong ideological underpinnings. Right from its inception, with Dadasaheb Phalke’s Raja Harishchandra (1913), it has shaped the public narrative in India.
 

While the themes of Hindi films have changed over the years --from the patriotic ‘Mother India’ to the sports-feminist ‘Dangal’, the presentation of nationalism, sports and sexualities may just be old wine in new bottles. We will examine these ideologies primarily through the lens of gender.
 

We will also explore how the language, fashion, music, dance, and social values embedded in Bollywood films are disseminated. International theoretical readings from ideas of nationalism, film, gender, class, and cultural studies, and literature from various parts of the world will underpin our discussions of Bombay’s film industry and our exploration of the values and ideologies embedded in apparently innocent entertainment.
 

One of the course’s goals is to recognize these themes and develop the analytical tools to effectively “read” a text/film, empowering us to identify and challenge mainstream norms.

[Please note –Supplementary readings and films may be assigned during the course of the semester. Film viewing is mandatory. Even if you have seen the film before it is important to see it again for this class and with a view to the topics and ideas being discussed. Please find a way to view the films on your own. Ashoka may not be able to arrange screenings.]

Learn film language

understand the subtext and ideologies the films are trying to convey

See the history of Bollywood cinema

Explore the roles of women and men in Bollywood

Overview

This course will examine the aesthetic identity of criticism as a genre of world English literature. “Creative Criticism” implies a convergence of the intellectual and the imaginative to produce a new understanding of the relationship between reading, writing, teaching, and activism. Our focus will be on themes that emerge from the convergence of art and thought, practice and analysis, immediate experience and historical consciousness, which can be neither exclusively theorized, nor exclusively embodied. Our goal is to understand criticism as a literary practice that originates from the entanglements of self and archive, subject and history, individual and community through intellectual voices that are only retrievable through artistic imagination.

Zero-Knowledge Proofs and zk-SNARKs [CS-4623] [CS-4623-1]

Faculty
Mahabir Prasad Jhanwar [mahavir.jhawar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Traditionally, a proof is a static object that can be checked step by step to verify the correctness of a statement. Modern cryptography has greatly expanded this notion by introducing interactive proofs, where a prover and a verifier engage in a protocol to convince the verifier that a computation has been carried out correctly. The course begins with the foundations of interactive proof systems, including their security guarantees of completeness and soundness, and classical protocols that illustrate the surprising power of interaction.

 

We then explore the broader landscape of information-theoretically secure interactive proof systems, including Multi-Prover Interactive Proofs (MIPs), Probabilistically Checkable Proofs (PCPs), and Interactive Oracle Proofs (IOPs). We discuss landmark results such as IP = PSPACE, and the PCP Theorem, which reveal the surprising expressive power of these proof models. Building on these foundations, we study how cryptographic techniques can be combined with these proof systems to construct efficient argument systems, enabling succinct and publicly verifiable proofs under standard computational assumptions. We then see how interactive arguments can be transformed into non-interactive arguments using techniques such as the Fiat-Shamir transformation.

 

The course next introduces zero-knowledge proofs, which allow a prover to convince a verifier of the correctness of a statement without revealing anything beyond the validity of the statement itself. We study the simulation paradigm underlying zero knowledge and see how privacy can be incorporated as an additional property of general-purpose argument systems.

 

Finally, we bring these ideas together in the study of zk-SNARKs - Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge - which combine succinctness, non-interactivity, zero knowledge, and proofs of knowledge in a single proof system. We study the fundamental ideas behind modern zk-SNARK constructions, including polynomial commitment schemes and other cryptographic building blocks, and gain an overview of widely used proof systems such as Groth16 and PLONK. 

 

The course concludes by exploring applications of zero-knowledge proofs in privacy-preserving authentication, digital identity, verifiable computation, blockchain technologies, and other emerging areas of modern cryptography.

courseTitle: Global Screen Archives: Histories, Curatorship, and Exhibitions
description:
Global Screen Archives: Histories, Curatorship, and Exhibitions [MS-3601] [MS-3601-1]

Faculty
Monia Acciari [monia.acciari@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

*** Welcome to this course brief ***

The moving image and the material culture that surrounds it constitute a crucial part of global screen heritage. Films, television broadcasts, photographs, posters, audio recordings, and other media artefacts are not only products of artistic and cultural production but also valuable historical sources that document social life, political change, and everyday cultural practices. Yet these materials are often fragile, ephemeral, and frequently overlooked as sources through which history can be written. Film stock decomposes, videotapes deteriorate, and digital formats quickly become obsolete. Preserving and interpreting audiovisual heritage therefore requires specialised knowledge, technical expertise, and the collaboration of archivists, historians, and cultural institutions.

This course introduces students to screen archives as dynamic spaces where histories are both constructed and questioned. Archives do not simply store materials; they shape what becomes visible, remembered, or marginalised within cultural memory. Through the study of archival collections and practices, you will explore how audiovisual materials contribute to the writing of film history as well as broader social and cultural histories.

At the same time, the course provides an introduction to the professional world of audiovisual archiving. Students will gain an overview of key archival practices, including preservation, cataloguing, storage, and access, while examining the technical and ethical challenges involved in caring for fragile media. By engaging with current archival standards and workflows, the course offers a practical insight into the professional practices that sustain film and media archives and enable researchers and the public to access these collections.

Beyond preservation and research, the course also examines the creative and public dimensions of archives. You will consider how archival materials can be mobilised for new creative projects, curatorial initiatives, exhibitions, and public engagement activities. In this context, the course explores how archives can be activated beyond the repository, becoming spaces where historical materials inspire new forms of storytelling, artistic practice, and collective reflection.

Drawing on perspectives from film history, and heritage studies, the course encourages students to think critically about archival processes and institutions. What kinds of materials are preserved? Which histories are prioritised, and which remain absent? How do environmental conditions, material degradation, selective acquisition practices, and institutional priorities shape the collections that survive? What other archives can we imagine? The course will combine lectures on selected readings, flipped classroom discussions, workshops, and practical archival exercises, allowing students to engage both theoretically and practically with the study of materials.

Learning Outcomes

On successful completion of this course, you will be able to:

1. Display a critical and practical understanding of archival material and handling of such items.

2. Demonstrate a historical and practical understanding of film memorabilia conservation and preservation procedures in line with international FIAF standards.

3. Identify film and film culture material’s state of condition/deterioration.

4. Engage with different theoretical, historical and practical discourses on international film archives.

5. Distinguish diverse type of archives, their preservation procedures and catalogues for accessibility.

6. Apply and exhibit archival material handling expertise to curate and execute the set-up of a public facing event.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Some of the key readings include;

Acciari, M. (2020) ‘From trash to shelves: Notes on the importance of satellite archives on Indian cinema heritage’, E-CineIndia, April–June, pp. 1–5.

Amad, P. (2010), Counter-Archive: Film, the Everyday, and Albert Kahn’s Archives de la Planète. New York: Columbia University Press. (Selected Reading)

Baron, J. (2014) The archive effect: Found footage and the audiovisual experience of history. Abingdon, Oxon and New York: Routledge. (Selected Reading)

Campagnoni, D.P. (2006) ‘The preservation, care and exploitation of documentation related to the cinema: An unresolved issue’, Film History, 18(3), pp. 306–318. (Selected Reading).

Chabria, S. (ed.) (2013) Light of Asia: Indian silent cinema, 1912–1934. New Delhi: Niyogi Books. (Selected Reading).

Cherchi Usai, P. (2019) Silent cinema: A guide to study, research and curatorship. London: BFI. (Selected Reading).

Douglas, Jennifer (2025) “Love in the Archive: Towards a theory and Praxis of Archival Care”, Archivaria, No. 100, Fall/Winter, pp 202-239.  

Edmonson, R. (1995) ‘Is film archiving a profession?’, Film History, 7(3), pp. 245–255.

Houston, P. (1994) The keeper of the frame. London: BFI Publishing. (Selected Reading).

Kumar, R. (2013) ‘The making of the National Film Archive of India: Notes from the archive of the archive’, The Moving Image: The Journal of the Association of Moving Image Archivists, 13(1), pp. 98–128.

Mazumdar, R. (2003) ‘The Bombay film posters: The journey from the street to the museum’, Film International, (3), pp. 13–18.

Bischoff Lizelle, Anna Grgic, Stephanie Van De Peer (eds.) (2025) Stretching the Archive, Towards a Woman Film Heritage, Archive Books (Film Series).

These are just a few texts we will be looking at in this course. A week by week reading requirement will be shared in due course.

Geoeconomics [IR-3046] [IR-3046-1]

Faculty
Arun Mohan Sukumar [arun.sukumar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In the summer of 1990, Edward Luttwak wrote about the rise of coercive economic statecraft: a new kind of “state action” that mixed "the logic of war with the grammar of commerce." In Luttwak’s framing, the unipolar world of the nineties was moving towards an extended era of peace. With the military might of states turning irrelevant – “geopolitical decay”, as he termed it -- they would turn to "geoeconomic" instruments to maintain their edge over rivals or competitors.

Has this thesis held? This course will study the evolution of economic statecraft from 1945, analysing in particular its place in the contemporary liberal, international order (LIO). Great Power competition has altered Luttwak’s landscape dramatically. The US, which once deployed sanctions and coercive measures to make smaller powers toe the line on fair trade, human rights, and non-proliferation, now wields them to upend some of the core tenets of the LIO. China, which once offered major concessions to join the WTO, is adopting the US’ playbook on sanctions. The signals and strategic objectives that both states may wish to send or pursue from geoeconomic manoeuvring are, however, different. This course foregrounds in students an ability to parse those signals. At the end of this course, we will have a broader appreciation of the role coercion plays in international political economy. While spending some time framing economic statecraft in its historical context, we will also explore its change in form and scope. International finance and competition over new technologies will figure prominently in class discussions, although you should expect readings drawing on theory and state practice across domains.

This is a reading-intensive course, designed as an advanced research seminar. The pre-requisites (waived if you have done IR theory + IR-2071 IPE) are meant to help you hit the ground running. Given the reading load and high grade allocation on class participation, please keep in mind your semester commitments at the time of enrolment.

Faculty
Nadeem Aktar [nadeem.akhtar@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course offers an introduction to the poetry of Zeb-un-Nissa Makhfi (1638–1702), the Mughal princess, scholar, and one of the most celebrated Persian poets of early modern South Asia. Writing under the pen name Makhfi ("The Hidden One"), Zeb-un-Nissa's poetry reflects themes of divine and earthly love, spirituality, longing, selfhood, and the rich literary traditions of Persianate culture.

Through close reading of selected verses, students will develop familiarity with her poetic language, literary style, and the historical and cultural milieu in which she composed. The course will situate her writings within the broader context of Mughal intellectual history and Persian literary traditions while strengthening students' skills in reading and interpreting classical Persian texts.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

  • Read and comprehend selected verses from the poetry of Zeb-un-Nissa Makhfi in the original Persian.
  • Develop an understanding of the linguistic, literary, and stylistic features of classical Persian poetry.
  • Analyse major themes in Zeb-un-Nissa's poetry, including love, mysticism, devotion, identity, and philosophical reflection.
  • Understand the historical and cultural context of Persian literary production in Mughal India.
  • Engage critically with classical Persian texts through close reading and discussion.
  • Improve Persian reading comprehension, vocabulary, and translation skills.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Course Readings

The course will primarily focus on selected verses from the poetry (Dīvān) of Zeb-un-Nissa Makhfi. Additional secondary readings on Mughal history, Persian literary traditions, and relevant scholarly scholarship may be assigned throughout the semester to provide historical and literary context.

Romanticism and Its Afterlives [ENG-2454] [ENG-2454-1]

Faculty
Alexander Robert Phillips [alexander.phillips@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

More than two centuries after the peak of European Romanticism, we continue to live in its cultural shadow. Romantic ideas about the author as genius continue to inform the reception of art and literature, beliefs that a given population has a unique spiritual bond remains core to nationalist ideology, the revaluation of "wild" nature remains at the core of much environmental politics, the fascination with the dark sides of human psychic experience would directly inspire psychoanalytic thinking, and the fascination with fairy tales and the fantastic persists in science fiction, horror, and most obviously the products of the Walt Disney Studios. The fact that Romanticism and its legacies continue to be objects of critique is a testament to its staying power. Much of this class will be spent exploring authors and texts that literary history typically groups together under the label Romanticism. We will also look to see the many ways that the Romantics' favorite themes show up later in the nineteenth century and beyond, even amongst their harshest critics.
