Explorations into Histories of Concepts [HIS-4851] [HIS-4851-1]

Faculty
Gaurav Churiwala Garg [gaurav.garg@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

One of the key challenges of the studying social world as opposed to the world of natural forces is that is that the very language that we use in order to comprehend it, also partly constitutes and changes that very world. For example, even if we do not comprehend that water douses fire it will retain that property, but in the social world, once we understand a social formation, like a city as an organism, we not only understand it in the particular way but we also intervene in ways that are determined by the terms in which we understand them.  Expressions such as parks are “lungs of the city” are part of this deep conceptual vocabulary.  All this means that concepts or broadly speaking the words through which we engage in abstractions of the real world to understand it, is also one of the prime ways in which we transform our world. Very often, however we deploy concepts innocently as mere descriptors of a reality or look for timeless, spaceless and universal definitions for them. But in doing so, we often misread the actions, intentions, and thoughts of others and indeed, miss out on the ways in which our ideas have made the world we live in. Concept History or what in the Anglophone world is known as History of Ideas can help us overcome this haze. By becoming sensitive to the idea that concepts have histories, how are such histories written, and most importantly how such concepts shape our world ( including our present and the future) this course will help students read the social world in a new light. In order to learn the nuances and the sheer importance of concept history, we will focus on the history of three major modern concepts that continue to shape our world and which we often continue to use innocently— progress, culture, and civilization.

Learning Outcomes

If the course succeeds words you often gloss over while reading or writing will appear to you in a new and rich light. The main outcome will be that you will have a new lens for making sense of the world we inhabit. 

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

This will be a reading heavy course. The focus will be on three concepts— culture, progress and civilization. 

You will be expected to read and engage. This will be a discussion based seminar. 

You will be given the chance to work with me on the history of a concept that you find interesting.

Introduction to Cognitive Disorders [PSY-4023] [PSY-4023-1]

Faculty
Lee David Cranberg [lee.cranberg@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Instructor: Lee Cranberg, MD (Visiting Professor)

How is it that a woman can write something and then not be able to read it? Or that a man can see his arm but be convinced it does not belong to him? In this course we will explore cognitive disorders, the often strange and fascinating ways they manifest, and the brain damage that produces them. Sources of information will include patient videos, textbook material, and classic case reports about patients whose deficits taught us much about the human mind. In addition, students will learn to administer many of the tests used by neuropsychologists to diagnose cognitive impairments.

Learning Outcomes

A) Identify the major brain structures pertinent to motor, sensory, and cognitive functions.

B) Explain core cognitive systems (language, memory, visuospatial skills, executive functions, etc.) and how they break down in specific disorders.

C) Describe major cognitive disorders, including clinical features, common causes, and expected brain damage.

D) Analyze case descriptions or patient videos to determine a patient's particular behavioral, emotional, and cognitive deficits (e.g., hemispatial neglect, conduction aphasia, anterograde amnesia), and use that information to formulate a hypothesis regarding the location and cause of the underlying brain damage.

E) Demonstrate facility in administering some of the key tests neuropsychologists use (Stroop test, Trail Making Test, etc.) to diagnose cognitive impairments.

F) Critically read and summarize case reports of patients with acquired cognitive deficits.

Hellenistic Philosophy [PHI-2441] [PHI-2441-1]

Faculty
Aditi Chaturvedi [aditi.chaturvedi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

It’s time for me to upload my course syllabus and I find that I’ve accidentally deleted the entire folder with all my course materials prepared for over a year. I have no backup. What do I do? The Stoics say that that I have a choice — I can refuse the panic, anger etc. that assails me. The Epicureans remind me that what is painful is easy to endure. The Cynics might support me in my decision to ignore the enforced convention of sharing a syllabus ahead of time. The Cyrenaics would incite me to give up on something this unpleasant and turn my attention to pleasanter pursuits. What they all have in common is a systematic account of how we should live, grounded in well-developed metaphysical and epistemological theories. This semester we will work our way through the fundamental ethical, political, metaphysical, and epistemological concerns that preoccupied the Hellenistic philosophers (3rd-1st century BCE) and which still occupy us today: How should we live? How can we be free and happy? What can we know? Do we have free will? What is the nature of reality? How should we live in communities? We will also situate these views in their historical contexts. The Hellenistic philosophers, both Greek and Roman, wrote during turbulent times and their doctrines were also meant to help those around them live through those times. In that spirit, we will analyse and respond to their arguments, but we will also consider what it means to live in accordance with these different schools of thought.

Decolonial Feminist Philosophy [PHI-3801] [PHI-3801-1]

Faculty
Merve Rumeysa Tapinc [merve.tapinc@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Description

What does it mean to speak of women's freedom across different historical, cultural, and political contexts? Can feminism advance universal ideals without reproducing colonial assumptions? How should we understand practices such as veiling, marriage, or gendered social roles when they are interpreted through radically different moral and cultural frameworks?

This course introduces students to contemporary debates in decolonial feminism by examining the philosophical assumptions underlying dominant feminist theories. Rather than treating feminism as a single, unified tradition, we will explore competing conceptions of autonomy, agency, oppression, and emancipation. Drawing on philosophers and feminist theorists from diverse intellectual traditions, we will ask whether concepts developed within liberal Western feminism adequately capture the experiences of women across the globe, or whether they inadvertently reproduce forms of epistemic and political domination.

Throughout the semester, we will critically examine topics including the politics of the Muslim veil, marriage, family, gendered norms, intersectionality, and colonial legacies. Students will leave the course with a deeper understanding of the philosophical debates surrounding universalism, relativism, coloniality, and the possibilities of a more inclusive feminist theory.

Learning Outcomes

Students will leave the course with a deeper understanding of the philosophical debates surrounding universalism, relativism, coloniality, and the possibilities of a more inclusive feminist theory.

Overview

Course Description

This course is designed for undergraduate program. Industrial Chemistry bridges the gap between fundamental chemical principles and their large-scale technological applications. This course introduces students to the processes, raw materials, engineering principles, economics, and environmental considerations involved in manufacturing chemicals on an industrial scale. Students will gain insight into how theoretical chemistry is translated into profitable, safe, and environmentally responsible industrial operations.

Course Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

- Understand the principles governing large-scale chemical manufacturing processes.

- Evaluate process economics, energy efficiency, and sustainability of chemical industries.

- Analyze environmental impacts and apply green chemistry principles to industrial processes.

- Apply knowledge of polymers, dyes, fuels, fertilizers, and electrochemistry to industrial contexts.

- Interpret process flow diagrams and basic reactor design concepts.

Learning Outcomes

- Fundamentals of chemical process technology, raw materials, and industrial economics.

- Illustrate the petrochemical processes and industrial synthesis of key components.

- Apply principles of electrochemistry to industrial processes and corrosion prevention.

- Evaluate the environmental impact of chemical industries and propose sustainable practices.

Introduction to Cancer [BIO-3450/ BIO-4211] [BIO-3450/ BIO-4211-1]

Faculty
Deblina Raychaudhuri [deblina.raychaudhuri@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces students to the world of cancer biology through an exploration of its history, causes, mechanisms, and treatments. Beginning with the global burden and societal impact of cancer, students will trace its historical roots and understand how pivotal discoveries shaped our understanding of the disease. Students will uncover how a “selfish” cell escapes normal control, evolves under selective pressures, and interacts dynamically with its microenvironment. The course will also examine the diverse causes of cancer, from genetic mutations to environmental and infectious agents, followed by discussions on prevention, early detection, and therapeutic strategies including surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. In the final weeks, students will learn about emerging frontiers in cancer research such as neoantigen vaccines, oncolytic viruses and microbiome modulation,. Each class will combine instruction with interactive discussions to encourage critical thinking about the biological, clinical, and societal dimensions of cancer. Seminal papers and discoveries in the field will be regularly discussed. Industry leaders in the field may be invited for guest lectures.

Learning Outcomes

Students will be expected to:

a) Understand the global burden and historical understanding of cancer (Week 1).

b) Explain key cellular and molecular mechanisms driving tumor growth and survival (Weeks 2–3).

c) Distinguish between genetic, epigenetic, environmental, and infectious causes of cancer (Weeks 4–5).

d) Understand how cancers spread (Week 6).

e) Analyze the role of the tumor microenvironment in shaping cancer progression and tumor immunity (Week 7).

f) Understand how tumors evolve (Week 9).

f) Evaluate approaches to cancer prevention, screening, and early diagnosis (Week 10).

g) Compare the principles, strengths, and limitations of major cancer therapies (Week 11).

h) Identify emerging trends in cancer research, including immunotherapy, vaccines, microbiome, approaches (Week 12-13).

Decision Theory [ECO-6105/ ECO-4105/ MAT-3217] [ECO-6105/ ECO-4105/ MAT-3217-1]

Faculty
Abhinash Borah [abhinash.borah@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course studies decisions under uncertainty. Its goal is to provide students with some of the theoretical language required to systematically study the problem of an intelligent agent who is embedded in an uncertain environment, receives observations about that environment, which are often noisy, and has to take actions either once or over time to best achieve certain objectives. For an economist, the agent is typically an individual decision maker like a consumer, investor, or firm. For others, that agent may be a robot or a purely non-physical entity, like a decision system whose existence is fully digital. The two sources of uncertainty that we will primarily deal with are:

  • Outcome uncertainty, where the effects of the agent’s actions are uncertain.
  • Model uncertainty, where the agent’s model of the problem is uncertain.

We will begin by studying two celebrated theorems. The first is the expected utility theorem of von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944), and then its generalization, the mixture space theorem of Herstein and Milnor (1953). We will thereafter examine the (behavioral) foundations of subjective probabilities and Bayesianism. We will study the classic approaches of de Finetti (1937), Savage (1954), and Anscombe and Aumann (1963) to this question.

After that, we will focus on the large and impressive literature on decision-making under ambiguity that has emerged over the last three decades or so. Ambiguity, here, refers to decision settings in which a decision-maker perceives "uncertainty about probability, created by missing information that is relevant and could be known" (Frisch and Baron, 1988). That such decision settings exist was pointed out by Ellsberg (1961). His work showed how ambiguity represents a normative criticism of the subjective expected utility framework of Savage (1954) and, by extension, of the Bayesian paradigm. David Schmeidler and Itzhak Gilboa’s work in the late 1980s revived interest in this area of research. We will cover important models like Schmeidler's Choquet expected utility (1989), Gilboa and Schmeidler's maximin expected utility (1989), Klibanoff, Marinacci, and Mukerji's smooth ambiguity model (2005), Maccheroni, Marinacci, and Rustichini’s variational preferences (2006), and Siniscalchi's vector expected utility (2009).

This discussion will be a natural segue into our study of model uncertainty. Here, we will see how entropy can be used to measure model misspecification and draw on concepts from robust control theory.

Along the way, we will study theories of stochastic choice to model decision-makers who act according to probabilistic rather than deterministic decision rules. We will look at the random utility model and its special case, the Luce/Logit model (Luce, 1959). Finally, since intelligent decision-making has a lot to do with learning about the uncertain environment, we will (time permitting) touch on some theories of learning, like Bayesian learning, maximum likelihood parameter learning, structure learning, reinforcement learning, and active learning.

courseTitle: Religious Authority: Conceptions, Contestations and Discourses from Early India
description:
Religious Authority: Conceptions, Contestations and Discourses from Early India [SAN-3007] [SAN-3007-1]

Overview

In this course we will focus on the formation of religious authority in Indian religions between 600 BCE and the first centuries of the Common Era, what we call the ‘early period’ of Indian history. The course will familiarise students with the development of religious ideas, institutions and sources of authority in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, thus giving an overview of early history of Indian religions. Through various themes and issues, the students will be able to understand: (1) how religious authority shaped various aspects of everyday life and society in early India and was in turn shaped by them; and (2) how Indian religious traditions engaged with each other in dialogues and contestations to present their own visions of religious authority. The commonalities and differences that resulted from these encounters will be explored to study the religious and intellectual histories of early India.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Develop a critical understanding of religion and its relationship with society.
  • Apply historical ideas to understand how we engage with religious ideas in everyday life.
  • Have a better knowledge of Indian religions and by extension, history of early India.
  • Recognise these religious traditions not as static or passive but dynamic and constantly evolving.
  • Identify on your own how religious authority percolates to socio-political and cultural spheres of human lives and situate historical concepts in conversations about the present.
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

Democracy: Origins, Crises, and Resilience [POL-3143] [POL-3143-1]

Faculty
Apurva Bamezai [apurva.bamezai@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why did some countries become democracies while others did not? Why, after decades in which democracy seemed to be winning, are democracies now breaking down — not through tanks and coups, but at the hands of elected leaders who were freely voted into power? And once that erosion begins, what, if anything, stops it? This seminar takes up these three questions in turn, treating contemporary democratic backsliding across the world as a puzzle that the comparative study of politics can help to explain.

 

The course proceeds in three parts. ‘Origins’ asks where democracy comes from: what democracy is and how social scientists measure it and the theories that explain its historical emergence. ‘Crises’ turns to how democracies die today — the slow, legal process of backsliding driven by polarization, populism, and disinformation, and the steady capture of courts, election management bodies, and the press. ‘Resilience’ asks how democracies defend themselves: how oppositions fight back, how civil resistance works, and which institutional reforms can halt or reverse decline. 

 

This course is part of the international Democratic Erosion Consortium and is taught in 100+ universities across 20+ countries. Students will build a semester-long case study of a single country's democratic trajectory and write for a public audience through a cross-university student blog. Not only will it allow you to interact with your classmates, but it will also allow you to interact with students from other universities as well.

 

The course is intended for two kinds of students. The first are those drawn to the empirical study of democracy — students considering research, graduate study, journalism, public policy, or work with civil-society organisations, who want to understand why regimes rise and fall and how that knowledge is produced. The second are students who have taken introductory comparative politics and want to see its concepts — regimes, institutions, parties, and accountability — put to work on one of the most consequential political developments of our time. This is a reading- and discussion-intensive seminar: students are expected to arrive prepared to argue.

Learning Outcomes
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course builds on the conceptual vocabulary of comparative politics — regime types, institutions, political parties, and accountability. The prerequisite is Introduction to Comparative Politics. Students who have not taken it but believe they have equivalent preparation should approach me before registration with a short description of their background. No prior knowledge of statistics or research methods is required.

Elementary Hindi-I [SAN-1501] [SAN-1501-1]

Overview

Elementary Hindi I introduces students to spoken Hindi and Devanagari through immediately useful communicative situations. Students learn to introduce themselves, exchange personal information, describe people and places through basic sentence formations, express preferences and needs, ask/tell time, and manage simple interactions on campus and in everyday public settings. Pronunciation, script, vocabulary, and grammar are developed together rather than sequentially. By the end of the course, students should be able to participate in short, predictable conversations and read and write simple connected sentences in Devanagari.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students should be able to:

  • recognise, pronounce, read, and write high-frequency Hindi words and simple sentences in Devanagari;
  • use culturally appropriate greetings, forms of address, introductions, and classroom expressions;
  • ask and answer basic questions about identity, family, study, location, routine, and preference;
  • describe familiar people, objects, and places using elementary gender, number, and agreement patterns;
  • talk about habitual and ongoing activities in the present;
  • perform simple transactions, requests, commands, and direction-seeking tasks;

Overview

Intermediate Hindi I helps students move from sentence-level communication to connected discourse. Students consolidate the tense–aspect system and develop greater control over direct and oblique formations, case marking, agreement, compound postpositions, compound and conjunct verbs, infinitives, participles, and relative-correlative structures. The course uses personal experiences, and contemporary life as contexts for sustained conversation, summarization, and explanation. Along with formal Hindi structure, colloquial and regionally varied forms of Hindi will receive regular attention throughout the course.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students should be able to:

  • sustain conversations and ask spontaneous follow-up questions on familiar and semi-familiar topics;
  • narrate connected events using habitual, progressive, and perfective contrasts;
  • apply major case and agreement patterns, including ने (ne), को (ko), and multifunctional से (se);
  • use common compound and conjunct verbs to express completion, inception, continuation (grammatically termed ‘vectors’), and speaker perspective.

Methods in Political Theory [POL-4015] [POL-4015-1]

Faculty
Vivek Yadav [vivek.yadav@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Any theory of politics presupposes an answer to the questions of what the task of political theory is, and how it ought to be done. This course makes these questions its main subject. Over the semester we shall work through the rival views within the discipline about its own tasks and how these are to be performed. The questions we shall discuss include the following: Is the study of politics a science, or something no science can capture? Should theory design the just society, as Rawls does, or expose that design as ideology? What role, if any, does history play in political theory? Do we understand a political idea by recovering what past authors meant by it, by tracing its genealogy, or by inheriting it through a living tradition? And whose experience has "universal" theory been built to overlook -- a question we press through realist, feminist, dalit, and non-Western critics. The couse not only introduces students to the different ways of doing political theory, but also helps them appreciate why the choice of method is never innocent.

Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Strategy is a product of mental models. Formulation of effective strategy requires abstract thinking as opposed to thinking of specific actions. We make judgements, weigh risks, and evaluate costs and benefits to make decisions. Decisions stem from rational and intuitive thinking. Intuition is a powerful involuntary and spontaneous thinking process. It is a marvel responsible for some of mankind’s greatest advances, creativity, and innovation. Unfortunately, it also occasionally causes bias that adversely affect judgements and decisions. Yet, it is an ally, a faculty that helps us make life and death decisions in the blink of an eye. As students of strategic thinking, we need to understand how it works, where it helps, and when it may not. This outline provides you a bird’s eye-view of the course, what you may gain from it, and the nature and extent of effort that will be expected of you.

Learning Outcomes

1. Achieve an appreciation of how we think. Become aware of the powers of the rational as well as the non-rational processes of the mind.

2. Acquire working knowledge of principles, theoretical models and concepts that can make decision making rigorous and effective.

3. Learn to apply the principles to everyday life and business to make sound decisions.

Entrepreneurial Mindset through Simple Thinking [ENT-1030] [ENT-1030-1]

Faculty
Mukesh Sud [mukesh.sud@ashoka.edu.in], Priyank Narayan [priyank.narayan@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course develops entrepreneurial thinking in conditions of complexity, uncertainty, and under constraint. The central premise is that entrepreneurship does not require more information or greater resources. It requires a better way of thinking, building and leading.
Simple thinking is the engine of that better way. It is the ability to identify what truly matters by cutting through the noise and making sound choices under ambiguity. Entrepreneurs who think simply move faster, waste less, and build more robustly than those who chase complexity.
Across twelve weeks and three modules, students will encounter frameworks drawn from strategy, entrepreneurship, and innovation. Through perspectives from stand-up comedy, persuasion, storytelling and authentic leadership, they will examine how entrepreneurial success depends not only on how people think and build, but also on how they infl uence and lead. Students will practice these capabilities through case analyses, refl ective exercises, live experiments, and a fi nal group project.

Learning Outcomes

1. See Clearly in Complexity
Recognize complexity bias, the tendency to favor complicated over clear, and use the principles of simple thinking to cut through noise, identify what actually matters, and build a clearer understanding of any problem or opportunity.
2. Act Decisively Under Uncertainty
Apply the principles of eff ectuation to make decisions without complete information, working with what you have, committing what you can aff ord to lose, and leveraging unexpected events to your advantage.
3. Build and Test Ideas with Minimal Waste
Use lean startup methodology, the build-measure-learn loop, and MVP (minimum viable product) approach to validate entrepreneurial ideas quickly and cheaply through experimentation and feedback.
4. Convert Constraints into a Creative Advantage
Reframe scarcity of resources, time, and information not as obstacles but as design conditions that force smarter, simpler, more scalable choices. Apply a LeanSpark framework to build ventures that are frugal by design and global in ambition.
5. Develop the Entrepreneur’s Human Advantage
Apply principles from humour, persuasion, storytelling and authentic leadership to build trust, infl uence decisions and communicate ideas in situations of uncertainty and change.

courseTitle: Profit, Power and Punishment - The Anatomy of a Business Organization
description:
Profit, Power and Punishment - The Anatomy of a Business Organization [ENT-3050] [ENT-3050-1]

Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The course cracks open the black box of the modern business – demystifying the legal and economic principles behind its inner workings, structure, and identity when the stakes are high: who controls the money, who calls the shots, and what happens when the whole thing blows up. You just bought an Apple computer. It does not work as advertised. Can you, as an Apple customer, show up at Tim Cook’s house with your receipt and demand reimbursement from his wallet? You also own Apple stock. The stock price falls sharply because thousands of mis-advertised computers are sold, thwarting the public’s expectations. Can you, as an Apple stockholder, show up at Tim Cook’s house, demanding from his wallet the returns you expected on your investment? The computers begin to explode due to a technical design flaw, injuring the public. Can the police drag Tim Cook to prison? Can an injured member of the public show up at your house and demand payment of damages, asserting that you, as a stockholder of Apple, are an owner of Apple, and thus bear ultimate responsibility? Imagine the answer to these questions is yes. Would you still want to hold Apple stock? Would Tim Cook still want to be CEO? These questions are of monumental importance; the answers decide whether businesses can even exist, let alone thrive. These and many similar questions implicate the subject of this course: the peculiar legal and economic characteristics that define business organizations – startups, Fortune 500 companies, and everything in between. If profit is the lifeblood of a business, these characteristics are the organization’s veins, arteries, and heart: They constitute an intricate framework designed – with attention to nuanced economic and legal principles – to facilitate profit; and any attempt to make profit can succeed only within their constraints. Understanding them is therefore critical for anyone who wants to build a business or advise one. Understanding them is also critical for any manager, because efficient management requires awareness of – and makes use of – the organization’s legal structure.

Learning Outcomes

In this course, you will gain: A thorough understanding of the nature, structure, and functioning of business organizations. See the Detailed Session Plan for week-wise sub-topics and objectives. Top-tier, world-class business strategic acumen backed by sophisticated economic and legal intuition. The selection of concepts taught in this course – and the angles from which we’ll approach the concepts – echoes courses taught at the preeminent business schools and law schools of the world. After this course, you will share a nucleus of sophisticated learning with graduates of schools like Wharton, Kellogg, NYU Stern, and Yale Law School – all of which offer courses similar to this one. Real-world insights into business organizations, built on a strong theoretical foundation. This course marries powerful high theory – which has shaped the field – with no-nonsense, rubber-hits-the-road practical application – which is the field. Whatever the differences between the average scholar and the average practitioner, the best minds in the academy and the best minds in industry are more alike than different: They share a strong understanding of both theory and practice, and are aware of the need for – and limits of – both. Breadth and (accessible) depth of knowledge from startup to conglomerate. This course marries breadth with depth – surveying a wide variety of big-ticket topics like an introductory lecture of general interest, while also probing several of them with the kind of nuance and sophistication that is at the cutting edge of the field, and is usually reserved for niche seminars. The way I teach this course makes even those cutting-edge concepts accessible to a fresh, inexperienced audience, which is rare for undergraduates at most schools. Professional readiness for the uppermost echelons of the corporate world. In addition to an understanding of concepts – both practical and theoretical – this course will polish you for the professional corporate world. A big part of succeeding in high-stakes business environments is a terrific work ethic, devotion to detail, a sparkling personality, and navigating difficult work environments. This is as true of ambitious startups exploding Page 4 of 14 with potential, as it is of elite global behemoths that have stood for decades (or even centuries; the financial law firm I worked at was born in 1849 on Wall Street). None of this is in textbooks. This course will impart this polish, including through discussions of exemplar situations and anecdotes, and unfiltered advice on matters small and big, all drawn from my own professional experiences – woven into the discussion of the class materials. The skill of critical, creative analysis of corporate puzzles. The skill of critical, creative analysis is the sharpest tool in the toolkit of any successful professional, and indeed any thinker, no matter the field. Whether you become a businessperson, or an adviser to businesspeople (like a consultant or commercial lawyer), or something else entirely, a pedantic knowledge of obscure facts will be secondary; clever thinking in the face of neverbefore-seen puzzles will be primary. This course will build this skill. Logical discipline in organizational reasoning. Analysis that is critical and creative is nothing if it isn’t also attuned to the unforgiving laws of logic: Curiosity and imagination don’t go far without clarity of thought. This course will prepare students to think with the unflinching discipline of a logician. Sophistication in the commercial world regularly requires grappling with complicated conceptual puzzles. The best business minds – like the best minds, period – have an appetite for fast and intricate mental gymnastics around the thorniest, messiest analytical puzzles with multiple overlapping and moving parts. They are able to discern the precise set of relevant parts, the precise shape of each part, and the precise relationships among all the parts – which allows them to play with those parts to dazzling ends. This involves more than business expertise, intuition, and casual cleverness; it involves mastery of the laws of logic: understanding precisely what follows from what, what doesn’t, what can, what can’t, and so on. This course will hone such mastery. The skill of clear, captivating communication. Communication – written and oral – is both an art and a science. Everyone does it, but few do it well. It is not easy, and it is crucial to succeeding in any analytical or professional environment. Whether you are pitching your business idea to an investor or defending a CEO in court, the better you are at communication the more effective you’ll be at your job. This course will teach this skill through in-class oral and written exercises

courseTitle: The Contract - Making and Breaking Promises in Business
description:
The Contract - Making and Breaking Promises in Business [ENT-2100] [ENT-2100-1]

Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course is a deep dive into the concept of the contract. It examines contracts both in principle and in practice through (1) an interdisciplinary analysis of the defining features of a contract, and (2) a rigorous, step-by-step journey through the life of a typical commercial contract – sprawling and intricate; often brutally contentious; often wildly counterintuitive. The contracts that bind a business determine the floor and the ceiling on the business’s success. Knowing how to read them, how to craft them, and when to break them is therefore essential to anyone looking to succeed in business. Indeed, familiarity with contracts is essential for even a baseline level of business-mindedness. Almost every relationship in the business world – between individuals, between companies, or between an individual and a company – is governed by a contract, and often a nexus of related contracts. Job offers. Supply deals. NDAs. Commercial leases. Online “I agree” terms and conditions. Every serious contract is a tricky, high-wire game that paradoxically involves both collaboration and conflict: How do you get what you want, limit what you owe, take the right risks, shift the rest – knowing the other side is trying to do the same?

courseTitle: Twisting the Tiger’s Tale: The Political Ecology of Conservation
description:
Twisting the Tiger’s Tale: The Political Ecology of Conservation [ES-2139] [ES-2139-1]

Faculty
Asmita Kabra [asmita.kabra@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course is meant for students who are passionate about biodiversity and wildlife, but are willing to challenge closely held beliefs about how to ‘do’ conservation. It highlights the tension between two big ideas of contemporary times – the right to life of nonhuman species, and social justice in human societies. By the end of the course, students will have a sense of why contemporary conservation creates trade-offs between these two imperatives, and how they can be reconciled.

Biodiversity loss and persistent poverty are major concerns that have been strongly articulated since the 1980s at the national and global levels. Is it a coincidence that the world’s most biodiversity rich areas are also home to some of the poorest human populations? Or that access to biodiversity is critical for survival needs of the world’s most vulnerable people? Lands set aside today as ‘pristine’ nature have been shaped by human actions over the millennia. Similarly, interaction of forest dwellers with their land/waterscapes has indelibly shaped their economy, politics, identity, culture, and cosmology. This course highlights the importance of an explicitly political understanding of conservation-livelihood linkages. It will familiarize students with theoretical and policy frameworks, and on-ground experiences that shape conservation and local livelihoods in ecologically diverse and increasingly fragile landscapes in the Global South.

Learning Outcomes

On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

  • Read and comprehend diverse perspectives from the natural and social sciences, law, history, and public policy on the links between biodiversity conservation and local livelihoods
  • Critically analyze and compare national and global law/policy frameworks governing conservation-livelihood linkages using evidence-based arguments
  • Critically engage with alternative discourses from ecology, conservation biology and political ecology to identify policies and practices for socially just biodiversity conservation
  • Understand the role of the state, markets, and society in shaping conservation-livelihood linkages in India and apply this conceptual understanding to real-world case studies
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The course will require students to attend regular lectures and invited talks by experts. They will be asked to engage closely with texts, films, blogs, and other study material circulated on Google Classroom. Detailed instructions and study material will be posted weekly for each module of the course.

Weekly Teaching Plan

  • Week 1: Biodiversity loss and the global conservation movement
  • Week 2: Fortress conservation and the nature-culture divide
  • Week 3: Forestlands in precolonial and colonial India
  • Week 4: Forests, commons, and local livelihoods
  • Week 5: Conservation through dispossession
  • Week 6: Participatory and community-based conservation
  • Week 7: Neoliberal and celebrity conservation
  • Week 8: Spectacular and militarized conservation
  • Week 9: ONEs and marine conservation
  • Week 10: Human-wildlife conflict and Unruly Natures
  • Week 11: The political ecology of rewilding and reintroduction
  • Week 12: Conservation in the Anthropocene – alternative visions

Birds and Wetlands [ES-2137] [ES-2137-1]

Faculty
Abdul Jamil Urfi [abdul.urfi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Course Title: Birds and Wetlands

Faculty Instructor: Professor A.J. Urfi, an ecologist who specializes in wetland birds. Former Senior Professor and Head of Environmental Studies Department, Delhi University.

Schedule: Wednesday–Friday | 11:50 AM – 1:20 PM

Wetlands were regarded as ‘wastelands’- breeding grounds for malaria and mosquitoes and fit only for land reclamation. Wetlands are actually highly productive ecosystems, refugia for highly diverse and specialized biodiversity and an important resource for human civilizations. This course will discuss wetlands within the  framework of international treatises and ecological processes. It is primarily designed for science students to raise their overall understanding about environmental issues in context of wetlands and their biodiversity, especially birds. The preliminary modules will focus on definitions under the Ramsar Convention, ecological processes such as succession, productivity and adaptations of living organisms for survival in an amphibious habitat and wetland values. Since, the most visible component of wetlands are birds, other teaching modules will focus on the ornithological dimension covering topics of wetland bird diversity, long distance migration, conservation issues etc. This will be accompanied by a few field visits to wetlands in the vicinity of Delhi for onsite discussions and  teaching.

 

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students:

  • Will have a good ecological understanding about wetland ecosystems, their importance, and conservation issues.
  • Students will have a thorough understanding of the ornithological dimension in context of wetlands and how international conventions help in conservation
  • A working knowledge about the diversity of wetland birds from field visits.
  • Students will have some understanding of web based data recording on wetland populations, species distributions and nesting success based on involvement from volunteers.

Introduction to Environmental Modelling and applications [ES-3179] [ES-3179-1]

Faculty
Meghna Agarwala [meghna.agarwala@ashoka.edu.in], Parthasarathi Mukhopadhyay [parthasarathi.mukhopadhyay@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In this time of AI/ML, there is a growing recognition that AI/ML needs to be tethered to traditional domain-specific models. For example, we can enhance prediction accuracy of weather by combining traditional weather models with AI/ML. In this course, we will work on environmental modeling, which requires understanding of the fundamental concepts in modeling. This course will cover a variety of environmental models to simulate natural systems, wind, precipitation and air pollution. It includes both deterministic and stochastic approaches to modeling pollutant transport, dispersion, and chemical transformation. The objective of the course is to:

1. Understand the idea, methodology and basic tools of environmental modeling

2. Understand the different modeling approaches, their scope and limitations

3. Understand the fate and transport of pollutants

4. Obtain practical ability to execute these models/simulations through weekly labs.

We will be using python for modeling. We will teach it from scratch in labs starting from week 1.

Pre-requisites:

Some exposure to a mathematics course that covered calculus.

description:
Introduction to Earth and Climate Sciences [ES-2260] [ES-2260-1]

Faculty
Meghna Agarwala [meghna.agarwala@ashoka.edu.in], Parthasarathi Mukhopadhyay [parthasarathi.mukhopadhyay@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Anyone interested in the environment needs to understand the basic science of earth and atmospheric systems. However, such material is often inaccessible for the non-science major. In this course, we introduce you to a basic understanding of earth and climate processes. Topics include geology (such as the rock cycle and plate tectonics), meteorology (including winds and weather), the hydrosphere (water in the geosphere, atmosphere and oceans), and climatology. The course will also include topics on general circulation of the atmosphere, global energy balance, radiative processes in the atmosphere, tropical dynamics, thermodynamics and severe storms to provide basic understanding about the important concepts and processes underlying the Earth and its climate-system.           

The objective of the class is to introduce the Earth to students interested in environmental studies. We expect the students to understand the mechanism of Earth’s processes and the essential principles of Earth's climate system. We expect the students to be able to apply this knowledge to important problems facing India and the world today, and to critically examine policy interventions associated with earth sciences such as roads, dams, zoning, floods, droughts, cyclones, climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation, and monetary evaluation of risk. The knowledge gained in this course will help students to better understand the coupled solid Earth and climate system and will work as the basis for the students to take up future courses related to climate change that will make the students ready to take up projects and jobs on climate risks etc.                     

The practical sessions in this course will train students on basic computer simulations of Earth systems and provide more intuitive understanding of the system as well as practical skills that they can carry to other statistical, modeling and ML classes.

Pre-requisites:

This course has no pre-requisites. We will be beginning from scratch and expect all students to reach a high level by the end of the course.

courseTitle: Return of the wild: the practice and science of ecological restoration and rewilding
description:
Return of the wild: the practice and science of ecological restoration and rewilding [ES-2722] [ES-2722-1]

Faculty
Akshay Surendra [akshay.surendra@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Small groups of people across India and around the world are regrowing forests, restoring grasslands, liberating rivers, and bringing back wildlife. This course will introduce students to the science and practice of such efforts across the country.

Students will learn the science behind planting trees, growing corals, reintroducing beavers, undamming rivers, and much more. This learning will be primarily situated in ecology  -- a study of the living organisms being brought back to their 'wild' state, their interactions with other living organisms of the same or different species, and the non-living template (soil, light, water and dispersing currents) that supports such interactions. In-class lectures, a field visit, regular assignments and the final exam will facilitate student learning of the science of restoration and rewilding.

Students will also be exposed to the practice of restoration and rewilding. This includes ethical and socioeconomic motivations for bringing back 'wild' nature, global regional  and local frameworks that support such action, market mechanisms that incentivize restoration of carbon and biodiversity, and monitoring and evaluation approaches used to measure restoration and rewilding success. In-class discussions, a mid-semester project, a field visit and two guest lectures will facilitate student  learning of the practice of restoration and rewilding.

Students from all concentrations are encouraged to apply. Enrolment is capped at 15 students.

Subject to students' interest, we will organise a bi-monthly series of (online and in-person) guest lectures on careers in restoration and rewilding.

Learning Outcomes
  • Students will learn the ecological concepts that underpin restoration and rewilding, through lectures and periodic assignments.
  • Students will be introduced to various motivations of stakeholders in bringing back Nature, through seminar-style discussions.
  • Students will learn approaches to monitor and evaluate restoration and rewilding success, through a mid-semester class project with subsequent presentations.
  • Students will have first-hand experience with the importance of local context in restoration and rewilding, through a field visit and two guest lectures.

Overview

Taught by Nadya


In this course, we will explore vocal techniques. What techniques are used in choral works from different eras?
What types of choirs exist (for example: women's choir, mixed choir, men's choir, etc.) and what is different between of them. The subtleties of choral performance in different eras of Western classical music? We will learn to read musical notation and analyze the basics of musical form in choral works (for example, what is counterpoint) as well as other forms of choral works. We will learn to understand the gestures of the conductor. It is important to understand the concept of inner hearing, and we will strive to develop it. The course will be filled with a wealth of information, both theoretical and practical.

Acting as performative research treats the stage not as a final destination but as a laboratory. In this course, the actor moves beyond the traditional interpretation of scripts to view the body and the performance space as sites for generating new knowledge. Through rigorous improvisation, auto-ethnographic exploration, and iterative experimentation, practitioners investigate the "in-between" spaces of theory and practice.

The curriculum prioritizes the creative process over the polished product, encouraging students to document their internal shifts and physical discoveries. By integrating critical inquiry with embodiment, students learn to use theatre as a methodology to dissect social structures and personal narratives, ultimately redefining performance as a continuous, lived inquiry.

Between Nostalgia and Memory [CVA-0120] [CVA-0120-1]

Overview

Taught by Vikrant Kano

Between Nostalgia and Memory is a twelve-session course that teaches you how to look closely at family photographs and creatively transform them into a handmade mini-document, a unique form between a photobook and a zine. We do not trust first glances. A family album is never a simple record. It holds longing, forgetting, grief, and love.

We treat every photograph as a doorway between what was and what might have been. You will write, sequence, annotate, draw,collage, and bind a small creative document .
We enter images from the side: through film grain, through captions, through politics (who is centered and who is cropped out), through imagination, and through tenderness toward the dead.

This is not therapy, but it is careful. Not professional design, but personal making. We practice looking as a way of staying close to someone across time and then we give that looking a physical, permanent form.

This course introduces students to the vibrant world of West African music through rhythm, movement, ensemble playing, listening, and collective creativity. Open to students of all experience levels, the course focuses on learning traditional and contemporary West African rhythmic forms such as Tiriba, Kuku, Garangedon, and Afro Mambo through hand percussion, body percussion, voice, and movement-based exercises. Through collaborative exercises, rhythmic compositions, and guided improvisations, students will gradually build confidence in performance and creative expression. courseTitle: Through the Looking Glass: Exploring Movement on Camera
description:
Through the Looking Glass: Exploring Movement on Camera [CPA-0125] [CPA-0125-1]

Faculty
Abhinaya Penneswaran [abhinaya.penneswaran@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Taught by Abhinaya Penneswaran
The camera in our phones has become the most accessible means of preserving memory, and acknowledging moments of beauty in our daily lives. It is also a means of scrutiny, one of the devices deployed to enforce rules of conduct, a tool to keep us in check. Through social media, we also see the camera turn into a device that creates visual, and vibes-based aspirations- the face, the body, the clothes, the voice, the dance that garners the most engagement becomes the most popular. This creates a hierarchy that influences our self-image, our choices/taste.

The course seeks to reorient the camera as a device for self expression and exploration. Some key questions that we will attempt to answer: How does the body respond to the eye of a camera? How does the camera become an active participant while negotiating with a body’s movement? What effect does a camera have on movement quality? Can a camera create new paths of movement exploration? Can we re-imagine the camera as a portal that could take us towards the surreal?

Phone cameras and our bodies will be the primary medium for this course. Participants will be able to share phone cameras , if the need arises. Prior experience in dance/dance forms will be helpful but not a requirement for this course.

courseTitle: Exploring Refusal and Its Afterlives in Punjabi Language, Literature, and Culture
description:
Exploring Refusal and Its Afterlives in Punjabi Language, Literature, and Culture [CLA-0056] [CLA-0056-1]

Overview

Taught by Gurshabadjeet Singh

Punjabi literature is full of figures who cannot stay where they are placed. This course studies qissas, sufi and revolutionary poetry, modern verse, song, oral memory, popular culture, and performance through questions of refusal, memory, and possibility. It asks what happens when characters, poets, lovers, faqirs, and rebels encounter worlds rather narrow for their desire, devotion, dignity, grief, or freedom. Where do their refusals lead? What forms of love, poetry, faith, protest, loss, or selfhood do they open? The course will place literary texts alongside contemporary songs, performances, videos, quotations, and social media fragments to explore how these figures continue to travel in the present. Figures explored may include Heer-Ranjha, Sahiban, Luna, Shah Hussain, Shiv Kumar Batalvi, Paash, Lal Singh Dil, Manjit Tiwana, and others. Through close reading, translation, discussion, media analysis, and workshop exercises, students will study them through their own poetry, poetry in which they appear, and popular forms of circulation, asking what their afterlives make available, obscure, or perhaps soften for present-day refusals and possibilities.

Brand Strategies for Impact [ENT-2075] [ENT-2075-1]

Faculty
Bibek Banerjee [bibek.banerjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Brands are among the most valuable assets a company owns. Consider the 2025 brand valuations of the top 100 brands published by the leading branding consultancy, Interbrand. The top three brands in the list, Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon, had a combined brand value of approximately US$1.2 trillion, roughly equal to the GDP of the top 3 Indian states: Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and UP (US$1.25 trillion in 2025)!

Building strong brands is fundamental to success in most industries as it enables companies to attract customers who are willing to buy more at higher prices while at the same time attracting top talent for lower salaries. Moreover, brands have long lives. Often, far longer than human lives. Consider the Tata and Godrej brands in India or globally ubiquitous brands like Coca Cola and Johnnie Walker; they have been around since the 1800s and are still going strong. Not surprisingly, the stock market returns of highly branded companies tend to outperform their less or unbranded counterparts.

Too often, however, marketing and broader business decisions are made in isolation, without taking into account their impact on brand equity. In this course, you will learn how to develop strategy from a branding perspective, to build strong brands and maximize the value of existing brands.

Learning Outcomes

The course is designed with the following specific objectives and learning outcomes:

A framework for understanding when and why consumers care about brands

We will draw on consumer psychology to understand how consumers perceive, evaluate, and respond to brands. This will help us understand why branding creates value, both for the consumer and for the firm.

A step-by-step approach to building strong brands

We will address the strategies and tactics involved in building brand equity. We will examine the concept of brand identity and understand how a brand’s identity can be decoded to provide guidance for driving business decisions. We will explore the different potential sources of differentiation, how to select and activate traditional media and channels alongside digital media and channels in an integrated way, to build brands.

3. Strategies for maximizing the value of mature brands

We will study strategies for expanding a brand’s footprint, product line mix and merchandising decisions, brand architecture decisions (corporate & umbrella brands), and brand extension decisions.

4. Strategies and tactics to penetrate less affluent customer segments

Understand the importance of and how to build brands that resonate with less affluent customers.

5. Build and manage brands in emerging markets

Understand the dynamics of emerging markets and the particularities of managing brands in such contexts.

6. Building brands from scratch with limited resources

We will examine how small entrepreneurial businesses can build strong brands, notwithstanding their limited resources.

By the end of the course, you will have the tools and capacity to build and manage brands independently or act in an advisory capacity to branded businesses. For those in general management roles at brand-owning firms, you will be able to ensure that the business decisions you take are aligned with and support this most valuable asset, owned by the organization.

Performing Masculinities

This course will focus on the self-consciousness of being male within Modernity, i.e., colonialism, post-colonialism and now within a variety of ethicized nationalisms. We will study how masculinity and muscularity have historically been used as a means of creating identities, binaries and hierarchies for the purpose of control and hegemony; and its ramifications and expressions today. Examining the populist images and narratives of masculinity that abound, the performative component of this course will explore if the image can speak back to dismantle itself.  Apart from the moral and erotic appeal of the muscular we will look at the tradition of female-impersonators as well as queer performances to see how the ethicized image of the masculine is valorized, subverted or questioned in performance.

description:
Creating Value with AI for Entrepreneurs [ENT-2055] [ENT-2055-1]

Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Artificial intelligence is the most consequential business technology of this generation, yet most organisations struggle to convert it into measurable value. Surveys consistently show that while the overwhelming majority of companies are experimenting with AI, only a small fraction report material impact on revenue or cost. The gap between AI's promise and its realised value is the defining strategic problem of the decade, and the defining entrepreneurial opportunity. This course teaches students how businesses and organisations actually capture value from AI, in a real and practical sense, and how to recognise and pursue the entrepreneurial and transformation opportunities that arise from it. It is grounded not in technical theory but in deployment reality: what works, what fails, why most pilots never scale, and what separates the organisations that compound value from AI from those that merely accumulate proofs of concept. The course draws on the instructor's three decades of experience advising global corporations on strategy and technology transformation, including direct involvement in AI deployments across financial services, automotive, consumer, and healthcare. It combines first-hand deployment examples, publicly available case studies, and original frameworks developed and published by the instructor, including the Five Archetypes of AI Value Creation. Across six weeks and two modules, students will first build a rigorous understanding of how AI creates value inside organisations, and then apply that understanding to the entrepreneurial frontier: full-stack industry transformation, AI-native professional services, and deep tech. The course closes by mapping the biggest unsolved gaps and problems in the AI economy, the white spaces where the next generation of ventures will be built.

Learning Outcomes

1. Separate AI Value from AI Hype Develop a clear-eyed, evidence-based view of where AI is genuinely creating business value today, distinguish realised value from announced ambition, and understand why most enterprise AI initiatives fail to scale beyond pilots. Page 3 of 7

2. Apply the Five Archetypes of AI Value Creation Use the Five Archetypes framework, Labor Productivity, Operational Optimization, Expert Workflow Augmentation, Autonomous Revenue Growth, and Innovation & Discovery, to help identify the most valuable AI initiatives, assess their value potential, and identify what it takes to capture that value in practice.

3. Diagnose Real Deployments Analyse real-world AI deployments, drawn from the instructor's direct experience and from public case studies, to identify the organisational, data, talent, and change-management conditions that determine success or failure.

4. Recognise the Entrepreneurial Opportunity Blocks Understand the three major blocks of entrepreneurial opportunity arising from the AI transition, full-stack transformation, AI-native professional services, and deep tech, including the economics, moats, and execution challenges of each.

5. Identify Gaps and Build an Opportunity Thesis Map the biggest unsolved gaps and problems in the AI economy, from trust and evaluation to last-mile deployment and vertical depth, and develop a defensible, original thesis for a venture or transformation opportunity.

Overview

Traditional models of finance assume that individuals are rational decision-makers and that financial markets efficiently process available information. Yet, evidence from psychology, economics, and finance shows that individuals often depart systematically from these assumptions when making decisions under risk and uncertainty. This course explores how cognitive processes, biases, attention, and beliefs influence financial decision-making and market outcomes. By implementing insights from behavioral economics into traditional finance models, the course develops a broader understanding of investor behavior, financial market dynamics, and observed patterns in financial markets. The course will engage with theoretical models as well as empirical evidence from experimental and market-based studies. Towards the end of the course, students will be expected to present research papers from the behavioural finance literature.

Faculty
Mrinalini Sil [mrinalini.sil@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Empires in Motion: Art and Imperial Encounters in the Early Modern World (15th -19th C)

Course Instructor: Mrinalini Sil

Spanning roughly between the 15th and 19th centuries, this course explores the rise of major empires across Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas through the study of art and material culture. It examines how artistic production was shaped by trade, diplomacy, warfare, and religious exchange, and how objects such as paintings, manuscripts, textiles, ceramics, and luxury goods circulated across vast imperial networks. Adopting a transregional and comparative perspective, the course will focus on interconnected empires including the Mughal, Ottoman, Safavid, Qing, Spanish, Dutch, and British. Through the movement of objects, artists, and ideas, students will investigate how art contributed to imperial expansion, cultural negotiation, and the formation of new visual languages. The course also considers the afterlives of these objects in modern museums, encouraging critical engagement with histories of collecting, colonialism, cultural heritage, restitution, repatriation, and their relevance to contemporary museum debates.

The course will include two field trips and several guest lectures by leading international scholars and museum curators.

Learning Outcomes

On successful completion of the course, the students will be able to:

  Analyse early modern artworks within transregional contexts of mobility and exchange.

  Apply object-based and visual analysis to artworks in classroom and field settings.

  Evaluate the role of art and material culture in imperial systems of power.

  Critically assess museum practices and the afterlives of objects.

  Develop and present coherent curatorial arguments in written and visual formats.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

A selected reading list is included in the course description, and additional weekly readings will be uploaded and shared with those who choose to pursue the course. Students are encouraged to engage with materials across disciplines, not limited to art history, and to draw on a range of supplementary resources such as online museum collections, podcasts, press reports, newspaper clippings, works of historical fiction, and scholarly blog posts to support their learning.

No prior training in Visual Arts or Art History Required.

courseTitle: Experimental Design and Analysis in Psychological and Cognitive Science Research
description:
Experimental Design and Analysis in Psychological and Cognitive Science Research [PSY-4025] [PSY-4025-1]

Faculty
Sneha Shashidhara [sneha.shashidhara@ashoka.edu.in], Nandini Chatterjee Singh . [nandini.singh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course provides a practical foundation in experimental research for students preparing to undertake independent research/thesis in psychological and cognitive sciences. It will guide students through the complete research process, from formulating research questions and designing rigorous experiments to implementing behavioural studies, analysing data, and communicating scientific findings. Emphasis is placed on developing a strong understanding of experimental design, statistical reasoning, data visualization, reproducible research practices, and ethical decision-making. The course combines conceptual foundations with practical implementation using contemporary research tools and culminates in the design, execution, analysis, and presentation of an original research study.

Course Objectives
1. To guide students through the complete research workflow, from question formulation to the communication of original findings.
2. To develop principled intuition for experimental design, validity, and the logic of causal inference.
3. To build practical competence in PsychoPy and analysis without requiring prior programming or statistical expertise.
4. To provide hands-on experience with the core paradigms of cognitive science through guided experiment building and data collection.
5. To cultivate statistical reasoning grounded in effect sizes, power, and honest interpretation of evidence.

6. To embed ethical thinking as a constituent part of research practice, not a procedural afterthought.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Formulate a testable research question and translate it into a controlled, well-powered experimental design.
2. Implement behavioural experiments in PsychoPy.
3. Analyse data and produce quality figures, interpreting results beyond binary significance.
4. Critically evaluate experimental designs.
5. Apply ethical frameworks to the design and review of research protocols involving human participants.
6. Execute and publicly present an original empirical study, defending design and interpretation under questioning.

 

Themes we will cover:

1. The Logic of Experimental Design

Formulating testable research questions and translating them into controlled designs. Independent and dependent variables, confounds, sampling, validity, and the reasoning behind causal inference. Critical evaluation of published methods and researchers' degrees of freedom.

2. Statistical Reasoning and Data Communication

Hypothesis testing as intuition rather than recipe. Planning analysis alongside design, choosing appropriate tests, and interpreting evidence beyond binary significance through effect sizes and power. Data wrangling, visualisation, and the clear communication of findings.

3. Research Ethics in Practice

Ethics as a constituent part of research rather than a procedural afterthought. Informed consent, deception, confidentiality, data management, and research integrity, applied through IRB-style review of real protocols.

4. Building Experiments

Translating a design into a working behavioural experiment. Experiment structure, stimulus presentation, trial logic, randomisation, and data collection using contemporary research tools.

5. Core Paradigms of Cognitive Science

The classic experimental traditions in psychophysics, attention, memory, and decision making, and what each paradigm allows researchers to measure and infer.

6. The Research Project

An original empirical study carried end to end, from design and piloting through data collection, analysis, and public presentation with viva.

courseTitle: Brand Management for New Age Enterprises
description:
Brand Management for New Age Enterprises [ENT-3027] [ENT-3027-1]

Faculty
Vani Dandia [vani.dandia@ashoka.edu.in]
Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why do consumers choose one brand over another? Why do some brands become memorable while others are forgotten? Why do people often say one thing but do another?
This course explores the intersection of brand management, consumer psychology, and neuroscience to answer these questions. Using real-world cases from India and around the world, students will examine how the brain processes information, forms memories, categorises brands, responds to emotion, trusts influencers, and makes purchase decisions. The course connects key marketing decisions—pricing, positioning, brand architecture, media planning, influencer marketing, consumer research, and purpose-led branding—to the psychological and behavioural mechanisms that drive them.
Through cases such as Fit & Flex, The Baker's Dozen, Fidele, Bisk Farm, The Wishing Chair, and Amrutam, students will learn not just what successful marketers do, but why these strategies work in the minds of consumers.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:
•
Choose and defend a brand architecture for a real portfolio, and explain how categorisation in the consumer mind makes that structure work or fail.
•
Build distinctiveness within category codes — distinguishing points of parity (category membership) from points of difference (memorable, ownable assets).
•
Apply the laws of growth — mental and physical availability, Double Jeopardy, reach over depth — to challenger and small-brand strategy.
•
Design good consumer research that works around human bias (the say–do gap, social desirability, the introspection illusion) instead of being fooled by it.
•
Plan media against clear objectives and measure effectiveness across the funnel.
•
Judge when purpose, emotion, and influencer strategies create real value — and when they invite scepticism or backlash.

Arindam Chakrabarti [arindam.chakrabarti@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Philosophy of the Body From Mahābhārata to Merleau Ponty: Classical Indian and Contemporary Western

Code: PHI-2219/ PHI-2107-1

Course Description:

The ‘subject-matter’ of the course is the human body as a living and lived, conscious, material subject. Drawing upon contemporary analytic philosophy of mind, phenomenology, J.J.Gibson’s ecological psychology, neuro-cognitive science and selected Indian philosophical perspectives (e.g. of the Upanishads and Bhagavadgita), the course explores how human sense-experience, proprioception, imagination, consciousness, agency and selfhood are fundamentally shaped by the body (including cranial and gut brain).

Starting with the Bhagavadgita(XIII) conception of “this body as a field” and the conscious first person as “knower of the field”,  the notions of cognitive and active sense-organs, topics discussed  would include: 1. The Human Body as Object and Subject: Metaphysical debates on Embodiment and Consciousness: Phenomenological versus Neuro-cognitive accounts,  2. Birth and Death of the body/person, 3. The Senses as Active Perceptual Systems, 4.Embodied Perception and Environmental Affordances, 5. The Gut–Brain Axis and Visceral Consciousness, 6. The Hand, Touch, Muscular Motility, Vision, Hearing, Enteric-Digestive system and Human Agency, 7.Face, Mouth, and Feet: Expression, Speech and Movement. 8. Breath, 'prāṇa', and the breathing-attention connection. 

No prior course in Philosophy needed.  Attendance and Class/DS Participation=20% of Total Grade. Writing Assigned: 5 Reading Responses, and Final Short Essay preceded by brief oral presentation to TF/ Instructor in office hours.

Each student will be encouraged to generate at least one new philosophical question of their own, bridging classical Indian and contemporary Western metaphysical, medical, conceptual, epistemological, contemplative, and ethical research and reflections on our bodies and our senses.

Learning Outcomes

1. Practice of Reading Philosophical, Neuro-Psychological, and Phenomenology texts, book chapters, research papers under pressure of time, with making notes for oneself

2. Ability to reformulate the philosophical issues raised and arguments proposed in class lectures and readings in the form of succinct premises and conclusions.

3. Practice of writing and editing and revising one's own writing, without use of AI.

The Hand: A Philosophical Inquiry into Human Being, Edinburgh University Press, 2003, Noë, Alva. courseTitle: Melodious History: Music, Society, and Politics in India
description:
Melodious History: Music, Society, and Politics in India [HIS-4207/ PA-4700/ MS-3022] [HIS-4207/ PA-4700/ MS-3022-1]

Faculty
Pratyay Nath [pratyay.nath@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview
  • This course is cross-listed with Performing Arts

What did it mean to be male connoisseurs and female performers at Mughal mehfils? How did nationalism and colonialism shape classical music in modern India? In what ways did World War II contribute to the spread of jazz in urban milieus? What is the politics of language and identity in Hindi film songs? These are some of the questions the present course addresses. It explores the changing worlds of music in the last five hundred years (c. 1500 - c. 2000) of Indian history at the intersection of social, political, and cultural processes. Being a seminar course, it is geared heavily towards collective reading and discussion of a set of recent books from music history, ethnomusicology, and cultural studies, with every week focusing on one particular book and its themes. The various topics include the nature of music in sufi and bhakti mileus, the dynamics of music in the Mughal Empire, the coming with European music with colonialism, the nationalist politics around canonising musical knowledge, and the changing patronage, pedagogy, and performance of classical music in modern India. We will also investigate the politics of culture around the spread of jazz, the intersection of gender and identity in the making of folk music, the dynamics of performing religious music, and the social equations of bhangra among the Indian diaspora. Within this broad rubric, students will get room to pursue their own interests (in terms of topics and readings), and based on that write a research paper as the final assignment. Classes will involve a few guest lectures by scholars researching music, as well as collective listening of and discussion on relevant recorded pieces of music. Overall, this interdisciplinary course helps students understand how music has always been as much about the art as about the changing processes of culture, society, and politics.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students will able to 

  • look at music from a historical perspective and
  • understand how social, cultural, and political processes have shaped the performance and reception of music in India over the last four hundred years
  • see how different fields like history, ethnomusicology, and cultural studies appreach music studies.

courseTitle: Medicine Culture Power: An Introduction to Medical Anthropology
description:
Medicine Culture Power: An Introduction to Medical Anthropology [SOA-2256] [SOA-2256-1]

Overview

Medical anthropology is one of the fastest growing fields of study in the health and social sciences. In this introductory lecture course, we take a deep dive into the world of medical anthropology, exploring the myriad ways that matters of disease, health, the body, and wellbeing are negotiated at the individual and collective levels across cultures.

We begin by examining the intellectual origins of the field, learning about medical anthropologists, focusing on who they are, what they do, and where they work. This background establishes the ethical and philosophical underpinnings of medical anthropology and provides a handle on longstanding debates surrounding disease and illness, the normal and the pathological, and cure and prevention.

In turn, we will undertake a comparative cross-cultural analysis of healing systems, the growing dominance of Western biomedicine, the emergence of global public health, the transnational political economy of healthcare, the treatment of the human body vis-à-vis social and other inequities, and the significance of a “biocultural” and “ecosocial” turn.

In the second half of this course, we will examine the contributions of medical anthropologists to theorizing health, illness, recovery, and well-being in relation to a range of special topics — pandemics, war, psychiatric disorders, reproductive health and stem cells, the management of death and dying, and the prospects of digital health and artificial intelligence.

description:
Technoscientific Imaginaries in a Post-Truth World: STS and Its Futures-Past [SOA-3171] [SOA-3171-1]

Overview

Science and Technology Studies (STS) is an interdisciplinary field that examines the historical, philosophical, social, cultural, political, economic, and ecological constitution of science and technology. This course offers an overview of the history, key concepts and thinkers, methods and emergent directions in STS.

We begin by situating the natural and physical sciences in the matrix of modernity and inquire into the historical and cultural specificity of the knowledge cultures we call scientific. Proceeding through debates around “real” and “constructed” of scientific knowledge production and the perils of the post-truth era, this course shows how objectivity is fashioned in social worlds, addresses the significant interventions of feminist and postcolonial thinkers, and charts an agenda for anthropology in the critical study of the sciences. As we take on topics ranging from management science and gambling to algorithmic governance and the colonization of outer space, we will ask:

What forms of knowledge production are deemed scientific? How are human and nonhuman lives technologically configured? How is technoscientific expertise crafted and sustained through new forms of colonialism? What are our technological futures?

Overview

This course offers a rigorous introduction to the anthropology and sociology of caste through the lens of social stratification, hierarchy, and lived experience. Beginning with canonical debates centered on Louis Dumont’s Homo Hierarchicus and BR Ambedkar’s foundational text Annihilation of Caste, the course will move through successive layers of theoretical and ethnographic focus on caste, stratification, and hierarchy. Students will grapple with questions and debates at the heart of social theory on caste: Is caste best treated as a religious system, a political one, or something that defies domains altogether? How has caste shaped broader struggles of recognition and self- making? How does caste articulate with other markers of identity and hierarchy, such as gender, class, and religion?
