Global Film Histories Reimagined [MS-1401/ HIS-1802] [MS-1401/ HIS-1802-1]

Faculty
Monia Acciari [monia.acciari@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

*** Welcome to Global Film History Reimagined ***

This course invites you to look explore global film history not as a fixed chronology of movements, masterpieces, and technological innovations, but as a contested field of memory, circulation, interpretation, and cultural power. Rather than treating cinema history as a stable narrative organised exclusively through canonical films and directors, the course invites you to examine the processes through which film histories are produced, preserved, forgotten, reinterpreted, and transformed across different historical and geographical contexts.

Drawing from film historiography, media archaeology, fan studies, visual culture, and cultural memory studies, the course foregrounds the relationship between cinema and the institutions that shape historical knowledge, including archives, festivals, museums, studios, collectors, fan communities, and digital platforms. You will investigate how film histories are constructed through systems of preservation and circulation, while also examining what remains excluded, erased, or marginalised within dominant narratives of cinema globally.

The course is organised around three interconnected conceptual frameworks: canon, apocrypha, and fanon. Canon refers to officially recognised narratives of film history and the institutional processes that determine cultural value and historical legitimacy. Apocrypha explores neglected, forgotten, or alternative histories that exist outside dominant historiographical traditions, including personal archives, material artefacts, migration histories, and ephemeral media cultures. Fanon examines the interpretative and DiY practices generated by audiences and fan communities and consider how spectators themselves become historians, archivists, collectors, and producers of cultural memory.

Alongside these conceptual frameworks, students will engage with the material and technological histories of cinema. The course examines how media formats and infrastructures, from nitrate film stock and silent cinema exhibition to VHS circulation, streaming platforms, digital archives, and online fan communities, shape not only how films are experienced, but also how they survive historically. Through a combination of lectures, seminars, screenings, archival encounters, and media lab engagement, you will critically rethink the making of global film history through interdisciplinary perspectives.

Learning Outcomes

On successful completion of this course, you will be able to:

1. Critically analyse global cinema history as a phenomenon to be reimagined through peripheral narratives and fan intervention. 

2. Identify and evaluate the roles of canon, apocrypha, and fanon in constructing and contesting film histories.

3. Assess the journey of cinema historically, geographically, technologically and through fan cultures.

4. Assess changing media formats to evaluate the evolution of historiography of cinema.

5. Interpret fan cultures and audience agency.

6. Work and familiarise with international case-studies, silent cinema, sound transitions, digital cinema, etc.) to research and construct nuanced, multi-perspective interpretations of film history.

Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

The following are some of the key readings in this course:

Geoffrey Nowell-Smith (2023, Latest edition), The Oxford History of World History, Oxford University Press: Oxford. (Selected Chapters).

Glyn Davis, Kay Dickison, Lisa Patti, Amy Villarejo, Film Studies, A Global Introduction, Routledge Edition: London. (Selected Chapters).

Bhaumik, Kaushik, Debashree Mukherjee, and Rahaab Allana, (2014) Filmi Jagat: A Scrapbook: Shared Universe of Early Hindi Cinema, New Delhi: Niyogi Books, 2014. (Selected Chapters).

Richard Maltby, Daniel Biltereyst, Philippe Meers (2011), Explorations in New Cinema History: Approaches and Case Studies, Wiley: Hoboken. (Selected Chapters).

Malte Hagener, methods, Discourses (2024) How Film Histories were Made, AUP, Amsterdam. (Selected Chapters).

Lucia Cesalkova (2017), “Feel the Film: Film Projectionists and professional Memory”, Memory Studies, Vol 10 (1), 49-62.

The Indian Ocean World [HIS-3523/ IR-3047] [HIS-3523/ IR-3047-1]

Faculty
Seema Alavi [seema.alavi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The Indian Ocean saw people from East Asia, the Middle East, South East Asia and Europe meet and mix over many centuries. This course will look at the histories of these interactions and what they meant to world history. It traces patterns of mobility in the ocean to reflect on the nature of the connections forged and what they tell us about the longer histories of globalization and International Relations.  The many intersecting histories that constitute the Indian Ocean are: maritime studies, weather patterns and the monsoon, religious networks (Buddhist, Christianity and Islam), diasporas, and the patterns of commerce. Through an exploration of these histories the course will offer insights on the making of the Indian Ocean as a textured canvas that sustained Asian and African Sultanates in the high period of imperialism (19th century) which is conventionally viewed as the Ocean’s European century.  It will reflect on what these Asian political aspirations lent to the making of the modern world order.

Learning Outcomes

Offers a fresh perspective on the History of Internationl Relations; Global History and World History

courseTitle: History and the Art of Reading
description:
History and the Art of Reading [HIS-5850/ ENG-4678/ SOA-4012] [HIS-5850/ ENG-4678/ SOA-4012-1]

Faculty
Eloise Wright [eloise.wright@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How is it the case that two people can read the same text and come up with contrasting interpretations? Why does a reader encountering a newly-written text find a different meaning in it than readers years or generations later? Can we ever really know what meaning an author intended? As historians, we read constantly: historical sources from different time periods and places, empirical and theoretical work by historians and scholars from other disciplines. We read in different languages and formats, on screens, paper, stone, or bronze, via images and material objects. In this class, we will examine the processes by which readers make meaning out of texts, that is, hermeneutics, in the context of historical scholarship.

In the first half of the class we will explore three historical hermeneutical traditions: German phenomenology, Chinese classicism, and Russian Marxism. By reading key texts from each tradition, we will encounter a range of approaches to the problems of reading and interpretation. In the second half of the class, we will consider these ideas (and others) applied to real-world situations: ethnographic studies of reading as an embodied practice, problems of translation between languages and scripts, and social practices of reading within the university context.

This course is open to fourth years and above only.

Faculty
Sandeep Juneja . [sandeep.juneja@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

In autonomous vehicles, robots, and many other physical settings, at any state a number of decisions need to be made. Each decision comes with an immediate reward but more importantly leads to another probabilistically selected state. In reinforcement learning, we learn optimal decisions through trial and error where good decisions are reinforced and bad ones are punished. This learning regime, especially when combined with deep learning, is an incredibly powerful tool for artificial and augmented intelligence. In this course we will study the underlying theory and learn to code-up many practical and intricate applications.

 

Topics covered:

Markov Chains, Markov Decision Processes, Dynamic Programming, Value and Policy Iteration, Temporal Difference Learning, Q-Learning, functional approximations,  Bandit methods, Neural Networks and Deep Q learning, other deep RL methods

Introduction to Single Cell Technologies [BIO-4555/ BIO-6004] [BIO-4555/ BIO-6004-1]

Faculty
Kedar Nath Natarajan [kedar.natarajan@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course aims to build a basic understanding of different technologies and approaches used to isolate single cells, perform different workflows to extract and measure cellular macromolecules (DNA, chromatin, peptides/proteins) at single-cell level through high-throughput technologies within mammalian cell systems. We will discuss single-cell transcriptomics, chromatin accessiblity and other multi-modal assays. This course will also have a brief, short data analysis component and provide the students with skills to understand and interpret different data analysis steps (quality control, dimensionality reduction, clustering etc.). We will briefly introduce concepts of microscopy and spatial transcriptomics as well. The course will include guest speakers applying experimental single-cell omics across different tissues and developing computational methods. 

 

Overall students will obtain critical knowledge for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of various single cell technologies, appreciate concepts relating to data interpretation on highly multi-dimensional datasets, and application of single-cell technologies in health and disease.

Learning Outcomes

The student who has met the objectives of the course will be able to:

  • Understand and appreciate cellular heterogeneity within biological systems and the need for single-cell resolution
  • Explain different approaches to isolate single cells from complex tissues
  • Explain the underlying principles for extracting different macromolecules from single-cell assays, including transcriptome, chromatin accessibility, and regulatory networks
  • Evaluate the strengths and limitations of various adaptations of these technologies
  • Appreciate concepts in spatial transcriptomics
  • Be aware of the basic data analysis steps involved in multi-dimensional single-cell omics datasets
Requirements (Reading List and other materials)

We will be updating the requirements, reading list and other materials. 

In addition, students are expected to know basic familarity with molecular biology, biochemistry including bulk omics concepts (Genomics, Transcriptomics, Proteomics).

Pandemics, Virulence, Terror: Apocalypse Redux [SOA-3172] [SOA-3172-1]

Faculty
Harish Naraindas [harish.naraindas@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course on pandemics is an attempt to break down territorial and scholarly silos, and transpose explanatory tropes, by bringing South Asia, the UK and the US, indexed by Calcutta, London, and Boston, into a single analytical framework.

Promiscuous pandemics – driven by zoonotic spillover, bacterial exchange and indiscriminate border crossing – not only tear down geopolitical boundaries by their sheer virulence but, as Covid 19 proved, invariably raise the haunting question of whether it is a catastrophe of nature, an unintended accident, or an intended act of terror.

The attempt to address real pandemics by sovereign states through measures such as quarantine, lockdowns and vaccines, or virtual ones through table top war games played in “real” time, are often experienced by real and virtual citizens as “carceral and invasive”, and raise difficult questions of bodily sovereignty, civil liberty, religious freedom and the more easily overlooked question of therapeutic freedom based on epistemic difference. The refusal to follow these “carceral” measures, or submit to invasive ones such as vaccines – vaccine hesitancy in contemporary parlance - disrupts public health and raises the spectre of the apocalypse.

We intend to examine the above themes by starting with a smallpox epidemic in 1721 Boston, and the April 1722 public inoculation of King George’s granddaughters in London, based on techniques and protocols (read theories) practiced in, and borrowed from, Istanbul and then Calcutta. We will then pivot from there to the recent past through war games like Dark Winter, and eerily prescient ones like Event 201, and set them against the lived experience of the last pandemic. We will then do a double genealogical excavation: by a) tracing the theological roots of vaccine hesitancy, first to the Civil War in England where the radical working class (not John Locke) rearticulates ideas of both bodily sovereignty and the apocalypse, which in turn can be traced to the 1527 drowning of the anabaptists in Zurich as its ground zero; and b) trace the epistemic roots of smallpox variolation and vaccination to Bengal and their tikkadars, which the colonial state tied to worship and superstition rather than religion or reason, despite the British governor of Bengal arguing to the contrary. This leads to several ironies and paradoxes, and, in a reversal of tropes, shows that religious reasons, against the ever-present idea of End-Times (apocalypse redux), underpins anti-vaccination protests in the West, while South Asian scholarly tropes continue to see religion rather than reason as the terra firma of protests in the East – while it is the very East that had bequeathed to the West both smallpox variolation and its attendant theoretical scaffolding.  

It should be evident that this course is as much a course on method as it is on pandemics, as it invites students to reconsider, through the study of pandemics, how ethnographic and historical objects need to be framed if we are to escape received explanatory tropes. It is an invitation to reflect on the possibility of theorizing at once about the North and South, rather than the current preoccupation of doing “Theory from the South”, that runs the risk of once again being anchored to the South.

courseTitle: The Techniques of Daily Life: Histories of Everyday Technology in the Modern World
description:
The Techniques of Daily Life: Histories of Everyday Technology in the Modern World [HIS-3162] [HIS-3162-1]

Faculty
Siddhartha Mukherjee [siddhartha.mukherjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

What role did punch cards play in the extermination of the Jews? Were people scared of telephones?  How does the use of two-wheelers challenge social order? What does security have to do with etiquette? How did watches challenge colonialism? What were eyeglasses doing in the Victorian period? By focusing on case studies that answer such questions, the course will demonstrate how the history of small-scale technologies that enable everyday work and leisure addresses socio-political and cultural issues and concerns like freedom, racial politics, hygiene, gender relations, and surveillance. Such connections will be unveiled by showcasing the entanglement of states, manufacturers, medical doctors, print media, businessmen, and consumers with objects like spectacles, electric push buttons, hand-pulled fans, hearing aids, shirt-pocket radios, phones, home computers, cars, and biometrics. We will conclude by arguing for a broadening of focus from large-scale operations of systems like dams, railways, or telegraphs to much smaller and more intimate objects to understand the expanse of modernity across the globe. 

Learning Outcomes

Along with familiarising students with some of the emerging global histories of everyday technology, the course will emphasize how their lives can be studied and written about through analyses of films, policy documents, advertisements, newspapers, technical handbooks, and short stories. It will provide them with a robust understanding of the methods of engaging with micro-histories of technology, many of which continue to shape our lives.

description:

Operational Support

Faculty
Vani Dandia [vani.dandia@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

‘The Psychology of Consumption and Markets’ examines how consumers make decisions, form preferences, assign value, and respond to brands in an increasingly complex marketplace. Integrating perspectives from psychology, behavioural economics, and marketing, the course challenges the assumption that consumers are purely rational actors and explores the cognitive, emotional, social, and cultural forces that influence consumption.
Students will learn how psychological biases and social influences affect choices, and how marketers use these insights to build brands, influence behaviour, and create competitive advantage. Through a combination of real-world business cases, advertising analysis, challenger brand strategies, consumer insight development, and decision-making frameworks, the course bridges theory and practice to explain how markets work and why consumers buy.
By the end of the course, students will be able to better understand consumption, evaluate business decisions, and design more effective products, brands, and communications.

Learning Outcomes

1.
Understand how psychology shapes consumer behaviour and market outcomes.
2.
Analyse brands, advertising, and consumption using theories from psychology, and marketing.
3.
Generate consumer insights by uncovering the motivations, emotions, and social influences underlying behaviour.
4.
Evaluate marketing decisions through evidence from behavioural science rather than managerial intuition alone.
5.
Design products, brands, and communications that align with how people actually think, decide, and behave.

Overview

The course will focus on why and how political institutions and culture affect economic outcomes and how they are shaped by economic development and policy choices. The goal is to understand core theoretical concepts in political economy, understand determinants of voting behaviour and learn how to understand and evaluate empirical evidence. The course starts with the literature on the classical political economy and discusses how contemporary economists study the questions raised by it. Energy Systems, Society, and Sustainability [ES-3012/ ECO-3564/ POL-3147] [ES-3012/ ECO-3564/ POL-3147-1]

Faculty
Sumedha Basu [sumedha.basu@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

“Everything is energy, and that is all there is to it.” – Albert Einstein

Energy is at the heart of our modern world. Nearly 75% of global carbon emissions come from energy-related activities, making the sustainable transformation of energy systems one of the most urgent strategies for addressing climate change. But energy is not just about technology—it is deeply connected to society, shaping how we live, work, and interact, while also being shaped by social, political, and economic forces.

This course introduces you to the fundamentals of today’s energy systems and explores the multiple dimensions of their sustainable transition. We will move beyond questions of cost and efficiency to examine broader issues such as equity, justice, politics, geopolitics, and broader socio-ecological impacts.

Through a mix of theory and practice, you will:

  • Learn key concepts in energy policy, economics, and governance.
  • Engage with social science and critical theory frameworks to analyse energy transitions.
  • Explore justice-focused themes such as just transitions, energy poverty, fossil fuel lock-in, and energy democracy.
  • Apply practical tools like systems mapping, stakeholder analysis, and scenario planning.
  • Study case examples from around the world, with a special focus on India’s energy transition.

By the end of the course, you will have the analytical skills to critically evaluate energy challenges and propose creative solutions. Whether you aspire to work in policy, research, industry, or activism, this course will strengthen your foundation and encourage independent thinking about one of the most pressing issues of our time.

As an interactive course, you will have a chance to shape it, ensuring we focus on the areas and tools most relevant to your interests and future goals.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course:

  • You will have a systemic understanding of the energy sector and sustainable energy transitions and their deep interdependence on society, economy, and geopolitics.
  • You will have a fundamental understanding of important concepts in energy technologies and economics.
  • You will be able to engage critically with the ongoing sustainability energy transition and form an assessment of the power structures and injustices across different dimensions and scales.
  • You will develop practical skills to contribute towards policy analysis, energy roadmaps, and strategy development.

courseTitle: Politics of Hierarchy: Caste, Race, and Ethnicity in Comparative Perspective
description:
Politics of Hierarchy: Caste, Race, and Ethnicity in Comparative Perspective [POL-3145/ ECO-3565] [POL-3145/ ECO-3565-1]

Faculty
Poulomi Dhar Chakrabarti [poulomi.chakrabarti@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Why do some human differences harden into durable inequalities between groups? How are these hierarchies created, reproduced, and justified? And how can they be dismantled? This seminar examines the politics of group-based inequality across societies, placing caste, race, and ethnicity within a single comparative framework. Rather than treating any one system of hierarchy as unique, we ask what caste in India, race in the United States and South Africa, and indigeneity in the Americas share as systems of ranking, exclusion, and dominance – and where they diverge.

We begin with the conceptual and social-psychological foundations of hierarchy: What is ethnic hierarchy? How do group identities acquire status and become organized into relations of superiority and subordination? We then examine how hierarchies are historically constructed and reproduced through institutions and networks, everyday social norms and practices, and ideologies that legitimize inequality. The second part of the course turns to the consequences of ethnic hierarchy for socioeconomic inequality, state formation, and public goods provision. The final part examines the politics of hierarchy: how subordinated groups organize to challenge entrenched systems of dominance, and how dominant groups respond through backlash and retrenchment.

By placing group subordination at the center of ethnic politics, the course challenges mainstream approaches to ethnicity that focus primarily on difference rather than inequality. Throughout, we ask not simply why ethnic identities matter, but why some come to carry durable advantage and disadvantage, and what happens when those hierarchies are contested. Drawing on political science, social psychology, sociology, economics, and history, the course trains students not merely to absorb scholarly findings but to interrogate them: to reconstruct arguments, evaluate evidence, compare explanations, and use comparison to think critically about how hierarchies are made, sustained, and undone.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students should have an overview of the major debates and issues in the field of ethnic politics and its intersection with group-based inequality. The course emphasizes critical thinking and students should be able to distinguish between different theoretical explanations and evaluate the merit of evidence used to support them. The focus on interdisciplinary perspectives is designed to train students to develop research questions that have broad theoretical relevance. Finally, the evaluation methods strengthen analytical writing and oral communication skills.

description:
Global Investments, Geopolitics and Leadership [ENT-2056/ IR-2278] [ENT-2056/ IR-2278-1]

Operational Support
Sagar Singhal [sagar.singhal@ashoka.edu.in], Soumyajit Bhattacharjee [soumyajit.bhattacharjee@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

Capital does not move in a vacuum. It is shaped by institutions, political risk, technology, conflict, regulatory choices, social expectations, and leadership judgement. This course introduces students to the strategic and ethical complexities of global capital allocation in a world marked by geopolitical uncertainty and institutional flux.

The course is designed as an intensive academic-practitioner module. It combines the experience of senior leaders in responsible investing, sovereign and institutional capital, Indian foreign policy, and global governance with structured classroom discussion, case-based reflection, and written analysis.

The animating question of the course is: how should leaders allocate capital, manage risk, and exercise judgement when economic opportunity, geopolitical uncertainty, and long-term responsibility collide?

Global Investments, Geopolitics, and Leadership is an intensive elective that examines how global capital is deployed, governed, and contested in complex environments. The course moves between three levels of analysis: investment decision-making, geopolitical context, and leadership under uncertainty.

Students will study the evolution of responsible investing, ESG integration, portfolio construction, sovereign wealth and institutional capital, geopolitical risk, foreign direct investment, and the role of leadership judgement in moments when there are no clean answers. The course is deliberately cross-disciplinary and is intended for students of economics, political science, international relations, business, public policy, entrepreneurship, finance, history, sociology, and related fields.

The course is not a technical finance course. Nor is it a conventional international relations course. Its intellectual contribution lies in bringing these domains together: how capital responds to geopolitical risk, how institutions manage competing stakeholder expectations, and how leaders make consequential decisions under uncertainty.

The course is an Initiative in Global Learning | Centre for Entrepreneurship, Ashoka University, in collaboration with Iron Pillar. The format is a one-week module; three hours of classroom engagement per day, supplemented by instructor office hours.

Learning Outcomes

The course is designed with the following specific objectives and learning outcomes:

●   Understand how global investors allocate capital across markets and how they balance risk, return, responsibility, and long-term value creation.

●   Analyse the evolution of responsible investing from ethical exclusion to ESG integration, sustainability, active ownership, and politically contested approaches to corporate responsibility.

●   Develop a working understanding of geopolitical risk and its implications for capital flows, markets, firm strategy, and national economic choices.

●   Evaluate how sovereign wealth funds, institutional investors, and boards define purpose, constraints, risk appetite, and investment boundaries.

●   Apply scenario thinking and stress testing to assess portfolio vulnerability and institutional resilience in volatile environments.

●   Examine how leaders exercise judgement amid imperfect information, competing priorities, stakeholder pressures, and high-stakes uncertainty.

courseTitle: The Eighteenth Century in Indian History
description:
The Eighteenth Century in Indian History [HIS-3213/ POL-3146] [HIS-3213/ POL-3146-1]

Faculty
Seema Alavi [seema.alavi@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course will span from the later half of Aurangzeb’s period (end of 17th century) to the age of reforms (1820-30s). It will offer new perspectives on how to understand the British conquest of india and the transition to colonialism.  It will look at changes in economy, society and culture that shaped regions, social groups and individual careers in the period of transition to English Company rule. An important part of this course will be to move the gaze away from the state and the meta-narrative of its oppression to in- house debates and discussions in the military, legal, medical and commercial cultures that determined the course of politics in the period of transition to British rule.

Learning Outcomes

Offers fresh perspective on the British conquest of India and the transition to colonial rule, the nature and origins of colonialism, and its ramifications in the long 18th cnetury.

Political Economy of International Development [IR-2077/ POL-2149] [IR-2077/ POL-2149-1]

Faculty
Aashna Khanna [aashna.khanna@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

The focus of this course is to examine the economics and politics of development, comparing how countries have pursued economic progress across space and time. Development is a multi-faceted concept and its study allows us to answer questions such as:
Why are some countries rich and some countries poor?
What does development mean, and how can we measure it?
What is political about development?
What is the relationship between development and economic growth?
Who are the key actors and institutions in international development and how do they promote development?

This course begins with an examination of how actors have pursued development starting from historical structures of empires & colonisation tracing the current state of the global economy, covering globalisation, neoliberalism, and the role of international institutions. In the second half, we will systematically discuss development topics such as foreign aid, gender and development, resource curse and civil conflict, thinking about the winners and losers of development. Lastly, we examine the economic and political strategies pursued by developing countries and connect these theories and topics to actual problems faced by countries today.

Political Ethnography [POL-3144/ SOA-3173] [POL-3144/ SOA-3173-1]

Faculty
Uday Chandra [uday.chandra@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

How might we learn to notice power? Political life does not unfold only in legislatures, elections, courts, parties, and other formal institutions. Power is also embedded in ordinary routines: waiting, speaking, listening, joking, eating, working, moving through space, filling out forms, negotiating access, observing silence, and managing bodily proximity. It may be sensed in the organization of a room, the authority of a uniform, the tone of a command, the smell of labour, or the rhythms of bureaucratic delay.

This course introduces political ethnography as a way of studying such forms of lived power. Students will learn to read ethnographies as arguments rather than as collections of colourful detail. We shall examine how ethnographers use multisensory immersion, observation, conversation, fieldnotes, and narrative scenes to interpret politics and society. The course aims, above all, to cultivate habits of attention, ethical awareness, and political judgment.

Students will also undertake a small ethnographic project of their own. Through field-based exercises, repeated observation, fieldnotes, peer workshops, and revision, they will learn how to move from perception to description and from description to argument

Faculty
Sanjana Ghosh [sanjana.ghosh@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

This course introduces students to the economics of environmental pollution, regulation,
and welfare, with a focus on emerging market settings. We begin with what markets do
well, where they fail, and how efficiency and equity interact in environmental decisions. The
course heavily focuses on local externalities — the costs imposed by pollution, congestion,
and industrial activity that markets tend to underprice. The bulk of the course examines the
main policy tools used to address these problems, economists think about correcting these
market failures, including property rights and the Coase theorem, Pigouvian taxes, environmental
standards, and tradeable permits, along with the practical limits of these approaches
under weak enforcement and informality. The course also introduces non-market valuation
methods, especially hedonic pricing, to understand how environmental quality affects welfare.

Metaphysics of Politics [PHI-4809/ POL-4017/ PHI-4509] [PHI-4809/ POL-4017/ PHI-4509-1]

Faculty
Arindam Chakrabarti [arindam.chakrabarti@ashoka.edu.in]
Overview

METAPHYSICS OF POLITICAL RELATIONS (PHI- 4809-1)

MONSOON 2026

COURSE DESCRIPTION:

Speaking of the uniquely human practice of politics, Hannah Arendt famously remarked: “We call this reality the ‘web of human relationships’.” The heart of politics has thus been regarded as a network of specific relations between people. A historically and phenomenologically sensitive analytical study of this reality would amount to a Metaphysics of Politics. Relations are everywhere in the world. The relation between speaker and listener, writer and reader, makes communication possible. Words stand in relations of meaning with what they signify and in relations of synonymy with words in other languages. Relations occur in the list of the ten categories in Aristotle’s metaphysics. Specific relations such as inherence (samavāya), the whole-to-part or quality-to-substance relationship, take centre stage in ancient Indian debates between realist Vaiśeṣika and nominalist Buddhist philosophers. Of course, political scientists teach and research International Relations. And, in this course, conceptual and metaphysical investigation of political relations will be aimed at actual public-policy applications, and currently burning issues of global justice and world politics (a la Mathias Risse, and Yaqing Qin) and   But in this course, we shall focus on five politically crucial relations:

  • Private Property/ Ownership
  • Authority and Internal and External Sovereignty
  • Membership and Part-Whole Relation between the Nation, Communities, and Citizens
  • Inequality of Power
  • Representation (most importantly: in democracy, and its current perverted form “populism”, what exactly does it mean for an elected legislator to "speak for" an entire community of voters?)

We shall analytically and critically explore the following questions:

What is a relation, and what does it mean to study politics relationally?

What does it mean to understand political realities in terms of ontological concepts that are culture-transcending? How can something as purposive, practical, and policy-oriented as politics be illuminated by something as theoretical as metaphysics?

How can we infuse the metaphysics of political relations with a ‘science of social change’ to make it relevant to politics as it is actually practiced?

What are the fundamental relations that structure political life, and how do they shape political institutions and practices?
Keeping these basic questions in mind, we shall focus particular attention to the relations of power, authority, property ownership, participation in a plurality, “selving” versus “othering”, inequality, and representation.
 

Note: No prior course in Philosophy is required.

Learning Outcomes

1. Practice of reading philosophical texts, book chapters and research papers under pressure of time, while making notes for oneself.

2. Ability to reformulate the philosophical issues raised and arguments proposed in class lectures and readings in the form of succinct premises and conclusions.

3. Practice of writing, editing and revising one's own writing, without the use of AI.
